rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that the Income Tax Department had not complied with the statutory requirements of **section 245 of the Income-tax Act** before adjusting Tata Communications Ltd.’s refund against tax demand. The case arose in the context of **AY 2019-20**, and the judgment was pronounced on **6 April 2021** (published **24 April 2021**). The Court criticized the Department’s position that the High Court’s order would not govern matters/orders passed by the **ITAT** merely because the **Union of India was not a party** to that proceeding, and said that this justification and approach could not be approved.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that **refund adjustments cannot be made casually or without following section 245’s procedure**, which requires proper statutory compliance before set-off of a refund against outstanding demand. The Court also emphasized that the tax authorities are expected to act as a **model litigant**, and that the Department’s failure to follow the legal requirements was especially inappropriate for a state authority. In practical terms, the decision reinforces that before withholding or adjusting a taxpayer’s refund, the Department must ensure the section 245 conditions and process are satisfied and cannot rely on a broad assertion that a High Court order does not bind related proceedings simply because a particular government entity was not formally a party.

Deshmukh J SECTION(S): 147, 148 GENRE: CATCH WORDS: dead person, Reopening of assessment, Writ jurisdiction COUNSEL: Atul Jasani, J.D. Mistri, Madhur Agrawal, Shyam Walve DATE: April 9, 2021 (Date of pronouncement) DATE: April 24, 2021 (Date of publication) AY: 2012-13 FILE: Click here to download the file in pdf format CITATION: Article 226/ s. 147: (i) A Writ Petition can be filed in the Bombay High Court against an order passed in Delhi if the assessee is based in Mumbai. The litigant has the right to go to ‘a Court’ where part of cause of action arises. (ii) A s. 148 notice & s. 147 reassessment order passed against an amalgamated (non-existing) company is without jurisdiction. The defect cannot be treated as procedural defect. Mere participation of the assessee in the assessment proceedings is of no effect as there is no estoppel against law. Such a defect cannot be cured by invoking section 292B (All imp judgements referred) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT BOMBAY ORDINARY ORIGINAL CIVIL JURISDICTION Teleperformance Towers Mindspace, ) Goregaon (West), Mumbai 400 104, ) Maharashtra, India … Petitioner Vs. 1. Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax ) Central Circle 25(1), New Delhi, ) C R Building, ITO, I P Estate, 104B, ) Indrapastha Marg, New Delhi 110 002 ) 2. Principal Commissioner of Income-tax 25(1), C R Building, ITO, I P Estate, 104B, ) Indrapastha Marg, New Delhi 110 002 ) 3.
rows.summary: This Bombay High Court decision concerns a reopening of assessment for AY 2012–13 under sections 147 and 148 against Teleperformance Global Services Private Limited, and the Court held that the reassessment notice and resulting reassessment order were invalid because they were issued to an amalgamated company that no longer existed. The Court treated this as a jurisdictional defect, not a mere procedural irregularity, and held it could not be cured by section 292B; the fact that the assessee participated in the proceedings did not help because there is no estoppel against law. For compliance purposes, the key point is that once an entity has amalgamated, tax notices and reassessment proceedings must be addressed to the surviving/transferee entity, not the extinguished transferor company, or the entire proceeding is vulnerable to being quashed. The judgment also confirms that a writ petition can be filed in the Bombay High Court even where the impugned order was passed in Delhi, so long as the assessee is based in Mumbai and part of the cause of action arises there. The operative dates shown are the pronouncement date of April 9, 2021 and publication date of April 24, 2021.

However, shares issued to shareholders of an amalgamating company in terms of a scheme of amalgamation does not fall within the sweep of the deeming provisions of s. 56(2) (viib). The so-called excess value of assets vested on amalgamation cannot be notionally termed as premium over the face value for the purposes of the deeming provision (AS-14 issued by the ICAI & CBDT Circular No 3/2012 dated 12-6-2012 referred) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Income from other sources DCIT v. Facts: The assessee company filed its return of income for AY 2013-14 in question which was subjected to scrutiny assessment. In the course of assessment proceedings, it was gathered by the AO that one M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL) amalgamated with the assessee company under the scheme of amalgamation.
rows.summary:
The ITAT Ahmedabad held that section 56(2)(viib) of the Income-tax Act, which taxes unjustified excess share premium received by a closely held company on issue of shares above fair market value, does **not** apply where shares are issued pursuant to a genuine **scheme of amalgamation**. In this case, Ozone India Ltd. had filed its return for **AY 2013-14**, and during scrutiny the Assessing Officer found that **M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL)** had amalgamated into the assessee company under a court-approved amalgamation scheme. As part of that merger, shares were issued to the shareholders of the amalgamating company, and the tax department attempted to treat the value attributed to the amalgamation as “excess premium” / deemed income under section **56(2)(viib)**.  

The Tribunal rejected that approach, explaining that the legislative purpose of section 56(2)(viib) is to tax cases where a private company issues shares at an unjustifiably high premium without real underlying value, not to tax allotment of shares made under an amalgamation arrangement. It specifically held that the value transferred on amalgamation cannot be artificially recharacterized as share premium merely because the resulting share issuance reflects the asset value of the merged entity. The decision relied on the accounting treatment recognized under **AS-14** and also referred to **CBDT Circular No. 3/2012 dated 12-6-2012**, which supports the amalgamation treatment.  

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that share issuances made strictly in accordance with a bona fide amalgamation scheme are outside the sweep of section 56(2)(viib), so long as the transaction is genuinely a merger and not a disguised premium-heavy equity infusion. The ruling was pronounced on **13 April 2021** and published on **24 April 2021**, and it applies to the facts of **AY 2013-14**.

The Tribunal held that the **third proviso to Section 50C**, inserted by the **Finance Act, 2018**, which prevents Section 50C from applying where the difference between the **stamp duty valuation** and the **actual sale consideration** does not exceed **5%**, is a **curative amendment** and should be treated as having retrospective effect from the date Section 50C was originally inserted, i.e. **1 April 2003**. Although the order references the amendments as prospectively stated in the statute, the Tribunal treated them as remedial and applicable to earlier years as well. The case is an **income-tax capital gains** matter, and the ruling is specifically relevant to taxpayers and tax teams dealing with **real estate transfers** where stamp duty value may exceed the reported consideration. rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that **Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016** because Section 238A of the IBC incorporates the Limitation Act “**as far as may be**.” As a result, if a corporate debtor makes a **written and signed acknowledgement of debt before expiry of the limitation period**, that acknowledgement can extend the limitation period for filing an insolvency application. The Court specifically rejected the contrary view of the NCLAT Full Bench in **V. Padmakumar v. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund**, thereby restoring the ordinary limitation principle that while time starts running when the cause of action accrues, it can only be extended in the manner recognized by law.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that an **entry in the company’s books of account, including the balance sheet, can amount to an acknowledgement of liability under Section 18** if it reflects an admission of the debt. The Court further clarified that the **notes to the balance sheet and the auditor’s report cannot be read in isolation**; they must be read together with the balance sheet to determine whether there is an acknowledgement. This means that disclosures, qualifications, and explanatory notes in financial statements may have legal consequences for limitation in recovery or insolvency actions, even if the company did not intend to create a formal admission for litigation purposes.

The decision affects **corporate debtors, lenders, resolution applicants, and insolvency professionals** because it broadens the kinds of documentary admissions that can restart or extend limitation for IBC claims. There was **no new filing deadline created**, but the ruling reinforces that companies should treat financial statement language carefully, since balance sheet disclosures, accounting entries, and audit-note wording may later be relied upon as evidence of acknowledgement of debt. The judgment was delivered on **April 15, 2021** and published on **April 17, 2021** by a three-judge bench consisting of **B.R. Gavai, Hrishikesh Roy, and Rohinton Fali Nariman, JJ.**

The Bombay High Court held that, under the Direct Tax Vivad se Vishwas Act, 2020 (“DTVSV Act”), the Designated Authority cannot refuse to accept a valid declaration merely because it disputes the merits of the taxpayer’s position. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that taxpayers who are eligible appellants under the scheme and who do not fall into the specific statutory exclusions should expect the declaration to be accepted and processed, not substantively denied on extraneous grounds. rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **DCIT v. Pepsi Foods Ltd.** interpreted and effectively revised the operation of **section 254(2A)** of the Income-tax Act, which governs **stay orders granted by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT)**. The Court held that the **third proviso to section 254(2A)**, as originally written, was unconstitutional because it required **automatic vacation of a stay after 365 days** even where the assessee was **not responsible for the delay** in hearing the appeal; the Court found this discriminatory and violative of **Article 14**. It also noted the proviso could unfairly benefit the Revenue by vacating stay even when the **Revenue itself caused the delay**, making the provision **manifestly arbitrary, capricious, irrational, and disproportionate** as applied to taxpayers.

As a result, the Court directed that the third proviso be **read down** by deleting the word **“even”** and the words **“is not”** after the phrase **“delay in disposing of the appeal”**. The practical effect is that a stay granted by the ITAT will **not automatically lapse merely because 365 days have elapsed**; instead, it will stand vacated after the applicable period only **if the delay in disposal of the appeal is attributable to the assessee**. For compliance purposes, this means taxpayers with pending appeals and stay orders should track whether any delay is being attributed to them, because that attribution—not the mere passage of time—now determines whether the stay continues. The judgment was pronounced on **April 6, 2021** and published on **April 7, 2021**.

The Bombay High Court in **Little Angels Education Society & Anr. v. UOI & Ors.** dealt with a charitable trust/school seeking exemption under **section 11** despite a delay in filing **Form No. 10B** for **AY 2018-19**. The Court upheld that 365-day limit as neither arbitrary nor irrational, meaning routine condonation by the CIT is capped at one year under that circular.

At the same time, the Court clarified an important compliance point: **section 119(2)(b) does not prevent the CBDT from granting a special order in an individual case even where the delay is beyond 365 days**. In other words, if the Form 10B delay exceeds the one-year limit, the taxpayer is not automatically barred from relief; instead, the matter may still be considered by the **CBDT on merits and in accordance with law**. In other words, a taxpayer is not automatically blocked from the Vivad se Vishwas scheme for an entire assessment year just because a prosecution exists for that year; the prosecution must relate to the **same tax arrear/issue** covered by the declaration.

The Delhi High Court held, in an appeal concerning **AY 1995-96 under Section 68 of the Income-tax Act**, that an assessee who claims the benefit of **“peak credit”** in an accommodation-entry case must fully and candidly disclose all facts within its knowledge about the credit entries in the accounts. The court said the assessee must explain, with sufficient detail, **the source of all deposits into the relevant bank accounts and the destination of all payments made out of those accounts**, not merely rely on a general assertion that transactions are circular or routed through banking channels. The court emphasized that the **primary onus of disclosure** rests on the assessee/accommodation-entry provider; if it wants the tax benefit of peak credit, it must make a “clean breast” of the entire transaction trail.

The decision signals that, in such cases, compliance and evidentiary support must be robust: merely showing bank movements is not enough unless the taxpayer can tie the full chain together with credible identity, source, and destination information. For a corporate compliance team, the key takeaway is that any involvement in or exposure to accommodation-entry style transactions creates a serious Section 68 risk unless the company can substantiate the entire money trail and the real counterparties involved. The decision was pronounced on **August 4, 2017** and published on **August 16, 2017**.

The functions performed, assets used and risk assumed, is not a proper and appropriate test to determine whether there is a location PE (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The assessing authority decided that the assessees had a permanent establishment (hereinafter referred to as PE) as they had a fixed place where they carried on their own business in Delhi, and that, consequently, Article 5 of the India U.S. Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement of 1990 (hereinafter referred to as DTAA) was attracted. Consequently, the assessees were liable to pay tax in respect of what they earned from the aforesaid fixed place PE in India. The CIT (Appeals) dismissed the appeals of the assessees holding that Article 5 was attracted, not only because there was a fixed place where the assessees carried on their business, but also because they were “service PEs” and “agency PEs” under Article 5. In an appea
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that the U.S. entities did **not** have a taxable permanent establishment (PE) in India under Article 5 of the **India–U.S. DTAA, 1990**, and therefore the Indian tax authorities could not tax the foreign companies on the basis of a supposed Indian PE. The assessing officer had treated the companies as having a **fixed place PE** in Delhi and concluded they were carrying on their own business there; the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld PE status, additionally characterizing the arrangement as a **service PE** and **agency PE**. The Supreme Court rejected those conclusions and emphasized that the mere existence of **close association and dependence** between the U.S. company and the Indian companies is **not enough** to create a PE.

The Court explained that the proper test is whether the foreign enterprise has a real **fixed place of business** in India through which its business is carried on, and it clarified that the analysis must not be reduced to a mechanical “functions performed, assets used, and risk assumed” comparison as the sole determinant of a location PE. In other words, the fact that some activities are carried out in India, or that Indian entities support the foreign business, does not by itself establish a PE unless the treaty requirements for a fixed place, service PE, or agency PE are actually met. For compliance purposes, this decision is important because it narrows the circumstances in which foreign companies with Indian affiliates, vendors, or support arrangements can be treated as having a taxable presence in India merely due to operational integration or dependence. No specific filing deadline or rate change is announced in the excerpt; the key holding is the treaty interpretation that, on these facts, **PE attribution in India was not sustainable**.

rows.summary:
This circular explains how the GST return filings for the initial implementation period were to be handled and reconciled, specifically for FORM GSTR-1, FORM GSTR-2, and the simplified FORM GSTR-3B under sections 37, 38, and 39 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with rules 59, 60, and 61 of the CGST Rules, 2017. It notes that, although the normal statutory framework requires monthly filing of outward supplies in GSTR-1 by the 10th of the next month, inward supplies in GSTR-2 by the 15th, and the return in GSTR-3 by the 20th, the GST Council extended the filing deadlines for GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 for July and August 2017 and allowed filing of a simplified GSTR-3B for those two months, with tax to be paid by the notified due dates. For taxpayers using transitional credit under section 140 to pay July 2017 liability, FORM GST TRAN-1 had to be filed on or before 28 August 2017, and the credit claimed was to be reflected in the electronic credit ledger for use against tax liability.

The key compliance point is that once FORM GSTR-3B is filed, the system-based reconciliation process begins against the data later furnished in GSTR-1 and GSTR-2, so taxpayers must ensure that the liability declared and tax paid through GSTR-3B are consistent with the detailed outward and inward supply returns ultimately filed. The circular is directed to all Principal Chief Commissioners/Chief Commissioners/Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax and all Principal Director Generals/Director Generals, indicating nationwide application to registered persons affected by the extended-return regime for the first two months of GST. In practical terms, this means compliance teams needed to track the simplified monthly payment return separately from the detailed return cycle and be prepared for reconciliation of reported supplies, input tax credit, and tax paid once the detailed forms were submitted.

rows.title:
CGST dated 27.08.2017 is issued to clarify classification and GST
                            rate on lottery
rows.desc: Circular No.06/06/2017-CGST F. No. 354/149/2017-TRU Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Tax Research Unit ***** New Delhi, the 27 th August, 2017 To, The Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioners/ Principal Commissioner/ Commissioner of Central Tax (All) / Director General of Systems Madam/Sir, Subject: - Issue related to classification and GST rate on lottery tickets – regarding Supply of lottery has been treated as supply of goods under the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017. 2. Accordingly, based on the recommendation of the GST Council, the GST rate for supply of lottery has been notified under relevant GST rate notification relating to CGST/IGST/UTGST/SGST. However, entries in the respective notifications mention classification for lottery as “-”. 3. In this connection, references have been received, inter-alia, stating that due to discrepancy in code allotted, i.e., lottery is defined as goods but code allotted for lottery is under services, the assessees are not able to upload return or deposit tax in time. 4. The matter has been examined. It should be noted that the process of filing return is linked with rate of tax specified for supply. Further, there is complete clarity about rate of tax on lotteries. As mentioned above, in GST, lottery is goods and the classification indicated in relevant notification for lottery is “-”, which means any chapter. 5. That being so, it is clarified that the classification for lottery in respective CGST, IGST, UTGST and SGST notifications shall be ‘Any Chapter’ of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (51 of 1975) and tax on lottery should be paid accordingly at prescribed rates, 12% or 28%, as the case may be. (Ruchi Bisht) Under Secretary (TRU)
rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 27 August 2017 by the Ministry of Finance, clarifies the GST classification and applicable tax rate for lottery tickets under the CGST/IGST/UTGST/SGST rate notifications. It confirms that the supply of lottery is to be treated as a **supply of goods** under the CGST Act, 2017, not as a service, even though some system/code references had described lottery under services. The document explains that the “-” classification shown in the relevant notifications is to be read as **“Any Chapter”** of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

The practical reason for the clarification is that assessees were reportedly unable to upload returns or deposit tax on time because the code/classification in the system did not align with the legal treatment of lottery as goods. The circular states that return filing is linked to the rate of tax for the supply, and emphasizes that the GST rate on lottery is already clear; the issue was only the classification entry. Compliance teams dealing with lottery supplies should therefore ensure that tax is reported and paid under the correct goods classification and not be misled by the “services” code in the system.

For tax compliance purposes, the circular directs that lottery should be taxed at the **prescribed GST rates of 12% or 28%, as applicable**, under the relevant CGST, IGST, UTGST, or SGST notifications. There is no new substantive tax liability created here; rather, the circular resolves a classification mismatch so that filings, payments, and return uploads can proceed correctly. Entities involved in the supply of lottery tickets should align their GST return/tax payment processes with this clarification immediately, as of the circular date, to avoid filing delays or errors.

This means that only such exporters are eligible to LUT facilities who have received a remittance of Rs. one crore or 10% of export turnover, whichever is a higher amount, in the previous financial
rows.summary:
The circular clarifies the rules for exporting goods or services without payment of integrated tax under a Bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT), issued under section 168(1) of the CGST Act to ensure uniform implementation of Notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax dated 7 July 2017 and related circulars. Its main substantive change is that the LUT facility is not limited to manufacturer-exporters; it is available to any registered person, but only if they satisfy the foreign inward remittance condition from the preceding financial year. Specifically, an exporter is eligible to furnish an LUT only if it has received foreign inward remittances equal to at least 10% of export turnover in the previous financial year and the remittance amount is not less than Rs. 1 crore; the circular states this as effectively requiring Rs. 1 crore or 10% of export turnover, whichever is higher, in the prior year.

For compliance purposes, this means companies seeking to export without paying IGST should verify their prior-year export turnover and inward remittance receipts before using the LUT route, because failure to meet this threshold would require export under bond instead. The document is intended to resolve inconsistent interpretations in the field and expand LUT access, but it also imposes a clear quantitative eligibility test that customs/GST teams should document and track annually. The effective framework is tied to the July 2017 notification and circulars, with this clarification issued on 11 August 2017.

A clarification has been soughtas to whether bond to be furnished for exports is a running bond (with debit / credit facility) or a one-time bond (separate bond for each consignment / export). It is observed consign
rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the procedure for exporting goods or services **without payment of integrated tax (IGST)** under **rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017**, because exporters and field officers reported practical difficulties with the required **bond/Letter of Undertaking (LUT)** process. Issued by the CBEC GST Policy Wing on **7 July 2017** under **section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017**, it is intended to ensure uniform implementation across all Central Tax field formations.

The circular confirms that any **registered person** making such zero-IGST exports must furnish either a **bond or a Letter of Undertaking in FORM GST RFD-11**. It further states that **Notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax dated 1 July 2017** identifies which exporters are eligible to export under an LUT and sets out the related conditions and safeguards; **all exporters not covered by that notification must furnish a bond instead of an LUT**. The circular also notes that the procedure for submitting and accepting the bond had already been prescribed in **Circular No. 2/2/2017-GST dated 4 July 2017**.

A specific compliance point is that the **bond must be executed on non-judicial stamp paper of the value applicable in the State where the bond is furnished**. The circular also addresses a key procedural question: for export bonds, the document is to function as a **running bond with debit/credit facility**, rather than requiring a separate one-time bond for each consignment/export. This means exporters can use a continuing bond balance for multiple export transactions, with debits for each export and replenishment as needed, rather than executing a fresh bond each time.

rows.summary:
This circular, dated **5 July 2017** and issued by the **Central Board of Excise and Customs, GST Policy Wing**, assigns the “proper officer” for administering specific **GST functions other than Registration and Composition** under the **Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017**, read with the IGST Act and subject to section 5(2) of the CGST Act. It does not change tax rates or substantive liability rules; instead, it allocates enforcement and procedural authority to particular levels of Central Tax officers, which is important for determining which officer is legally empowered to issue notices, conduct proceedings, and exercise specified statutory powers.

The circular states that the **Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Central Tax** is the proper officer for **section 67(7)** and the **proviso to section 78**. The **Additional or Joint Commissioner of Central Tax** is assigned functions under **sections 67(1), (2), (5), and (9)**; **sections 71(1) and (2)**; the **proviso to section 81**; the **proviso to section 129(6)**; **rules 139(1)–(4)**; and **rule 140(2)**. For compliance purposes, the key implication is that **taxpayers and internal teams must direct responses, filings, and litigation/administrative coordination to the officer level authorized for the specific provision involved**; actions taken by the wrong rank could raise authority/challenge issues. The circular is effective from its issuance date and is intended to standardize officer jurisdiction for GST proceedings such as scrutiny, inspection, audit-related powers, recovery-related steps, provisional/release procedures, and refund-related functions to the extent covered by the listed statutory sections and rules.

Various communications have been received from the field formations and exporters on the issue of difficulties being faced while supplying the goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax and filing the FORM GST RFD -11 on the common portal (www.gst.gov.in), because of which exports are being held up. 2. Whereas, as per rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017, any registered person availing the option to supply goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax shall furnish, prior to export, a bond or a Letter of Undertaking. This bond or Letter of Undertaking is required to be furnished in FORM GST RFD-11 on the common portal. Further, Circular No. 26/2017- Customs dated 1 st July, 2017 has clarified that the procedure as prescribed under rule 96A of the said rules requires to be followed for the export of goods from 1 st July, 2017. 3. Another issue being raised by various stakeholders is that the Bond/Letter of Undertaking is required to be given through the proper officer which is to be furnished to the jurisdictional Commissioner as per sub-rule (1) of rule 96A of the said rules. Taking cognizance of the fact that a large number of such Bonds/Letter of Undertakings would be required to be filed by the registered exporters who would be located at a distance from the office of the jurisdictional Commissioner, it is understood that the furnishing of such bonds/undertakings before the jurisdictional Commissioner may cause hardship to the exporters. 4. Thus, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (
rows.summary:
This circular addresses the procedure for exporters who want to supply goods or services for export **without payment of integrated tax** and clarifies how the required **Bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT)** should be filed. Under **rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017**, any registered person using this export-without-tax option must furnish a **bond or LUT before export**, and this is to be done in **FORM GST RFD-11 on the common portal (www.gst.gov.in)**. The circular notes that exporters and field offices reported practical difficulties in filing RFD-11 on the portal, which was delaying exports, and also highlights that a previous customs circular, **Circular No. 26/2017-Customs dated 1 July 2017**, had already clarified that the rule 96A procedure applies to exports of goods starting **1 July 2017**.

The main change introduced is a relaxation in the filing process: although rule 96A refers to furnishing the bond/LUT through the proper officer and jurisdictional Commissioner, the government recognized that requiring exporters to appear before the **jurisdictional Commissioner** could cause hardship, especially because many exporters are located far away from that office. As a result, the circular uses the power granted under the GST law to permit bonds/LUTs to be furnished in a more practical manner, removing the need for exporters to physically submit them only to the jurisdictional Commissioner. For compliance purposes, the requirement to have a valid bond/LUT **before making zero-rated exports without payment of integrated tax** remains in force; what changes is the administrative procedure for furnishing it, intended to prevent export delays. The document is addressed to all Central Tax field formations and is meant to be implemented immediately in relation to the export procedures already effective from **1 July 2017**.

rows.summary:
This circular amends Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST, which deals with who is the “proper officer” for adjudicating show cause notices under sections 73 and 74 of the CGST Act, 2017 and the corresponding IGST provisions. The key change is that, following Notification No. 02/2022-Central Tax dated 11 March 2022 and the later substitution of Table V by Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax dated 25 November 2024, additional Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners of Central Tax in specified Central Tax Commissionerates have been given all-India jurisdiction to adjudicate show cause notices issued by officers of the Directorate General of Goods and Services Tax Intelligence (DGGI). Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax took effect on 1 December 2024, and this circular is issued on 4 December 2024 to align the earlier circular with that expanded jurisdiction.

As a result, paragraph 7.1 of Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST (as already amended by Circular No. 169/01/2022-GST dated 12 March 2022) is being substituted. The revised paragraph begins by addressing show cause notices issued by DGGI officers and indicates that there may be situations where a notice is issued to multiple noticees; the circular text provided cuts off before the full revised procedure is visible, but the substantive regulatory effect is clear: adjudication authority for DGGI-originated notices now includes the newly empowered officers listed under the amended notification, with all-India jurisdiction. For compliance teams, the practical implication is that DGGI notices may now be adjudicated by a broader set of Central Tax Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners than before, so internal routing, jurisdiction checks, and litigation/response tracking should be updated to reflect the post-1 December 2024 framework.

rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court, Circuit Bench at Jalpaiguri, dealt with a writ petition by Umen Chandra Roy challenging denial of Input Tax Credit (ITC) relief under Section 16(5) of the CGST Act, 2017, read with Section 39. The petitioner had filed the relevant return up to November 30, 2021, which the court noted was within the statutory cut-off contemplated under Section 16(5), and later submitted a rectification application on January 12, 2026 seeking the ITC benefit. That application was rejected by the tax authority by order dated April 8, 2026 on the ground that it was not filed within the period stated in departmental circular/notification dated April 8, 2024, as read with a circular dated October 15, 2024.

A key issue in the judgment was the time limit for rectification: the original judgment text in paragraph 3 referred to a period of “six weeks,” but the later correction order dated August 21, 2026 clarified that this was a clerical/error correction and the intended period was “six months,” and that the word “communication” should be read as “circular.” The petitioner’s position was that the rectification period could be extended because Section 16(5) itself does not prescribe a specific filing deadline for the rectification application. The revenue opposed this by stating that the original order dated March 6, 2024 had already been served on the petitioner the same day by post, implying the challenge was time-barred under the departmental timeline.

For compliance purposes, the case is significant because it shows the court engaging with whether taxpayers can seek rectification/ITC relief beyond the strict time period referenced in departmental circulars when the statute itself is silent on a rectification filing deadline. Entities claiming transitional or delayed ITC relief under Section 16(5) should note the factual dates emphasized by the court: the relevant return cutoff of November 30, 2021, the order in original dated March 6, 2024, the departmental circulars dated April 8, 2024 and October 15, 2024, the rectification filing on January 12, 2026, the rejection order dated April 8, 2026, and the correction order dated August 21, 2026. The practical compliance implication is that businesses seeking ITC restoration or rectification should not assume a statutory extension exists merely because the section itself does not specify a deadline; they must still monitor and act within the deadlines imposed by applicable circulars, while also preserving service-date evidence and documentary support to contest any limitation objection.

rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court upheld the deduction/allowability of a provision for major repairs made by ECA Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd. for Assessment Year 2015–16, rejecting the Revenue’s Section 260A appeal against the ITAT Mumbai order dated 8 February 2023 and the CIT(A), Pune order dated 23 March 2022. The assessee was a special purpose vehicle engaged in road construction and toll collection under a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) concession with the Government of Maharashtra, and under that 30-year concession it was contractually required to carry out major repairs during the concession period. The document states that the first major repair was due after seven years (in the eighth year) and the last major repair in the 30th year; the assessee argued that the liability accrued over time and could be recognized using a reliable scientific estimate, rather than waiting until the actual repair outlay occurred.

For AY 2015–16, the assessee had reported a book loss of Rs. 4,48,91,467 and an income-tax loss of Rs. 8,46,64,672. The Assessing Officer disallowed the provision for major repairs and added Rs. 7,47,00,000 to income. In support of its position, the assessee relied on the BOT agreement and CBDT Circular No. 9/2014 on expenditure incurred for development of roads/highways under BOT arrangements. The CIT(A) had examined the concession agreement’s relevant clauses (Articles 17, 37, 38 and 39) and allowed the claim, and the Tribunal affirmed that view.

The High Court agreed with the lower authorities that the provision was not a mere contingent liability but a contractual and ascertainable obligation arising under the BOT arrangement, and that a scientifically estimated provision was deductible when properly supported. For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that BOT concessionaires in road/highway projects may recognize provisions for mandated future major repairs where the obligation is fixed by contract and the amount is estimated on a rational basis; however, the deduction will depend on the concession terms, the reliability of the estimate, and the ability to show that the liability has accrued over the concession period.

The Appellant/Applicant submitted that it had filed an appeal before the First Appellate Authority in APL-01 and also filed the GSTAT appeal in APL-05 on the same day, 19.03.2026, stating that the Department was undertaking recovery proceedings. The Respondent-State Government drew the Bench’s attention to its submissions dated 28.07.2026 and, particularly, to APL-02, which had been rejected on 24.06.2026 by the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals, being the First Appellate Authority. The Registry raised a defect because the GSTAT appeal had been filed before the rejection order of the First Appellate Authority came into existence. After hearing both sides and examining the records, the Bench found that Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 had been filed on 19.03.2026, whereas no order under Section 112(1) of the CGST Act, 2017 was then in existence because the First Appellate Authority had not yet passed its order. The central question before the Bench was whether an aggrieved person could approach GSTAT under Section 112 of the CGST Act, 2017 in the absence of an order passed under Section 107 or Section 108. The Bench reproduced the substance of Section 112(1), under which an aggrieved person may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against an order passed unde
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench held that an appeal filed before the First Appellate Authority had passed its Section 107 order is not maintainable. In this case, Pankajam Plastics filed APL-01 before the First Appellate Authority and also filed the GSTAT appeal in APL-05 on the same day, 19.03.2026, arguing that recovery proceedings had begun and that it needed to protect its position. However, the record showed that the First Appellate Authority’s rejection/order in APL-02 was not passed until 24.06.2026, so when Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 was submitted on 19.03.2026, there was no existing order under Section 107 or Section 108 that could be appealed against under Section 112(1) of the CGST Act, 2017.

The Tribunal emphasized the core statutory requirement that GSTAT jurisdiction is triggered only by an appeal from an actual order passed by the appropriate lower authority; a taxpayer cannot file a valid Tribunal appeal in anticipation of a future appellate order. Because the appeal was lodged before the First Appellate Authority’s order came into existence, the Registry’s defect objection was upheld and the filing was treated as premature and therefore not maintainable. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that a GSTAT appeal must be filed only after the relevant Section 107/108 order is issued, even if recovery proceedings are underway; the pendency or threat of recovery does not by itself create a right to move the Tribunal before the statutory order exists.

Abhilash Mohanty alleging that M/s Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. had failed to pass on the benefit of Input Tax Credit (ITC) to homebuyers in its “Vertex Panache” project following the introduction of GST from 01.07.2017, thereby contravening Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017. The Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering referred the matter to the DGAP, which initially reported profiteering of Rs. 73,00,010/-, comprising a base profiteered amount of Rs. 65,17,866/- and GST of Rs. 7,82,144/-, allegedly required to be passed on to 140 eligible homebuyers. The Respondent contended that substantial escalation in construction costs had materially offset the additional ITC benefit. The budgeted construction cost was Rs. 1,56,94,91,872/-, whereas actual expenditure amounted to Rs. 1,61,06,72,320/-, resulting in an overall cost increase of Rs. 4,11,80,448/- including indirect cost. The Respondent specifically identified increases of 19.87% in Ready-Mix Concrete (RMC), 62.98% in Sand and 73.17% in Bricks. Based on actual quantities consumed and costs incurred, the additional expenditure attributable to these major inputs was stated to be Rs. 3,49,87,499/-. The Respondent relied upon the Delhi High Court judgment in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, particularly paragraph 118, concerning price increases based on genuine commercial factors despite reduction in tax or availability of ITC. rows.summary:
This GST anti-profiteering matter concerned M/s Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd.’s “Vertex Panache” real estate project and whether it failed to pass on the benefit of additional Input Tax Credit (ITC) after GST took effect on 01.07.2017, as prohibited by Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017. The complaint was filed by Sh. Abhilash Mohanty, and the Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering referred the matter to the DGAP, which initially concluded that Vertex Homes had profiteered by Rs. 73,00,010/-, made up of Rs. 65,17,866/- as the base profiteered amount and Rs. 7,82,144/- as GST, allegedly due to 140 eligible homebuyers. Vertex Homes disputed the allegation and argued that the expected benefit from ITC had been substantially neutralized by steep construction-cost inflation, pointing to a budgeted construction cost of Rs. 1,56,94,91,872/- versus actual expenditure of Rs. 1,61,06,72,320/-, creating an overall cost overrun of Rs. 4,11,80,448/- including indirect cost. It highlighted specific input cost increases of 19.87% for Ready-Mix Concrete, 62.98% for sand, and 73.17% for bricks, and said that, based on actual quantities and costs, these three inputs alone added Rs. 3,49,87,499/- in expenditure.

The respondent relied on the Delhi High Court’s decision in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, especially paragraph 118, to support the position that price increases driven by genuine commercial factors can justify not fully passing through a tax benefit. It also submitted a Chartered Accountant’s Certificate dated 25.06.2026 from M/s Tukaram & Co. The material point for compliance purposes is that the case turns on whether the statutory anti-profiteering obligation under Section 171 was actually breached, or whether increased input/construction costs offset the ITC benefit such that no net profiteering occurred. The document excerpt itself indicates that the GSTAT ultimately found nil profiteering, meaning the tribunal accepted that cost escalation absorbed the ITC advantage rather than requiring a passing-on adjustment to the homebuyers. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that GST-related benefit pass-through under anti-profiteering rules must be assessed against actual commercial cost movements, with project-specific cost records, quantity consumption data, and professional certifications being central evidence when defending against allegations of non-passing of ITC benefits.

rows.summary:
The document concerns an anti-profiteering proceeding against **M/s Sane Retails Pvt. Ltd.** arising from a complaint by **Shri Rohit Kumar Agrawal** alleging that the company did **not pass on the benefit of GST rate reduction** on **“MI LED Television 4A 80 cm”** when the applicable GST rate dropped from **28% to 18%**, effective **01.01.2019**, under **Notification No. 24/2018-Central Tax (Rate) dated 31.12.2018**. The matter was referred by the **Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering** to the **DGAP** under **Rule 129 of the CGST Rules, 2017**, and the DGAP reviewed invoices and outward taxable supply data for the period **01.11.2018 to 31.12.2018** (pre-reduction) and **01.01.2019 to 31.12.2019** (post-reduction). On that basis, DGAP initially calculated profiteering at **₹7,79,947**.

After the abolition of the **National Anti-Profiteering Authority**, the case was transferred via the **Competition Commission of India** to the **GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT)**. The Tribunal directed the respondent to prove that the profiteered amount had been refunded to affected customers, and the respondent produced **Electronic Gift Voucher (EGV)** screenshots, an **Excel mapping** linking vouchers to customer orders and invoices, and later **credit notes**. DGAP objected that the EGVs were **conditional, time-bound, and restricted**, and that the system label **“Offers and cash back”** did not by itself establish that the GST benefit had actually been passed on. DGAP did, however, accept **credit notes totaling ₹2,21,056** for **174 customers** whose orders were cancelled or whose goods were returned, which reduced the alleged profiteering to **₹5,58,891**.

The key issue before the Tribunal was whether the **EGVs constituted valid transfer of the GST benefit**. The Tribunal ultimately **upheld the EGVs as a legitimate mode of passing on the benefit**, meaning the respondent’s vouchers were accepted as evidence of benefit transfer to customers. After allowing for the credit notes and accepting the EGV-based benefit transfer, the Tribunal found that only **₹10,241** remained unaccounted for and **ordered that amount to be deposited into the fund**. For compliance purposes, the document shows that businesses subject to GST anti-profiteering scrutiny may be required to substantiate benefit pass-through with customer-specific records, and that the Tribunal accepted EGVs when adequately mapped to transactions, while also enforcing deposit of any residual amount not shown to have been refunded or passed on.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST ITC on Immovable Property: Eligibility & Risks
rows.desc: Summary: The article examines the restriction of input tax credit under Section 17(5)(c) and (d) of the CGST Act on works contract services, goods and services used for constructing immovable property, and the statutory exceptions for plant and machinery and construction not undertaken on a taxable person’s own account. It explains the meaning of immovable property through the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act and judicial tests concerning the nature, object, intention, functionality, permanency and marketability of annexation. It also discusses ITC eligibility for movable installations, HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems and other business equipment, and recommends separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery and movable goods to reduce the risk of denial of otherwise eligible credit. Table of Contents▸ Background: Blocked credit under section 17(5)(c/d) Comments: What is immovable property? Movable vs immovable property test-various judgements The principles laid down by the Apex Court in the case of Bharti Airtel Limited v The Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune Eligibility to Input tax credit and immovable property under GST Way ahead and conclusion Possible issues when there is a Single contract for construction of building and supply of machineries, other moveable goods: ACTION POINTS FOR ITC OPTIMISATION: Show all 10 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background: It is being observed that the assesses are receiving notices requiring to reverse/pay back ITC availed pertaining to newly constructed building projects used for business operations[such as factory premise/warehouses], alleging such credit is restricted being of nature of “immovable property”. However in addition to civil works, such projects involve installation of electrical fittings, cabling, STP, security, fire fighting, machines for manufacture of
rows.summary:
The article explains that GST input tax credit is often being challenged for credits taken on newly constructed business premises such as factories and warehouses, because tax authorities are treating the underlying expenditure as “immovable property” and therefore blocked under Section 17(5)(c) and (d) of the CGST Act. It emphasizes that the restriction applies to input tax credit on works contract services and on goods/services used for construction of immovable property on a taxpayer’s own account, but there are statutory exceptions where credit may still be available, especially for “plant and machinery” and for construction that is not undertaken for the taxpayer’s own account. The document says the immovable-versus-movable determination is not based only on whether something is attached to the building, but on legal tests drawn from the General Clauses Act and Transfer of Property Act, plus judicial factors such as the nature of the attachment, intention, functionality, permanency, and marketability of the item once annexed.

It specifically discusses that credit eligibility can differ for items installed in a facility, and that business equipment such as HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems, and other movable installations may qualify for ITC depending on how they are structured and whether they fall within the blocked-credit rule or the plant-and-machinery exception. A major compliance concern highlighted is that where a single contract covers both civil construction and supply/installation of machinery or other movable assets, the tax risk increases because authorities may deny the entire or part of the credit by characterizing the spend as construction of immovable property. To reduce this risk, the article recommends structuring the project through separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery, and movable goods/services, so eligible credits are not contaminated by ineligible construction credits.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that newly constructed operational sites can trigger notices and demands for reversal of ITC already availed, so taxpayers should review project documentation, contract scope, invoicing, and asset characterization before claiming credit. The document does not give a new filing deadline or a change in rate; instead, it is a risk-and-eligibility guide focused on how Section 17(5)(c) and (d) should be applied to construction-related spending and how to preserve credit where the underlying items are truly movable or qualify as plant and machinery.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Vague Fraud Allegation Cannot Invoke GST Section 74: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court: Mere Words “Fraud” or “Suppression of Facts” in a GST Show Cause Notice Are Not Enough to Invoke Section 74 Summary: The Supreme Court in M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. held that merely using the expressions “fraud” or “suppression of facts” in a GST show cause notice is insufficient to invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act. M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam challenged an SCN dated 13.06.2025 concerning FY 2018-19 and raising a demand of Rs.1,52,56,431/-. The company argued that the ordinary limitation period applicable under Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025 and that the department had mechanically invoked Section 74 without identifying any conduct constituting fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Although the department sought to explain the allegations through its counter affidavit, the Court refused to consider those subsequent explanations. It reiterated that the legal validity of a notice must be determined from the notice itself and that deficiencies affecting jurisdiction cannot be cured through pleadings filed later before a court. The SCN contained only a bland reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining how fraud was inferred or concealment detected. The use of the expression “or” also indicated uncertainty regarding the allegation being made. Holding that the foundational facts and reasoning supporting the invocation of the extended limitation period must be disclosed in the notice, the Supreme Court set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order as well as the SCN and restrained the department from proceeding further on its basis. Table of Contents▸ Background of the Case What the Company Argued What the Department Argued What the Supreme Court Held Key Takeaways for Practitioners Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background of the Case This case deals with a Show Cause Notice (SCN) iss
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held in **M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.** that a GST notice cannot validly invoke the **extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act** merely by using the words **“fraud”** or **“suppression of facts”** without stating the actual facts that allegedly amount to fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression. The case involved an **SCN dated 13.06.2025** for **FY 2018–19** demanding **Rs. 1,52,56,431**, and the taxpayer argued that the normal limitation under **Section 73** had already expired on **28.02.2025**, so the department could not bypass that deadline with a mechanical Section 74 invocation.

The Court emphasized that the **validity and jurisdictional basis of a show cause notice must be judged from the notice itself**, and the department cannot later cure a defective notice by adding explanations in a counter affidavit or court pleadings. Here, the SCN contained only a vague reference to **“fraud or concealment of facts”** and did not explain **what conduct was fraudulent, how any concealment was discovered, or why the extended-period provisions applied**. The Court also noted that the use of the word **“or”** reflected uncertainty about the actual allegation, further undermining the notice.

As a result, the Supreme Court **set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order and quashed the SCN**, and it **restrained the department from proceeding further on the basis of that notice**. For compliance teams, the practical point is that if a GST notice seeks to use **Section 74** rather than **Section 73**, it must contain **specific, fact-based allegations** showing fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression; a bare label is not enough. This ruling is especially relevant where the department tries to preserve a time-barred demand by inserting fraud language without detailed supporting facts in the notice itself.

rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench held that goods transported without an E-Way Bill could justify detention and penalty under Section 129 of the UPGST Act, 2017 where the surrounding facts indicated an intention to evade tax. The case concerned 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods transported by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018; the vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018, and the E-Way Bill was not available with the driver at the time of interception. On those facts, the department had originally imposed tax of Rs. 47,844 and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844 under Section 129(3), but the first appellate authority had later set aside both demands by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018.  

The department’s position was that the failure to carry the mandatory E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules, and that later production of the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns, and proof of tax payment did not erase the original non-compliance. It argued that the nature of the goods, the interception itself, the route, and the later documents together supported a finding of evasion intent, so penalty under Section 129 remained warranted. The order text also contains an internal party-description inconsistency: the cause title identifies Santosh Mani Mishra as the appellant and a party linked to Islam Trading Company as respondent, while the opening paragraph describes the appellant as Revenue and later refers to M/s Islam Trading Company as the appellant.  

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that transport of taxable goods without a valid E-Way Bill at the time of movement/interception can result in detention plus tax and penalty exposure, even if supporting tax documents are produced later. The case reinforces that businesses moving goods should ensure the E-Way Bill is generated and available with the driver before dispatch, because post-interception document production may not prevent a Section 129 penalty if authorities infer an attempt to evade tax.

rows.summary:
The Tribunal considered three connected appeals involving real-estate developers in Tamil Nadu—Real Value Promoters Pvt. Ltd., Ceebros Property Development, and Prime Developers—arising from orders dated 6.1.2010, 10.5.2010, and 16.8.2010, respectively, and heard together at Chennai. The core issue was whether construction activity undertaken for buyers under separate arrangements for supply of goods and for provision of construction services, or under ECIS/works-contract-style billing, should be treated as a “works contract service” for service tax purposes, and whether the department could deny composition scheme treatment after 1.6.2007. The department had issued show cause notices alleging short payment of service tax under Commercial or Industrial Construction Services, and in the case of Real Value Promoters specifically disputed the composition levy for three projects—Sananda Brindavan, Sujeet, and Surya Skanda—on the grounds that the services were not properly classifiable as Works Contract Service and that the appellants had not exercised the required option for the composition scheme.

The appellants’ position was that their arrangements involved separate supply and service elements and that the post-1.6.2007 regime for works contract/composition should apply to their construction activities. The Tribunal’s order is a final appellate decision dated 18.09.2018 (Final Order Nos. 42436-42438/2018), and it was heard on 16.08.2018. Although the excerpt provided does not contain the full operative findings, the document clearly concerns the classification of real-estate construction contracts for service tax liability, the availability of composition treatment from 1.6.2007 onward, and the validity of departmental demands alleging underpayment where builders used separate supply/service structures rather than being taxed as works contracts. For compliance purposes, the material point is that developers engaged in commercial and residential construction needed to evaluate whether their contract structure and election of the composition scheme satisfied the legal requirements applicable after 1.6.2007, because the department challenged such treatment for specific projects and sought service tax under a different category.

The prayer for bail was opposed by the learned A.G.A. as well as the counsel appearing for the GST Department. rows.summary:
The Allahabad High Court granted bail to Waseem Akram @ Monu in a criminal case arising out of an alleged GST fraud involving a non-existing/bogus firm, M/s Super Power Industries. The case was registered as Case Crime No. 539 of 2025 at Police Station Brahampuri, District Meerut, under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, and 120-B of the IPC. The applicant argued that he was falsely implicated, that his name did not appear in the FIR, and that he had no ownership or direct connection with the alleged bogus firm, which was said to have been declared bogus in November 2021; he also said his name surfaced only through the statement of Sakeel Khan and that he was not a beneficiary of the alleged fraud.

From a compliance perspective, the order is a bail decision rather than a substantive GST ruling, so it does not create a new filing, tax-payment, or registration requirement. However, it underscores that allegations tied to fictitious GST entities can lead to serious criminal exposure, including prosecution under IPC fraud and forgery provisions, even where the FIR initially does not name a person directly. The court also noted the applicant’s lack of criminal history and the fact that he had been in custody since 05.04.2026, and it accepted the argument that trial completion was unlikely soon because of case backlog. The bail application was opposed by the State A.G.A. and counsel for the GST Department, but the court nevertheless allowed bail pending trial, based on the overall facts, evidence, and nature of allegations.

The Department proposed service tax of Rs. 39,22,945/- together with interest, penalties and late fee for non-filing of ST-3 returns. The demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals), leading to the appeal before the Tribunal. The appellant contended that the expression “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been incorrectly interpreted. It argued, relying particularly on Cuddalore Municipality Vs Joint Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, that the expression “any other person” meant a person other than the owner. It also argued that vacant land was excluded from the relevant definition and that arrears of rent had been taxed at an incorrect service tax rate. rows.summary:
The CESTAT Delhi considered a municipality’s liability to service tax on two separate streams of income: charges received for allowing advertisements on hoardings, and rent/licence fees received from letting immovable property, including vacant land, to agencies, persons, and traders. The dispute covered financial years 2009-10 through 2014-15, spanning both the pre-negative-list and post-negative-list service tax regimes. The municipality had received Rs. 3,06,738 from hoarding rent between April 2009 and June 2012, and Rs. 3,39,22,974 from various immovable properties between April 2009 and July 2014; the Department demanded Rs. 39,22,945 in service tax, plus interest, penalties, and late fee for failure to file ST-3 returns.

On the renting issue, the municipality argued that “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been wrongly applied, contending that the phrase “any other person” in the statutory definition should be read as someone other than the owner, that vacant land was excluded from the taxable category, and that some arrears of rent were taxed at the wrong rate. The Tribunal rejected that broad challenge to taxability and held that the municipality’s activity of renting/licensing immovable property and vacant land was within the taxable service framework for the relevant period. However, on the hoarding/advertisement receipts, the municipality argued that it was only collecting statutory licence fees under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 for allotting land on which advertisers erected hoardings, rather than itself providing a taxable advertising service.

The Tribunal’s ruling is significant for compliance because it confirms that municipal income from hoarding space and property-rental arrangements can attract service tax exposure, but it also limits the Department’s recovery in this case by quashing the extended-period demand. In other words, the Tribunal did not accept the Department’s full attempt to invoke the longer limitation period for tax recovery, which means any demand beyond the normal limitation period could not be sustained on the facts found. The decision therefore matters both for classification of municipal receipts and for limitation/penalty exposure: entities performing similar municipal or licensing functions should review whether they are receiving taxable consideration for immovable-property use or advertisement rights, whether the correct service tax rate was applied to each payment period, and whether any non-filing of ST-3 returns or related late-fee/penalty liabilities may arise for historical periods.

rows.summary:
This Madras High Court decision concerns AY 2015–16 and arises from a writ petition by Sankaran Mekala challenging a demand order dated 16.07.2026 passed under sections 147, 271(1)(b), and 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The petitioner had earlier filed W.P. No. 1242 of 2026 against an assessment order dated 16.01.2024 and a notice dated 12.04.2022; that earlier writ was disposed of on 09.02.2026 with a direction to file the return of income for AY 2015–16 and to reply to the notice issued under section 148.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Court accepted the taxpayer’s evidence of technical inability to upload the return on the income-tax e-filing portal, including a screenshot showing the failure, and treated that as sufficient reason to grant another opportunity to comply. The petitioner also showed proof that she had already deposited Rs. 5 lakhs pursuant to the earlier High Court order, which the Court noted as part of her attempted compliance.

The High Court held that, in the interests of justice, the petitioner should be allowed to file the return despite the portal issue, and it disposed of the writ petition by directing that portal access be reopened / made available so the return could be uploaded in accordance with the earlier order. The practical compliance implication is that when a court has directed filing through the e-filing portal, contemporaneous proof of technical failure on the portal and proof of partial compliance can justify relief, and the taxpayer should preserve screenshots and payment evidence to support any request for extension or reopening of filing access.

Significantly, the CBI had investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report recording that the available evidence indicated that
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals filed by Chessman Impex Private Limited and co-appellants and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017. As a result, the customs duty demand of Rs. 2,16,93,068, the consequential interest, and the penalties of Rs. 20 lakh each imposed under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, as well as the penalties imposed on the co-appellants, were held unsustainable. The dispute arose from a DEEC licence issued under the EXIM Policy 1997-2002, which allowed duty-free import of 5,350 MT of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against an export obligation of 5,000 MT of non-alloy steel bars and rods.

Revenue’s case was that the imported scrap had been diverted into the domestic market and that, instead of exporting the stipulated steel products, the appellant had fraudulently exported maize to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export. The Tribunal rejected the demand because the record contained multiple corroborating materials supporting the appellant’s explanation: special permission for exports through Ghojadanga Land Customs Station, Customs examination of the export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai’s confirmation of manufacture by Goyal Ispat Ltd., permission from the foreign buyer to segregate and export unprocessed scrap, undisputed realization of export proceeds, and issuance of the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate by the competent DGFT authority. The Tribunal also noted that the CBI had investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and, in its final report, recorded that the available evidence did not support the allegations in the manner asserted by Revenue.

For compliance purposes, this case underscores that when an export obligation has been discharged through the competent DGFT process and the contemporaneous customs/excise record supports the shipments and manufacture, a later customs demand alleging diversion or sham exports may fail if it is not backed by reliable, corroborative evidence. It also highlights the importance of preserving export permissions, customs examination records, excise certifications, foreign buyer correspondence, export proceeds realization evidence, and the EODC, because those documents were decisive in defeating the duty, interest, and penalty demands in this matter.

(Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered a challenge to a customs penalty of Rs. 425,27,99,100/- imposed on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962. The penalty arose from an allegation that a consignment of natural diamonds had been mis-declared as lab-grown diamonds to pay a lower tariff. The Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025 was challenged before the Gujarat High Court, but the challenge failed when the High Court dismissed the appeal on 20.01.2026. The matter then reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court did not enter into the merits of the underlying customs dispute. Instead, the appellant contended that several judgments and articles relied upon by the second respondent in the Order-in-Original had been generated using Artificial Intelligence. The Court independently verified the material relied upon in the customs order and found that the second respondent had relied upon case laws that were either non-existent or had fake citations. The Court further found that some case laws which did exist did not lay down the legal propositions attributed to them. The Court observed that the material appeared to be a hallucination of AI. This discovery led the Supreme Court to rely upon its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh Vs Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd., where the Court had adopted a zero-tolerance approach towards producing, citing or relying upon artificial-intelligence-generated precedents without verification. The Supreme
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court set aside the Gujarat High Court’s dismissal of a challenge to a customs penalty of ₹425,27,99,100 imposed on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962. The penalty had been imposed by Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025 on the allegation that a consignment of natural diamonds had been misdeclared as lab-grown diamonds to evade a lower tariff. The High Court had rejected the appeal on 20.01.2026, but the Supreme Court did not decide the underlying customs classification or penalty merits; instead, it focused on the integrity of the legal authorities cited in the customs order.

The key compliance-relevant holding is that the appellant showed several judgments and articles relied upon in the Order-in-Original were generated using artificial intelligence, and the Court independently verified that the decision-maker had cited case law that was either nonexistent, had fake citations, or did not support the legal propositions attributed to it. The Supreme Court said the material appeared to be an AI “hallucination,” and it relied on its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd., which adopts a zero-tolerance approach to producing, citing, or relying on AI-generated precedents without verification. The practical implication for compliance teams is that customs orders, internal legal submissions, and any regulatory filings or defenses must be checked for authenticity and legal accuracy before reliance; unsupported AI-generated authorities can undermine enforcement actions and judicial outcomes.

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court disposed of three connected writ petitions filed by Reckitt Benckiser (India) Private Limited concerning GST matters for the tax period 2019–2020. One petition challenged a show cause notice in Form GST DRC-01 dated 31.05.2024, another challenged an order/reply dated 29.05.2024, and the third challenged Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023 and the related State/Government orders issued under Section 168A of the GST laws that extended limitation periods. The limitation-extension issue was the key compliance point in the case, but the Court did not rule on the substantive validity of that notification or on the underlying tax dispute.

At admission, the Court had granted interim protection on 13.08.2024. After that, the jurisdictional State Tax Officer submitted a detailed report dated 27.01.2026, and the Court recorded that the report’s conclusion prima facie supported the petitioner’s position. Based on that report and the subsequent developments, the petitioner stated that no further adjudication was necessary for the DRC-01 challenge, and the Court accepted that position.

As a result, the Court held that the challenge in W.P. No. 20657 of 2024 no longer required adjudication, and the challenges in W.P. Nos. 20652 and 20655 of 2024 had become academic. The Court therefore closed W.P. Nos. 20652 and 20655 of 2024 and disposed of W.P. No. 20657 of 2024. No costs were awarded, and the connected miscellaneous petitions were also closed.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is procedural rather than substantive: this order does not create a new GST rule or invalidate the limitation-extension notifications on the merits, but it shows that limitation-related GST challenges can be rendered moot by later departmental developments and officer reports. Entities facing GST notices for older tax periods, especially where limitation extension under Section 168A and Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax is involved, should note the dates involved here—31.03.2023 for the notification, 29.05.2024 for the order/reply, 31.05.2024 for the DRC-01, 13.08.2024 for interim protection, and 27.01.2026 for the officer’s report—because the court treated those later developments as decisive in closing the litigation.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST appeal should not be rejected solely as time-barred where the delay was caused by medical circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control. In this case, Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd. challenged the rejection of its GST appeal by the appellate authority’s order dated 27.02.2026, and also sought quashing of the underlying order dated 07.02.2024 as well as restoration of its GST registration. The Court set aside the appellate authority’s limitation-based rejection and directed that the appeal be entertained and decided on its merits in accordance with law.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Court recognized that although appellate authorities remain bound by the limitation rules under Section 107 of the Rajasthan/CGST GST framework, writ jurisdiction under Articles 226/227 may be used in exceptional cases where strict adherence to limitation would cause grave prejudice and the delay arose from reasons outside the taxpayer’s control. The judgment relied on prior Rajasthan High Court cases, especially M/s. Pratap Power Spares, where a 99-day delay was condoned after the Court granted relaxation of the 120-day statutory appeal window under Section 107 and directed the appeal to be heard if filed within 30 days. The Court also referred to other decisions supporting delayed GST appeals in exceptional circumstances, while acknowledging the general rule that writ jurisdiction should not be used to bypass statutory limitation.

The relief was not unconditional: the Court made it subject to the petitioner depositing the late fee, penalty, and other statutory amounts required for entertaining the appeal, “as admissible.” The appellate authority must now consider the appeal on merits rather than refuse it on limitation alone. All pending applications were disposed of. From a compliance perspective, this decision underscores that delayed GST appeals may still be pursued where there is documented, compelling hardship such as medical incapacity, but the taxpayer should expect to satisfy all statutory deposit requirements and should not assume that ordinary limitation deadlines will be excused absent exceptional facts.
