rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court considered a writ petition by M/s Jagdish Prasad Agrawal, a partnership firm, challenging the blocking of Input Tax Credit (ITC) in its Electronic Credit Ledger, specifically an IGST ITC block shown with a negative balance. The petitioner asked for the blocking action to be declared illegal, inoperative, and void, for the ledger to be re-credited with any ITC that had been wrongly set off against the disputed demand, and for other appropriate relief. By the time of hearing, the blocking had already automatically ceased to operate because the statutory one-year period had expired, and the Electronic Credit Ledger had been reactivated; as a result, the live dispute narrowed to whether the ITC could have been blocked at all without following Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017.

The respondents conceded that the ledger was operational again, but they could not show that the mandatory preconditions under Rule 86A had been satisfied before the block was imposed. The Court noted that Rule 86A requires the competent authority to have “reasons to believe” that ITC was fraudulently availed or was ineligible, and then, for reasons recorded in writing, to disallow debit of an equivalent amount from the Electronic Credit Ledger for payment of tax liability under section 49 or for refund of unutilised credit; the Court also specifically referred to Rule 86A(1)(d). The respondents admitted the omission was a bona fide mistake, acknowledged that no proper reasoned order had been passed, and conceded that the petitioner had not been given an opportunity of hearing before the blocking. They undertook that any future blocking would be done only by the competent authority through a proper, reasoned order and strictly in accordance with Rule 86A, and an unconditional apology was tendered on behalf of the concerned officer.

Although the Court found on the record that the mandatory requirements of Rule 86A had not been complied with, it treated the matter as exceptional because the restriction had already lapsed and the ledger had been restored. The writ petition was therefore disposed of rather than decided on broader merits, and pending applications were also disposed of. Importantly for compliance purposes, the Court issued a clear warning that if the respondents in future block ITC without due compliance with Rule 86A, they may be liable to pay appropriate compensation to the aggrieved party. The practical compliance takeaway is that any ITC-blocking action under Rule 86A must be supported by recorded reasons, based on the statutory “reasons to believe” standard, and carried out by the proper authority with a reasoned order; otherwise, the action risks being treated as non-compliant and exposing the department to compensation claims.

The appellant was a 100% export unit providing Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas entities under specific service agreements and exported those services without payment of service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. It had claimed refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. Refund of ₹78,79,939 was rejected in respect of General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services on the ground that the services lacked nexus with exported output services. It further submitted that the disputed services fell within the definition of “input service” under Rule 2(l), relying on numerous judicial decisions, and that direct nexus with the final output services was not n
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chandigarh held that M/s Agilent Technologies International Pvt. Ltd., a 100% export-oriented service provider, was entitled to refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The company provided Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas clients under service agreements and exported those services without payment of service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. The specific refund claim rejected by the department was ₹78,79,939, and the rejection related only to credit taken on General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services, and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services on the theory that those services lacked nexus with the exported output services.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that where the Department has not first challenged the availment of CENVAT credit under Rule 14, it cannot later deny refund of the accumulated credit under Rule 5 by questioning whether the credit was eligible in the first place. The Tribunal treated availment, utilisation, and refund of credit as distinct issues and relied on prior case law to conclude that refund proceedings are not the proper stage to re-litigate the underlying eligibility of credit that was never put in dispute under Rule 14. It also reaffirmed that, during the relevant period, the definition of “input service” under Rule 2(l) was broad/exhaustive enough to cover General Insurance Service, Commercial or Industrial Construction Service, and Works Contract Service, and that a strict direct nexus with the exported output service was not required.

The Tribunal specifically relied on Circular No. 120/1/2010-ST dated 19.01.2010 and the decision in Reliance Corporate IT Park Ltd. for the proposition that direct one-to-one linkage between each input service and the exported output service is not necessary for refund eligibility. Accordingly, the impugned order rejecting the refund was set aside and the appeal was allowed with consequential relief, if any, as per law. The practical compliance takeaway is that exporters claiming Rule 5 refunds should ensure credits are properly availed and documented as input services, but if the department intends to dispute eligibility, it should do so at the credit-availment stage under Rule 14; otherwise, a later refund denial on nexus grounds is vulnerable.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12613 Case Name Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Hyderabad considered an appeal by M/s Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. against an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 confirming Service Tax demands, interest and penalties principally under “Banking and Other Financial Services” and “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” for 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The first dispute concerned charges deducted by foreign/intermediary banks while export proceeds were transmitted from foreign buyers through banking channels. The appellant, a manufacture-exporter of pharmaceutical products, contended that the foreign buyers remitted consideration through their banking arrangements and that the foreign/intermediary banks deducted charges before the balance reached the appellant’s Indian bank. The Department proceeded on the basis that, because the deductions economically reduced the amount received by the appellant, the appellant was the recipient of banking services and was liable to Service Tax under Reverse Charge Mechanism. The Tribunal rejected that approach. It found no evidence that the appellant had engaged the foreign banks, entered into contractual arrangements with them, or was otherwise obliged to pay consideration to them for services rendered to it. Merely bearing the economic impact of deductions did not establish a service provider-service recipient relationship. The Tribunal also relied on the appellant’s own earlier decision, Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020,
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad allowed Aurobindo Pharma Ltd.’s appeal and set aside service tax, interest, and penalties confirmed by the Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 for the periods 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The dispute involved two categories of alleged taxability: first, deductions made by foreign/intermediary banks from export remittances received by the company from overseas buyers; and second, payments to overseas/regulatory consultancy vendors M/s DADA Consultancy and M/s Pharpe Dr. D.R. Iban for preparing clinical/non-clinical overviews and regulatory documents to obtain foreign pharmaceutical product approvals. For the bank charges, the Tribunal held that Aurobindo was not the recipient of “Banking and Other Financial Services” merely because the banks’ fees reduced the net remittance amount; there was no evidence of any contract, engagement, or obligation by Aurobindo to pay those foreign banks, so reverse charge liability did not arise.

For the regulatory documentation work, the Tribunal rejected Revenue’s attempt to classify the services as “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services.” It found that the consultants were mainly compiling existing data, published materials, and dossier/form submissions for regulatory filings, not performing independent scientific research, experimentation, technical studies, or giving advice in a scientific discipline. The Tribunal emphasized that classification must be based on the actual nature of the work performed, not simply on the scientific/technical background of the personnel doing it, and held that services rendered to obtain overseas registrations/permissions do not become scientific or technical consultancy just because they relate to regulated pharma approvals. It also relied on Aurobindo’s own earlier favorable order (Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020) and on the IPCA Laboratories line of cases, noting that no material change in facts or service nature had been shown.

A further point important for compliance is that Aurobindo had already discharged service tax on these consultancy payments under “Management or Business Consultant Service,” and the Department had appropriated that amount in the impugned order while simultaneously reclassifying the same services under another taxable head; once the reclassification failed, the demand could not stand. Because the underlying tax demands were set aside, the related interest and penalties were also cancelled. The Tribunal did not separately decide the appellant’s argument about penalty computation under Section 76 of the Finance Act, 1994, in light of the amendment effective 08.04.2011, because that issue became moot after the substantive liabilities were deleted. For compliance teams, the case reinforces that export-remittance bank deductions are not automatically reverse-charge taxable absent a direct service relationship, and that pharma regulatory dossier preparation/compilation for foreign approvals is not, by itself, scientific or technical consultancy.

rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai decision in **Ranjita Rajendra Bane v. Commissioner of Customs** set aside personal penalties of **₹2,50,000** and **₹1,00,000** that had been imposed under **Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962** on the late **Rajendra Bane**, a **Customs Hawaldar**, whose widow appealed as his legal successor. The case arose from a **smuggled-gold investigation at Pune International Airport** involving gold recovered from the **gent’s toilet** after passengers arrived from **Dubai on SpiceJet Flight SG 52 on 16.08.2018**; the department alleged that Bane, despite being on **sanctioned leave** and at his **native place near Ratnagiri**, had facilitated the smuggling operation. The evidence relied on by Customs included **statements recorded under Section 108**, especially those of **co-accused/accomplices**, **telephone call records**, and the physical recovery of gold from the airport and from a passenger.

The Tribunal found that the department had **not proved any credible link** between Bane and the alleged smuggling scheme sufficient to sustain a penalty under Section 112(a). The defence had consistently denied involvement and maintained that Bane was on leave on the relevant date; it also asserted that he had actually **passed information to the Superintendent on duty** at the airport and that this came from a **privileged informer communication** whose source could not be disclosed. The Commissioner (Appeals) had rejected that explanation, but the Tribunal held that the available material, including accomplice statements and call records, did not establish culpability with the level of proof required for penal action. As a result, the **personal penalties were deleted**, and the ruling is significant for compliance purposes because it underscores that customs penalties against employees or officers cannot rest on suspicion or uncorroborated statements alone; there must be **reliable, affirmative evidence** connecting the person to the prohibited act.

rows.summary:
The Patna High Court dealt with a GST dispute involving M/s Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal, a registered taxpayer that performs Nukkad Natak (street plays) for public awareness campaigns, mainly on assignments from government departments. For financial year 2022-23, the department issued a notice under Section 73 of the CGST Act, 2017 on gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100 received from the District Public Relations Officer, Gaya, and the adjudicating authority later confirmed a combined tax, interest, and penalty demand of Rs. 1,63,452 by order dated 20.08.2025. The petitioner appealed under Section 107(1), but the Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on 28.02.2026 solely because it was filed 21 days late.

The petitioner argued that the tax issue should be reconsidered in light of Collectorate, Gaya Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025, which reportedly said GST was not applicable to receipts from sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in Nukkad Natak and that Nukkad Natak teams consisting of 4, 6, 8, or 10 members were exempt from GST. The High Court did not itself decide the merits of the exemption claim; instead, it remitted the matter back to the Appellate Authority for reconsideration. Practically, this means the appellate dismissal on limitation was set aside for further review, and the compliance issue remains whether the petitioner’s Nukkad Natak receipts fall within the stated exemption/ गैर-applicability position reflected in the later government memo.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Remands GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A ITC Mismatch for Fresh Verification
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12609 Case Name N. R. Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GSTAT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); N. R. Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Summary: The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, allowed the appeal of M/s. N. R. Builders by way of remand in a dispute concerning alleged excess Input Tax Credit (ITC) of ₹2,33,502/- for Financial Year 2018–19. The disputed amount comprised CGST of ₹1,16,751/- and SGST of ₹1,16,751/-. Interest of ₹2,03,730/- and penalty of ₹23,350/- had also been imposed, resulting in a total demand of ₹4,60,582/-. The Appellant, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, contended that the apparent mismatch between FORM GSTR-3B and FORM GSTR-2A did not represent excess ITC. According to the Appellant, the disputed credit related to Financial Year 2017–18 invoices but was availed in Financial Year 2018–19 within the permissible period under Section 16(4). The Appellant also challenged the proceedings on the ground that no personal hearing was granted and that no notice in FORM GST ASMT-10 had preceded the proceedings. A pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A was issued on 22.01.2024, followed by a Show Cause Notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 under Section 73. The Show Cause Notice itself recorded the date, time and venue of personal hearing as “NA”. The Proper Officer subsequently confirmed the entire demand ex parte. The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal and upheld the demand. The Tribunal first considered whether the GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A difference could be treated as inadmissible ITC without examining the Appellant’s explanation concerning Financial Year 2017–18 invoices.
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, remanded the matter of **M/s. N. R. Builders v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes** for **fresh verification** after finding that the tax department had not properly examined the taxpayer’s explanation for the input tax credit mismatch. The dispute involved an alleged **excess ITC of ₹2,33,502 for FY 2018–19**, split equally into **CGST ₹1,16,751 and SGST ₹1,16,751**, with additional **interest of ₹2,03,730** and **penalty of ₹23,350**, bringing the total confirmed demand to **₹4,60,582**. The taxpayer, a proprietary concern engaged in **quarrying and sale of crushed stones**, argued that the credit reflected in the GSTR-3B versus GSTR-2A mismatch was not actually excess credit because it related to **FY 2017–18 invoices** but was claimed in **FY 2018–19** within the time limit permitted under **Section 16(4) of the CGST Act**.

Procedurally, the department had issued a **pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A on 22.01.2024**, followed by a **Show Cause Notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 under Section 73**. The notice recorded the date/time/venue of personal hearing as **“NA,”** and the proper officer then **confirmed the entire demand ex parte**. The taxpayer also challenged the case on the grounds that **no personal hearing was granted** and that **no FORM GST ASMT-10 notice** had preceded the proceedings. Although the **First Appellate Authority** dismissed the appeal and upheld the demand, the Tribunal held that the **GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A mismatch could not be treated as inadmissible ITC without first examining the taxpayer’s claim that the invoices belonged to the prior financial year and were claimed within the statutory period**.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that **mismatch between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A alone was not enough to sustain the disallowance where the taxpayer asserted a valid timing-based claim under Section 16(4)**; the department must verify the underlying invoice period and eligibility before confirming tax, interest, and penalty. The remand means the assessment is not finally settled and the authority must conduct **fresh verification**, including consideration of the taxpayer’s explanation and procedural fairness concerns. No new general rule was announced, but the case reinforces that businesses claiming ITC across financial years should retain invoice-level support showing that the credit was availed **within the statutory deadline under Section 16(4)** and be prepared to substantiate any GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A differences during assessment.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative & Judicial Developments
rows.desc: Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative and Judicial Developments – Period covered: September 2025 to September 2026 Summary: The period from September 2025 to September 2026 witnessed substantial changes in India’s GST framework across legislation, tax rates, refunds, return filing, appellate remedies and judicial interpretation. The Finance Act, 2026 amended provisions governing post-supply discounts, credit notes, provisional refunds and appellate arrangements, while omitting Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act concerning intermediary services. Commencement differs across provisions, and the amendments to Sections 15, 34 and 54 of the CGST Act await notification. Rate rationalisation was completed through the withdrawal of compensation cess and migration of specified tobacco and pan masala products to the 40 per cent slab. Risk-based provisional refunds were expanded, GSTAT benches became operational and revised limitation dates were prescribed for legacy appeals. The return architecture increasingly requires verification and reconciliation before filing, supported by GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B and the Invoice Management System. Judicial developments clarified buyer exposure where suppliers fail to deposit tax, statutory timelines for detention orders and the prospective application of penalty-related pre-deposit requirements. With the 57th GST Council meeting scheduled for 12 September 2026, further proposals concerning ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds and small-business compliance remain under consideration but cannot be treated as operative law until formally implemented. The twelve months preceding the 57th meeting of the GST Council have produced the densest concentration of change since the levy was introduced in July 2017. Three distinct layers moved at once. The rate architecture recommended by the 56th Council was completed with the withdrawal of compensation cess and the migration of tobacco and pan mas
rows.summary:
The document summarizes major GST changes in India during September 2025 to September 2026, with the most important compliance point being that the Finance Act, 2026 amended the GST framework on post-supply discounts, credit notes, provisional refunds, and appellate arrangements, while also omitting Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act for intermediary services. The summary notes that the commencement of these amendments is not uniform: some provisions are already in force, but the amendments to Sections 15, 34, and 54 of the CGST Act are still pending notification, so compliance teams should not treat those specific changes as operative until the government issues the commencement notification.

On indirect tax rates, the period saw rate rationalization through the withdrawal of compensation cess and the movement of specified tobacco and pan masala products into the 40% GST slab. That means businesses dealing in those products need to update pricing, tax coding, invoicing, and product-specific compliance controls to reflect the new rate structure and the end of the cess regime. The document also states that risk-based provisional refunds were expanded, which implies that refund claims will increasingly be subject to the revised risk-based process rather than routine processing, and organizations filing refunds should expect more scrutiny and evidence requirements.

The return and data-reconciliation regime has become more control-heavy: filing is increasingly expected to be preceded by verification and reconciliation using GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B, and the Invoice Management System. In practical terms, companies should reconcile outward supplies, inward tax credit, and invoice-level mismatches before filing returns, because the system is moving toward pre-filing validation rather than post-filing correction. This is particularly relevant for input tax credit governance, because the document indicates that the architecture is designed to catch discrepancies earlier in the filing cycle.

On dispute resolution and legacy matters, GSTAT benches have become operational, giving taxpayers a functioning appellate forum, and revised limitation dates were prescribed for old appeals. Compliance teams with pending or historical GST disputes need to check whether any appeal is subject to the newly prescribed deadlines, because missing the revised limitation window could foreclose appellate rights. The summary also reports judicial developments that clarified buyer exposure when suppliers fail to deposit tax, statutory timelines for detention orders, and that penalty-related pre-deposit requirements apply prospectively, meaning they should not be applied retrospectively to older matters unless the ruling or statute expressly says so.

Finally, the document flags that the 57th GST Council meeting was scheduled for 12 September 2026 and may consider proposals on ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds, and small-business compliance, but none of those proposals are operative unless formally implemented. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that several major rule changes are already effective or operational, but some are still pending notification or are only proposals, so internal tax policies, return workflows, and litigation calendars should distinguish carefully between enacted law, notified commencement, and items still under consideration.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaulting Sellers
rows.desc: Why Does the GST Department Chase Bona Fide Buyers Under Section 16(2)(c) Instead of Defaulting Sellers Under Section 76? Summary: Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act makes a recipient’s entitlement to Input Tax Credit conditional upon the tax charged by the supplier having actually been paid to the government. Consequently, even a bona fide buyer who possesses a genuine invoice, receives the goods or services, pays the entire consideration including GST and files returns correctly may be required to reverse ITC if the supplier defaults. Section 76, however, independently empowers the GST department to recover tax collected but not deposited from the person who collected it, together with applicable interest and penalty. Despite this direct remedy, enforcement action is frequently taken against compliant buyers because they are easier to trace, possess identifiable assets and remain active within the GST system, whereas defaulting suppliers may have closed operations, disappeared or operated through shell entities. Automated GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch identification also makes buyer-side proceedings administratively easier than investigation and recovery against sellers. The Supreme Court’s decision in Bhandari Scrap Traders upheld the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), recognising ITC as a statutory benefit subject to legislative conditions, including supplier payment of tax. Nevertheless, questions of fairness and enforcement sequencing remain. A balanced approach would prioritise recovery under Section 76 from the defaulting supplier and reserve ITC denial for transactions involving collusion, fraud or failure to establish genuineness. Until legislation or binding precedent clarifies the sequencing of these provisions, buyers should maintain comprehensive evidence of supplier verification, invoices, receipt of supplies, e-way bills, transport records, banking payments and return reconciliation. rows.summary:
The document explains that under Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act, a buyer’s right to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC) is conditional on the supplier actually paying the GST collected to the government. That means even a bona fide purchaser who has a valid invoice, has received the goods or services, paid the full consideration including GST, and filed returns correctly can still be forced to reverse ITC if the supplier defaults on depositing the tax.  

It contrasts that with Section 76, which separately authorizes the GST department to recover tax that was collected but not deposited from the person who collected it, along with applicable interest and penalty. In principle, this gives the department a direct remedy against the defaulting seller, but in practice the document says authorities often proceed against compliant buyers instead because buyers are easier to locate, have identifiable assets, remain active in the GST system, and are easier to assess through automated GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch checks, whereas defaulting suppliers may have shut down, vanished, or operated through shell entities.  

The document notes that the Supreme Court in *Bhandari Scrap Traders* upheld the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), treating ITC as a statutory benefit that can be conditioned on supplier payment of tax. At the same time, it says fairness concerns remain because enforcement is often aimed first at the buyer even though the seller is the party that collected and failed to remit the tax.  

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that businesses should assume ITC may be challenged if the supplier does not pay GST, even when the transaction is genuine, and they should preserve detailed proof of supplier due diligence and transaction genuineness. The document specifically recommends retaining records of supplier verification, invoices, receipt of supplies, e-way bills, transport documents, banking payment evidence, and return reconciliations to defend against notices. It also argues that a more balanced enforcement approach would prioritize recovery from the defaulting supplier under Section 76 and reserve ITC denial for cases involving collusion, fraud, or inability to prove the transaction was genuine, but it does not say that this sequencing requirement is currently binding law.

rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court dealt with a dispute arising out of insolvency proceedings involving Byju’s K3 Education Private Limited (“Byju’s K3”) and Think and Learn Private Limited, where competing Resolution Professionals were contesting control over certain assets at the IndoSpace Logistics Complex, Bommasandra, Bengaluru. The petitioner, the Resolution Professional of Byju’s K3, asked the High Court to set aside the NCLT Bengaluru Bench’s order dated 13.08.2026 in I.A. No. 768/2026 in C.P. (IB) No. 29/2025 and to quash a public announcement dated 02.08.2026 for sale of those assets, on the ground that the sale proposal would wrongly dispose of property allegedly belonging to Byju’s K3 and harm its insolvency resolution process. The High Court did not decide the ownership dispute itself, holding instead that the matter was already pending before the National Company Law Tribunal and that both companies’ assets were under the Tribunal’s custody, so parallel writ proceedings were not appropriate, especially in a conflict between two Resolution Professionals.

For compliance and insolvency-process purposes, the practical effect is that any challenge to the proposed sale or asset ownership issues must be pursued before the NCLT, not by a parallel writ petition in the High Court. The Court expressly disposed of the petition while granting liberty to the petitioner to move the pending proceedings before the NCLT on 20.08.2026, and it directed the NCLT to take up the matter and pass appropriate orders expeditiously. The High Court also allowed the petitioner to place before the NCLT any documents that came into his possession after the earlier proceedings, signaling that the asset-sale dispute remains live and may be supplemented with additional evidence before the tribunal.

rows.title: Service Tax | STPI’s SOFTEX Certification Charges Taxable as Business Support Service: CESTAT Hyderabad
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12593 Case Name Software Technology Park of India Vs Pr. Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The two appeals concern a common dispute regarding the levy of Service Tax on charges collected by M/s Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) towards certification of SOFTEX forms and issuance of No Objection Certificates (NoCs). The Department classified these activities under “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994. In appeal no. ST/20226/2014, the dispute covered the period from 2007-08 to 2011-12 and involved Service Tax of Rs. 5,15,53,520/- along with interest and penalties. Appeal no. ST/30531/2016 concerned the period April 2012 to June 2012 and involved Service Tax of Rs. 2,06,792/- along with interest and penalties. The Commissioner (Appeals), in the latter appeal, upheld the demand while extending cum-tax benefit. STPI contended that it is an autonomous society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 and functioning under the administrative control of the Department of Electronics and Information Technology, Government of India. It was established, inter alia, to administer and facilitate implementation of the Software Technology Park Scheme. STPI was separately registered with the Service Tax Department and admittedly paid Service Tax on various services including renting of immovable property, bandwidth services, co-location services and project consultancy. The controversy was confined to charges connected with activities under the STP Scheme, particularly SOFTEX certification and issuance of NoCs. The appellan
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that charges collected by Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) for certifying SOFTEX forms and issuing No Objection Certificates (NoCs) are taxable under Service Tax as “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994, rather than being treated as exempt sovereign/statutory functions. The dispute covered two appeal periods: 2007-08 to 2011-12, involving Service Tax demand of Rs. 5,15,53,520 plus interest and penalties, and April 2012 to June 2012, involving Service Tax demand of Rs. 2,06,792 plus interest and penalties; in the later matter, the Commissioner (Appeals) had already upheld the demand while granting cum-tax benefit. STPI argued that it is an autonomous society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, operating under the Department of Electronics and Information Technology, and that SOFTEX certification/NoC issuance were statutory functions under the Foreign Trade Policy, FEMA, and RBI circulars, so they should not be taxed; it relied on Board Circulars No. 89/2006-ST dated 18.12.2006 and No. 96/07/2007-ST dated 23.08.2007, which it claimed exempted statutory-fee activities performed by public authorities. The Department countered that STPI is not a Central Government department, that the charges were collected from STP units as consideration for facilitating their export business, and that the amounts were retained by STPI and used for administrative and establishment expenses rather than being collected as a compulsory statutory levy paid into the Government treasury or a consultation fund.

The Tribunal accepted the Department’s position and emphasized that merely because an activity is regulated by law or an organization is authorized by the Government does not make every such activity a sovereign function. It distinguished between truly sovereign acts that only the State can perform and services provided by an autonomous body to support business operations; it found that SOFTEX certification, NoCs, and related assistance are directly connected with software exporters’ business, foreign exchange realization, and regulatory compliance. On that basis, the Tribunal concluded STPI was providing business facilitation/support to STP units and that the resulting charges were taxable as Business Support Service. Practically, the ruling means STPI’s SOFTEX certification and NoC charges for the relevant periods remain liable to Service Tax, along with the associated interest and penalties, and the earlier cum-tax relief in the 2012 period did not alter the underlying taxability finding.

After adjudication, the Commissioner confirmed the demand only for the normal period and dropped the extended-period demand. Thereafter, the respondent opted for settlement under the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme, 2019. Its declaration was accepted, the amount determined was paid and Form SVLDRS-4 dated 10.02.2020 was issued as a discharge certificate for full and final settlement. The Tribunal held that the legal effect of such certificate, particularly under Section 129 of the Finance Act, 2019, was to bring finality to the matter and period covered by the declaration. It relied upon Astute Valuers and Consultants Pvt. Ltd. Vs Union of India (Bombay High Court), where continuation of proceedings after issuance of a discharge certificate was held inconsistent with the object and statutory finality of the Scheme. The Tribunal also independently examined limitation. The Show Cause Notice dated 21.12.2018 was the fifth n
rows.summary:
The Revenue appealed an Order-in-Original dated 18.12.2019 that had confirmed service tax only for the normal limitation period and had dropped the demand for the extended period. The underlying dispute arose from Show Cause Notice No. 20/2018-19 dated 21.12.2018, issued to Big C Mobiles Pvt. Ltd., which sells mobile phones through retail outlets in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, alleging non-payment of service tax on insurance coverage charges collected from customers during the period 2013-14 through June 2018. The Commissioner ultimately confirmed service tax of Rs. 1,43,75,615/- only for the normal period and granted consequential relief by rejecting the extended-period allegation.

After that adjudication, the taxpayer opted into the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme, 2019 (SVLDRS). Its declaration was accepted, the determined amount was paid, and Form SVLDRS-4 was issued on 10.02.2020 as a discharge certificate signifying full and final settlement. The CESTAT held that once a discharge certificate is issued under Section 127 of the Finance Act, 2019, Section 129 gives finality to the dispute for the period covered by the declaration, so the Department cannot continue pursuing an appeal on the same dispute; the Tribunal relied on Astute Valuers and Consultants Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India for that proposition. Independently, the Tribunal also agreed with the Commissioner on limitation: this was the fifth show-cause notice on substantially the same issue, earlier notices had already been adjudicated, and the Department therefore already knew the relevant facts about the company’s accounting method, collection of insurance charges, and service-tax treatment. Because those facts were already within the Department’s knowledge, the Tribunal applied the Supreme Court’s ruling in Nizam Sugar Factory to hold that suppression could not be alleged again to invoke the extended period. On both grounds—the SVLDRS discharge certificate and the merits of the limitation finding—the Revenue’s appeal was dismissed.

rows.summary: The Patna High Court granted regular bail to Jaswant Singh @ Rolly Babu in Complaint Case No. 49 of 2026, arising from allegations under Section 132(1)(a), (b), (c) and (d) of the CGST Act, 2017. The prosecution alleged a GST evasion scheme involving issuance of tax invoices without actual movement or supply of goods, fraudulent availment of input tax credit without receipt of goods or services and without corresponding e-way bills, falsification of accounts and financial records, and operation of shell entities by controlling GST credentials, banking operations, passwords, and compliance activities; the alleged revenue implication was approximately ₹73.75 crore. The petitioner denied wrongdoing and challenged the arrest as lacking the required “reason to believe” under Section 69 of the CGST Act, arguing that the arrest memo and authorization did not disclose the monetary threshold or the basis for arrest, that the evidence largely consisted of statements of proprietors/co-accused without cross-examination, and that no incriminating material was found at his residence; he also pointed out that filing work had been handled by his accountant and that investigation of the relevant IP address would be needed before attributing electronic filings to him. He relied on Supreme Court authorities such as Arnesh Kumar and Satender Kumar Antil to argue that arrest and continued detention must be justified by necessity and proper judicial scrutiny, and noted that the investigation was complete, the charge sheet had been filed, there was no risk of tampering with evidence, and he had been in judicial custody since 26.05.2026. The Union of India opposed bail, emphasizing that this was an economic offence requiring strict treatment and arguing that under Section 132, where wrongly availed/utilised input tax credit or refund exceeds ₹5 crore, the punishment may extend to five years. The Court ultimately leaned in favor of bail and ordered release upon furnishing a bail bond of ₹10,000 with two sureties of the like amount each to the satisfaction of the Special Judge, Economic Offence, Patna/concerned court; the order is limited to pre-trial release and does not decide the merits of the alleged fake invoicing, ITC fraud, record falsification, or shell-entity allegations.

rows.summary:
This Calcutta High Court decision concerns GST adjudication and appeal proceedings under Section 107 of the West Bengal GST Act and the Central GST Act, 2017. The petitioner challenged an adjudication order dated 28.07.2024 and an appellate order dated 29.05.2025, after the appeal was rejected solely as time-barred. The underlying dispute began with a show cause notice in Form GST DRC-01 No. ZD190524017416E dated 12.05.2024, proposing tax, interest, and penalty; the petitioner argued that the notice was uploaded only in the GST portal’s “Additional Notice and Orders” tab and no separate intimation was sent, so it was never seen in time and no reply could be filed. The court accepted that this portal-only upload, without separate notice, prevented a response and amounted to a violation of natural justice, and it noted that the appellate authority had not examined the merits at all, but had dismissed the appeal only on limitation.

As a result, the High Court quashed both the appellate order dated 29.05.2025 and the adjudication order dated 28.07.2024, and also set aside the consequential bank attachment. The matter was sent back to respondent no. 1 to reconsider the case on the merits of the grounds raised in the appeal, give the petitioner an opportunity of hearing, and pass a fresh reasoned adjudication order in accordance with law within 12 weeks. The court further directed that the decision be communicated to the petitioner within one week after the fresh order is passed. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that GST notices placed only in the portal’s “Additional Notice and Orders” section, without effective intimation, may be vulnerable to challenge on natural justice grounds, especially where the taxpayer is deprived of any chance to respond before adjudication.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Unsigned GST Show Cause Notice & Order Invalid: Rajasthan High Court
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12580 Case Name Mayur Timber Vs State of Rajasthan & Ors. (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court allowed the writ petition filed by M/s Mayur Timber challenging the show-cause notice dated 13.06.2024 and consequential order dated 15.10.2024 passed under Section 74 of the CGST Act, 2017, whereby GST demand of Rs.3,13,894, interest of Rs.4,26,002 and penalty of Rs.3,13,894 had been confirmed on the allegation of ITC availment without actual receipt of goods. The Court found that the show-cause notice, reminder and adjudication order bore neither digital nor physical signatures. Examining Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules, 2017, the Court held that electronic issuance and authentication are distinct and cumulative requirements and that mere generation of a document on the GST portal or allotment of a reference number cannot substitute authentication by signature. A signature authenticates the document, fixes accountability on the issuing officer and safeguards against arbitrariness by evidencing application of mind. Consequently, an unsigned show-cause notice or order is no notice or order in the eyes of law, and the defect is not a curable irregularity but goes to the root of the authority to proceed. The Court further noted that the documents had been uploaded only under “Additional Notices and Orders”, the petitioner learnt about the demand only upon bank recovery proceedings, and no effective personal hearing had been afforded contrary to Section 75(4). The plea of alternative remedy was therefore rejected. The show-cause notice, consequential order dated 15.10.2024
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST show-cause notice and adjudication order issued under Section 74 of the CGST Act, 2017 are invalid if they are not authenticated by signature. In this case, M/s Mayur Timber challenged a show-cause notice dated 13.06.2024 and the consequential order dated 15.10.2024 confirming GST demand of Rs. 3,13,894, interest of Rs. 4,26,002, and penalty of Rs. 3,13,894, all based on the allegation that the taxpayer had wrongly availed ITC of Rs. 3,13,894 without actual receipt of goods. The Court found that the show-cause notice, reminder, and order bore neither digital nor physical signatures; under Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules, electronic issuance and authentication are separate and cumulative requirements, so mere upload on the GST portal or allotment of a reference number does not amount to lawful authentication. Because a signature is what shows the issuing officer applied mind and takes responsibility for the document, the Court treated an unsigned notice or order as no notice or order in law, not a curable technical defect.

The Court also noted serious service and hearing defects: the order was uploaded only under “Additional Notices and Orders,” not the normal “Notices and Orders” section; it was never manually served; and the taxpayer first learned of it only when its bank informed it on 21.08.2025 that recovery had been initiated. The department had issued FORM GST DRC-13 on 20.08.2025 under Section 79(1)(c) to Kotak Mahindra Bank, directing recovery of Rs. 9,00,820 from the taxpayer’s account, and the bank account was provisionally attached before being released after the taxpayer filed an affidavit dated 22.08.2025. The Court further held that no effective personal hearing had been granted, contrary to Section 75(4), so the alternative-remedy objection was rejected. As a result, the Court set aside the show-cause notice dated 13.06.2024, the order dated 15.10.2024, and the recovery notice in FORM GST DRC-13 dated 20.08.2025, but it expressly allowed the department to start again with a duly authenticated show-cause notice and by giving an effective opportunity of hearing; the merits of the alleged tax demand were left open.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Penalty Not Automatic for Delayed Foreign Travel Tax Payment: SC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12577 Case Name Saudi Arabian Airlines Vs Union of India & Ors. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Saudi Arabian Airlines Vs Union of India & Ors. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by M/s. Saudi Arabian Airlines and set aside the penalty imposed for delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT), holding that delayed payment of FTT cannot be equated with failure or non-payment of tax for the purposes of Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979. The Court held that while Section 38(3) deals with non-payment of FTT, delayed deposit falls within Section 38(4) read with the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979. It further held that imposition of penalty under Section 38 is not automatic merely because a statutory timeline has been breached. The dispute arose from six instances of delayed deposit of FTT collected by the appellant airline. In five instances, the delay ranged from one day to eleven days, though the demand drafts had been purchased before the respective due dates. The appellant explained that the drafts could not be deposited because of security restrictions. In the sixth instance, involving December 1995, there was a delay of 63 days, which was attributed to the concerned employee being on emergency leave. The initial adjudication order had imposed a penalty of Rs.12,000 for the six cases of late payment, but after remand the penalty was enhanced drastically to Rs.71,29,140. Examining Section 38(3), the Supreme Court emphasised the expressions “fails to pay the foreign travel tax” and “the amount of the tax not so paid”. The Court held that “failure to pay” means non-payment and cannot be equated with delay in making payment.
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT) by a carrier is **not the same as non-payment or failure to pay tax** for purposes of **Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979**. In this case, Saudi Arabian Airlines had six delayed remittances of collected FTT: in five instances the delay was only **1 to 11 days** and the demand drafts had been purchased before the due dates but could not be deposited because of security restrictions; in the sixth instance, relating to **December 1995**, the delay was **63 days** because the relevant employee was on emergency leave. An initial penalty of **Rs. 12,000** was later drastically enhanced after remand to **Rs. 71,29,140**, but the Supreme Court set aside the penalty and allowed the airline’s appeal.

The Court interpreted the statutory language in Section 38(3) — “**fails to pay the foreign travel tax**” and “**the amount of the tax not so paid**” — to mean **actual non-payment**, not mere late payment. It held that if Parliament intended delayed payment to be covered by Section 38(3), it would have used express language to that effect, and courts cannot expand fiscal penalty provisions by implication. Instead, the Court said delayed deposit falls within **Section 38(4)** read with the **Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979**, which specifically address delayed compliance and allow flexibility.

Under **Rule 4**, collected FTT had to be deposited **within 30 days from the end of the month**, but the **Collector of Customs** could extend that period on **sufficient cause** and having regard to the carrier’s accounting system. **Rule 9** similarly required monthly returns within the prescribed time but also allowed extension. The Court emphasized that this framework shows the deadlines are **not inflexible**; where delay is explained and condoned under the rules, the situation is not one of punishable non-payment. The Court further stated that payment made **before a show-cause notice is issued** is to be treated as **delayed payment**, not failure to pay.

On penalty, the Court relied on **Rule 12**, which requires a **written show-cause notice**, an opportunity to make a **representation**, and a **reasonable opportunity of hearing** before any penalty can be imposed. That procedural structure means the authority must exercise **discretion**; penalty is **not automatic** merely because a deadline was missed. The Court distinguished between cases where mens rea is not required and cases where penalty still remains discretionary, and it reaffirmed the principle from **Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa** that penalty for breach of a statutory obligation depends on the facts and surrounding circumstances. The decision therefore protects carriers and other entities subject to the FTT regime from automatic penalty exposure for late deposit where the tax was in fact collected and the delay is explainable or otherwise dealt with under the rules.

Ltd. v. DCIT, where PMS fees were allowed as a deduction while computing capital gains. The assessee also submitted that although the Revenue had challenged KRA Holding and Trading before the Bombay High Court, th
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that Portfolio Management Service (PMS) fees are deductible while computing capital gains under section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, at least on the facts of this case, where the assessee had paid **Rs. 8,42,360** to **Trust Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd.** for PMS. The assessee, **Ameeta Jagdish Thackersey**, had returned **total income of Rs. 72,26,297** for **Assessment Year 2011-12**, comprising salary, short-term capital gains, and income from other sources; the Assessing Officer disallowed the PMS charges in a **section 143(3)** assessment on the ground that they were not expenditure incurred “wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer” of capital assets under section 48. The **CIT(A) order dated 28.08.2025** upheld that disallowance, relying mainly on **ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah**, where the Mumbai Bench had held PMS fees and performance-linked charges not deductible under section 48.

On appeal, the assessee argued that the law was unsettled because different ITAT Benches had taken different views, citing **KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT** (Pune ITAT), **Zarah Rafik Malik v. ITO** (Mumbai ITAT), and **ACIT v. Vireet Investment Pvt. Ltd.** (Delhi ITAT), all of which had accepted deduction of PMS-related expenses in the circumstances before them. The assessee also pointed out that although the Revenue had challenged **KRA Holding** before the Bombay High Court, the substantial question there concerned whether the income was taxable as **capital gains** or **business income**; it did **not** specifically raise the deductibility of PMS charges under section 48. The Revenue maintained that PMS charges were composite advisory/management/consultancy fees and not directly linked to the acquisition or transfer of any particular security, so they should not qualify under section 48.

The Tribunal noted the existence of divergent coordinate Bench rulings and found no binding judgment of either the **Bombay High Court** or the **Supreme Court** squarely holding that PMS charges are not deductible under section 48. Applying the Supreme Court’s rule in **CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd. (88 ITR 192)**—that where two reasonable interpretations of a taxing provision exist, the interpretation favorable to the assessee should be adopted—the Tribunal chose the assessee-favouring view. It therefore **allowed the deduction of Rs. 8,42,360 as PMS charges** in computing capital gains, **set aside the revenue authorities’ orders on this issue, and directed the Assessing Officer to allow the claim**. The appeal was consequently allowed.

Ltd. challenging an assessment order dated 15.10.2018 to the extent it disallowed refund of input tax credit lying in the Electronic Credit Ledger under the head SGST credit. rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court dismissed AVT McCormick Ingredients Pvt. Ltd.’s writ challenge to an assessment order dated 15.10.2018 that had disallowed its GST refund claim to the extent of SGST input tax credit lying in the Electronic Credit Ledger. The company, an exporter of spice extracts and oleoresins, had earlier been registered under the Kerala VAT regime and had filed Form GST TRAN-1 in November 2017 to transition excess pre-GST input tax credit into the GST Electronic Credit Ledger; it claimed that this transitional credit was reflected in the ledger on 27.12.2017 and used that balance to support a refund claim for November 2017. The Department rejected the refund on the ground that transitional credit is not “Net ITC” for purposes of Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017, as clarified by Circular No. 37/11/2018-GST dated 15.03.2018, and therefore could not be included in the refund computation.

On the legal position, the Court accepted that Section 140 of the CGST Act and Rule 117 of the CGST Rules permit eligible closing credit under the pre-GST regime as on 30.06.2017 to be carried forward into the Electronic Credit Ledger on 01.07.2017, so that unutilised ITC under the earlier regime could form the opening balance under GST. However, the petitioner failed on proof: it did not produce a copy of the TRAN-1 declaration filed within the prescribed period and did not produce satisfactory evidence showing the credit standing in its Electronic Credit Ledger as on 01.07.2017. The Court held that refund could be allowed only if the claimant proves that the amount claimed was actually credited in the ledger as of 01.07.2017, and in the absence of such material, there was no basis to interfere with the adjudication order.

The Court also rejected the writ petition on maintainability grounds because the company had not exhausted statutory remedies and had approached the High Court only after the limitation period for appeal had expired. It noted that Sections 107 and 108 of the CGST Act provide appeal and revision mechanisms against adjudication orders, and that a taxpayer cannot let the statutory appeal period lapse and then use that lapse as a basis to invoke Article 226. The Court relied on Supreme Court authority, including A.V. Venkateswaran, Rikhab Chand Jain, and Glaxo Smith Kline Consumer Health Care, to emphasize that writ jurisdiction must be exercised promptly and consistently with the legislative scheme; it also noted that the petitioner’s reliance on Moriroku UT India was undermined because that High Court decision had been set aside by the Supreme Court. In practical compliance terms, the decision underscores that refund claims based on transitional credit must be supported by timely filed TRAN-1 documentation and evidence of the exact ledger position as on 01.07.2017, and that missed statutory appeal deadlines are unlikely to be cured by later filing a writ petition.

Vs Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Vs Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The CESTAT Hyderabad partly allowed the appeal of Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd. against an Order-in-Original confirming service tax of Rs.1,63,15,458/- with interest under “Club or Association Service”, besides penalties under Sections 76, 77 and 78 of the Finance Act, 1994 and smaller demands under Mandap Keeper Service, Internet Café Service, Rent-a-Cab Scheme Operator Service and Renting of Immovable Property Service. The appellant operated Lahari Resorts and had introduced a Time Share Holiday Scheme under which customers acquired a contractual right to occupy specified accommodation for one week every year for 12 years against predetermined consideration. The Tribunal examined whether persons enrolled under the Time Share Scheme could be regarded as “members” of a club or association merely because the agreement used that terminology. It held that taxability must depend upon the real legal and commercial character of the arrangement rather than nomenclature. The customers acquired no proprietary, voting, management or shareholding rights in the appellant company. Their relationship with the appellant remained that of customer and service provider, and they merely purchased accommodation rights for specified periods. The Tribunal also noted that the appellant was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and that the time-share customers did not become members of the company in accordance with that Act. They neither subscribed to the memorandum, became shareholders, nor had the
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd.’s time-share holiday scheme was **not taxable as “Club or Association Service”** under the Finance Act, 1994, because the customers were not actually members of a club or association in the legal sense. The company operated Lahari Resorts and offered customers a contractual right to occupy specified accommodation for **one week every year for 12 years** in exchange for predetermined consideration; although the agreement used “member”-type language, the Tribunal said taxability depends on the **real legal and commercial substance**, not labels.

The Tribunal emphasized that the time-share customers had **no proprietary, voting, management, or shareholding rights** in the company and did not become members of the company under the Companies Act, 1956. They did not subscribe to the memorandum, become shareholders, or have their names entered in the register of members, so the legal basis for treating them as “members” of a club/association was absent. The relationship was therefore one of **customer and service provider**, not members of a mutual club or association, and the dominant object of the scheme was **accommodation**, not club privileges, sports, recreation, or similar facilities.

A significant point in the decision was the Tribunal’s reliance on the later introduction of **“Short Term Accommodation Service” under Section 65(105)(zzzzw)** of the Finance Act, 1994, effective **1 May 2011**. The Tribunal viewed this as supporting the conclusion that hotel/resort accommodation was not meant to be taxed earlier under the “Club or Association Service” head merely because it involved a membership-style arrangement. It also relied on the Supreme Court’s reasoning in **State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club Ltd.** and on prior hospitality-sector cases such as **Bharat Hotels Ltd.** and **Adarsh Realty & Hotel Pvt. Ltd.**, which treated similar membership/loyalty arrangements as commercial hospitality transactions rather than club services.

On the tax demand side, the original order had confirmed **service tax of Rs. 1,63,15,458/-** along with interest under “Club or Association Service,” plus smaller demands under **Mandap Keeper Service, Internet Café Service, Rent-a-Cab Scheme Operator Service, and Renting of Immovable Property Service**, and penalties under **Sections 76, 77, and 78** of the Finance Act, 1994. The Tribunal set aside the entire **Club or Association Service** demand, but upheld the view that the smaller category-wise liabilities had already been **voluntarily paid in full along with applicable interest before the show-cause notice was issued**. Because the Department did not dispute the payment or quantum, and there was no evidence of fraud, wilful suppression, or clandestine conduct, the Tribunal held the appellant was entitled to the protection of **Section 73(3)**, and therefore the penalties under Sections 76, 77, and 78 were not sustainable. The Tribunal also noted that the appellant had maintained regular books, the time-share receipts were disclosed in audited financial statements, and the Department’s case was built on the appellant’s own records, showing that the dispute was about **classification and interpretation**, not concealment.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Customs Cannot Indefinitely Detain Imported Car Without Seizure Order: Gujarat HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12569 Case Name Pranavbhai Ambalal Patel Vs Additional Director General (Gujarat High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Gujarat High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pranavbhai Ambalal Patel Vs Additional Director General (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court allowed a writ petition challenging the prolonged detention and subsequent seizure of a Toyota Land Cruiser imported from Japan. The petitioner purchased the vehicle for USD 54,000, filed Bill of Entry No.7472252 dated 26.12.2024 and paid customs duty of Rs.99,78,795. Out-of-charge was granted on 02.01.2025. On 07.02.2025, however, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the petitioner’s residence, prepared a Panchnama and directed him not to deal with or part with the vehicle. No contemporaneous seizure order under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 was passed. During pendency of the writ petition, the DRI ultimately issued a seizure memo only on 17.04.2026, more than one year after the original detention, followed by a show-cause notice dated 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4). The Department also passed a provisional release order on 18.05.2026 requiring a bond for Rs.85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs.1.20 crore by relying upon paragraph 2 of Circular No.35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017. The High Court noted that the relied-upon part of the Circular had already been struck down by the Delhi High Court in Shanus Impex Vs Union of India & Ors. to the extent it curtailed the adjudicating authority’s discretion. The Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated the Department’s continued reliance upon that paragraph. The Court rejected the Department’s attempt to attribute the delay in initiating Section 110 proceedings
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court held that customs authorities cannot keep imported goods—here, a Toyota Land Cruiser imported from Japan—under indefinite “detention” through a Panchnama and then much later issue a seizure memo under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 in an attempt to restart the limitation clock for notice and confiscation proceedings. In this case, the importer filed Bill of Entry No. 7472252 dated 26.12.2024 and paid customs duty of Rs. 99,78,795; out-of-charge was granted on 02.01.2025. The DRI searched the importer’s residence on 07.02.2025, recorded a Panchnama, and directed him not to deal with or part with the vehicle, but did not contemporaneously pass a seizure order; only on 17.04.2026 did it issue a seizure memo, followed by a show-cause notice on 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4).

The Court emphasized the legal distinction between detention and seizure: a Panchnama restraining the owner from dealing with the goods is not, by itself, a valid Section 110 seizure, and if seizure is intended the proper officer must record “reasons to believe” that the goods are liable to confiscation. The Court relied on Supreme Court authority in Union of India v. Jatin Ahuja, reiterating that where goods are seized under Section 110(1), notice under Section 124(a) must be issued within six months, extendable by another six months under Section 110(2), and absent timely notice the goods must be released. It also relied on Worldline Tradex Pvt. Ltd. and Instruction No. 01/2017-Cus. dated 08.02.2017, which require an actual seizure memo/order in addition to the Panchnama and require that, where immediate seizure is impracticable, an appropriate statutory order restricting dealings be served and the investigation fast-tracked.

The Court rejected the Department’s argument that pendency of the writ petition prevented it from initiating proper Section 110 action, noting that the record showed no court order restraining investigation; instead, the Court had repeatedly directed completion of the investigation. It treated the Department’s claim as a bald assertion and found that the delay was attributable to the Department’s own inaction. Critically, the Court held that customs cannot hold goods indefinitely and then issue a Section 110(1) seizure later merely to reset the six-month period under Section 110(2); time ran from the actual detention under the 07.02.2025 Panchnama, so the 17.04.2026 seizure memo could not validate the later notice.

The Court also set aside the provisional release order dated 18.05.2026 because it required a bond of Rs. 85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs. 1.20 crore based on paragraph 2 of Circular No. 35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017, which the Delhi High Court had already struck down in Shanus Impex to the extent it curtailed the adjudicating authority’s discretion. The Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated continued departmental reliance on that paragraph and held the provisional release conditions unlawful. In practical compliance terms, the decision warns customs officers that if imported goods are to be restrained or seized, the statutory seizure process must be followed promptly and cannot be backfilled later to extend limitation periods; for importers, it strengthens the position that prolonged detention without a valid seizure order is challengeable and that release conditions must have a lawful statutory basis.

(CESTAT Kolkata) Summary: CESTAT Kolkata allowed the appeal filed by Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. and set aside the demand for reversal of CENVAT credit of Rs.83,839. The appellant had availed credit on the basis of three invoices, two issued in 2011 and one dated 22.01.2014. The Department sought reversal on the ground that the appellant had purchased the goods through M/s Ashis Enterprise, which did not possess dealer registration. The appellant contended that the invoices issued by M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal specifically showed Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. as the consignee, while Ashis Enterprise was shown as the buyer. The goods were directly dispatched to the appellant and were duly accounted for in RG 23A Part I. Ashis Enterprise separately issued a commercial invoice to facilitate payment, which could be correlated with the invoice issued by Roshanlal Bhagirathmal. On examining the invoices, the Tribunal found that the appellant was expressly shown as the consignee and that all particulars required for an invoice under Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 were fulfilled. The Tribunal further noted that there was no allegation that the goods had not actually been received by the appellant. The goods had also been accounted for in RG 23A Part I after receipt at the appellant’s factory. In these circumstances, the Tribunal held that the Revenue had failed to establish any contravention of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The demand was accordingly set as
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Kolkata held that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely because the assessee purchased goods through another party if the underlying manufacturer’s invoice correctly names the assessee as consignee and the goods were actually received. In this case, Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. had taken credit of Rs. 83,839 based on three invoices, two dated in 2011 and one dated 22.01.2014; the Department had proposed reversal on the theory that the purchases were routed through M/s Ashis Enterprise, which was not a registered dealer. The Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position that M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal’s invoices expressly showed Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. as consignee, while Ashis Enterprise appeared only as buyer for payment/commercial invoicing purposes, and that the goods were directly dispatched to the assessee.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Tribunal treated the invoice documentation as sufficient under Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 because the required particulars were present, the goods were actually received, and the receipts were duly recorded in RG 23A Part I after arrival at the factory. The Revenue had not alleged, and did not prove, that the goods were not received by the assessee. On that basis, the Tribunal found no contravention of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and set aside the demand for reversal of credit. The practical takeaway for manufacturers is that credit is supportable when the manufacturer’s invoice properly identifies the assessee as consignee and receipt/accounting records corroborate actual receipt, even if another intermediary is involved in the commercial chain; however, the documentation must be internally consistent and capable of correlation.

rows.summary:
The document concerns a CESTAT Hyderabad decision in **ECI BJCL JV v. Commissioner of Central Excise and Service Tax** involving a service tax dispute on **EPC/works contract activities** carried out for the **Government of Andhra Pradesh** for the period **June 2007 to March 2012**. A **show-cause notice dated 23.10.2012** demanded **service tax of Rs. 43,86,471** under **Works Contract Service**, and the adjudicating authority confirmed the demand on **09.01.2014**. When the assessee appealed and sought waiver of pre-deposit, the Commissioner (Appeals) heard the stay application on **12.06.2014**, refused an adjournment request, and by order dated **13.06.2014** directed the appellant to deposit **50% of the adjudged service tax demand** as a condition for pursuing the appeal.

The appellant did **not comply** with the pre-deposit direction. Instead, it asked for a speaking order taking into account its legal submissions and cited precedents, but the appeal was nevertheless **dismissed on 23.07.2014** for non-compliance with the deposit requirement. Before the Tribunal, the appellant argued that dismissal without a merits decision was improper and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had not adequately considered **prima facie case, balance of convenience, or financial hardship**, relying on several case authorities. The Tribunal, however, **upheld the dismissal**, holding in substance that failure to comply with the mandated pre-deposit justified dismissal of the service tax appeal. For compliance purposes, the key point is that an assessee challenging a service tax demand must strictly satisfy any ordered pre-deposit condition—in this case **50% of Rs. 43,86,471**—or risk dismissal of the appeal without merits review.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vodafone Idea Limited Vs ACIT (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court allowed the connected writ petitions filed by Vodafone Idea Limited, seeking release of pending TDS refunds with applicable interest for Assessment Years 2003-04, 2008-09 to 2013-14. The petitions stated that the refunds had remained unpaid for about two years even after orders of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and subsequent orders passed by the Assessing Officer giving effect to those appellate decisions. For AY 2012-13, the Tribunal’s order dated 05.06.2024 was followed by an appeal-effect order dated 30.10.2024, with refund quantified by the assessee at Rs.11,06,37,172; the Form 26B applications dated 25.04.2025 were rejected. For AY 2013-14, the Tribunal’s order dated 30.04.2024 was followed by an appeal-effect order dated 14.10.2024, with refund quantified at Rs.7,57,50,048; the Form 26B application dated 01.02.2025 was rejected. For AYs 2003-04 and 2008-09 to 2011-12, the relevant Tribunal orders were dated 26.11.2024 and 03.02.2025, followed by an appeal-effect order dated 15.05.2026, with refund quantified at Rs.34,45,69,250. The total amount found payable by the Assessing Officer was Rs.53,09,56,470. The petitioner argued that Section 200A, Section 201, Rule 31A and Form 26B address the processing of TDS statements and refunds arising from excess or incorrect deduction/deposit. According to the petitioner, they do not govern a refund that crystallises after an assessment under Section 201 or after an appellate order. The respondents relied on departmental practice and the Standard Operating Pr
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court held that Vodafone Idea Limited was entitled to immediate release of pending TDS refunds for Assessment Years 2003-04, 2008-09 to 2013-14, together with applicable interest, because the refunds had already crystallized through appellate proceedings and appeal-effect orders but had remained unpaid for roughly two years. The Court accepted the company’s position that the procedural requirements in Section 200A, Section 201, Rule 31A, and Form 26B govern processing of TDS statements and refunds arising from excess/incorrect deduction or deposit, but do not control a refund that becomes due only after an assessment under Section 201 or after an appellate order giving effect to that decision.

On the facts, for AY 2012-13, the ITAT order dated 05.06.2024 was followed by an appeal-effect order dated 30.10.2024, and the assessee quantified the refund at Rs.11,06,37,172; the Form 26B application dated 25.04.2025 was rejected. For AY 2013-14, the ITAT order dated 30.04.2024 was followed by an appeal-effect order dated 14.10.2024, and the refund was quantified at Rs.7,57,50,048; the Form 26B application dated 01.02.2025 was also rejected. For AYs 2003-04 and 2008-09 to 2011-12, the relevant ITAT orders were dated 26.11.2024 and 03.02.2025, followed by an appeal-effect order dated 15.05.2026, and the refund was quantified at Rs.34,45,69,250. The Assessing Officer’s total amount found payable across all years was Rs.53,09,56,470.

The practical compliance takeaway is that the tax department cannot withhold a refund that has already become payable pursuant to final appellate/appeal-effect orders merely because the taxpayer has not secured or obtained Form 26B processing; the Court directed release of the pending refund amount with interest as applicable. This ruling is relevant to entities facing TDS-related refund delays after Section 201 proceedings or appellate relief, because it confirms that a post-assessment/post-appeal refund is not necessarily dependent on the standard TDS statement correction workflow.
