rows.summary:
The Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, has notified the **Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2026** by **S.O. 4870(E) dated 2 September 2026**, issued under **clauses (aa) and (ab) of section 46(2) of FEMA, 1999**. The amendment is effective **from the date of publication in the Official Gazette** and further amends the **Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019**.

The substantive change is the insertion of **serial number 15.2.5 in Schedule I** of the 2019 rules. This new entry expressly permits an **e-commerce entity** to operate an **inventory-based model of e-commerce** **only for exporting goods or products manufactured or produced in India**, and only in a manner consistent with the **Foreign Trade Policy 2023**, the **Handbook of Procedures (HBP)**, and the **Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods & Services) Regulations, 2015**. In other words, the amendment creates a specific export-only carveout for inventory-based e-commerce, rather than a general relaxation for domestic or broader cross-border inventory models.

The notification also states that the usual restrictions on **Business-to-Consumer (B2C) transactions** and on the **inventory-based model of e-commerce** contained in **serial numbers 15.2.1 to 15.2.4** will **not apply** when the goods or products are exported through e-commerce under this new permitted provision. For compliance purposes, this means entities involved in e-commerce exports of Indian-made products should assess whether their model falls within the new Schedule I entry and ensure their export operations continue to comply with the FTP 2023, HBP, and FEMA export regulations, since the exemption is limited to that specific export context.

The notification also notes that the principal NDI Rules were originally published on **17 October 2019** and have been amended through the listed notifications up to **S.O. 3030(E) dated 12 June 2026**. No numeric thresholds, monetary limits, or filing deadlines are introduced in the text provided beyond the effective date tied to Gazette publication.

rows.title: Corporate Law | ECLGS 5.0: ₹2.55 Lakh Crore Credit Support for MSMEs, Non-MSMEs and Airlines
rows.desc: Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Summary: The Press Information Bureau (PIB) Backgrounder on Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) 5.0, posted on 5 September 2026, explains the Government-backed credit support available to businesses affected by external disruptions. The scheme, approved on 5 May 2026 and implemented by the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC), aims to facilitate additional credit flow of up to ₹2.55 lakh crore through Member Lending Institutions. ECLGS 5.0 covers MSMEs, eligible non-MSME business borrowers and scheduled passenger airline companies. Eligible MSMEs receive 100% guarantee coverage, while eligible non-MSMEs and scheduled passenger airlines receive 90% coverage. For MSMEs and eligible non-MSMEs, additional credit can generally be provided up to 20% of peak fund-based working capital outstanding during Q4 FY 2025–26, subject to a ceiling of ₹100 crore per borrower. Airlines can receive additional credit up to 100%, subject to a ceiling of ₹1,500 crore per borrower and specified equity conditions for amounts exceeding ₹1,000 crore. The scheme is operational until 31 March 2027 or until guarantees of ₹2.55 lakh crore are issued, whichever is earlier. Loans to MSMEs and eligible non-MSMEs have a five-year tenure including a one-year moratorium, while airline loans have a seven-year tenure including a two-year moratorium. The PIB Backgrounder on Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) 5.0, posted on 5 September 2026 and approved on 5 May 2026, sets out a government-backed credit support program designed to provide additional lending to businesses affected by external disruptions. It is implemented by the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC) through Member Lending Institutions and is intended to facilitate up to ₹2.55 lakh crore of additional credit flow. The scheme applies to MSMEs, eligible non-MSME business borrowers, and scheduled passenger airline companies, so compliance teams at banks and lending institutions need to identify borrowers in those categories and apply the scheme-specific eligibility and guarantee rules.

For MSMEs, the scheme provides 100% guarantee coverage and allows additional credit generally up to 20% of the borrower’s peak fund-based working capital outstanding in Q4 FY 2025–26, subject to a cap of ₹100 crore per borrower. For eligible non-MSMEs, the same general credit limit and cap apply—up to 20% of peak fund-based working capital outstanding in Q4 FY 2025–26, capped at ₹100 crore per borrower—but with only 90% guarantee coverage. Scheduled passenger airlines also receive 90% guarantee coverage, but their credit terms are different: they may receive additional credit up to 100% subject to a ceiling of ₹1,500 crore per borrower, and any amount above ₹1,000 crore must satisfy specified equity conditions.

The scheme is operational until 31 March 2027 or until guarantees totaling ₹2.55 lakh crore are issued, whichever comes first. Repayment terms also differ by borrower type: MSME and eligible non-MSME loans have a five-year tenure including a one-year moratorium, while airline loans have a seven-year tenure including a two-year moratorium. As of 20 August 2026, the Backgrounder states that 6,73,979 guarantees had been issued covering ₹2,50,024 crore, with MSMEs accounting for 97.3% of guarantees by number and 80.79% of the guaranteed amount. The document also notes outreach efforts and that applications/access are available through the Jan Samarth Portal, which is relevant operationally for borrower onboarding and scheme access.

rows.summary:
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of ₹10 lakh on Dial4Trade Technologies Private Limited after finding that the company facilitated the online listing, hosting, advertising, and sale of ammonium nitrate without the mandatory safeguards required for a regulated explosive substance. The CCPA also ordered Dial4Trade to immediately stop listing, hosting, advertising, or otherwise facilitating the sale of ammonium nitrate, as well as any other substance classified as an explosive under the Explosives Act, 1884.

The enforcement action was based on the Authority’s finding that Dial4Trade’s platform did not properly disclose the seller’s valid PESO licence details, did not verify the buyer’s identity or licensed status, did not provide transaction-traceability mechanisms required under the Ammonium Nitrate Rules, 2012, and did not warn users about the legal restrictions and penalties associated with unauthorized possession or handling. The listing also used imagery showing explosions and blast effects, which reinforced the CCPA’s view that the item was being presented to the public in a misleading way, as if it were an ordinary consumer product rather than a controlled hazardous substance.

The CCPA held that a product listing available to the public over the internet is an “advertisement” under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and that advertising a regulated explosive without the required disclosures and controls constitutes both a misleading advertisement and an unfair trade practice. It rejected Dial4Trade’s argument that it was merely a B2B marketplace or intermediary and therefore exempt, stating that marketplace e-commerce entities are still subject to the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 and the associated due-diligence obligations. This action is part of a broader sector-wide review of online platforms dealing with hazardous chemicals and explosive substances, so compliance teams in marketplace, e-commerce, and classified-listing businesses should treat the decision as a warning that they must screen regulated goods, verify licenses and buyer eligibility, maintain traceability, and ensure all public listings avoid misleading presentation.

rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court directed the Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Bengaluru-3, to consider and decide the assessee’s application under section 119(2)(b) of the Income-tax Act seeking condonation of delay in filing a revised return for AY 2019-20. The practical issue was that compensation for compulsory acquisition of agricultural land was not actually received until 2025, after a long-running title dispute was resolved by a civil court decree in the assessee’s favour, even though the tax year involved was much earlier. Because the compensation was paid only after the dispute ended, the assessee sought refund of TDS deducted by the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB) and contended that the compensation was exempt under section 96 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.

For compliance purposes, the decision matters to any entity that acquires land compulsorily or pays acquisition compensation, especially where payment is delayed by ownership or title litigation. The court’s direction does not itself decide the taxability or refund entitlement, but it requires the tax authority to examine whether delay relief should be granted so the assessee can pursue a refund claim tied to exempt land-acquisition compensation. The case highlights that when compensation is received years after the relevant assessment year, taxpayers may need to seek condonation under section 119(2)(b) to permit a late/revised filing that aligns the return with the actual year of receipt. The underlying factual trigger was acquisition of 3 acres and 20 guntas in Survey Nos. 87/3 and 87/4 of Kothanur Village, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bengaluru South Taluk, with payment withheld until the title issue was judicially settled.

rows.title: Company Law | Annual ROC Compliance 2026: Beyond AOC-4 and MGT-7
rows.desc: Summary: Annual ROC compliance for FY 2025-26 should be approached as a complete corporate compliance closure exercise rather than merely filing AOC-4 and MGT-7/MGT-7A. The process covers finalisation and audit of financial statements, Board approval, Board’s Report, AGM, annual financial-statement and annual-return filings, auditor-related filings, DPT-3, MSME-1, director KYC, CSR, share capital, charges, related-party transactions and other event-based compliances. The FY 2025-26 cycle is particularly significant because the small-company thresholds were enhanced with effect from 1 December 2025 to ₹10 crore paid-up capital and ₹100 crore turnover, while the director KYC framework moved from annual compliance to a three-year cycle effective 31 March 2026. Companies should therefore reassess MGT-7/MGT-7A applicability, XBRL applicability, MGT-8 requirements and the applicable DIR-3 KYC cycle rather than relying on older checklists. AOC-4 should reconcile with the signed financial statements, while MGT-7/MGT-7A should agree with statutory registers, share capital records and MCA master data. Similar reconciliations should be undertaken for borrowings and DPT-3, MSME dues and MSME-1, related-party transactions, charges, CSR and share capital. The article also highlights the distinction between additional filing fees and statutory penalties, potential director-disqualification consequences, the continuing obligations of companies with no business activity, and the increasing importance of consistency between books, GST returns, Income-tax filings and MCA records. The recommended professional approach is Review → Reconcile → Identify Exceptions → Rectify → Approve → File, ensuring that annual ROC filings are the final output of a broader annual corporate compliance review. rows.summary:
This document says that FY 2025–26 annual ROC compliance should be treated as a full corporate compliance closure exercise, not just the mechanical filing of AOC-4 and MGT-7/MGT-7A. It covers the entire annual cycle: finalizing and auditing financial statements, Board approval, preparation of the Board’s Report, holding the AGM, and then making the annual filing of financial statements and annual return, along with auditor-related filings and event-based compliances such as DPT-3, MSME-1, director KYC, CSR, share capital changes, charges, and related-party transactions. The key practical instruction is that companies should reconcile the information across statutory registers, share capital records, MCA master data, books of account, GST returns, and Income-tax filings before filing, because the article treats ROC filings as the final output of a broader compliance review rather than a standalone form-filing exercise.

A major change highlighted is that the small-company thresholds were increased effective 1 December 2025 to paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore and turnover of ₹100 crore. Companies should therefore re-check whether they qualify as a small company for MGT-7A purposes, and also reassess whether XBRL filing applies and whether MGT-8 certification is required, instead of relying on older threshold checks. Another important change is for director KYC: the framework moves from an annual filing expectation to a three-year cycle effective 31 March 2026, so companies must identify which directors are due for DIR-3 KYC in the relevant cycle rather than treating it as a routine annual item for every director.

The document emphasizes that AOC-4 must match the signed financial statements exactly, and MGT-7/MGT-7A must align with statutory registers, share capital records, and MCA master data. Similar reconciliation is expected for borrowings reported in DPT-3, dues to MSMEs reported in MSME-1, related-party transaction disclosures, charge-related filings, CSR disclosures, and any changes in share capital. It also warns that missing or incorrect filings may lead not only to additional filing fees but also to statutory penalties and, in some cases, director-disqualification consequences.

The article notes that companies with no business activity still have ongoing compliance obligations and do not escape annual ROC responsibilities merely because operations are dormant. It also stresses the need for consistency between corporate records and external filings, particularly between the company’s books, GST returns, Income-tax filings, and MCA records, because discrepancies can create compliance exposure and filing errors. The recommended compliance workflow is explicitly “Review → Reconcile → Identify Exceptions → Rectify → Approve → File,” meaning the filings should only be made after discrepancies have been identified and corrected.

rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court, Circuit Bench at Jalpaiguri, considered a GST writ petition by Umen Chandra Roy challenging denial of Input Tax Credit (ITC) relief under Section 16(5) of the CGST Act, 2017, read with Section 39. The petitioner had filed the relevant return up to November 30, 2021, which the Court noted was within the statutory cut-off contemplated by Section 16(5). He later filed a rectification application on January 12, 2026 seeking the ITC benefit, but the revenue authority rejected it by order dated April 8, 2026.

The rejection was based on the department’s view that the rectification application was not filed within the period prescribed in a departmental circular/notification dated April 8, 2024, read with a circular dated October 15, 2024. The judgment originally referred in paragraph 3 to a period of “six weeks,” but a later correction order dated August 21, 2026 expressly corrected that to “six months” and also corrected the word “communication” to “circular.” In substance, the case turns on whether the rectification period for claiming the Section 16(5) ITC benefit can be extended, because the petitioner argued that Section 16(5) itself does not prescribe a time limit for filing such a rectification application.

The revenue opposed relief by stating that the original order dated March 6, 2024 had been served on the petitioner by post on the same day, and therefore contended that the petitioner was outside the applicable time limit. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this ruling concerns the procedural window for rectification applications tied to Section 16(5) ITC claims and the interaction between the statute and later departmental circular guidance, with the operative period reflected in the record being corrected from six weeks to six months. No broader change to GST rates or general filing deadlines is described in the document; the issue is specifically the timing and maintainability of a rectification request for ITC eligibility under Section 16(5).

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court judgment dated 27.03.2017 concerns the Revenue’s appeals under Section 260A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 against a common ITAT order dated 12.05.2016 for Assessment Years 2007-08 and 2010-11 in the case of M/s. Ennore Cargo Container Terminal P. Ltd. The key substantive tax issue raised is whether the assessee, which operated a Container Freight Station (CFS), was entitled to deduction under Section 80IA(4) as an “infrastructure facility,” especially after the statutory amendment to Section 80IA(4) that introduced an Explanation with effect from 01.04.2002 and omitted the phrase “any other public facility of similar nature.” The Revenue’s position, as framed in its questions of law, was that a CFS should not qualify after that amendment and that the assessee was merely acting as a custodian handling movement and containerized import/export consignments rather than developing an infrastructure facility.

The document also shows that, for Assessment Year 2007-08, the Revenue challenged the Tribunal’s treatment of deemed dividend, indicating that the Tribunal had held such income must be assessed only in the hands of the shareholder/recipient rather than elsewhere. Beyond identifying these issues, the excerpt does not provide the Court’s final holding or operational directions, but it establishes the compliance-relevant controversy: whether CFS operators can claim Section 80IA(4) infrastructure deductions for AY 2007-08 and AY 2010-11 despite the post-01.04.2002 statutory explanation, and how deemed dividend income should be taxed for AY 2007-08. For a compliance team, the document signals that entities running CFS-type operations should closely review whether their activities meet the legal definition of “infrastructure facility” under Section 80IA(4) for the relevant years, and whether their role is that of a developer of infrastructure or merely a custodian/service operator.

The Revenue challenged the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai order dated 8 February 2023, which had dismissed the Revenue’s appeal against the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), Pune order dated 23 March 2022. The assessee was a special purpose vehicle engaged in road construction on Build Operate Transfer (BOT) basis and collection of toll. The Assessing Officer made an addition of Rs.7,47,00,000/- by disallowing the provision for major repairs. The assessee relied upon its BOT agreement with the Government of Maharashtra, under which it had a 30-year concession and was contractually required to undertake major repairs during the concession period. The assessee contended that the liability accrued over the period and that the expenditure could be provided for on the basis of reliable estimates. It also relied upon CBDT Circular No. 9/2014 concerning expenditure incurred for development of roads/highways under BOT agreements. The CIT(Appeals) examined the Concession Agreement, including Articles 17, 37, 38 and 39, and
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court upheld the allowability of a scientifically estimated provision for major repairs made by ECA Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd. under Section 260A of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and dismissed the Revenue’s challenge to the ITAT’s order dated 8 February 2023 and the CIT(A), Pune order dated 23 March 2022. The assessee was an SPV engaged in road construction on a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) basis and toll collection under a 30-year concession agreement with the Government of Maharashtra; the agreement required it to carry out major repairs during the concession period, with the first major repair due after seven years (in the eighth year) and the last one in the 30th year. For Assessment Year 2015-16, the company reported a book loss of Rs. 4,48,91,467 and an income-tax loss of Rs. 8,46,64,672, but the Assessing Officer disallowed a provision for major repairs and made an addition of Rs. 7,47,00,000.

The assessee argued that the repair obligation was contractual, that the liability accrued over time, and that the amount could be provided for using reliable estimates; it also relied on CBDT Circular No. 9/2014 relating to road/highway development expenditure under BOT arrangements. The CIT(A) reviewed the Concession Agreement, including Articles 17, 37, 38, and 39, and accepted the assessee’s case. On further appeal, the High Court agreed that the provision was not a contingent or speculative claim but a deductible liability based on a reasonable, scientifically determined estimate for an obligation arising under the BOT contract. For compliance purposes, the decision confirms that BOT concessionaires in road infrastructure projects may support deductions for major repair provisions where the contractual obligation is clear and the estimate is reliably and scientifically computed, but they should retain the concession agreement, the basis of estimation, and supporting documentation showing how the provision was calculated and how the obligation accrues over the concession period.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12640 Case Name Pankajam Plastics Vs Muthiah Athinarayanan & Ors (GSTAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GSTAT, National Anti-Profiteering Authority Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pankajam Plastics Vs Muthiah Athinarayanan & Ors (GSTAT Chennai) Summary: The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench considered whether Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 filed by Pankajam Plastics was maintainable when the appeal before the First Appellate Authority had not yet resulted in an order. The Appellant/Applicant submitted that it had filed an appeal before the First Appellate Authority in APL-01 and also filed the GSTAT appeal in APL-05 on the same day, 19.03.2026, stating that the Department was undertaking recovery proceedings. The Respondent-State Government drew the Bench’s attention to its submissions dated 28.07.2026 and, particularly, to APL-02, which had been rejected on 24.06.2026 by the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals, being the First Appellate Authority. The Registry raised a defect because the GSTAT appeal had been filed before the rejection order of the First Appellate Authority came into existence. After hearing both sides and examining the records, the Bench found that Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 had been filed on 19.03.2026, whereas no order under Section 112(1) of the CGST Act, 2017 was then in existence because the First Appellate Authority had not yet passed its order. The central question before the Bench was whether an aggrieved person could approach GSTAT under Section 112 of the CGST Act, 2017 in the absence of an order passed under Section 107 or Section 108. The Bench reproduced the substance of Section 112(1), under which an aggrieved person may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against an order passed unde
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench held that an appeal to GSTAT is **not maintainable if it is filed before the First Appellate Authority has actually passed its order under Section 107 of the CGST Act, 2017**. In this matter, Pankajam Plastics filed an appeal in **APL-01** before the First Appellate Authority and also filed the GSTAT appeal in **APL-05** on the same day, **19.03.2026**, apparently because recovery proceedings had begun. The Tribunal noted, however, that the First Appellate Authority’s rejection/order in **APL-02** was only passed later, on **24.06.2026** by the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals, so when the GSTAT filing was made, **no order under Section 112(1) existed yet**.

The key compliance/legal point is that **Section 112 appeal rights arise only after an order is passed under Section 107 or Section 108**; a party cannot pre-emptively move the Appellate Tribunal before the underlying appellate order exists. The Registry had flagged the filing as defective on that basis, and after reviewing the filings and hearing both sides, the Bench agreed that the appeal filed on 19.03.2026 was premature. The decision therefore reinforces that taxpayers and advisors should **wait for the First Appellate Authority’s order before filing GSTAT appeals**, even if departmental recovery action is underway, because recovery concerns do not create a right to bypass the statutory sequencing of appeals.

According to the petitioner, the credit notes were declared through the e-invoice portal and the corresponding outward tax liability was adjusted against sales effected during previous months/financial years. It contended that this reduced its output tax liability but did not result in any short payment of tax because the liability had ultimately been discharged. It also furnished a “NEGATIVE LIABILITY STATEMENT” generated through the common portal for 01/09/2024 to 27/03/2025. The petitioner referred
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court considered a GST recovery dispute involving Best Agrolife Limited and a notice dated 25/03/2025 that required payment of tax and interest within seven days, warning that if payment was not made, recovery proceedings would be started under Section 79 of the Maharashtra GST Act, 2017. Best Agrolife did not pay; instead, it replied by email on 11/04/2025 saying it had issued credit notes under Section 34 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with Rule 53 of the CGST Rules, 2017 for returned goods and rate differences, had declared those credit notes through the e-invoice portal, and had adjusted the corresponding outward tax liability against sales from earlier months/financial years. It argued that this meant there was no actual short payment because the output tax liability had ultimately been discharged, and it supported this with a GSTN “Tax Liability Report” for April 2022 to February 2025 and a “NEGATIVE LIABILITY STATEMENT” for 01/09/2024 to 27/03/2025 showing negative sales/negative liability carried forward and automatically adjusted against later liability. The petitioner also relied on Notification No. 12/2024 – Central Tax dated 10/07/2024, saying the reporting facility from September 2024 onward was intended to improve reconciliation, and complained that the Revenue ignored its representations made in April 2025, May 2025, October 2025, and later in 2025.

The Revenue nonetheless issued recovery notices under Section 79, including a notice to ICICI Bank on 18/07/2025 and later notices to State Bank of India, Akola Branch dated 26/02/2026 and State Bank of India, New Delhi Branch dated 09/03/2026. Best Agrolife sought interim relief from the Court against these recovery actions, but the Court refused it because the petitioner had not acted promptly: the Court held that once the 25/03/2025 notice expressly warned of Section 79 recovery after seven days, the petitioner should have approached the Court in April or May 2025, not much later. The Court therefore rejected interim relief on the ground of unjustified delay, but it did not decide the underlying GST merits or whether the tax demand was correct. At the same time, the Court issued notice to the respondents, returnable on 10/04/2026, and specifically asked the Revenue to explain why the petitioner’s representation was not considered and why recovery action was not taken immediately after the seven-day period expired.

rows.title: Income Tax | Pune ITAT Restores ₹1.73-Crore Penalty U/s 271(1)(c) on Capital Expenditure Claim
rows.desc: IN THE INCOME TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL PUNE BENCH “B”, PUNE BEFORE SHRI INTURI RAMA RAO, ACCOUNTANT MEMBER AND SHRI S. S. VISWANETHRA RAVI, JUDICIAL MEMBER . / ITA No.386/PUN/2020 ᭅ ᭅ / Assessment Year : 2014-15 ITO, Ward-7(1), Pune. Vs. M/s. Sarsan Developers, 14A & B, Elephinstone Stone, Opp. East Street Post Office, Camp, Pune- 411001. PAN : ABJFS4506M Appellant Respondent / ORDER PER INTURI RAMA RAO, AM: This is an appeal filed by the Revenue directed against the order of ld. Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals)-8, Pune [‘the CIT(A)’] dated 13.12.2019 for the assessment year 2014-15. 2. Briefly, the facts of the case are that the assessee is a partnership firm engaged in the business of development of lands. The Return of Income for the assessment year 2014-15 was filed on 29.11.2014 declaring Rs.Nil income. Against the said return of income, the assessment was completed by the Income Tax Officer, Revenue by : Shri M. G. Jasnani Assessee by : Shri Kishor Phadke Shir Suhas P. Bora Date of hearing : 08.09.2023 Date of pronouncement : 10.10.2023 ITA No.386/PUN/2020 2 Ward-7(1), Pune (‘the Assessing Officer’) vide order dated 23.12.2016 passed u/s 143(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (‘the Act’) at a total income of Rs.Nil after making addition of Rs.5,60,73,319/- being the amount paid to be retiring partner, namely, Kumar Housing Corporation Limited. The factual background of the case is as under : During the previous year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, the assessee firm debited development expenses of Rs.13,40,50,885/- which includes an amount of Rs.5,60,73,319/- paid to retiring partner, namely, Kumar Housing Corporation Limited. The factual background of the issue was explained by the assessee vide his letter dated 30.11.2016, which is extracted by the Assessing Officer vide para no.4.1 of the assessment order, which reads as under :- “Sarsan Developers Private Limited (SDPL) and Kumar Housing Corporation Limited (KHCL) had entered into an agre
rows.summary:
For assessment year 2014–15, the Pune ITAT in **ITO, Ward-7(1), Pune v. M/s. Sarsan Developers** restored a large disallowance/penalty-related tax consequence arising from the assessee’s claim of a **₹5,60,73,319 payment to an outgoing partner** as deductible business expenditure. The assessee, a partnership firm engaged in land development, had filed its return on **29.11.2014** declaring **nil income**, but in assessment under **section 143(3)** dated **23.12.2016**, the Assessing Officer added the amount paid to the retiring partner, **Kumar Housing Corporation Limited (KHCL)**, and treated it as not allowable under **section 37(1)**, effectively increasing closing work-in-progress rather than allowing an immediate deduction. The factual basis was that Sarsan Developers and KHCL had formed a registered firm, **Sarsan Kumar Developers (SKD)**, on **21.10.2006** to develop a Pune property, but due to a weak market between **2009 and 2013**, the project stalled; under the partnership deed’s **Clause 16**, compensation was payable if a partner exited before project completion at market rate, and the assessee stated it paid **₹10,000** against fixed capital, **₹1,22,25,442** against current capital, **₹78,26,720** for the period **01.04.2013 to 01.08.2013**, and an additional **₹4,99,90,000** as exit/settlement cost, totaling **₹5,60,73,319**. The assessee’s position was that this amount was a project-related settlement cost transferred to capital work-in-progress and should, if not immediately deductible, be amortized/revenue-expensed when sales commenced; it also projected the project would yield about **48,000 sq. ft.** of saleable area and approximately **₹72 crore** in revenue at an average realization of **₹15,000 per sq. ft.**

The **CIT(A)** reversed the Assessing Officer and held that **section 45(4)** did not apply, so the payment should be allowed as **revenue expenditure** rather than being capitalized. On Revenue’s appeal, the ITAT examined the settlement deed and the surrounding facts and ultimately **restored the tax authority’s treatment adverse to the assessee**, concluding that the amount paid in connection with the retiring partner’s exit was not allowable as a current revenue deduction under the assessee’s claimed theory. For compliance purposes, the key point is that amounts paid to remove or settle with a partner in a project-development partnership can be recharacterized as capital/project costs rather than deductible operating expenses, especially where the payment is tied to withdrawal from a development venture and is connected to capital formation or settlement of partnership rights. There were no new procedural filing deadlines announced in the order, but the case underscores the need for careful documentation of partner exit payments, the contractual basis for compensation, and the tax treatment of such amounts in project accounts and returns, because the revenue authorities challenged the deduction and the tribunal sided against the assessee’s revenue-expense characterization.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12642 Case Name Ekviradevi Gramin Bigarsheti Sahakari Patsanstha Maryadit Vs ITO (ITAT, Pune Bench) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2018-19 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Pune Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Following the jurisdictional Bombay High Court decision in CIT v. Jet Airways (I) Ltd., the Tribunal held that the AO could not independently assess an altogether different item after abandoning the very issue for which reassessment jurisdiction had been assumed. Reopening Triggered by Cash & Time Deposits The assessee was a co-operative credit society. It had not filed its return of income for AY 2018-19, reportedly because its audit report was not received in time. Information available on the Insight Portal indicated that the assessee had made cash deposits of ₹91,86,100 in The RDCC Urban Bank and had also invested ₹55,50,000 in time deposits. Since no return had been filed, the AO formed the view that these transactions aggregating to ₹1,47,36,100 represented income that had escaped assessment. After issuing a show-cause notice u/s 148A(b), the AO passed an order u/s 148A(d) on 07.04.2022. The AO recorded that the cash deposits & time deposits remained undisclosed and constituted information sug
rows.summary:
The Pune ITAT quashed the reassessment of Ekviradevi Gramin Bigarsheti Sahakari Patsanstha Maryadit for AY 2018-19 because the Assessing Officer (AO) reopened the case only to examine alleged undisclosed cash deposits of ₹91,86,100 and time deposits of ₹55,50,000 in The RDCC Urban Bank, totaling ₹1,47,36,100, but ultimately made no addition on those transactions. The reopening had been initiated through a notice under section 148A(b), followed by an order under section 148A(d) dated 07.04.2022, and then a notice under section 148 on the same date, on the basis that these deposits appeared to be escaped income.  

During the reassessment completed on 20.03.2024 under section 147 read with section 144B, the AO abandoned the original deposit issue and instead disallowed the assessee’s deduction claim of ₹7,06,146 under section 80P(2)(a)(i). The CIT(A)-NFAC upheld that disallowance, but the Tribunal held that this was legally impermissible because the income that formed the recorded basis for reopening was never actually assessed or reassessed.  

Relying on the Bombay High Court’s decision in CIT v. Jet Airways (I) Ltd. and supporting authorities such as Ranbaxy Laboratories and Mohmed Juned Dadani, the ITAT reaffirmed that section 147 does not permit a “roving” reassessment on an unrelated issue once the original reason for reopening falls away. In other words, the AO must first assess the very income that justified the reopening; only then can any other escaped income noticed during the proceedings also be brought to tax.  

Because the AO accepted the assessee’s explanation on the cash and time deposits and made no addition on those items, the reassessment lacked jurisdiction once it was used solely to disallow the section 80P deduction instead. The Tribunal therefore quashed the entire reassessment and the resulting addition. This decision is mainly relevant for tax compliance and audit teams of co-operative societies and similar assessees: if a reopening notice is issued for one specific item, the department cannot lawfully complete the reassessment only on a different, unrelated issue unless it first taxes the originally recorded escaped income or starts a fresh reassessment proceeding.

Abhilash Mohanty alleging that M/s Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. had failed to pass on the benefit of Input Tax Credit (ITC) to homebuyers in its “Vertex Panache” project following the introduction of GST from 01.07.2017, thereby contravening Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017. The Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering referred the matter to the DGAP, which initially reported profiteering of Rs. 73,00,010/-, comprising a base profiteered amount of Rs. 65,17,866/- and GST of Rs. 7,82,144/-, allegedly required to be passed on to 140 eligible homebuyers. The Respondent contended that substantial escalation in construction costs had materially offset the additional ITC benefit. The budgeted construction cost was Rs. 1,56,94,91,872/-, whereas actual expenditure amounted to Rs. 1,61,06,72,320/-, resulting in an overall cost increase of Rs. 4,11,80,448/- including indirect cost. The Respondent specifically identified increases of 19.87% in Ready-Mix Concrete (RMC), 62.98% in Sand and 73.17% in Bricks. Based on actual quantities consumed and costs incurred, the additional expenditure attributable to these major inputs was stated to be Rs. 3,49,87,499/-. The Respondent relied upon the Delhi High Court judgment in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, particularly paragraph 118, concerning price increases based on genuine commercial factors despite reduction in tax or availability of ITC. The Respondent also produced a Chartered Accountant’s Certificate dated 25.06.2026 from M/s Tukaram & Co.
rows.summary:
This case concerned an anti-profiteering allegation under Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017, arising from a complaint by a homebuyer in Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd.’s residential project “Vertex Panache” in Kokapet, Hyderabad. The complainant alleged that after GST came into force on 01.07.2017, the developer did not pass on the benefit of additional Input Tax Credit (ITC) through a commensurate price reduction for the unit purchased, which triggered an investigation by the Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering and then the DGAP under Rule 129 of the CGST Rules, 2017.  

The DGAP’s original report dated 27.08.2025 had found profiteering of Rs. 73,00,010/-, made up of Rs. 65,17,866/- as the base profiteered amount and Rs. 7,82,144/- as GST, allegedly attributable to 140 eligible homebuyers. Vertex Homes contested that conclusion by arguing that construction costs had risen substantially and had offset the GST/ITC benefit; it said its budgeted construction cost was Rs. 1,56,94,91,872/- but actual expenditure was Rs. 1,61,06,72,320/-, an increase of Rs. 4,11,80,448/- overall including indirect costs. It specifically pointed to sharp increases in key material inputs—RMC up 19.87%, sand up 62.98%, and bricks up 73.17%—and said the additional expenditure attributable to those major inputs alone was Rs. 3,49,87,499/-.  

In support, the respondent relied on a Chartered Accountant’s certificate dated 25.06.2026 from M/s Tukaram & Co. LLP and on the Delhi High Court’s reasoning in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, which recognizes that genuine commercial cost increases can affect anti-profiteering calculations. In its clarification dated 30.07.2026, the DGAP accepted the claimed additional expenditure after verifying the certificate and sample invoices, and revised its computation accordingly. On that revised basis, total ITC-related savings were Rs. 2,47,02,175/-, but cost escalation of Rs. 3,49,87,499/- exceeded those savings, producing negative net savings of Rs. 1,02,85,324/- and therefore nil profiteering.  

The Tribunal accepted the DGAP’s revised methodology and concluded that the respondent had demonstrated genuine cost escalation in major construction materials, verified by the DGAP, sufficient to fully absorb the benefit of additional ITC. It held that the revised approach—subtracting proven cost increases from the ITC benefit—was legally sound, found no contravention of Section 171 of the CGST Act, and disposed of the matter with a finding of “Nil” profiteering. For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that GST/ITC anti-profiteering exposure in real estate can be negated where a developer can substantiate that bona fide construction cost escalation offset the tax benefit, but that conclusion depended here on documentary support, CA certification, and DGAP verification.

Ltd. failed to pass on the benefit of reduction in GST rate from 28% to 18% on “MI LED Television 4A 80 cm” with effect from 01.01.2019, pursuant to Notification No. 24/2018-Central Tax (Rate) dated 31.12.2018. The matter was referred by the Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering to the DGAP under Rule 129 of the CGST Rules, 2017. The DGAP examined invoices and outward taxable supply details for the pre-rate-reduction period from 01.11.2018 to 31.12.2018 and the post-rate-reduction period from 01.01.2019 to 31.12.2019 and initially determined profiteering of Rs. 7,79,947/-. Following cessation of the National Anti-Profiteering Authority, the matter was transferred through the Competition Commission of India to the GST Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal directed the Respondent to establish that the profiteered amount had been refunded to affected customers. The Respondent submitted Electronic Gift Voucher (EGV) screenshots, an Excel mapping of vouchers to customer orders and invoices, and subsequently credit notes. The DGAP initially objected that the EGVs were conditional, time-bound and restricted and that their system description, “Offers and cash back”, did not establish that the GST benefit had been passed on. The DGAP accepted credit notes of Rs. 2,21,056/- issued to 174 customers whose orders had been cancelled or goods returned. After this adjustment, the profiteering amount was revised to Rs. 5,58,891/-. The Respondent contended th
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal held that Electronic Gift Vouchers (EGVs) can constitute a valid and direct mode of passing on GST rate-reduction benefit under Section 171 of the CGST Act, provided they are credited to customers without expiry, are not tied to purchase of a particular product or category, and can be used broadly across the platform. The case arose from a complaint that Sane Retails Pvt. Ltd. did not pass on the benefit of the GST rate cut on “MI LED Television 4A 80 cm” from 28% to 18%, effective 1 January 2019, under Notification No. 24/2018-Central Tax (Rate) dated 31 December 2018; the DGAP had examined invoices and outward supplies for 1 November 2018 to 31 December 2018 versus 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2019 and initially quantified profiteering at ₹7,79,947. After the Respondent produced voucher screenshots, order/invoice mapping, and credit notes, the DGAP accepted credit notes of ₹2,21,056 issued to 174 customers for cancelled or returned orders and revised the alleged profiteering to ₹5,58,891.

The Tribunal rejected the DGAP’s argument that the EGVs were ineffective because they were described in the system as “Offers and cash back,” holding that nomenclature does not control where the underlying credits can be traced to specific customer orders, invoices, dates, prices, and the GST-linked differential. It emphasized that the EGVs were activated into customer wallets, had no expiry, were unrestricted in use across the platform, and therefore represented monetary value standing to the customer’s credit; this was treated as a direct and unconditional transfer of the benefit, distinguishable from the Delhi High Court’s Reckitt Benckiser decision because the present case involved actual wallet credits rather than indirect discounting or promotional schemes. The Respondent stated that EGVs totaling ₹5,48,650 had been issued to 488 customers, of which ₹3,17,965 had already been used by 291 customers and ₹2,30,685 remained available in e-wallets.

On reconciliation, the Tribunal found a shortfall of ₹10,241 between the DGAP’s revised profiteering figure of ₹5,58,891 and the EGVs issued of ₹5,48,650. Because the Respondent could not identify any corresponding customer or invoice for that residual amount, it accepted the Respondent’s offer to deposit the difference into the Central Consumer Welfare Fund. The Tribunal therefore directed deposit of ₹10,241 into the Fund and also ordered interest at 18% under Rule 133(3)(c) of the CGST Rules, calculated from the date the higher amount was collected until the date of deposit. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that voucher-based transfers can satisfy anti-profiteering obligations if they are unconditional, traceable, and usable by customers, but any unreconciled balance must still be deposited with statutory interest.

The assessee contended that he regularly followed the cash system of accounting & had received the balance interest in subsequent years. The Tribunal held that recognition of interest income on actual receipt basis is permissible u/s 145(1). Therefore, a mismatch between interest paid & interest received in a particular year cannot, by itself, justify complete disallowance. However, deduction u/s 57(iii) would be available only after establishing a direct nexus between the borrowed funds, the interest-bearing advance & the corresponding income offered to tax. His case was selected for limited scrutiny & notice u/s 143(2) was issued. During assessment proceedings, the AO noticed that the assessee had claimed interest expenditure of ₹65,47,089 against interest income of ₹58,81,505 offered under the head “Income from other sources.” In the preceding year, the assessee had reported interest income of ₹65,26,481, while the interest expend
rows.summary:
This ITAT Hyderabad decision for AY 2018-19 addresses how interest income and interest expense are to be matched for tax purposes when an assessee follows the cash system of accounting. The assessee, Ravi Kumar Gollapudi, returned total income of ₹30,33,940 and was selected for limited scrutiny under notice u/s 143(2). During assessment, the Assessing Officer found that the assessee had claimed interest expenditure of ₹65,47,089 against only ₹58,81,505 of interest income shown under “Income from other sources,” and noted that in the prior year the assessee had reported interest income of ₹65,26,481. On that basis, the AO disallowed the excess interest outgo, apparently treating the mismatch between interest paid and interest received as a reason to deny the deduction.

The Tribunal held that, because the assessee follows the cash system, recognition of interest income on actual receipt basis is permitted u/s 145(1), so the mere fact that interest income in the year was lower than interest paid does not automatically justify a full disallowance. At the same time, the Tribunal emphasized that deduction u/s 57(iii) is not automatic and can be allowed only if the assessee proves a direct nexus between the borrowed funds, the interest-bearing advance, and the income actually offered to tax. In other words, the taxpayer cannot rely only on the existence of borrowing and interest payment; the interest expense must be shown to have been incurred wholly and exclusively for earning the relevant income from other sources.

The practical outcome is that the ITAT did not uphold a blanket denial based solely on the mismatch; instead, it remanded the matter relating to the ₹13.66 lakh disallowance for verification of nexus and corresponding facts. For compliance purposes, the case reinforces that taxpayers using the cash method may defer recognition of interest receipts until actually received, but they must maintain documentation proving the exact linkage between borrowings, advances, and taxable interest income when claiming interest deductions under s. 57(iii).

Having regard to the dictum of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Competition Commission of India v. Ste
rows.summary:
The Competition Commission of India has refused to grant interim relief in a competition-law dispute between Smt. Rinima Borah Agarwal and Mrs. India Inc., a sole proprietorship operated by Smt. Mohini Sharma. The complaint had been filed under Section 19(1)(a) of the Competition Act, 2002, alleging violations of Sections 3 and 4, and by order dated 02.06.2026 the CCI had already directed a Director General investigation under Section 26(1), which is still pending.  

In the same matter, the Informant filed IA No. 178A of 2025 seeking emergency/interim directions under Section 33. Specifically, she asked the CCI to stay certain clauses in the Participant Terms and Conditions dated 23.10.2024 and the Winner’s Terms and Conditions dated 27.10.2024, and to restrain Mrs. India Inc. from sending communications that would restrict or discourage her from joining or competing in other competitions while the case was ongoing.  

The CCI held that the requested measures were effectively final reliefs, not true interim protection, because they would grant substantive relief before the investigation had concluded. Since the Commission had already formed only a prima facie view and the DG inquiry was still underway, granting the requested stay and restraint order would amount to prejudging the issues under investigation. As a result, the Commission found the interim relief neither appropriate nor warranted at this stage, leaving the DG investigation to continue.  

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that the impugned participation and winner terms remain under regulatory scrutiny, but no interim prohibition was imposed against their operation or against the respondent’s communications pending investigation. The document does not announce a new general rule for all market participants; it is a case-specific refusal of interim relief while preserving the ongoing DG process under the Competition Act.

rows.title: Corporate Law | DNA Evidence Establishes Paternity, Not Consent: Delhi HC Upholds Acquittal
rows.desc: Summary: The Delhi High Court, in KXXXXX v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr., upheld the acquittal of Respondent No. 2 and dismissed the complainant’s appeal. The Court held that a DNA report establishing biological paternity proves the fact of sexual intercourse but does not, by itself, establish whether the relationship was consensual. It considered the allegations of repeated sexual acts, threats, coercion and administration of an intoxicating substance, along with the DNA evidence. The Court examined the Trial Court’s assessment of inconsistencies in the complainant’s testimony, the delay in disclosure and reporting, the surrounding circumstances and the defence of a consensual relationship. Relying on the principles governing appeals against acquittal, including the Supreme Court’s decision in Tulasareddi @ Mudakappa & Anr. v. State of Karnataka & Ors., the Court held that an acquittal should not be disturbed where the Trial Court’s view is reasonably possible. Interference requires patent perversity, manifest illegality, misreading or omission of material evidence, or other compelling and substantial reasons. The Court also cautioned that the conduct of a complainant in a sexual-offence case cannot be assessed through stereotypical assumptions. It ultimately held that the gravity of an accusation cannot substitute the requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr., CRL.A. 320/2026 and CRL.M.A. 10175/2026, Neutral Citation No. 2026:DHC:7451, considered an appeal against the a
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court in **KXXXXX v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr.** (CRL.A. 320/2026; CRL.M.A. 10175/2026; Neutral Citation **2026:DHC:7451**) **dismissed the complainant’s appeal and upheld the respondent’s acquittal**. The Court’s core holding was that a **DNA report showing biological paternity only proves that sexual intercourse occurred; it does not, by itself, prove that the intercourse was non-consensual**. In other words, even where DNA establishes that the accused is the biological father of the child, that evidence cannot substitute for proof on the crucial issue of consent in a sexual-offence prosecution.

The Court reviewed allegations that the complainant had been subjected to **repeated sexual acts, threats, coercion, and administration of an intoxicating substance**, and it considered those allegations together with the DNA evidence. It nevertheless agreed with the Trial Court’s assessment that the complainant’s evidence contained **material inconsistencies**, there had been **delay in disclosure/reporting**, and the surrounding circumstances supported the defence theory of a **consensual relationship**. The Court also reiterated the governing rule for appeals against acquittal, relying on **Tulasareddi @ Mudakappa & Anr. v. State of Karnataka & Ors.**, namely that an acquittal should not be interfered with if the Trial Court’s view is a **reasonably possible view**.

For a compliance team, the decision is important as a statement of proof standards in sexual-offence litigation: the Court emphasized that appellate interference with acquittals is warranted only where there is **patent perversity, manifest illegality, misreading or omission of material evidence, or other compelling and substantial reasons**. It also cautioned that a complainant’s conduct in a sexual-offence case cannot be judged through **stereotypical assumptions**, but it still held that the **gravity of the allegation cannot replace the requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt**. No new reporting deadline, monetary threshold, regulatory filing obligation, or operational compliance procedure was created by this judgment; its practical effect is to reinforce evidentiary and appellate standards in criminal cases involving sexual-offence allegations and DNA proof.

He genuinely believed that the appeal would be filed within the prescribed period. After returning from Saudi Arabia, the assessee contacted the Chartered Accountant & the appeal was filed immediately. The assessee supported his explanation with an affid
rows.summary:
This Hyderabad ITAT ruling for AY 2018-19 involves Shri Ahmed Altaf Sayeed’s challenge to a penalty order of ₹2,13,664 imposed under section 270A after reassessment proceedings under section 147/148. The Tribunal first condoned a 110-day delay in filing the appeal, accepting the assessee’s explanation that the matter had been handed to his Chartered Accountant before his trip to Saudi Arabia for pilgrimage, and that the appeal was filed immediately after he returned and followed up, with the delay attributed to the professional lapse of the CA.

The substantive holding is that the assessee was allowed to challenge the legality of the underlying reassessment proceedings in an appeal against the penalty order because the reassessment order was the foundation for the penalty. The Tribunal found that the notice under section 148 had been issued with the approval of an authority that was not competent under section 151, meaning the reassessment initiation suffered from a jurisdictional defect. Because the reassessment itself was invalid, the consequential penalty under section 270A could not survive and was also quashed.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that penalty exposure linked to reassessment can collapse if the reassessment notice was not properly sanctioned by the specified authority required under section 151. The ruling reinforces that approval hierarchy for reassessment notices is not a technicality; if the wrong approving authority is used, both the reassessment and any downstream penalty based on it may be invalidated.

rows.summary:
The document explains that GST input tax credit can be denied even where expenses are otherwise incurred for business if they fall within the blocked-credit rules in Section 17(5)(c) and 17(5)(d) of the CGST Act. In particular, Section 17(5)(c) blocks credit on works contract services used for the construction of immovable property, except when the same works contract service is taken as an input service for further supply of works contract service; “construction” for this purpose includes reconstruction, renovation, additions, alterations, and repairs to the extent capitalized to the immovable property. The article also clarifies that “plant and machinery” is a key carve-out: it means apparatus, equipment, and machinery fixed to earth by foundation or structural support and used for making outward supplies, including those foundations/supports, but excluding land, buildings or other civil structures, telecommunication towers, and pipelines laid outside factory premises.

A separate exception under Section 17(5)(c) allows ITC where the works contract service is received for construction of “plant and machinery.” The article gives the example of a material-and-labour works contract that results in HVAC plant, stating that such a case can qualify for credit because the contract is tied to plant and machinery rather than blocked civil construction. It also notes the second exception for further supply of works contract service, illustrated by a developer constructing mall units for sale during construction: the developer may take credit to the extent the work relates to units sold during construction.

Section 17(5)(d) is described as blocking credit on goods or services received for construction of immovable property other than plant and machinery when the construction is for the taxpayer’s own account, including use in the course or furtherance of business. The text specifically notes an amendment replacing the phrase “plant or machinery” with “plant and machinery” retrospectively from 1 July 2017 through Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax dated 17.09.2025. This means compliance teams should treat the plant-and-machinery carve-out as applying consistently back to GST’s start date, and review any prior positions or disputes in light of that retrospective correction.

The article highlights a recurring compliance problem: taxpayers are receiving notices to reverse or repay ITC claimed on newly constructed business premises such as factories and warehouses, on the theory that the underlying project is immovable property. It emphasizes that such projects often include more than civil construction and may also involve electrical fittings, cabling, sewage treatment plants, security systems, fire-fighting systems, and manufacturing equipment, so the tax treatment depends on whether each component is truly part of blocked immovable property or is separate movable/plant-and-machinery equipment eligible for ITC. The document recommends structuring transactions through separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery, and movable goods/services so that eligible credits are less likely to be denied in an audit or notice proceeding.

Finally, the document explains that whether something is “immovable property” is not determined just by attachment to land; the analysis depends on statutory definitions and judicial tests such as the nature of annexation, intention, functionality, permanency, and marketability. It specifically discusses movable-vs-immovable treatment for installations like HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems, and other business equipment, implying that compliance teams should assess each item separately rather than assuming all fitters, systems, or equipment embedded in a facility are automatically blocked. The practical takeaway is that businesses constructing operational facilities should document classification carefully, segregate contracts and invoices, and retain evidence showing which items are civil construction, which are plant and machinery, and which are movable business assets to support ITC eligibility.

rows.title: Income Tax | Builder Delay Can Trigger TDS Interest for Homebuyers
rows.desc: How Home Buyers Get Trapped into Paying TDS Interest When Builders Delay Telling Them About TDS on Installments Summary: Homebuyers purchasing property from builders through construction-linked installments may incur substantial interest liability if tax is not deducted at source from each payment. Under Section 194-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a buyer acquiring qualifying immovable property from a resident seller must deduct TDS at 1% at the time of payment or credit, whichever is earlier. For transactions governed by the 1961 Act, the buyer must furnish Form 26QB within 30 days from the end of the month of deduction and issue Form 16B to the seller. From 1 April 2026, the corresponding obligation continues under Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with Form 141 replacing Form 26QB for applicable transactions. Problems arise when builders raise installment demands without informing buyers about TDS and communicate the requirement only near possession or final payment. Earlier installments may consequently remain subject to delayed deduction. Interest is then payable from the date on which tax should have been deducted, even if the buyer was unaware of the obligation. Under Section 201(1A) of the 1961 Act, interest applies at 1% per month or part thereof for delayed deduction and 1.5% per month or part thereof for delayed deposit after deduction. Buyers should independently monitor every installment, deduct TDS within the applicable timeline and complete the prescribed statement and certificate requirements without waiting for instructions from the builder. rows.summary:
The document explains that homebuyers purchasing immovable property from builders under construction-linked installment plans can unknowingly trigger TDS default interest if they do not deduct tax on each installment as required. Under Section 194-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, where the property is not agricultural land and the purchase price is Rs. 50 lakh or more, the buyer must deduct TDS at 1% from each payment or credit to the resident seller, whichever is earlier; this applies installment by installment, not only at possession or final settlement. After deduction, the buyer must deposit the TDS using Form 26QB within 30 days from the end of the month in which the deduction was made, and must also issue Form 16B to the seller as evidence of deduction.

The document highlights a change in the governing statute: from 1 April 2026, the corresponding obligation continues under Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with Form 141 replacing Form 26QB for applicable transactions. Substantively, however, the duty remains the same: buyers still must deduct 1% TDS at each installment payment where the transaction value is Rs. 50 lakh or more. If a buyer pays, for example, eight installments over two years, the compliance expectation is eight separate TDS deductions and filings, one for each installment, rather than a single deduction at the end.

The compliance risk arises when builders do not tell buyers about the TDS requirement until late in the project, often near possession or final demand. By then, earlier installments may already have been paid in full without TDS, and the buyer is then forced to make delayed deductions and filings. The document states that ignorance of the obligation does not avoid the tax consequence: interest becomes payable from the date on which TDS should originally have been deducted.

Under Section 201(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the interest rates are 1% per month or part of a month for delayed deduction and 1.5% per month or part of a month for delayed deposit after deduction. The practical compliance instruction for buyers is to monitor every installment independently, deduct and deposit TDS on time for each payment, and complete the prescribed statement and certificate process without waiting for the builder to prompt them. The key operational issue for corporate compliance teams handling employee housing benefits, real estate payments, or advising customers is that each construction-linked installment is a separate TDS event, and late awareness does not protect against interest exposure.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Vague Fraud Allegation Cannot Invoke GST Section 74: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court: Mere Words “Fraud” or “Suppression of Facts” in a GST Show Cause Notice Are Not Enough to Invoke Section 74 Summary: The Supreme Court in M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. held that merely using the expressions “fraud” or “suppression of facts” in a GST show cause notice is insufficient to invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act. M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam challenged an SCN dated 13.06.2025 concerning FY 2018-19 and raising a demand of Rs.1,52,56,431/-. The company argued that the ordinary limitation period applicable under Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025 and that the department had mechanically invoked Section 74 without identifying any conduct constituting fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Although the department sought to explain the allegations through its counter affidavit, the Court refused to consider those subsequent explanations. It reiterated that the legal validity of a notice must be determined from the notice itself and that deficiencies affecting jurisdiction cannot be cured through pleadings filed later before a court. The SCN contained only a bland reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining how fraud was inferred or concealment detected. The use of the expression “or” also indicated uncertainty regarding the allegation being made. Holding that the foundational facts and reasoning supporting the invocation of the extended limitation period must be disclosed in the notice, the Supreme Court set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order as well as the SCN and restrained the department from proceeding further on its basis. Table of Contents▸ Background of the Case What the Company Argued What the Department Argued What the Supreme Court Held Key Takeaways for Practitioners Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background of the Case This case deals with a Show Cause Notice (SCN) iss
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that a GST show cause notice cannot validly invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act merely by reciting the words “fraud,” “wilful misstatement,” or “suppression of facts.” In **M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.**, the department had issued an SCN dated **13.06.2025** for **FY 2018-19** demanding **Rs. 1,52,56,431**, and the taxpayer argued that the normal Section 73 limitation had already expired on **28.02.2025** after applying the relevant return-due-date extensions and the COVID-related limitation exclusions. The Court agreed that if the department wants to rely on the **five-year** period under Section 74 instead of the ordinary **three-year** period under Section 73, the notice itself must set out the specific foundational facts showing how fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression occurred; a bare or mechanical reference to those terms is not enough.

The Court rejected the department’s attempt to cure the defect by relying on explanations in its counter affidavit, holding that a notice’s legal validity must be tested on the face of the notice itself and that jurisdictional defects cannot be repaired later in litigation. Here, the SCN contained only a vague reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining what conduct constituted fraud, how concealment was discovered, or why Section 74 was being invoked; the Court also noted that the use of the word “or” suggested uncertainty about the actual allegation. As a result, the Supreme Court set aside the **Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order** and also quashed the **SCN itself**, and it restrained the department from proceeding further on the basis of that notice.

For compliance teams, the key point is procedural and jurisdictional: where the department seeks to use Section 74 rather than Section 73, the SCN must contain concrete facts and reasoning supporting the fraud/suppression allegation at the time of issuance. A notice that simply uses statutory buzzwords without particulars may be vulnerable to challenge, even if the department later supplies details in court filings. This decision reinforces the importance of scrutinizing GST notices for limitation and for whether the jurisdictional basis for invoking the extended period is actually pleaded in the notice itself.

The source order contains a party-description inconsistency: its cause title identifies Santosh Mani Mishra as the appellant and the Islam Trading Company-related party as respondent, while paragraph 1 describes the appellant as Revenue and paragraph 1.2 refers to M/s Islam Trading Company as the appellant. The proceedings arose from transportation of 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly, under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018. The vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018. The E-Way Bill was not available with the driver at the time of interception. Tax of Rs. 47,844/- and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844/- were imposed under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017. The first appellate authority, however, set aside the tax and penalty by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018. The Department contended that transportation without the mandatory E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules and that subsequent production of the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns and proof of tax payment could not retrospectively cure the statutory violation. It further argued that the interception of the vehicle, nature of the goods, route and subsequent production of documents cumulatively indicated an intention to evade tax. The authorised representative also submitted that an E-Way
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench, restored a detention-cum-penalty order under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017 for movement of iron goods without an E-Way Bill, holding that the facts showed an intention to evade tax rather than a mere technical lapse. The case involved 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods transported by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018; the vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018, and the driver did not have the E-Way Bill at the time of interception. On that basis, the Proper Officer had imposed tax of Rs. 47,844 and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844 under Section 129(3).  

The First Appellate Authority had later set aside both the tax and penalty by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018, but the Department appealed, arguing that transportation without a mandatory E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules and that producing the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns, and proof of tax payment only after interception could not cure the violation. The Department also stressed that the E-Way Bill is generated online while the invoice is manually issued, creating scope for later manipulation of records, and that the route, nature of goods, and post-interception documents together indicated evasion; no one appeared for the respondent despite opportunity.  

The Tribunal accepted the Department’s position and distinguished the precedents relied upon by the first appellate authority, including Sarva Shri Singh Tire, Shri KL Industries, Harley Foods Products, Modern Traders, and Rai Prexim India, on the facts. It specifically noted that the goods were loaded at Baheri, Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh for delivery to Kichha, Uttarakhand, about 25 km away, and treated the short-distance movement, the absence of the E-Way Bill, and the interception circumstances as supporting an inference of intent to evade tax. The Tribunal also relied on its own later order dated 20.08.2026 in Appeal No. APL/79/LKC/2026, Om Prakash v. M/s Islam Trading Company, involving the same goods, same destination, and a similar pattern where the E-Way Bill was produced only after interception, and held that the repeated post-interception production of the E-Way Bill showed a recurring modus operandi rather than a harmless procedural lapse.  

As a result, the Tribunal held that the First Appellate Authority erred in interfering with the Section 129(3) detention order, allowed the Revenue’s appeal, set aside the appellate order dated 24.09.2021, and restored the original order dated 09.03.2018 imposing the Rs. 47,844 tax and Rs. 47,844 penalty. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that transporting goods without the E-Way Bill at the time of interception can sustain Section 129 detention and penalty where the authorities infer evasive intent from the surrounding facts, and post-interception production of supporting documents may not be enough to avoid penalty.

Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, Chennai Arising out of Order-in-Original No.9/2010 dated 16.8.2010 passed by Commissioner of Central Excise, Chennai – IV ST/350/2010 Ceebros Property Development Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, Chennai Arising out of Order-in-Original No.1/2010 dated 6.1.2010 passed by Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, Chennai ST/528/2010 Prime Developers Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, Coimbatore Arising out of Order-in-Original No.4/2010 dated 10.5.2010 passed by Commissioner of Customs, Central Excise and Service Tax, Coimbatore – IV Appearance Shri G. Commissioner (AR) for the Respondent CORAM Hon‟ble Ms. Sulekha Beevi C.S., Member (Judicial) Hon‟ble Shri Madhu Mohan Damodhar, Member (Technical) Date of Hearing : 16.08.2018 Date of Pronouncement: 18.09.2018 Final Order Nos. 42436-42438 / 2018 Per Bench The issue involved in all these appeals being similar, they were heard together and are disposed by this common order. 2. The appellant M/s. Real Value Promoters (P) Ltd. are involved in activity of constructing commercial projects PRGT www.taxguru.in 2 and residential projects. The appellants were issued show cause notices alleging short-payment of service tax under Commercial or Industrial Construction Services. After 1.6.2007, though they discharged service tax under works contract services under the composition scheme, for three of their four projects namely Sananda Brindavan, Sujeet, Surya Skanda, the department was of the view that such payment is not proper for the reason that the services cannot be classified as Works Contract Service and also because appellants have not exercised their opt
rows.summary:
This common CESTAT Chennai order (pronounced 18.09.2018) disposed of three appeals involving real-estate developers and the levy of service tax on property-construction transactions. The core dispute was whether the appellants’ arrangements should be taxed as “construction of complex / commercial or industrial construction services” under the Finance Act, 1994, or as “works contract service” after 1.6.2007; the department also argued that, even where works contract composition was claimed, the assessees had not validly opted into the composition scheme by notifying the department as required under the Works Contract (Composition Scheme for Payment of Service Tax) Rules, 2007. In the Real Value Promoters matter, the department issued SCN No. 351/2008 dated 23.10.2008 for the period 1.4.2007 to 31.3.2008, proposing service tax of Rs. 2,06,20,252 plus interest and penalties under sections 76 and 78, split across buyer-facing and landowner-facing development projects: commercial PRGT (Rs. 34,38,337), residential The Lords / Sananda Brindavan / Sujeet / Surya Skanda (Rs. 1,07,33,392), commercial PRGT Amarasri (Rs. 48,98,579), and residential Sai Brindavan (Rs. 15,49,944). A second SCN, No. 570/2009 dated 20.10.2009, covered amounts received for construction of residential apartments and commercial complexes and proposed an additional Rs. 1,05,99,978 on Commercial PRGT for the allegation of non-payment on services provided to buyers.

The adjudicating authority’s common order dated 16.8.2010 confirmed the entire demand raised in those notices, with interest, imposed a penalty equal to Rs. 2,06,20,252 under section 78, and also imposed penalties under sections 76 and 77. In the Prime Developers appeal, the developer had entered into a Joint Development Agreement dated 17.1.2005 with the landowner (Prime Textiles Ltd.) for a 432-apartment residential complex, and sold units to ultimate buyers under separate agreements; SCN dated 10.8.2009 covered the period January 2005 to August 2008 and the original authority confirmed Rs. 1,16,42,448, holding that service tax was payable under CICS at least for the period before 1.6.2007. For compliance teams, the practical issue is that the department treated the construction activity as taxable both where developers contracted with buyers and where they received consideration from landowners in JDA-style structures, and it specifically challenged the availability of works-contract classification and the procedural validity of the composition option. The final outcome of the Tribunal’s legal analysis is not fully shown in the excerpt provided, so the safe compliance takeaway from the document content alone is that these construction/JDA arrangements were under active tax scrutiny for the stated periods, with large confirmed demands, interest exposure, and section 76/77/78 penalty risk, particularly where no documented works-contract composition option had been exercised before the department.
