The applicant’s counsel submitted that he was innocent and had been falsely implicated. It was argued that the FIR concerning the alleged GST fraud did not name the applicant and that he had no connection with the allegations. The applicant also asserted that he was not the owner of M/s Super Power Industries, which had allegedly been declared bogus in November 2021, whereas the FIR was lodged approximately four years later on 04.11.2025. It was further submitted that the applicant’s name surfaced in the matter through the statement of Sakeel Khan and that he was not a beneficiary in any manner. The applicant was stated to have no criminal history apart from the present case and had been in jail since 05.04.2026. It was also submitted that, considering the heavy pendency of cases, there was no likelihood of an early conclusion of the trial. The prayer for bail was opposed by the learned A.G.A. as well as the counsel appearing for the GST Department. After considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the record, evidence, nature of allegations and submissions of the parties, the Court held that the applicant was entitled to be enlarged on bail during pendency of the trial. Ac
rows.summary:
This is an Allahabad High Court bail order in a criminal prosecution arising out of an alleged GST fraud connected to a non-existing/bogus firm, M/s Super Power Industries, and it does **not** announce any new GST rule, filing requirement, tax rate, or compliance deadline. The underlying case is Case Crime No. 539 of 2025 at Police Station Brahampuri, District Meerut, registered under Sections **420, 467, 468, 471, and 120-B of the IPC**. The applicant, **Waseem Akram @ Monu**, argued that he was not named in the FIR, had no connection with the alleged fraud, was not the owner of the firm, and was not a beneficiary; his name allegedly surfaced only from the statement of **Sakeel Khan**. He also pointed out that the firm had been declared bogus in **November 2021**, while the FIR was filed on **04.11.2025**, and that he had no criminal history apart from this case and had been in custody since **05.04.2026**.

The State and GST Department opposed bail, but the Court held that, based on the record, allegations, and submissions, the applicant was entitled to bail during trial. The Court ordered release on bail upon execution of a **personal bond** and furnishing **two sureties of like amount**, subject to standard compliance conditions: he must not tamper with evidence, threaten or influence prosecution witnesses, commit a similar offence, or make inducements/threats/promises to persons connected with the case to prevent disclosure of facts to the Court or police. He must appear before the trial court on all dates unless exempted, and the trial court must verify the **identity, status, and residence proof** of the sureties before accepting them. If any condition is breached, the trial court may cancel bail. The Court expressly said its observations were limited to the bail decision and would not affect the merits of the case at trial.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Holds Municipal Hoarding Space Taxable, But Quashes Extended-Period Service Tax Demand
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12629 Case Name Chief Municipal Officer Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Chief Municipal Officer Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Delhi) Summary: The CESTAT New Delhi considered whether a municipality was liable to service tax on two activities: providing space for display of advertisements through hoardings and renting/licensing its immovable properties, including vacant land, to agencies, persons and traders. The disputed period was 2009-10 to 2014-15, covering both the pre-negative-list and post-negative-list service tax regimes. The appellant had received Rs. 3,06,738/- from hoarding rent during April 2009 to June 2012 and Rs. 3,39,22,974/- as rent from various immovable properties during April 2009 to July 2014. The Department proposed service tax of Rs. 39,22,945/- together with interest, penalties and late fee for non-filing of ST-3 returns. The demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals), leading to the appeal before the Tribunal. The appellant contended that the expression “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been incorrectly interpreted. It argued, relying particularly on Cuddalore Municipality Vs Joint Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, that the expression “any other person” meant a person other than the owner. It also argued that vacant land was excluded from the relevant definition and that arrears of rent had been taxed at an incorrect service tax rate. On advertisement receipts, the appellant maintained that it merely collected statutory licence fees under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 for allotting land on which advertisers erected hoardings, rather than selling advertisin
rows.summary:
The CESTAT, New Delhi held that a municipality’s activity of giving space on hoardings for advertisements was taxable as “sale of space or time for advertisement services” for the period up to 01.07.2012 under section 65(105)(zzzm) of the Finance Act, 1994, because the statutory explanation expressly covered space used for display, advertising, or showcasing products or services on billboards and in public places. The Tribunal also held that the municipality’s leasing/licensing of immovable property, including vacant land, for commercial use was taxable both before and after 01.07.2012: for the pre-negative-list period, it rejected the argument that “any other person” meant only a person other than the owner and found that the vacant land used as market space was not within the claimed exclusion; for the post-01.07.2012 period, it found the activity fell within the broad definition of “service” in section 65B(44) and was not covered by the negative list because the property was provided to business entities for commercial activities such as “Flee Markets.”

The dispute covered the period 2009-10 to 2014-15. The municipality had received Rs. 3,06,738 from hoarding rent during April 2009 to June 2012 and Rs. 3,39,22,974 as rent from various immovable properties during April 2009 to July 2014. The Department had proposed service tax of Rs. 39,22,945, along with interest, penalties, and a late fee for failure to file ST-3 returns, and the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals) had upheld the demand before the matter reached the Tribunal.

A key compliance outcome is that the Tribunal accepted the Department’s substantive position on taxability of both revenue streams, including amounts described as “licence fee” rather than rent, because the underlying activity was commercial and for consideration. However, it granted major relief on limitation: because the appellant was a government authority and there was no evidence of a positive act of suppression with intent to evade tax, the extended limitation period could not be invoked. The Tribunal relied on the principle from Anand Nishikawa Co. Ltd. that mere non-payment or non-declaration is not enough to establish wilful suppression; a positive act is required.

For compliance purposes, the practical result is that similar municipal or local-authority monetization of hoardings, advertising space, vacant land, market space, or other immovable property for commercial use can be subject to service tax/GST-era successor analysis depending on the period and facts, especially where the recipient is a trader or business entity and the arrangement is for consideration. In this case, the demand survived only for the normal limitation period, with proportionate reduction in penalty, while the extended-period demand was set aside. The appeal was therefore partly allowed.

rows.title: Income Tax | MEIS Rewards Taxable as Revenue Receipt from AY 2016-17: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12628 Case Name DCIT Vs Aarti Drugs Ltd. (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2016-17 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT Vs Aarti Drugs Ltd. (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The ITAT Mumbai Special Bench was constituted to decide whether the amount received by the assessee under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015 is taxable as a revenue receipt in view of the amendment to Section 2(24) of the Income-tax Act by insertion of clause (xviii) with effect from Assessment Year 2016-17. The assessee, engaged in manufacturing specialty chemicals and bulk drugs, had initially claimed the MEIS assistance as a revenue receipt, but subsequently contended before the CIT(A) that it was a capital receipt. The CIT(A) accepted the assessee’s contention for AYs 2016-17 and 2017-18, leading to the Revenue’s appeals. The Revenue argued that MEIS constitutes government assistance and falls within the amended definition of income under Section 2(24)(xviii), irrespective of the nomenclature of the benefit as a “reward”. It relied upon the objective of the Foreign Trade Policy, the expression “by whatever name called”, the Supreme Court’s decisions in Sahney Steel Press Works Ltd. and Ponni Sugars & Chemicals Ltd., and various Tribunal decisions. The assessee, on the other hand, contended that MEIS was a reward intended to improve the export competitiveness of the country and did not constitute the forms of assistance contemplated by Section 2(24)(xviii). It relied, among others, upon Ponni Sugars, CIT v. Chaphalkar Brothers, DCIT v. Munjal Auto Industries and Shree Balaji Alloys. The Special Bench first examined the “purpose test” laid down by the Supreme Court. In Sahney S
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai Special Bench held that incentives received under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015 are taxable as revenue receipts and therefore form part of business income, beginning with AY 2016-17, because of the amendment to section 2(24) of the Income-tax Act inserting clause (xviii). The dispute arose in the case of Aarti Drugs Ltd., a manufacturer of specialty chemicals and bulk drugs, which had initially treated the MEIS benefit as revenue receipt, later argued before the CIT(A) that it was a capital receipt, and succeeded before the CIT(A) for AYs 2016-17 and 2017-18; the Revenue appealed. The Revenue’s position was that MEIS is government assistance covered by section 2(24)(xviii), and that the label “reward” does not matter because the statute includes assistance “by whatever name called.”

The Special Bench applied the Supreme Court’s “purpose test” and concluded that MEIS was designed to offset export-related infrastructural inefficiencies and other ordinary export costs, and to improve India’s export competitiveness, not to help set up a new unit, expand capacity, or make capital investment. It noted that MEIS duty credit scrips are freely transferable, can be used to pay various duties and taxes, and do not carry any condition that they be used to acquire capital assets or repay capital borrowings; the benefit is computed with reference to the FOB value of exports and is available to qualifying manufacturer and merchant exporters. On that basis, the Bench held MEIS rewards are revenue in nature and are taxable as business income.

The Bench also held that section 2(24)(xviii) is drafted broadly enough to include assistance in the form of subsidy, grant, cash incentive, duty drawback, waiver, concession, reimbursement, or other similar government assistance “by whatever name called,” and rejected the assessee’s attempt to narrow the provision through ejusdem generis. It specifically found that the term “reward” used under MEIS falls within this broad language and that the MEIS benefit is, in substance, a cash incentive because it is linked to a percentage of FOB exports. The two statutory exclusions in section 2(24)(xviii) did not apply: MEIS was not an amount linked to the actual cost of a depreciable asset, and it was not a corpus donation to a trust or institution.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that, for AY 2016-17 onward, MEIS receipts should be treated as taxable income and included in business income rather than booked as a capital receipt. The decision also signals that exporters and other recipients of similar government export incentives should review their tax positions, accounting treatment, and return disclosures for periods covered by the amended definition of income, particularly where benefits are structured as duty credit scrips or “rewards” rather than explicitly labeled subsidies or grants.

rows.title: Income Tax | Gujarat HC Dismisses Reassessment Appeal Where Recorded Reasons Produced No Addition
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12627 Case Name PCIT Vs NK Proteins Pvt. Ltd (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court considered the Revenue’s appeal under section 260A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 arising from the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal order dated 12.11.2024 for A.Y. 2009-10. The assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing edible and non-edible oil products and byproducts. The original assessment under section 143(3) was completed on 29.12.2011. The source records total income at Rs. 22,55,48,605/- in paragraph 3.1, while paragraph 7 records Rs. 22,55,48,602/-. A notice under section 148 was issued on 09.03.2015 beyond four years from the end of the relevant assessment year. The recorded reasons concerned two matters: an alleged short computation of disallowance under section 14A read with Rule 8D, and an alleged income of Rs.244.98 crores said to have been received from National Stock Exchange Ltd. (NSEL) through so-called paper trade. In reassessment, however, the Assessing Officer made a disallowance of Rs.13,89,08,810/- under section 43(5) read with section 73 and section 40A(2)(b), along with excess disallowance of Rs.1,04,652/- under section 14A. The assessee challenged the reopening before the CIT(Appeals), pointing out that no addition had ultimately been made on either recorded reason. The CIT(Appeals) found that the NSEL figure of Rs.244.98 crores related to an addition in the assessee’s own case for A.Y. 2011-12 and that the assessee had not carried out NSEL transactions in the year under consideration. The CIT(Appeals) also noted that the original section 14A disallowance had been deleted by th
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court dismissed the Revenue’s section 260A appeal in **PCIT v. NK Proteins Pvt. Ltd.** for A.Y. **2009-10**, upholding the Tribunal’s order that had quashed the reassessment as **without jurisdiction**. The reassessment notice under **section 148** had been issued on **09.03.2015**, which was **beyond four years** from the end of the assessment year, so the reopening could stand only if the Revenue could show that income had escaped assessment because of the assessee’s **failure to disclose truly and fully all material facts**. The recorded reasons for reopening were limited to two alleged escapement items: an alleged under-disallowance under **section 14A read with Rule 8D**, and an alleged **Rs. 244.98 crore** receipt from **National Stock Exchange Ltd. (NSEL)** through a supposed paper trade.

The reassessment ultimately did **not** make any addition on either of those recorded reasons. Instead, the Assessing Officer made a different addition of **Rs. 13,89,08,810/-** under **sections 43(5), 73, and 40A(2)(b)**, plus an alleged excess disallowance of **Rs. 1,04,652/-** under **section 14A**. The CIT(A) and Tribunal both held that this could not sustain the reassessment because the NSEL figure related to an addition made in the assessee’s **A.Y. 2011-12** proceedings and the assessee had **not carried out NSEL transactions in the year under review**, while the original section 14A disallowance had already been deleted by the Ahmedabad ITAT on the ground that the assessee had **not earned exempt dividend income**. The Court agreed that the reopening failed at the threshold because the recorded reasons produced **no addition**, there was **no allegation of failure to disclose fully and truly all material facts**, and the Revenue had brought **no new tangible material** on record.

The High Court also rejected the Revenue’s reliance on **Explanation 3 to section 147**, holding that while that Explanation may allow the Assessing Officer, after a **valid** reopening, to assess other income that comes to notice during reassessment, it does **not** override the basic jurisdictional requirements of section 147. The Court applied the principle from **CIT v. Mohmed Juned Dadani** that if the **foundation** for reopening collapses, the reassessment cannot survive; it also reiterated that an Explanation cannot enlarge the scope of the main statutory provision. Practically, the ruling means that where a reassessment is initiated **after four years** and the recorded grounds themselves do not result in any addition, the Revenue cannot salvage the reassessment by making unrelated additions discovered later in the process.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 272A(2)(e) Penalty Cannot Continue Beyond Section 139(4): Chennai ITAT
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12626 Case Name Swamy Vivekanandha Vidhyala Trust Vs ITO (ITAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2013-14 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Chennai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Swamy Vivekanandha Vidhyala Trust Vs ITO (ITAT Chennai) Summary: The appeal concerned levy of penalty under section 272A(2)(e) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for failure by a charitable trust to furnish its return of income. The assessee, a charitable trust running an educational institution and registered under section 12A, had not filed its return for AY 2013-14. The Assessing Officer received information that the assessee had deposited cash of Rs. 75,55,200/- into its bank account. Consequently, assessment proceedings were reopened by issuing notice under section 147. In response, the assessee filed a return declaring Nil income after claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(iiiad). The assessment under section 147 accepted the returned income. Subsequently, penalty proceedings under section 272A(2)(e) were initiated. The assessee explained that the return had not been filed because of a bona fide belief that no return was required where the income was exempt. It also contended that there was no loss to the Revenue and no intention to conceal income. The Assessing Officer rejected these submissions and levied penalty of Rs. 3,04,300/-. The CIT(A) confirmed the penalty, holding, among other things, that the assessee had failed to comply with section 139(4C), that ignorance of law was not an acceptable excuse, absence of revenue loss and mens rea was irrelevant, and that the penalty was mandatory in the absence of reasonable cause under section 273B. At the hearing before the Tribunal, the assessee pressed only ground No.8 and did not press the remaining gro
rows.summary:
The Chennai ITAT held that a penalty under section 272A(2)(e) of the Income-tax Act for failure to furnish a return cannot run indefinitely past the point at which the assessee was still legally able to file a valid voluntary return under section 139(4). The case involved a charitable trust registered under section 12A and running an educational institution, which had not filed its return for AY 2013-14; the Assessing Officer reopened the case under section 147 after finding cash deposits of Rs. 75,55,200 in the trust’s bank account, and the trust then filed a return declaring nil income and claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(iiiad). Although the assessment was completed on the returned income, the Assessing Officer levied penalty of Rs. 3,04,300 under section 272A(2)(e), and the CIT(A) upheld it, taking the view that the trust had failed to comply with section 139(4C), that ignorance of law and absence of revenue loss were irrelevant, and that no relief was available absent “reasonable cause” under section 273B.

Before the Tribunal, the trust pressed only the issue that the penalty period should stop when the time for filing a valid belated return under section 139(4) expired, rather than continuing until the return was actually filed in response to notice under section 148. The Revenue argued that because section 272A(2)(e) applies for every day during which the failure continues, the default should be treated as continuing up to the eventual filing date. The Tribunal rejected that approach, holding that once the section 139(4) deadline passed, the assessee no longer had the statutory ability to voluntarily furnish a valid return, so the failure could not be treated as continuing beyond that point for purposes of section 272A(2)(e).

Relying on Bethany Seva Sangam v. ITO [2023] 155 taxmann.com 352 (Raipur Tribunal) and also noting G. Pulla Reddy v. JCIT (2010) 47 DTR 1 (Hyd.), the Tribunal ruled that the penalty must be restricted to the period up to the last date permitted under section 139(4), and not extended to the date of filing in response to the section 148 notice. It therefore set aside the penalty computation and remanded the matter to the Assessing Officer solely to recompute the penalty by limiting the default period to the section 139(4) window. The appeal was partly allowed.

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court considered a writ petition by Sankaran Mekala challenging a demand order dated 16.07.2026 passed under sections 147, 271(1)(b), and 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for Assessment Year 2015–16. The petitioner asked the Court to quash the demand and to direct reopening of the income-tax e-filing portal so she could upload her return in compliance with an earlier Madras High Court order dated 09.02.2026 in W.P. No. 1242 of 2026. In that earlier proceeding, the Court had already directed her to file the return of income for AY 2015–16 and respond to the section 148 notice; she stated she complied in part by depositing Rs. 5 lakhs, but technical problems prevented her from uploading the return on the portal.

For compliance purposes, the important point is that the Court accepted the petitioner’s screenshot as evidence of portal upload failure and held that, where a taxpayer has attempted to comply but is blocked by technical issues, justice requires another opportunity to file. The Revenue had notice of the petition, and the petitioner also produced proof of the Rs. 5 lakh deposit and other supporting documents. The Court therefore disposed of the writ petition by directing that she be allowed access to the portal / given an opportunity to file the return, rather than treating the portal failure as non-compliance. The document does not set out any broader system-wide rule change, but it confirms that documented evidence of technical inability to upload a return can support relief from adverse consequences where a prior court order required filing.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12624 Case Name DCIT-2(1)(1) Vs Bank of Baroda (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2003-04 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT-2(1)(1) Vs Bank of Baroda (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal dismissed the Revenue’s appeals concerning the manner in which refunds payable to M/s. Bank of Baroda were required to be adjusted between the interest component and the principal tax component. The consolidated order covered AYs 2003-04, 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10, 2016-17 and 2005-06, with ITA No.5707/Mum/2025 for AY 2003-04 taken as the lead case. The Revenue challenged the order of the CIT(A), NFAC, contending that where a refund comprised both tax and interest under section 244A, any refund payment should first be appropriated towards the principal tax component rather than the interest component. According to the Revenue, section 244A contained no express provision prescribing that interest should be adjusted first. It was also argued that adjusting the refund against interest would result in further interest liability on the unpaid tax component and would effectively amount to charging interest on interest. The assessee contended that the issue had already been settled by various judicial decisions and by decisions of the Tribunal in its own case. It relied on the principle of consistency and submitted that, in the absence of any change in facts or circumstances, the earlier view should be followed. The assessee also relied upon decisions concerning Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, Bank of India, IDBI Bank, Reliance Industries Limited, State Bank of India and Tata Sons Limited, among others. The Tribunal noted that section 244A provides
rows.summary:
The Mumbai ITAT dismissed the Revenue’s appeals and upheld the CIT(A), NFAC view on how tax refunds under section 244A must be adjusted for M/s. Bank of Baroda. The dispute covered multiple assessment years—AY 2003-04, 2005-06, 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10, and 2016-17—with ITA No. 5707/Mum/2025 for AY 2003-04 treated as the lead matter. The Revenue’s position was that when a refund contains both principal tax and section 244A interest, the refund should be applied first against the tax component because section 244A does not expressly say interest must be adjusted first; it argued that otherwise the unpaid tax balance would keep generating additional interest and this would amount to “interest on interest.”  

The assessee argued that the issue was already settled by prior judicial decisions, including decisions in its own case, and that the principle of consistency required the same treatment absent any change in facts or law. It also cited supporting rulings involving Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, Bank of India, IDBI Bank, Reliance Industries Limited, State Bank of India, and Tata Sons Limited. The Tribunal held that section 244A contemplates interest on refundable amounts and that, for the purpose of refund adjustment, the interest component must be given priority before the principal tax component; accordingly, the Revenue’s appeals were rejected.  

For compliance purposes, this means refund-setoff processing in these matters should follow an interest-first approach when a taxpayer’s entitlement includes both tax refund and section 244A interest, and the department cannot insist on applying the refund first to principal tax merely because the statute does not spell out the order in express terms. The ruling is relevant for taxpayers receiving income-tax refunds with a section 244A interest element, particularly where the department seeks to net off against outstanding tax liabilities, because the adjustment sequence directly affects whether any residual tax balance continues to accrue further interest. No separate prospective deadline or filing date was stated in the text; the decision is case-law guidance applicable to the covered assessment years and similar refund-adjustment disputes.

Chessman Impex Private Limited Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Chennai) Summary: CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017, holding that the customs duty demand of Rs.2,16,93,068/- against Chessman Impex Pvt. Ltd., consequential interest, penalties of Rs.20 lakh each under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962 and penalties imposed on the co-appellants could not be sustained in the absence of reliable and corroborative evidence. Chessman Impex had obtained a DEEC licence under the EXIM Policy 1997-2002 permitting duty-free import of 5350 MTs of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against export obligation of 5000 MTs of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue alleged that the imported scrap was diverted in the domestic market and maize was fraudulently exported to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export instead of the stipulated steel products. The Tribunal found material support for the appellant’s case in the special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, Customs examination of export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai’s confirmation regarding manufacture by Goyal Ispat Ltd., the foreign buyer’s permission for segregation and export of unprocessed scrap, undisputed realisation of export proceeds and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority. rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals filed by Chessman Impex Private Limited and co-appellants and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017 in full. The customs department’s demand of ₹2,16,93,068 in duty, along with consequential interest, and penalties of ₹20 lakh each imposed under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, as well as the penalties levied on the other appellants, were held unsustainable because the Revenue did not establish its allegations with reliable, corroborative evidence.

The underlying dispute concerned a DEEC licence issued under the EXIM Policy 1997–2002 that allowed duty-free import of 5,350 MT of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against an export obligation of 5,000 MT of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue alleged that the imported scrap had been diverted into the domestic market and that, instead of exporting the required steel products, the appellant had fraudulently exported maize to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export. The Tribunal rejected that allegation after finding supporting evidence for the appellant’s version, including special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, Customs examination of the export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, confirmation from DRI Chennai that the goods were manufactured by Goyal Ispat Ltd., and permission from the foreign buyer allowing segregation and export of unprocessed scrap.

The Tribunal also relied on the fact that export proceeds had been realized without dispute and that the competent DGFT authority had issued an Export Obligation Discharge Certificate, indicating completion of the licensing conditions. In addition, the CBI had investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report stating that the material on record supported the conclusion that the exports had in fact been made from the actual address of the company. For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Tribunal’s decision turns on the absence of firm evidence of diversion or sham exports and on the existence of contemporaneous official certifications and discharge of export obligations; the customs demand, interest, and penalties were therefore quashed.

(Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered a challenge to a customs penalty of Rs. 425,27,99,100/- imposed on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962. The penalty arose from an allegation that a consignment of natural diamonds had been mis-declared as lab-grown diamonds to pay a lower tariff. The Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025 was challenged before the Gujarat High Court, but the challenge failed when the High Court dismissed the appeal on 20.01.2026. The matter then reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court did not enter into the merits of the underlying customs dispute. Instead, the appellant contended that several judgments and articles relied upon by the second respondent in the Order-in-Original had been generated using Artificial Intelligence. The Court independently verified the material relied upon in the customs order and found that the second respondent had relied upon case laws that were either non-existent or had fake citations. The Court further found that some case laws which did exist did not lay down the legal propositions attributed to them. The Court observed that the material appeared to be a hallucination of AI. This discovery led the Supreme Court to rely upon its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh Vs Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd., where the Court had adopted a zero-tolerance approach towards producing, citing or relying upon artificial-intelligence-generated precedents without verification. The Supreme
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court set aside the customs penalty matter not on the merits of the underlying import allegation, but because the customs adjudication record was found to contain fake or misrepresented legal authorities. The case involved a penalty of ₹425,27,99,100 (about ₹425 crore) imposed by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962, based on an allegation that a consignment of natural diamonds had been wrongly declared as lab-grown diamonds to obtain a lower customs duty. The Order-in-Original was dated 08.10.2025, the Gujarat High Court rejected the challenge on 20.01.2026, and the matter then reached the Supreme Court.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that the Supreme Court did not decide whether the customs classification/misdeclaration allegation was correct; instead, it focused on the integrity of the adjudicatory materials relied on by the customs authority. The appellant argued that several judgments and articles cited in the Order-in-Original had been generated using artificial intelligence, and the Court independently checked the cited authorities. It found that some of the case laws were entirely non-existent or had fake citations, while others existed but did not support the legal propositions attributed to them. The Court described the apparent result as an AI “hallucination.”

The Supreme Court tied this finding to its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd., emphasizing a zero-tolerance approach to producing, citing, or relying on AI-generated precedents without verification. The practical compliance implication is that any adjudication, appeal, internal legal memo, or regulatory submission must verify every cited case, quotation, and proposition against authentic primary sources before filing or relying on it. For customs and other regulated matters, this decision reinforces that fabricated, hallucinated, or unverified AI-assisted legal citations can undermine the validity and credibility of the entire proceeding and may trigger judicial reproach even where the substantive enforcement issue remains unresolved.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Madras HC Upholds Negative Blocking of Electronic Credit Ledger Under Section 79

The petitioner sought a direction to the respondent to lift the blockage and permit free utilisation of the Input Tax Credit available in the electronic credit ledger. An assessment order dated 17.03.2023 had been issued for the assessment period 2017-2020. Primarily challenging the clubbing of assessments relating to multiple assessment periods, the petitioner had filed W.P.No.41890 of 2025. An interim stay concerning recovery measures was granted on 25.02.2026. The electronic credit ledger, however, had already been blocked on 04.02.2025, and that blocking order was challenged in the present writ petition. The petitioner contended that the blocking could not survive in view of the interim order dated 25.02.2026. It was further argued that the blocking travelled beyond the scope of Section 79 of the CGST Act. Comparing Section 79 with Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, learned counsel contended that negative blocking was impermissible under Section 79. The Revenue submitted that there was no infirmity in the blocking. It also contended that the interim order dated 25.02.2026 merely directed that recovery proceedings be kept in abeyance and did not affect the earlier blocking order. The Court accepted the Revenue’s inter
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court upheld the blocking/freezing of M/s. Zigma Machinery & Equipment Solutions’ electronic credit ledger that had been imposed by reference No. BL3302250000152 dated 04.02.2025, rejecting the taxpayer’s request to have the blockage lifted and to be allowed free use of input tax credit in the ledger. The taxpayer had argued that the blocking could not continue because of an interim stay granted on 25.02.2026 in a separate writ petition challenging an assessment order dated 17.03.2023 for the 2017–2020 assessment period, and that the blockage exceeded the scope of Section 79 of the CGST Act because, according to the taxpayer, “negative blocking” is not permitted under that provision when compared with Rule 86A of the CGST Rules. The Revenue responded that the interim order only put recovery proceedings in abeyance and did not invalidate or override the earlier ledger-blocking action, and the Court agreed with the Revenue’s position.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that, at least on these facts, an electronic credit ledger blockage imposed before an interim stay on recovery can remain effective even if litigation later results in temporary protection against recovery actions; the stay on recovery does not automatically解除 or nullify the earlier blocking measure. The decision also indicates that the Court did not accept the argument that the blocking was impermissible merely because it was characterized as “negative blocking” under Section 79. Entities facing GST enforcement should therefore treat a separate credit-ledger blocking order as an independent compliance constraint unless and until it is specifically set aside or withdrawn, and they should not assume that a stay on recovery proceedings restores unrestricted access to input tax credit.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12620 Case Name Nahas Kakkattummal Vs ITO (Kerala High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Kerala High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. The dispute concerned amounts received by the appellant while pursuing postgraduate medical studies. According to the appellant, the amounts were stipend and not salary. The appellant’s counsel contended that the assessment order had been issued by relying “blindly” on documents supplied by the University where the appellant was studying and drawing stipend, in which the sums were shown as salary. It was submitted that the appellant was admittedly a postgraduate student and that the amount received was stipend statutorily paid under law and in accordance with mandatory guidelines of the National Medical Commission. On that basis, it was argued that the Assessing Authority could not assess the receipts as salary. Alternatively, the appellant sought liberty to produce additional documents before the Assessing Authority. Counsel pointed out that even the University communication relied upon by the Assessing Authority categorically certified that the appellant had been admitted to an MD/MS postgraduate course as a Junior Resident. It was submitted that such students were covered by the regulations of the NMC, which prohibited payment of salary but mandated stipend. The appellant also relied upon Ext.P5, which certified that he was a bona fide PG student of the University, and contended that the letters relied upon by th
rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court considered a dispute over the tax characterization of amounts paid to a postgraduate medical student while he was enrolled in an MD/MS program. The taxpayer argued that the receipts were a statutory stipend paid to him as a bona fide PG student, not “salary,” and therefore should not have been assessed as salary income under the Income Tax Act, 1961. He contended that the Assessing Authority had relied mechanically on university documents that described the payments as salary, even though the university communication also stated that he had been admitted as a Junior Resident in a postgraduate course, and that the National Medical Commission’s regulations for such students require stipend payments rather than salary. The taxpayer also relied on a certificate (Ext. P5) confirming his status as a bona fide postgraduate student, and he sought permission to produce additional documents before the tax authority to establish the true nature of the payments.

Procedurally, the case reached the High Court after a Single Judge had declined to exercise writ jurisdiction and directed the appellant to pursue the ordinary statutory remedy under the Income Tax Act. On appeal, the High Court did not itself finally decide whether the stipend was taxable as salary; instead, it remanded the matter for fresh assessment so that the relevant factual materials could be properly considered. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the tax treatment of medical postgraduate stipends may turn on documentary proof of student status, the governing university/NMC framework, and the actual nature of the payment, and that assessments based solely on a document labeling the amount as salary may be vulnerable if contrary evidence shows the recipient was a PG trainee entitled to stipend.

rows.summary:
For AY 2015-16, the Kolkata ITAT considered an appeal by Sandhya Roy arising from a reassessment based on a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) dated 22.01.2015 with a co-owner/developer arrangement. The assessee had not filed an original return of income and also did not file a return in response to the section 148 notice issued on 31.03.2022. In reassessment, the Assessing Officer treated the JDA as a “transfer” under section 2(47), adopted total sale consideration of ₹48,68,542 based on fair market value plus cash consideration, assumed a nil cost of acquisition, and completed assessment under sections 147, 144 and 144B at total income of ₹48,68,542, entirely as long-term capital gains.

Before the CIT(A), the assessee challenged both the validity of the reassessment and the capital-gains addition. On limitation, the assessee invoked the Supreme Court’s reassessment-transition rulings, including Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal and Union of India & Ors. v. Rajeev Bansal, but the CIT(A) held that because the section 148 notice was issued on 31.03.2022, before 01.04.2022, the case was not covered by the Department’s concession regarding time-barred notices and therefore the Ashish Agarwal directions applied; the limitation objection was rejected. On the capital-gains issue, the CIT(A) did not finally decide the merits against the assessee in a way that the ITAT found acceptable for final disposal on the existing record.

The ITAT Kolkata did not finally affirm the capital-gains addition; instead, it remanded the matter back for fresh adjudication on merits. The practical compliance takeaway is that the reassessment framework and the JDA-based capital gains treatment remain under reconsideration, and the addition of ₹48,68,542 as long-term capital gains was not allowed to stand without further fact-finding and examination. No new general compliance rule was announced, but the case underscores that JDA transactions can be scrutinized as transfers for capital-gains purposes, especially where the taxpayer has not filed returns and the department proceeds under reassessment, best-judgment, and faceless appeal procedures.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Allahabad HC Quashes GST Order for Notice Served Only Through Portal After Cancellation
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12618 Case Name Ved Enterprises Unnao Vs State of U.P (Allahabad High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Allahabad High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ved Enterprises Unnao Vs State of U.P (Allahabad High Court) Summary: The petitioner challenged the order dated May 28, 2022 passed by the Deputy Commissioner, State Tax, Sector-1, District Unnao under Section 74 of the Uttar Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. The writ petition was filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The petitioner’s registration under the Act had been cancelled on 16.11.2021. Thereafter, the petitioner did not carry on any business. A show cause notice was uploaded on the GST portal and, subsequently, the impugned order was passed under Section 74. The Court held that once the registration had been cancelled, the petitioner was not obligated to check the GST portal. The Court observed that the mode of service of any show cause notice had to be by way of alternative means to the petitioner. The petitioner relied upon the coordinate Bench decision in M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others, Neutral Citation No.2024:AHC:23697-DB. The Court stated that it was essentially in agreement with the principle enunciated by the coordinate Bench. Finding a violation of the principle of natural justice, the Allahabad High Court quashed and set aside the impugned order dated May 28, 2022. The Department was left at liberty to issue a proper notice to the petitioner and act in accordance with law. The writ petition was accordingly disposed of. Cases Discussed M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others, Neutral Citation No.2024:AHC:23697-DB FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF ALLAHABAD HIGH COURT 1. Heard Sri Mukesh Kumar Tewa
rows.summary: The Allahabad High Court quashed a GST demand/order passed under Section 74 of the Uttar Pradesh GST Act, 2017 against Ved Enterprises Unnao because the only show-cause notice had been uploaded on the GST portal after the taxpayer’s registration had already been cancelled. The petitioner’s GST registration was cancelled on 16.11.2021, and the impugned order was issued on 28.05.2022 by the Deputy Commissioner, State Tax, Sector-1, District Unnao; the petitioner had not been carrying on business after cancellation. The Court held that once registration is cancelled, the taxpayer is not expected to keep checking the GST portal, so service of notice only through the portal is not adequate; the department was required to use an alternative/appropriate mode of service to ensure the notice actually reached the taxpayer. In reaching this conclusion, the Court said it agreed with the principle laid down in the coordinate-bench decision in M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others (Neutral Citation No. 2024:AHC:23697-DB), and found that failure to properly serve notice amounted to a breach of natural justice. The consequence is that the order dated 28.05.2022 was set aside, but the tax department was expressly left free to issue a fresh, proper notice and proceed in accordance with law. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that where a GST registration has been cancelled, portal-only service may be legally vulnerable, and authorities must use a service method that actually reaches the former registrant before passing adverse orders, especially under Section 74.

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court disposed of three connected writ petitions filed by Reckitt Benckiser (India) Private Limited by common order dated 24.04.2026. All three matters arose from the same GST dispute concerning the 2019–2020 tax period and, in particular, the legality of the extension of limitation under the GST laws: one petition challenged an impugned order/reply dated 29.05.2024 for the 2019–2020 period, another challenged Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023 and the consequential State/UT Government Orders issued under Section 168A of the respective GST enactments extending limitation periods, and the third challenged a show cause notice dated 31.05.2024 issued in Form GST DRC-01 for the same period.

The Court had earlier granted interim protection on 13.08.2024. After that, the jurisdictional State Tax Officer filed a detailed report dated 27.01.2026, and the Court noted that the report’s conclusion prima facie supported the petitioner’s position. In light of that report and the later developments, the Court closed the writ petitions rather than continuing the limitation challenge, effectively ending the immediate litigation on the notices and the extension issue for this assessee. The document does not set out a new general compliance rule or a fresh substantive tax rate/threshold; the material point for compliance teams is that the case concerned whether limitation could validly be extended under Section 168A through Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023 and related Government Orders, and that a Form GST DRC-01 show cause notice dated 31.05.2024 for the 2019–2020 period was part of the challenge.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court in **Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan** held that a **GST appeal rejected as time-barred** could not be shut out where the delay was attributable to **medical reasons beyond the taxpayer’s control**. The Court **set aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026** that had dismissed the petitioner’s appeal on limitation and directed the **Appellate Authority to hear and decide the appeal on merits**, but only after the petitioner makes the **required statutory payments**, including **late fees, penalty, and other admissible deposits**.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the petitioner had sought relief against the **order dated 07.02.2024** and also sought **restoration of GST registration**, showing that the dispute concerned both the underlying adverse GST action and the refusal to entertain the appeal. The Court relied on prior Rajasthan decisions, especially **M/s. Pratap Power Spares v. Union of India & Ors. (D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 9882/2024, decided 28.07.2026)**, where the Court had allowed a **99-day delay** by invoking a **120-day relaxation under Section 107 of the CGST Act**, and had directed that an appeal be entertained on merits if filed within **30 days**. The petitioner also cited **M/s. Molana Construction Company**, **Man Singh Tanwar v. Commissioner, CGST**, **RPC PSIPL JV** (two decisions), and **M/s. Kakar Automobiles**, indicating that the Court’s reasoning was consistent with a broader line of cases permitting relief from limitation where sufficient cause existed.

The practical compliance message is that, in Rajasthan High Court’s view, a GST appellate authority should not mechanically reject an appeal for delay where the taxpayer can establish **medical incapacity or similar circumstances beyond control**, but the taxpayer must still comply with the **monetary preconditions** for pursuing the appeal. The order does **not** create a blanket extension of limitation; it is a fact-specific judicial relief requiring the appellant to satisfy the authority on merits after making the prescribed deposits.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court considered a writ petition by M/s Jagdish Prasad Agrawal, a partnership firm, challenging the blocking of its Input Tax Credit (ITC) in the Electronic Credit Ledger, including an alleged blocking of IGST ITC with a negative balance. The petitioner asked the Court to declare the blocking illegal, inoperative, and void, to quash it, and to direct re-credit of any ITC unlawfully set off against the disputed demand. By the time of hearing, the blocking had already ceased automatically by operation of law after one year, and the Electronic Credit Ledger had been reactivated, so the dispute had narrowed to whether the ITC could lawfully have been blocked in the first place without following Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017.

The respondents conceded that the ledger was now operational, but they could not show that the mandatory conditions under Rule 86A had been satisfied before blocking the credit. They admitted that the action was a bona fide mistake and that, although the officer had reasons for action, no proper reasoned order had been passed and the petitioner had not been given an opportunity of hearing before the blockage. The Court specifically noted that Rule 86A requires the competent authority to have “reasons to believe” that ITC has been fraudulently availed or is ineligible, and to record those reasons in writing before disallowing debit of an equivalent amount from the Electronic Credit Ledger for payment of tax liability under section 49 or for a refund of unutilised credit. The Court found, on the record before it, that these mandatory preconditions were not complied with.

Because the restriction had already expired and the ledger had been restored, the Court did not grant further substantive relief in the petition; instead, it disposed of the matter after accepting the unconditional apology tendered on behalf of the concerned officer. However, the Court issued a clear warning for future cases: if the department blocks ITC without due compliance with Rule 86A, it may become liable to pay appropriate compensation to the affected taxpayer. For compliance purposes, the key point is that Rule 86A safeguards are mandatory before ITC blocking—specifically, a recorded written basis and proper legal satisfaction by the competent authority are required, and a failure to follow those steps can expose the department to compensation exposure and judicial censure.

rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chandigarh allowed Agilent Technologies International Pvt. Ltd.’s appeal against denial of refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Agilent was a 100% export unit providing Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas customers under service agreements and exporting those services without paying service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005; it had claimed refund of accumulated credit under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The refund amount at issue was ₹78,79,939, which the department had rejected on the ground that credit taken on General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services, and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services allegedly had no nexus with the exported output services.  

The Tribunal held that the department could not deny a Rule 5 refund by re-litigating the eligibility of credit where the availment of that CENVAT credit had never been challenged under Rule 14 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. In other words, the decision treats credit availment, its utilisation, and refund of unutilised credit as distinct issues, and says a refund objection under Rule 5 cannot be used as a substitute for an untimely or absent challenge to credit admissibility itself. The Tribunal also reiterated that, for the relevant period, the definition of “input service” under Rule 2(l) was exhaustive and that the disputed services had been accepted in various precedents as qualifying input services; it further accepted the appellant’s position that direct one-to-one nexus with the exported output services was not necessary, relying on Circular No. 120/1/2010-ST dated 19.01.2010 and case law including Reliance Corporate IT Park Ltd.  

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that exporters claiming Rule 5 refunds should retain documentation showing that the underlying credits were validly availed and not previously disputed, because the Tribunal emphasized that once the department has not invoked Rule 14 to challenge availment, it cannot later deny refund merely by questioning nexus at the refund stage. The order ultimately set aside the impugned denial and granted the refund with consequential relief, if any, as per law.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Hyderabad Sets Aside Tax on Pharma Regulatory Approval Support Services
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12613 Case Name Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Hyderabad considered an appeal by M/s Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. against an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 confirming Service Tax demands, interest and penalties principally under “Banking and Other Financial Services” and “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” for 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The first dispute concerned charges deducted by foreign/intermediary banks while export proceeds were transmitted from foreign buyers through banking channels. The appellant, a manufacture-exporter of pharmaceutical products, contended that the foreign buyers remitted consideration through their banking arrangements and that the foreign/intermediary banks deducted charges before the balance reached the appellant’s Indian bank. The Department proceeded on the basis that, because the deductions economically reduced the amount received by the appellant, the appellant was the recipient of banking services and was liable to Service Tax under Reverse Charge Mechanism. The Tribunal rejected that approach. It found no evidence that the appellant had engaged the foreign banks, entered into contractual arrangements with them, or was otherwise obliged to pay consideration to them for services rendered to it. Merely bearing the economic impact of deductions did not establish a service provider-service recipient relationship. The Tribunal also relied on the appellant’s own earlier decision, Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020,
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad set aside the Service Tax demands raised against Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. in an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 for the periods 2011-12 and up to June 2012, along with the related interest and penalties. Two categories of demand were in dispute: first, amounts deducted by foreign/intermediary banks from export remittances before the net proceeds reached the appellant’s Indian bank; and second, payments to overseas regulatory consultants for preparing clinical/non-clinical overviews and other documentation for foreign pharma product approvals.  

On the banking issue, the Tribunal held that Aurobindo was not the recipient of a taxable banking service merely because bank charges were economically borne through reduced export proceeds. The record did not show that the company had contracted with, engaged, or owed consideration to the foreign banks, so the reverse charge demand under “Banking and Other Financial Services” was unsustainable; the Tribunal also relied on its own earlier favourable order for an earlier period and the Eastman Exports decision.  

On the consultancy issue, the Tribunal rejected Revenue’s attempt to classify regulatory dossier preparation and compilation work performed by M/s DADA Consultancy and M/s Pharpe Dr. D.R. Iban as “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services.” It held that compiling already available information and published material for regulatory submissions, without independent scientific research, experimentation, technical studies, or actual advice in a scientific/technical discipline, does not become scientific/technical consultancy simply because the service providers have technical expertise or the documentation relates to scientific product particulars. The Tribunal emphasized that the true nature of the activity controls classification, and it followed the appellant’s earlier case and IPCA Laboratories Ltd. for the proposition that services connected with obtaining regulatory approvals/registrations abroad are not automatically taxable under that head.  

The order also noted that Aurobindo had already discharged Service Tax on these consultant payments under “Management or Business Consultant Service,” and the impugned order had appropriated that tax while simultaneously reclassifying the same activity under another taxable heading; once the reclassification failed, the demand could not survive. Because the substantive tax demands were set aside, the associated interest and penalties were also quashed, and the Tribunal did not separately rule on the appellant’s Section 76 penalty-computation argument tied to the amendment effective 08.04.2011.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ranjita Rajendra Bane Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Mumbai) Summary: The Customs, Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai considered the appeal filed by Ranjita Rajendra Bane, widow and successor in interest of deceased Rajendra Bane, challenging personal penalties of ₹2,50,000/- and ₹1,00,000/- imposed under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962. Rajendra Bane had been serving as a Customs Hawaldar. The penalties arose from an investigation into smuggled gold recovered from the gent’s toilet at Pune International Airport after passengers travelled from Dubai by Spice Jet Flight No. SG 52 on 16.08.2018. The allegation was that although Rajendra Bane was on sanctioned leave and staying at his native place near Ratnagiri, he had facilitated the smuggling of gold and assisted the smugglers. The material relied upon against him included statements recorded under Section 108 of the Customs Act, 1962, particularly statements of co-accused/accomplices, call records received from the telephone operator, and recovery of gold from the airport toilet and from a passenger. The defence completely denied involvement. It admitted that Rajendra Bane was on leave and at his native place on the relevant day, but contended that the seizure had actually followed information transmitted by him to the Superintendent on duty at Pune International Airport. The defence claimed that the information involved privileged communication with an informer and therefore its source could not be disclosed. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, rejected this explanation. He considered the statement
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai set aside the personal penalties of ₹2,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 imposed under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962 on late Rajendra Bane, a Customs Hawaldar, and deleted the penalties entirely for lack of proof that he knowingly aided the smuggling operation. The case arose from the recovery of smuggled gold from a men’s toilet at Pune International Airport after SpiceJet Flight SG 52 from Dubai arrived on 16.08.2018, with the Department alleging that Bane—though on sanctioned leave and at his native place near Ratnagiri—had facilitated the smuggling through statements of co-accused, call records, and the recovery of gold from the airport and a passenger.  

The Tribunal held that the Department’s case rested too heavily on accomplice/co-accused statements and that, under the evidentiary principle reflected in Section 114 illustration (b) of the Indian Evidence Act, a person cannot be implicated solely on such statements where no incriminating material was seized from him. It specifically noted that no incriminating article, including the allegedly relevant SIM card, had been recovered from Bane, and it distinguished the Commissioner (Appeals)’ reliance on the Supreme Court’s Naresh J. Sukhwani precedent as being in a materially different factual setting. The Tribunal also found weaknesses in the call-record theory: the Superintendent, Shri D.G. Nandanwar, had called Bane back and was told that the gold had been dumped in the Immigration Hall men’s lavatory, and the investigation showed calls from Bane’s son Prathmesh Rajendra Bane’s number between 03:04:03 A.M. and 05:33 A.M., whereas the CDR produced to the Superintendent for 5:00 A.M. to 6:00 A.M. did not show that number; the seizure itself occurred at 05:15 A.M.  

On the facts, the Tribunal concluded that the Department failed to establish that the later call to the Superintendent was a fabricated afterthought or that Bane was acting in connivance with the smugglers. It also rejected the adverse inference drawn by the lower authority from Bane’s alleged failure to contact another officer when the Superintendent did not answer the first call, finding that such reasoning did not overcome the absence of direct incriminating evidence. The Tribunal viewed the surrounding circumstances as more consistent with Bane having provided an actionable tip that led to recovery of more than 13 kg of smuggled gold, including about 10 kg found in the dustbin of the men’s toilet, rather than with his being part of the smuggling network. As a result, the Section 112(a) penalties were deleted in full.

The petitioner challenged the Appellate Authority’s order dated 28.02.2026 in Appeal Case No. GST/PTC-2—2025-26 and the underlying demand dated 20.08.2025 raising tax, interest and penalty of Rs. 1,63,452/-. The dispute arose for the financial year 2022-23. A notice had been issued against the petitioner under Section 73 of the CGST Act, 2017 on the basis of gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100/- received from the District Public Relations Officer, Gaya. The Adjudicating Authority subsequently imposed a liability of tax, interest and penalty amounting to Rs. 1,63,452/- on 20.08.2025. The petitioner thereafter filed an appeal under Section 107(1) of the CGST Act, 2017. The appeal was dismissed on 28.02.2026 because it was filed with a delay of 21 days. The petitioner, however, relied upon a subsequent memo issued by the Collectorate, Gaya, Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025. According to the petitioner, that communication stated that GST was not applicable to receipts against sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in the profession of Nukkad Natak and that Nukkad Natak teams comprising (4-6-8-10) members were exempted from the GST regime. Before the High Court, the petitioner therefore contended that the underlying issue was not merely
rows.summary:
The Patna High Court did **not** decide the merits of whether Nukkad Natak services are exempt from GST, but it held that the **exemption question must be examined on the merits** rather than being rejected solely as time-barred. The petitioner, **M/s Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal**, is a **GST-registered entity** engaged in **Nukkad Natak (street plays)** for public awareness programs assigned mainly by government departments; for **FY 2022–23**, it received **gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100** from the **District Public Relations Officer, Gaya**, leading to a **Section 73 CGST Act notice** and an adjudication order dated **20.08.2025** imposing **tax, interest, and penalty totaling Rs. 1,63,452**. The petitioner appealed under **Section 107(1)** of the CGST Act, but the Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on **28.02.2026** because it was filed **21 days late**.  

The petitioner relied on **Collectorate, Gaya Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025**, which allegedly stated that **GST is not applicable to receipts against sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in Nukkad Natak** and that **Nukkad Natak teams of 4–6–8–10 members are exempt from GST**; however, the State argued that this communication did not identify any statutory exemption provision or GST Council decision and that the appeal was simply out of time. The High Court treated the exemption issue as one going to the **root of tax jurisdiction** and faulted the Appellate Authority for dismissing the appeal on limitation without deciding the substantive claim. Accordingly, the Court **set aside the 28.02.2026 appellate order** and **remitted the matter back to the Appellate Authority** to decide whether the petitioner, as a registered person performing Nukkad Natak, is actually **exempt from GST liability**, in accordance with law.  

For procedure, the petitioner must **produce a copy of the High Court order and appear before the Appellate Authority within one week** for fixation of a hearing date. Upon production, the Appellate Authority must provide a **personal hearing** and dispose of the appeal **within a maximum of two months** from receipt/production of the High Court order. Compliance takeaway: this ruling does **not** create a general GST exemption for Nukkad Natak teams; it only requires the appellate forum to determine the exemption claim on its legal merits in this case.

rows.summary: This ITAT Mumbai decision concerns an AY 2014-15 penalty dispute under section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, arising from the assessee’s claim of section 54 capital gains exemption after selling a residential house for Rs.1,35,00,000 and computing long-term capital gain of Rs.72,19,588. The assessee initially claimed exemption for the full capital gain, stating that Rs.68,25,500 had been invested with M/s Damodar Suruchi Developers for a proposed residential project and Rs.10,00,000 had been deposited in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme with SBI; when the project stalled, he later entered into a compromise and purchased another residential property for Rs.49,95,000, leaving a shortfall of Rs.24,40,579 that was ultimately admitted to be taxable. The Assessing Officer taxed that Rs.24,40,579 in AY 2014-15 and imposed a penalty of Rs.5,25,923, equal to 100% of the tax sought to be evaded, and the CIT(A)/NFAC upheld the penalty on the theory that the assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars by claiming excess exemption and had not voluntarily disclosed the shortfall before scrutiny, relying on MAK Data (P.) Ltd. The Tribunal disagreed and held that, under section 54(2), the shortfall could not be taxed in AY 2014-15 because the statutory investment period had not yet expired when the original return was filed, and by the time it became clear that the full investment would not materialize, the time limit for filing a revised return under section 139(5) had already lapsed; the Tribunal also noted that a fresh purchase agreement was entered into on 28.05.2015, relevant to AY 2016-17. Although the proviso to section 54(2) technically applies to unutilised amounts in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme, the Tribunal treated the legislative intent as supporting the view that taxability arises only in the year of expiry of the prescribed period, not immediately in the original assessment year. Because the Rs.24,40,579 was held not taxable in AY 2014-15, the Tribunal found that there was no basis for alleging concealment or furnishing of inaccurate particulars for that year and deleted the entire penalty of Rs.5,25,923; the assessee’s appeal was allowed.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Remands GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A ITC Mismatch for Fresh Verification
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12609 Case Name N. R. Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GSTAT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); N. R. Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Summary: The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, allowed the appeal of M/s. N. R. Builders by way of remand in a dispute concerning alleged excess Input Tax Credit (ITC) of ₹2,33,502/- for Financial Year 2018–19. The disputed amount comprised CGST of ₹1,16,751/- and SGST of ₹1,16,751/-. Interest of ₹2,03,730/- and penalty of ₹23,350/- had also been imposed, resulting in a total demand of ₹4,60,582/-. The Appellant, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, contended that the apparent mismatch between FORM GSTR-3B and FORM GSTR-2A did not represent excess ITC. According to the Appellant, the disputed credit related to Financial Year 2017–18 invoices but was availed in Financial Year 2018–19 within the permissible period under Section 16(4). The Appellant also challenged the proceedings on the ground that no personal hearing was granted and that no notice in FORM GST ASMT-10 had preceded the proceedings. A pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A was issued on 22.01.2024, followed by a Show Cause Notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 under Section 73. The Show Cause Notice itself recorded the date, time and venue of personal hearing as “NA”. The Proper Officer subsequently confirmed the entire demand ex parte. The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal and upheld the demand. The Tribunal first considered whether the GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A difference could be treated as inadmissible ITC without examining the Appellant’s explanation concerning Financial Year 2017–18 invoices.
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, remanded a GST input tax credit dispute involving M/s. N. R. Builders, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, after setting aside both the Order-in-Original dated 20.04.2024 and the Order-in-Appeal dated 07.11.2024. The case involved an alleged excess ITC of ₹2,33,502 for FY 2018–19, split equally into CGST of ₹1,16,751 and SGST of ₹1,16,751, with related interest of ₹2,03,730 and penalty of ₹23,350, taking the total demand to ₹4,60,582. The department had issued a pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A on 22.01.2024 and then a show cause notice in FORM GST DRC-01 on 30.01.2024 under Section 73; the notice recorded the personal hearing details as “NA,” and the Proper Officer confirmed the demand ex parte. The Tribunal held that the dispute could not be resolved merely by pointing to a GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A mismatch, because the assessee’s explanation was that the credit related to FY 2017–18 invoices but was lawfully availed in FY 2018–19 within the period permitted by Section 16(4). It relied on CBIC Circular No. 183/15/2022-GST, which requires verification of such mismatches for FY 2017–18 and 2018–19 instead of automatic disallowance, and specifically found that non-appearance of an invoice in GSTR-2A does not by itself prove that the supplier failed to pay tax.

On facts, the Tribunal concluded that neither the adjudicating authority nor the first appellate authority had conducted the necessary invoice-wise verification of the appellant’s explanation, and therefore the demand could not be sustained on the existing record. It also rejected the first appellate authority’s reliance on Mahalakshmi Cotton Ginning Processing and Oil Industries v. State of Maharashtra, ALD Automotive Private Limited v. CTO, and Microqual Techno Ltd. v. State of Karnataka, holding that those cases were distinguishable because the statutory provisions and factual circumstances differed and there was no finding here that the underlying purchases were non-genuine. On natural justice, the Tribunal found a procedural defect: Section 75(4) requires an opportunity of hearing when an adverse decision is proposed, and since the notice itself showed “NA” for personal hearing and there was no evidence that any hearing was actually granted, the ex parte order was unsustainable. The Tribunal rejected the appellant’s argument that FORM GST ASMT-10 was mandatory, holding that Section 61 scrutiny and Section 73 demand proceedings are independent and that failure to issue ASMT-10 does not invalidate a directly initiated Section 73 proceeding. Interest and penalty were left to follow the outcome of the reassessment, with the Tribunal noting their dependence on the final tax determination and citing the compensatory nature of interest.

For compliance purposes, the remand order requires the Proper Officer to redo the adjudication de novo and specifically verify the ITC invoice-wise against FY 2017–18 GSTR-2A, suppliers’ GSTR-1, the assessee’s ITC register, books of account, and GSTR-9/GSTR-9C for both FY 2017–18 and FY 2018–19. The practical takeaway is that where a taxpayer claims that ITC appearing mismatched in GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A was actually eligible because it related to prior-year invoices booked and availed within the Section 16(4) time limit, the department must examine the underlying invoices and reconciliation before disallowing credit, and must also provide a genuine opportunity of hearing before confirming liability.
