(Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court has allowed the writ petition filed by Sheth Shree Karshandas Halu Dharamshala Jamnagar and quashed the order dated 19.11.2020 passed under Section 264 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, rejecting the Trust’s claim for exemption under Section 11(1A) in respect of capital gains reinvested in a fixed deposit. The petitioner, a public charitable trust registered under the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950 and under Section 12A of the Income-tax Act with effect from 01.04.2007, had sold its immovable property for Rs.4,87,50,000/- under a registered sale deed dated 11.07.2011. The entire sale proceeds were thereafter invested in a two-year Fixed Deposit Receipt with Canara Bank, Jamnagar, in accordance with the conditions imposed by the Joint Charity Commissioner. For A.Y. 2012-13, the Trust inadvertently failed to claim the exemption under Section 11(1A) for the reinvestment of the capital gains, although the capital gains were fully disclosed and tax was paid. The return was processed under Section 143(1), resulting in a demand of Rs.19,44,180/-. The Trust subsequently invoked Section 264. The High Court relied upon the principles laid down in C. Parikh & Co., Ramdev Exports and S.R. Koshti, holding that revisional jurisdiction under Section 264 is sufficiently wide to grant relief where an assessee has been over-assessed because of a mistake or omission. The fact that the assessee itself had disclosed the income in the o
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court held that a charitable trust could obtain exemption under Section 11(1A) of the Income-tax Act even though it had not claimed the exemption in its original return, and it quashed the Commissioner’s rejection of the trust’s Section 264 revision application dated 19.11.2020. The assessee, Sheth Shree Karshandas Halu Dharamshala Jamnagar, was a public charitable trust registered under the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950 and registered under Section 12A of the Income-tax Act with effect from 01.04.2007; it sold immovable property for Rs. 4,87,50,000 under a registered sale deed dated 11.07.2011 and then invested the entire sale consideration in a two-year fixed deposit receipt with Canara Bank, Jamnagar, pursuant to conditions imposed by the Joint Charity Commissioner. For A.Y. 2012-13, the trust inadvertently omitted the Section 11(1A) claim in its return, although the capital gains were fully disclosed and tax was paid, and the return was processed under Section 143(1) resulting in a tax demand of Rs. 19,44,180.

The Court accepted that Section 264 revisional jurisdiction is broad enough to grant relief where an assessee has been over-assessed because of a bona fide omission or mistake, even if the income was already disclosed in the original return. It relied on Gujarat and other precedents, including C. Parikh & Co., Ramdev Exports, S.R. Koshti, and Swaminarayan Mandir Trust, and held that the Commissioner should have examined whether the trust satisfied the substantive conditions for Section 11(1A) relief rather than refusing relief because the claim had not been made at the assessment stage. The Court specifically held that the relevant test was compliance with Section 11(1A) read with CBDT Instruction No. 883 dated 24.09.1975, and that because the sale proceeds were placed in an FDR with a scheduled bank for more than six months, the transaction qualified for the intended exemption treatment.

The Court also rejected the attempt to deny exemption by linking Section 11(1A) with Section 36(1)(a) of the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950, holding that Section 11(1A) is a standalone income-tax provision and cannot be curtailed by that state-law provision. It further held that the Supreme Court’s decision in Goetze (India) Ltd. was not controlling because that case dealt with claims before the Assessing Officer otherwise than by revised return, not the Commissioner’s powers under Section 264. Finding that the trust had acted bona fide, fully disclosed the capital gains, paid the tax, and suppressed nothing material, the Court allowed the Section 264 application, held that the trust was entitled to the Section 11(1A) exemption, and directed refund/payment of excess tax of Rs. 1,00,27,295 for A.Y. 2012-13 together with applicable interest under Section 244A, with consequential orders to be passed within four weeks. From a compliance perspective, the case reinforces that charitable trusts with qualifying reinvestment of sale proceeds should not assume a lost exemption claim is irrecoverable: if the facts and statutory conditions are satisfied, relief may still be available through revision, particularly where the omission was inadvertent and the tax position was otherwise fully disclosed.

rows.title: Income Tax | Bogus Purchases & Sales Cannot Justify Entire Purchase Addition; 5% GP Applied: Delhi ITAT
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12607 Case Name HSB Home Solutions Ltd. Vs ACIT (ITAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2012-13 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); HSB Home Solutions Ltd. Vs ACIT (ITAT Delhi) Summary: The Delhi ITAT partly allowed the assessee’s appeal for AY 2012-13. The Tribunal first upheld the validity of reassessment proceedings initiated after four years, holding that the subsequent survey conducted on 30.11.2018 revealed information regarding allegedly bogus transactions which had not been examined in the original assessment. The original assessment order itself recorded that the assessee had no business activity, despite substantial purchases, sales and disclosed profit. The Tribunal therefore found that the reopening was based on subsequent information and was not merely a change of opinion. On merits, however, the Tribunal held that the Assessing Officer could not simply treat the entire purchases of Rs.5,81,57,000/- as undisclosed income when the corresponding sales of Rs.5,94,91,966/- had also been treated as bogus. The Tribunal rejected the assessee’s contention that banking-channel transactions alone established genuineness, since physical movement of goods and existence of the parties had not been established. Considering the totality of circumstances, it directed the AO to apply a 5% gross profit rate on the turnover of Rs.5,94,91,966/-, while giving credit for the profit already disclosed by the assessee. List of Cases Discussed / Relied Upon New Delhi Television Limited v. DCIT, 424 ITR 607 (SC) Phool Chand Bajrang Lal v. ITO, 203 ITR 456 (SC) ITO v. Lakhmani Mewal Das, 103 ITR 437 (SC) High Gain Finvest (P) Ltd., 304 ITR 325 (Delhi) Raymond Woollen Mills Ltd. v. ITO, 236 ITR 34 (SC) Sanand Prop
rows.summary:
The Delhi ITAT dealt with AY 2012-13 in the case of HSB Home Solutions Ltd. and first upheld the validity of reopening under section 148 even though the notice was issued after four years from the end of the assessment year. The Tribunal accepted the Revenue’s position that the reassessment was based on fresh information from a survey conducted on 30.11.2018 under section 133A in the case of Shri Ashok Kumar Gupta and others, which allegedly exposed accommodation-entry activity through M/s Gayatri Maa Enterprise; this was not treated as a mere change of opinion because the original assessment had not examined the bogus-transaction issue and the survey material surfaced later. The original assessment record also noted that the assessee had no business activity despite reporting substantial purchases, sales, and profit, which supported the reopening.

On the merits, the Assessing Officer had treated the entire alleged bogus purchases of Rs. 5,81,57,000 as undisclosed income, and the CIT(A) upheld that full addition. The ITAT disagreed with the approach of taxing the entire purchases when the corresponding sales of Rs. 5,94,91,966 were also found to be bogus, holding that the Revenue could not simply select the purchase side for a 100% addition. At the same time, the Tribunal rejected the assessee’s argument that payments through banking channels alone proved genuineness, because the actual movement of goods and even the existence of the parties from whom purchases were allegedly made had not been established.

Instead of sustaining the full purchase disallowance, the ITAT directed the AO to apply a 5% gross profit rate on the turnover of Rs. 5,94,91,966, with credit allowed for profit already disclosed by the assessee. In practical compliance terms, the decision confirms that reassessment after four years can still be sustained where later survey material reveals previously unexamined bogus-entry activity, and it also confirms that in cases where both purchases and sales are treated as non-genuine, the tax addition should be based on a reasonable profit estimate rather than automatically adding the entire purchase figure.

The Assessing Officer/TPO had made an adjustment of Rs. 1,17,72,05,188/-, taking the position that electricity generate
rows.summary:
The Ahmedabad ITAT dismissed both Revenue appeals in **DCIT v. Nirma Limited**, being **ITA Nos. 1569 and 1570/AHD/2026**, which covered **Assessment Years 2018-19 and 2020-21** and arose from CIT(A), Ahmedabad-13 orders dated **09.02.2026** under **Section 250 of the Income-tax Act, 1961**. The Tribunal heard the matters together because they involved substantially identical issues and issued a common order on **21.08.2026**, ultimately confirming the CIT(A)’s relief to the taxpayer on every contested point.

For **AY 2018-19**, the Revenue’s challenge to deletion of **Rs. 4,09,94,465** of depreciation on **goodwill** created on amalgamation of **Saurashtra Chemicals Ltd.** was rejected; the Tribunal accepted that the issue was already covered by earlier Tribunal orders in the assessee’s own case for **AYs 2012-13 to 2016-17**. The Revenue’s challenge to deletion of **Rs. 1,73,64,613** of depreciation on **brands and names** transferred from a demerged unit was also dismissed on the same basis. The major transfer-pricing dispute for this year was the inter-unit sale of **electricity** from a captive power plant, where the AO/TPO had made an adjustment of **Rs. 1,17,72,05,188** by valuing the electricity not at the rate charged to the manufacturing unit, but at the price at which power-generating companies sell to distribution companies; the Tribunal upheld the CIT(A)’s reliance on **CIT v. Gujarat Alkalies & Chemicals Ltd. (395 ITR 247, Gujarat High Court)** and earlier assessee-favourable decisions, and sustained deletion of the adjustment.

For **AY 2020-21**, the Revenue again failed on depreciation claims: the Tribunal upheld deletion of **Rs. 97,67,598** on **brands and trade marks** transferred under demerger and **Rs. 2,30,59,386** on **goodwill** arising from the amalgamation of Saurashtra Chemicals Ltd., rejecting arguments that the intangible valuation had not attained finality and that the goodwill was artificially created. The Revenue also lost on inter-unit electricity benchmarking, where the CIT(A)’s deletion of **Rs. 20,17,23,105** was affirmed by following the Tribunal’s ruling on the AY 2018-19 issue.

The remaining substantive issue was valuation of **steam** transferred between eligible and non-eligible units for **AY 2020-21**. The AO/TPO had treated steam generated as a by-product of the captive power plant as having **nil arm’s length price** and made an adjustment of **Rs. 1,06,55,75,141**. The CIT(A) rejected that approach, relying on **Vishal Fabrics Ltd.**, **Star Paper Mill Ltd. v. DCIT (134 Taxmann.com 177 (2022))**, and **Gujarat Alkalies & Chemicals Ltd.**, holding that the fact steam is a by-product does not mean it has no cost or market value and that external market prices can be used as a benchmark if reliable data and appropriate adjustments are available. The Tribunal agreed, upheld the CIT(A)’s use of the prevailing market rate approach, and dismissed the Revenue’s ground challenging deletion of the steam adjustment.

In practical compliance terms, the order reinforces that, for this taxpayer and similar transfer-pricing fact patterns, **captive electricity and steam transfers cannot automatically be benchmarked at nil or at a generically higher external supply rate without regard to the actual inter-unit transaction and judicial precedent**, and that depreciation on **goodwill, brands, and trademarks** arising from amalgamation/demerger remains allowable where prior year rulings in the assessee’s own case have already settled the issue. The final outcome is that **both Revenue appeals were dismissed in full**.

rows.title: Income Tax | IBC Resolution Plan Bars Pending Pre-Approval Income Tax Proceedings: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12605 Case Name DCIT Vs Indusind General Insurance Company Limited (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2020-21 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT Vs Indusind General Insurance Company Limited (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai Bench, disposed of a consolidated batch comprising Revenue’s appeals for Assessment Years 2011-12 to 2018-19 and 2020-21 and the assessee’s appeals for Assessment Years 2012-13 and 2020-21. The appeals arose from orders of the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals) concerning, among other matters, disallowances relating to payments made to motor vehicle dealers. The Tribunal, however, decided the batch on a preliminary legal issue arising from a subsequent insolvency resolution process and did not adjudicate the merits of the individual additions or disallowances. The assessee, now IndusInd General Insurance Company Limited and formerly Reliance General Insurance Company Limited, was an unlisted subsidiary of Reliance Capital Limited (RCL), which held approximately 99.83% of its equity share capital during the relevant period. RCL was admitted into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The NCLT, Mumbai Bench, admitted the insolvency petition on 06.12.2021 and declared a moratorium under Section 14. A Resolution Plan submitted by IndusInd International Holdings Limited was approved by the Committee of Creditors in June 2023 and subsequently approved by the NCLT on 27.02.2024 under Section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The Income-tax Department had participated in the NCLT proceedings and had raised objections, principally concerning carry forward of losses under Section
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that once an insolvency resolution plan is approved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, pending income-tax proceedings relating to periods before the plan’s approval generally cannot be continued if the claims were not preserved in the approved plan. This ruling came in the consolidated appeals of the Revenue and the assessee (IndusInd General Insurance Company Limited, formerly Reliance General Insurance Company Limited) for Assessment Years 2011-12 to 2018-19 and 2020-21, but the Tribunal did not decide the underlying merits of the tax additions/disallowances; it disposed of the matters on the legal effect of the approved resolution plan.

The facts the Tribunal relied on were that Reliance Capital Limited, which held about 99.83% of the assessee’s equity, went into CIRP, the NCLT Mumbai admitted the insolvency petition on 06.12.2021 and imposed the Section 14 moratorium, and a resolution plan submitted by IndusInd International Holdings Limited was approved by the Committee of Creditors in June 2023 and then approved by the NCLT on 27.02.2024 under Section 31 of the IBC. The Income-tax Department had already participated in the NCLT process and objected mainly on Section 79 loss-carryforward issues, but those objections were considered and rejected. The assessee’s later name change effective 22.09.2025 did not alter the Tribunal’s analysis.

Procedurally, the Tribunal admitted additional grounds raised by the assessee and allowed the Revenue matter to be argued under Rule 27 of the ITAT Rules because the issue was a pure question of law based on undisputed later events, and no fresh fact-finding was needed. Substantively, the Tribunal placed weight on Section 31 of the IBC, which makes an approved resolution plan binding on the corporate debtor and its stakeholders, including governmental authorities, and on Clauses 9.1.8 and 9.1.9 of the approved plan. Clause 9.1.8 specifically addressed pending, threatened, present, or future tax proceedings and other proceedings relating to periods before the approval date for the corporate debtor and related entities, while Clause 9.1.9 barred governmental, judicial, and quasi-judicial authorities from acting contrary to the plan.

The Tribunal also relied on the NCLT’s approval order dated 27.02.2024, its corrective order dated 13.03.2024 clarifying that approval extended to Clauses 9.1.8 through 9.1.13, and the NCLT’s refusal to accept SEBI’s later attempt to limit relief only to Reliance Capital and exclude subsidiaries. Citing the Supreme Court’s decision in Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons and Bombay High Court decisions such as Uttam Value Steels and AMNS Gandhidham, the Tribunal held that claims not included in an approved resolution plan stand extinguished and cannot be pursued afterward. It rejected the Revenue’s reliance on S. V. Kondaskar as distinguishable because that case involved winding-up under the Companies Act, 1956, not the post-approval consequences of an IBC resolution plan. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that once a resolution plan with express tax-claim treatment is approved under the IBC, pre-approval tax proceedings against the corporate debtor covered by the plan may be barred from continuation, including proceedings involving subsidiary/affiliate periods if the plan and NCLT order expressly extend that far.

The assessee was engaged in manufacturing and trading agricultural products, principally guar gum and its by-products, Churi and Korma. During the relevant year, its factory and stock were taken over by the bank after the assessee’s Phalodi bank account became an NPA. The assessee subsequently found that its stock of guar gum had been damaged due to rain, germs, bacteria and alleged negligence while the premises remained under the bank’s possession. The damaged stock could not be sold as normal guar gum and was processed into Churi/Korma. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s valuation of the closing stock and adopted an NRV of Rs. 82.58 per kg based on an internet website, resulting in an addition of Rs. 2,79,03,981/-. The assessee contended that it had consistently followed Accounting Standard-2 (AS-2), under which inventories are valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. TaxGuru’s publication on AS-2 confirms that inventories are required to be valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value and explains that the cost may not be recoverable where inventories are damaged or their selling prices have declined. [Accounting Standard 2: ‘Valuation of Inventory’](htt
rows.summary:
For Assessment Year 2017–18, the ITAT Jodhpur dismissed the Revenue’s appeal in **ITO v. Varsha Mills** and upheld deletion of two major additions: **₹2,79,03,981** relating to alleged undervaluation of damaged guar gum stock and **₹3,36,49,500** added under **Section 69A** for cash deposits made during the demonetization period. The assessee was in the business of manufacturing and trading agricultural products, mainly guar gum and its by-products Churi and Korma; its Phalodi account had turned into an NPA, the bank took possession of the factory and residential premises on **29.09.2016**, and the stock was allegedly damaged by rain, germs, bacteria, and lack of proper care while in the bank’s possession. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s closing stock valuation and substituted a market-based **net realisable value (NRV) of ₹82.58 per kg** sourced from an internet website, but the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position that under **Accounting Standard 2 (AS-2)** inventories are valued at the **lower of cost and NRV**, and that damaged inventory must be written down rather than valued as normal stock. The Tribunal also relied on the fact that the damaged guar gum had actually been processed into **Churi/Korma** and sold for **₹2,02,69,593**, with that amount already offered to tax, so the stock addition was not sustainable.  

On the Section 69A issue, the disputed cash deposits were made in Mumbai bank accounts during **09.11.2016 to 25.11.2016**, and the Revenue objected because the assessee had a Phalodi account and questioned why cash from Phalodi sales was deposited elsewhere. The assessee explained that because the Phalodi account had become an NPA and the premises had been taken over, he and his family had shifted to Mumbai and therefore deposited the cash there instead. The Tribunal accepted this explanation and, importantly for compliance purposes, noted that the cash deposits were already recorded in the audited books as **cash sales**, supported by **sale bills, delivery challans, the sale register, and the stock register** produced before the Assessing Officer. Because the cash receipts had been duly recorded in the regular books and the related income had already been offered to tax, the same money could not be taxed again as unexplained under **Section 69A** absent contrary evidence. The practical takeaway is that properly documented, recorded cash sales—especially in exceptional circumstances like bank possession, relocation, and demonetization-era banking constraints—were sufficient here to defeat an unexplained-money addition, while damaged inventory supported by accounting policy, audit disclosure, and evidence of actual disposal at reduced value was also protected from arbitrary revaluation.

rows.summary:
For Assessment Year 2013-14, the Delhi ITAT disposed of cross appeals filed by both the assessee, Acme Cleantech Solutions Pvt. Ltd., and the Revenue, arising from transfer-pricing adjustments and a section 14A disallowance. The assessee had filed its return on 30.11.2013 declaring total income of INR 23,85,28,970, and because it had international transactions with associated enterprises, the matter was referred to the Transfer Pricing Officer. The TPO proposed total transfer-pricing adjustments of INR 60,57,12,301, made up of INR 47,52,09,333 for loans, INR 11,02,91,500 for the manufacturing segment, and INR 2,02,11,468 for receivables; the Assessing Officer then added the full TP adjustment plus INR 3,14,18,961 under section 14A, resulting in assessed income of INR 87,56,60,232.

The key ruling for compliance purposes concerns foreign-currency intercompany loans: the TPO had benchmarked the loan interest using SBI PLR of 12.6% even though the assessee had charged actual interest of 6.5% to 9.5%, while the CIT(A) directed that the correct benchmark was LIBOR plus 300 basis points. The Tribunal upheld that approach, following its own earlier decisions for AYs 2011-12 and 2012-13 and relying on the principle that where the loans are repayable in US dollars, LIBOR is the appropriate reference rate rather than an Indian rupee lending rate like SBI PLR. In practical terms, the order confirms that for foreign-currency loans between AEs, interest benchmarking should be based on LIBOR plus 300 bps, not domestic prime lending rates, and this standard was applied to the facts of this case for AY 2013-14.

The Tribunal ultimately dismissed both appeals and left the CIT(A)’s decision undisturbed. The document does not state any new statutory deadline or prospective compliance date; instead, it is a case-law determination that reinforces how transfer-pricing teams should benchmark cross-border intra-group loans denominated in foreign currency.

rows.summary:
The ITAT Delhi in **Addl. CIT vs. PNB Gilts Ltd.** dismissed the Revenue’s appeal for **Assessment Years 2012-13 and 2013-14** and upheld the relief granted by the CIT(A). For **AY 2012-13**, the Assessing Officer had made three major additions/disallowances: **₹4.26 crore under Section 14A read with Rule 8D**, **₹30.61 lakh under Section 36(1)(iii)**, and **₹6.56 crore** for alleged diminution in the market value of securities held as stock-in-trade. The Tribunal held that PNB Gilts, an **RBI-registered NBFC and Primary Dealer**, held the securities in question as **stock-in-trade in its ordinary securities-trading business**, and it had **interest-free funds of ₹577.64 crore**, which were far in excess of the investments/securities linked to exempt income. Because of that funding position, the Tribunal accepted the presumption that the investments were made out of interest-free funds, and it emphasized that a **proper, reasoned satisfaction** is required before Rule 8D can be applied; the Section 14A disallowance was therefore deleted.

The Tribunal also rejected the **₹30.61 lakh disallowance under Section 36(1)(iii)** on the ground that the borrowings were used for business purposes and the same interest cost could not effectively be disallowed again on a duplicative basis. On the securities valuation issue, the Tribunal accepted that the assessee had consistently valued securities at **cost or market value, whichever is lower**, in line with **RBI guidelines and accepted accounting principles**. On that basis, the **₹6.56 crore diminution** was treated as a legitimate **valuation loss on stock-in-trade**, not an unascertained provision, and was therefore allowable.

For compliance purposes, the decision is significant for financial-sector entities holding securities as stock-in-trade because it reinforces that **Section 14A/Rule 8D cannot be applied mechanically** and requires documented satisfaction by the Assessing Officer, while also supporting the position that **adequate interest-free funds can rebut interest disallowance assumptions**. It further confirms that, where RBI/recognized accounting norms are followed consistently, **mark-to-market diminution on stock-in-trade securities may be deductible as a real trading loss** rather than disallowed as a provision.

rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur restored the charitable trust’s applications for registration under section 12AB and approval under section 80G(5) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, after the Commissioner of Income-tax (Exemption), Jaipur had rejected them on the ground that the trust did not produce Rajasthan Public Trust Act, 1959 (RPT Act) registration or satisfactorily prove that it was exempt from that requirement. The trust, Veera Devi Ramchandra Jhanwar Charitable Trust, is a public charitable trust created by deed dated 11.11.2011 and earlier held registration under section 12AA from 11.11.2011 pursuant to an order dated 22.02.2012. Its stated charitable activity is operating “Veera Seva Sadan Dharamshala” at P.B.M. Hospital, Bikaner, to provide accommodation and related support to poor and needy patients and their attendants, on a “No Profit No Loss” basis with only subsidised room/user charges.

During the 12AB/80G proceedings, the CIT(E) specifically called for RPT Act registration or proof of exemption under the RPT Act. The trust argued that section 77(1) of the RPT Act exempted it because of the manner of administration and governmental control over the Dharamshala. The CIT(E) nevertheless denied both the 12AB registration application and the 80G(5) approval. On appeal, the Tribunal did not finally decide the exemption issue itself; instead, it set aside the rejection and restored the matter to the file of the CIT(E) for a fresh examination of whether the trust falls within the section 77(1) exemption from RPT Act registration. The practical compliance point is that the trust’s tax registration/approval cannot be denied solely on the earlier record without a proper determination of the RPT Act exemption question, and the CIT(E) must re-adjudicate that issue before deciding the 12AB and 80G applications.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative & Judicial Developments
rows.desc: Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative and Judicial Developments – Period covered: September 2025 to September 2026 Summary: The period from September 2025 to September 2026 witnessed substantial changes in India’s GST framework across legislation, tax rates, refunds, return filing, appellate remedies and judicial interpretation. The Finance Act, 2026 amended provisions governing post-supply discounts, credit notes, provisional refunds and appellate arrangements, while omitting Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act concerning intermediary services. Commencement differs across provisions, and the amendments to Sections 15, 34 and 54 of the CGST Act await notification. Rate rationalisation was completed through the withdrawal of compensation cess and migration of specified tobacco and pan masala products to the 40 per cent slab. Risk-based provisional refunds were expanded, GSTAT benches became operational and revised limitation dates were prescribed for legacy appeals. The return architecture increasingly requires verification and reconciliation before filing, supported by GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B and the Invoice Management System. Judicial developments clarified buyer exposure where suppliers fail to deposit tax, statutory timelines for detention orders and the prospective application of penalty-related pre-deposit requirements. With the 57th GST Council meeting scheduled for 12 September 2026, further proposals concerning ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds and small-business compliance remain under consideration but cannot be treated as operative law until formally implemented. The twelve months preceding the 57th meeting of the GST Council have produced the densest concentration of change since the levy was introduced in July 2017. Three distinct layers moved at once. The rate architecture recommended by the 56th Council was completed with the withdrawal of compensation cess and the migration of tobacco and pan mas
rows.summary:
This review covers GST developments in India from September 2025 to September 2026 and notes that the most significant changes came through the Finance Act, 2026, rate rationalisation measures, expanded refund and appellate processes, and several important court rulings. The Finance Act, 2026 amended the GST law on post-supply discounts, credit notes, provisional refunds, and appellate arrangements, and also omitted Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act relating to intermediary services; however, the document states that the amendments to Sections 15, 34, and 54 of the CGST Act are not yet operative and will take effect only when notified. It also highlights that the rate structure was completed by withdrawing compensation cess and moving specified tobacco and pan masala products into the 40% GST slab, which is a material change for businesses dealing in those products.

On refunds, the period saw an expansion of risk-based provisional refunds, meaning taxpayers in relevant risk categories may receive provisional refunds under a more structured, risk-based framework rather than the earlier narrower approach. On the returns side, the filing architecture is becoming more verification-heavy: taxpayers are expected to reconcile and validate data before filing, with GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B, and the Invoice Management System playing a larger role in checking inward and outward supply data and reducing mismatches. The document also notes that GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) benches became operational and that revised limitation dates were prescribed for legacy appeals, so taxpayers with older disputes need to check whether new filing deadlines apply to them.

The judicial developments summarized in the document are also compliance-relevant. Courts clarified that buyers can face exposure where suppliers fail to deposit tax, so input tax credit and vendor compliance monitoring remain critical. The document also says courts addressed statutory timelines for detention orders and held that penalty-related pre-deposit requirements apply prospectively, which affects how pending and future disputes should be handled. Finally, the document flags that the 57th GST Council meeting was scheduled for 12 September 2026 and that proposals concerning ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds, and small-business compliance were under consideration, but none of those proposals should be treated as binding law unless and until formally implemented.

rows.title: CA, CS, CMA | How Underpriced Audits Weaken Anti-Corruption Controls
rows.desc: Summary: Audits are a quiet but essential safeguard for bank deposits, investments, provident funds, companies and cooperative societies. However, the effectiveness of this safeguard is being weakened by declining real audit fees, market concentration and inadequate time for completing complex assignments. Between FY2018 and FY2023, the market value of Nifty 500 companies reportedly increased by about 92%, while their audit fees rose by only 28%. At the same time, six large audit networks handle around two-thirds of Nifty 500 companies, concentrating both influence and systemic risk. The problem is even sharper in cooperative societies, rural branches and local bodies, where auditors may have only a few days to examine cash-heavy, paper-based records. Professional restrictions also affect smaller practitioners: chartered accountants are generally restricted from undertaking business activities without ICAI permission, while the revised tax-audit ceiling treats assignments of widely different sizes as one audit each. Strengthening audit as an anti-corruption mechanism requires disclosure of the actual time available for an audit, scrutiny of abnormally low fees, development of capable mid-sized firms, risk- and complexity-based audit ceilings, and fair remuneration and timelines for rural and cooperative audits. Higher fees alone cannot guarantee quality, but persistent underpricing, rushed work, market concentration and conflicted incentives can collectively weaken independence and reduce the depth of scrutiny. N U M B E R S T E L L S T O R I E S The Underpriced Watchman Why fixing audit is one of the simplest ways to fight corruption — from an auditor’s chair Your salary lands in a bank. Your savings sit in a fixed deposit, a mutual fund, maybe a cooperative society your family has trusted for years. Your provident fund is invested in companies you have never heard of. The company you work for reports its numbers every year, and your job depends on those numbers be
rows.summary:
The document argues that audit is a critical anti-corruption safeguard for bank deposits, investments, provident funds, companies, and cooperative societies, but that this safeguard is being weakened by underpriced audit fees, high market concentration, and insufficient time for completing complex work. It cites FY2018 to FY2023 data showing that the market value of Nifty 500 companies reportedly rose by about 92%, while audit fees increased only 28%, implying that audit remuneration has lagged far behind the growth in scale and complexity of the entities being audited. It also states that six large audit networks now audit roughly two-thirds of Nifty 500 companies, creating concentration risk and making the audit market more systemically important.

The document highlights that the pressure is even more severe in cooperative societies, rural branches, and local bodies, where auditors may have only a few days to review cash-heavy, paper-based records. It does not describe a new law being imposed, but it identifies compliance-relevant gaps and calls for specific reforms: firms and regulators should disclose the actual time available for an audit, scrutinize unusually low audit fees, and move toward risk- and complexity-based audit ceilings rather than treating all assignments as equivalent. It also notes that small and mid-sized practitioners face structural constraints, including professional restrictions on chartered accountants undertaking business activities without ICAI permission and the current tax-audit ceiling that counts assignments of very different sizes as one audit each.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that low fees and compressed timelines should be treated as red flags because they can impair audit independence and depth of scrutiny even if the audit formally occurs. The document recommends fairer remuneration and realistic timelines for rural and cooperative audits, plus development of stronger mid-sized audit firms to reduce overreliance on the largest networks. No specific new statutory deadline is set in the document, but the substantive compliance message is that audit quality controls should account for actual audit effort, fee adequacy, concentration risk, and assignment complexity rather than relying on nominal audit completion alone.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaulting Sellers
rows.desc: Why Does the GST Department Chase Bona Fide Buyers Under Section 16(2)(c) Instead of Defaulting Sellers Under Section 76? Summary: Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act makes a recipient’s entitlement to Input Tax Credit conditional upon the tax charged by the supplier having actually been paid to the government. Consequently, even a bona fide buyer who possesses a genuine invoice, receives the goods or services, pays the entire consideration including GST and files returns correctly may be required to reverse ITC if the supplier defaults. Section 76, however, independently empowers the GST department to recover tax collected but not deposited from the person who collected it, together with applicable interest and penalty. Despite this direct remedy, enforcement action is frequently taken against compliant buyers because they are easier to trace, possess identifiable assets and remain active within the GST system, whereas defaulting suppliers may have closed operations, disappeared or operated through shell entities. Automated GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch identification also makes buyer-side proceedings administratively easier than investigation and recovery against sellers. The Supreme Court’s decision in Bhandari Scrap Traders upheld the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), recognising ITC as a statutory benefit subject to legislative conditions, including supplier payment of tax. Nevertheless, questions of fairness and enforcement sequencing remain. A balanced approach would prioritise recovery under Section 76 from the defaulting supplier and reserve ITC denial for transactions involving collusion, fraud or failure to establish genuineness. Until legislation or binding precedent clarifies the sequencing of these provisions, buyers should maintain comprehensive evidence of supplier verification, invoices, receipt of supplies, e-way bills, transport records, banking payments and return reconciliation. Anyone who has dealt with a GST department notice in the las
rows.summary:
The document explains that under **Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act**, a buyer’s entitlement to **input tax credit (ITC)** depends not only on having a valid invoice, receiving the goods or services, and paying the consideration including GST, but also on the **supplier actually remitting the tax to the government**. As a result, even a bona fide purchaser who has complied with its own filing and payment obligations can be forced to **reverse ITC** if the seller defaults on deposit of the tax.

It contrasts that with **Section 76**, which gives the GST department a direct recovery route against the person who **collected tax but did not pay it over**, including recovery of the unpaid tax along with **interest and penalty**. The article’s core criticism is that, despite this direct remedy against the defaulting seller, authorities often pursue the **buyer** instead because buyers are usually easier to locate, have traceable assets, remain active in the GST system, and are more readily flagged through automated **GSTR-2B / GSTR-3B mismatch** checks, while defaulting suppliers may have shut down, vanished, or operated through shell entities.

It notes that the **Supreme Court in Bhandari Scrap Traders** upheld the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), treating ITC as a **statutory benefit subject to legislative conditions**, including supplier payment of tax. However, the document says fairness and sequencing remain unresolved: in its view, the better policy would be to **first pursue recovery from the defaulting supplier under Section 76** and only deny ITC to the buyer where there is **collusion, fraud, or a failure to prove the transaction is genuine**.

There are **no new effective dates, deadlines, or numerical thresholds** in the text. The practical compliance takeaway is that buyers should preserve strong contemporaneous evidence showing they exercised due diligence and that the transaction was real, including **supplier verification records, invoices, proof of receipt of goods or services, e-way bills, transport documents, banking/payment records, and reconciliation of returns**.

rows.title: Income Tax | Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS 2026)
rows.desc: Summary: The Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS) provides a one-time, time-bound route for eligible taxpayers to declare specified foreign assets and foreign income omitted from earlier returns. The Scheme operates under Chapter IV of the Finance Act, 2026, comprising sections 130 to 144, together with the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers–Disclosure Scheme Rules, 2026. Form 1 may be filed electronically up to 31 December 2026. Section 133 creates two separate declaration routes: Row 1 covers undisclosed foreign assets or foreign income, subject to an aggregate ceiling of ₹1 crore and payment equal to 30% tax plus an amount equal to 100% of that tax, producing an effective burden of 60%; Row 2 covers specified foreign assets acquired from foreign income earned while non-resident or from income already offered to tax but omitted from Schedule FA, subject to a ₹5 crore ceiling and a flat ₹1 lakh fee. Rule 3 prescribes valuation as on 31 March 2026, including special rules for foreign bank accounts, sold assets, reinvestment and currency conversion. Rule 5 operationalises electronic filing and provides a 20% valuation-variance safeguard for assets other than bank accounts. The Scheme also prescribes Forms 2 to 4 for determination, payment intimation and certification. Full and timely payment is essential for immunity under the Black Money Act; false particulars, excluded cases, excess-value declarations and payment defaults may invalidate or bar relief. Who can declare (eligibility) 3.1 Residential status (section 131) 3.2 Grounds for declaration (section 132) 3.3 Who is excluded (section 140) 4. Section 133 — “Amount payable by declarant” (the core) Row 1 (Sl. No. 1) — Genuinely undisclosed money Row 2 (Sl. No. 2) — Clean money, just not reported 5. Why pay tax even if I’m voluntarily declaring? 6. Rule 5 — Declaration of asset/income located outside Indi
rows.summary:
The Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS) is a one-time, time-bound disclosure window for eligible taxpayers to voluntarily report specified foreign assets and foreign income that were omitted from earlier returns. It is created under Chapter IV of the Finance Act, 2026, specifically sections 130 to 144, and is implemented through the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers–Disclosure Scheme Rules, 2026. The prescribed declaration is Form 1, which must be filed electronically on or before 31 December 2026.

The scheme has two distinct declaration tracks under section 133, each with different eligibility and payment consequences. Under Row 1, a declarant may disclose undisclosed foreign assets or foreign income, but only if the aggregate value does not exceed ₹1 crore; the amount payable is 30% tax plus an additional amount equal to 100% of that tax, resulting in an effective burden of 60% of the disclosed amount. Under Row 2, a declarant may report specified foreign assets acquired from foreign income earned while the person was non-resident, or from income that was already offered to tax but was not reported in Schedule FA; this route is available only up to an aggregate ceiling of ₹5 crore and requires payment of a flat ₹1 lakh fee.

Valuation is governed by Rule 3, which requires foreign assets and income to be valued as on 31 March 2026, with special valuation rules for foreign bank accounts, assets that have been sold, assets that have been reinvested, and currency conversion. Rule 5 sets out the electronic filing process and includes a 20% valuation-variance safeguard for assets other than bank accounts. The scheme also uses Forms 2 to 4 for determination of the amount payable, intimation of payment, and certification.

From a compliance perspective, timely and complete payment is critical because relief under the Black Money Act depends on full compliance with the scheme requirements. False particulars, declarations by excluded persons or in excluded cases, declarations that exceed the applicable value limits, and payment defaults can invalidate the declaration or bar the taxpayer from receiving immunity or other relief. Although the scheme is framed as a disclosure opportunity, it is not a blanket amnesty: eligibility, asset classification, valuation, and payment conditions all have to be satisfied exactly for the declaration to be effective.

rows.summary:
This ITAT Jodhpur decision concerns **Urban Improvement Trust, Pali’s application in Form 10AB for renewal/continuation of registration under sections 12A/12AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961**, for the **assessment year 2026-27**. The **Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Jaipur** had rejected the application by order dated **20.03.2026**, mainly because (1) the Form 10AB was said to be incomplete and (2) the Trust had **not produced registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, 1959**. The CIT(E) relied on **section 12AB(1)(b)(i)** and took the view that compliance with other laws relevant to the institution’s objects had to be verified.

The Tribunal held that **non-registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act cannot by itself be used to deny renewal under section 12AB**, especially where the applicant is not an ordinary private trust but a **statutory public authority / urban improvement trust constituted under State law**. The assessee argued, and the Tribunal accepted as legally relevant, that **section 77 of the Rajasthan Public Trust Act** excludes from that Act’s application any public trust administered by an agency acting under the control of the State Government or by a local authority. In other words, the CIT(E) had to first examine the Trust’s **actual legal character and whether the Rajasthan Public Trust Act applied to it at all** before treating the absence of that registration as a disqualifying factor.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that **renewal/continuation under sections 12A/12AB should not be refused solely for failure to obtain Rajasthan Public Trust Act registration when the applicant is a state-created/local-authority-controlled statutory body**. The Tribunal’s ruling requires the tax authority to assess the institution’s statutory status and the applicability of other laws in context, rather than applying a blanket adverse inference from the absence of such registration. The order therefore supports continued exemption-regime registration for qualifying statutory urban development bodies, subject to the usual tax-law requirements, and limits the use of non-compliance with the Rajasthan Public Trust Act as an automatic bar.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12598 Case Name Mewar University Vs ITO (Exemption) (ITAT Jodhpur) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2017-18 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Jodhpur Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Mewar University Vs ITO (Exemption) (ITAT Jodhpur) Summary: The Jodhpur Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by Mewar University for Assessment Year 2017-18 and directed deletion of an addition of ₹26,50,000 representing corpus contributions. The dispute arose because the University had claimed exemption under section 10(23C)(vi), while the Assessing Officer and CIT(A) considered the specific exemption contemplated under section 11(1)(d) unavailable under that provision for the relevant year. Mewar University, Chittorgarh, was constituted under the Mewar University Act, 2009 enacted by the Rajasthan State Legislature. It was registered under section 12AA and also had approval under section 10(23C)(vi). It filed its return for AY 2017-18 declaring nil income. Assessment under section 143(3) was completed on 30.12.2019 determining total income at ₹15,61,58,900 after various additions and disallowances. The CIT(A) granted relief on the other substantive issues, but sustained the addition relating to the corpus contribution of ₹26,50,000. The disputed amount consisted of two donations: ₹1,50,000 received from Shri Ramesh Chandra Baser through NEFT and ₹25,00,000 received from Mundra International through cheque. Confirmations from the donors were furnished and specifically stated that the contributions were towards the corpus of the University. The Assessing Officer took the view that because the assessee had claimed exemption under section 10(23C)(vi), rather than under section 11, there was no question of allowing the corpus contrib
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur allowed Mewar University’s appeal for AY 2017-18 and deleted an addition of ₹26,50,000 treated by the tax authorities as taxable income, holding that corpus donations do not become taxable merely because the university was claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(vi) rather than section 11(1)(d). The university, established under the Mewar University Act, 2009, was registered under section 12AA and also had approval under section 10(23C)(vi); it filed a nil-return for the year, and its assessment under section 143(3) was completed on 30.12.2019 at total income of ₹15,61,58,900 after various additions and disallowances.  

The disputed receipts were two specific donations totaling ₹26,50,000: ₹1,50,000 from Shri Ramesh Chandra Baser via NEFT and ₹25,00,000 from Mundra International by cheque. The university produced donor confirmations stating that both payments were made specifically toward the corpus of the university, but the Assessing Officer and then the CIT(A) sustained the addition on the reasoning that the corpus exemption expressly mentioned in section 11(1)(d) was not available where the assessee was claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(vi).  

The Tribunal rejected that approach and directed deletion of the addition, effectively confirming that, on these facts, a corpus donation does not lose its character as a corpus contribution simply because the institution’s exemption claim is under section 10(23C)(vi). For compliance purposes, the key point is that institutions with approval under section 10(23C)(vi) should still be able to defend corpus receipts as non-taxable if they can substantiate that the donations were earmarked for corpus through proper donor confirmations and supporting banking records. The decision concerns AY 2017-18 and addresses the tax treatment of earmarked capital/corpus gifts to an educational institution, not a general change in filing or registration requirements.

rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai dealt with two linked appeals by the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON) against orders dated 30.03.2026 passed by the Commissioner of Income-tax (Exemptions), Mumbai, which had rejected ISKCON’s applications for renewal of its section 12AB registration and its section 80G approval. Because the section 80G approval depended on the section 12AB registration, the Tribunal treated the 80G matter as consequential and first examined the 12AB issue. ISKCON was already registered as a charitable institution under section 12A since 11.06.1975 and had held section 80G approval since 16.01.1971; the Tribunal noted that its objects and activities had not changed and that it operates more than 270 centres across India.

The CIT(E) had characterized several of ISKCON’s activities—such as meditation camps, scriptural courses, devotional books and articles, satvik food distribution, broadcasting and royalty income, agriculture and farm operations, and accommodation—as falling under the residuary limb of section 2(15) (“advancement of any other object of general public utility”). On that basis, he applied the proviso to section 2(15) and used selected data from the ISKCON Juhu centre to conclude that the institution was engaged in activities that allegedly took it outside charitable status. The Tribunal rejected that approach, holding that these activities were part of ISKCON’s religious/charitable work and that the CIT(E) had not shown any material change in ISKCON’s objects or core functioning that would justify denial of renewal. It also indicated that selective reliance on a single centre’s data was not a proper basis for refusing registration renewal when the organization’s overall record and nationwide activities were being ignored.

As a result, the ITAT set aside the order rejecting section 12AB registration renewal and, because the 80G issue was dependent on the registration issue, granted renewal of section 80G approval as well. For compliance purposes, the ruling preserves ISKCON’s charitable registration/approval status and confirms that the listed activities, on the facts presented, did not justify treating the organization as non-charitable or applying the section 2(15) proviso in a way that would block renewal. The document does not specify a separate future compliance deadline; the operative dates are the CIT(E)’s rejection orders on 30.03.2026 and the Tribunal’s corrective decision restoring the renewals.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); TPJ Carriers Theppala House Vs State of Karnataka (Karnataka High Court) Summary: The Karnataka High Court considered a writ petition filed by M/s. TPJ Carriers, owner of a 14-wheeler tanker bearing No. KL-40/S-7040, which had been hired by M/s. SVP Petro Products for transporting bulk bitumen. The conveyance was intercepted by the State GST Authorities and proceedings were initiated under Section 129(3) of the CGST/KSGST Act, 2017. A penalty of Rs.23,86,590/- was imposed. The petitioner, being the transporter, contended that it was entitled to release of the conveyance on payment of Rs.1,00,000/-. The Court noted that this was the lesser amount contemplated under the first proviso to Section 129(6), and recorded that the petitioner had paid the said amount. The petitioner’s grievance was that although approximately two and a half months had elapsed after the penalty order, the authorities had taken no action for sale of the seized goods. The respondents submitted that the goods had not been brought to sale because the period for filing an appeal might not have expired. The Court examined Section 129(6), which provides that where the person transporting the goods or the owner fails to pay the penalty within fifteen days from receipt of the order under Section 129(3), the detained or seized goods or conveyance become liable to be sold or otherwise disposed of for recovery of the penalty. The first proviso provides for release of the conveyance upon payment by the transporter of the penalty or one lakh rupees, whichever is less. The second proviso permits re
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court held that hazardous goods seized under GST enforcement may be sold by the authorities under section 129(6) after the required notice process, rather than being left in custody indefinitely. The case arose after a transporter paid ₹1 lakh, and the court directed the authorities to proceed with sale of the hazardous seized goods in accordance with section 129(6), indicating that the enforcement mechanism can extend to disposal/sale where the goods are hazardous and continued retention would be impractical or unsafe.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that seizure of hazardous goods does not necessarily mean they will remain stored until a prolonged adjudication is completed; instead, authorities may move to sale after issuing notice under the statute. This decision is relevant to taxpayers, transporters, and logistics operators handling hazardous consignments under GST because it underscores the need to respond promptly to detention/seizure notices, address any demanded payment or penalty exposure quickly, and recognize that the goods themselves may be liquidated by the department if statutory procedures are followed. No broader rate, deadline, or industry-wide threshold is stated in the summary beyond the ₹1 lakh payment noted in the case.

rows.title: Income Tax | GP Rate Cannot Be Uniform Across Pre and Post Survey Periods: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12595 Case Name GRP Auto Vs JCIT (ITAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2010-11 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); GRP Auto Vs JCIT (ITAT Delhi) Summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Delhi Bench “F”, allowed the appeal filed by GRP Auto for Assessment Year 2010-11 and deleted the addition of Rs. 1,08,51,505 made by the Assessing Officer by adopting a differential gross profit rate. The Tribunal also held that rejection of the assessee’s books of account under section 145(3) of the Act was not justified. The assessee, a firm engaged in trading auto parts, filed its return for AY 2010-11 declaring total income of Rs. 4,36,31,310. It belonged to a group of concerns engaged in manufacturing and trading auto parts and had made major purchases from sister concerns, including Swiss Auto Products, Swiss Lamps Pvt. Ltd., Swiss Auto Pvt. Ltd., Swiss Devices (1) and Taruna Auto Pvt. Ltd. A survey under section 133A was conducted at the assessee’s business premises on 21-01-2010. Following discrepancies noticed during the survey, the assessee declared additional income of Rs. 1,15,16,100 towards excess cash, Rs. 1,75,98,542 towards excess stock and Rs. 2,27,29,200 towards undisclosed investment in furniture and fixtures, aggregating to Rs. 5,18,43,842. The assessee incorporated the excess-stock amount of Rs. 1,75,98,542 in its profit and loss account under “Sales and Other Income”. After considering that amount, its gross profit worked out to Rs. 8,42,95,900, or 10.79%. The Assessing Officer, however, treated the excess-stock surrender as income from other sources and excluded it while computing the business gross profit. The resulting gross profit was Rs. 6,66,97,358, representing 8.53% of turnover. T
rows.summary: The ITAT Delhi held that the Assessing Officer could not reject the taxpayer’s books of account under Section 145(3) merely to make a gross profit (“GP”) addition on an ad hoc basis, and it deleted the GP addition made in this case. The key point of the ruling is that a GP rate cannot be mechanically applied as a uniform benchmark across pre-survey and post-survey periods without proper justification and factual support, so an assessment cannot rest solely on a generalized rate comparison. For compliance purposes, this means tax authorities must have a defensible basis before discarding books or imposing estimated profit adjustments, and companies should preserve books, inventory records, and supporting explanations for any margin changes around survey periods to rebut arbitrary GP extrapolations. No new statutory rate, threshold, filing deadline, or procedural change was announced in the document itself; the significance is the limitation it places on ad hoc profit estimation and the need for evidence-based assessments under Section 145(3).

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pankaj Kumar Singhal Vs Shailendra Ajmera (Karnataka High Court) Summary: The petitioner, who is the Resolution Professional of Byju’s K3 Education Private Limited (Byju’s K3), approached the High Court seeking, inter alia, setting aside of the order dated 13.08.2026 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench in I.A. No. 768/2026 in C.P. (IB) No. 29/2025, and quashing of the public announcement dated 02.08.2026 concerning sale of certain assets at IndoSpace Logistics Complex, Bommasandra, Bengaluru. The petitioner apprehended that Respondent No.1, being the Resolution Professional of Think and Learn Private Limited, a subsidiary or related company of Byju’s K3, was proposing to sell properties allegedly belonging to Byju’s K3, which could adversely affect the insolvency resolution process being conducted by the petitioner. The High Court noted that the matter was already seized of by the National Company Law Tribunal and that the assets of both companies were in the custody of the Tribunal. The Court therefore held that the petitioner should pursue the matter before the NCLT and that parallel proceedings could not be initiated before the High Court, particularly when the dispute was between two Resolution Professionals. The writ petition was accordingly disposed of by reserving liberty to the petitioner to move the pending proceedings before the NCLT on 20.08.2026 and directing the NCLT to take up the matter and pass appropriate orders. The High Court further permitted the petitioner to produce documents that subsequently came into his possession
rows.summary:
The document reports a Karnataka High Court order in a corporate insolvency dispute involving Byju’s, where the court declined to continue parallel proceedings against the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and instead directed the NCLT to promptly hear and decide the Resolution Professional’s application concerning the proposed sale of the company’s “K3 assets.” The key issue is whether those assets were already sold under an earlier process or whether the Resolution Professional can lawfully proceed with the proposed sale; the article indicates the assets are “allegedly” subject to dispute, which makes their ownership/status central to any transaction. For compliance purposes, the practical implication is that any contemplated sale, transfer, or related action involving these assets should be treated as legally uncertain until the NCLT rules, because the High Court has pushed the matter back to the insolvency forum rather than adjudicating it itself.

The order does not announce a new statutory rule, threshold, fee, or general compliance deadline. Instead, it imposes a procedural direction: the NCLT must consider the Resolution Professional’s request expeditiously, meaning parties affected by the insolvency proceedings should monitor the tribunal case closely and be prepared for a quick decision that could authorize, restrict, or invalidate a proposed asset sale. If a corporate compliance team is involved with the borrower, resolution process, bidders, or creditors, it should ensure no transaction steps assume clear title to the K3 assets until the tribunal’s decision is issued and any resulting legal constraints are reviewed.

The Department classified these activities under “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994. In appeal no. ST/20226/2014, the dispute covered the period from 2007-08 to 2011-12 and involved Service Tax of Rs. 5,15,53,520/- along with interest and penalties. Appeal no. ST/30531/2016 concerned the period April 2012 to June 2012 and involved Service Tax of Rs. 2,06,792/- along with interest and penalties. The Commissioner (Appeals), in the latter appeal, upheld the demand while extending cum-tax benefit. STPI contended that it is an autonomous society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 and functioning under the administrative control of the Department of Electronics and Information Technology, Government of India. It was established, inter alia, to administer and facilitate implementation of the Software Technology Park Scheme. STPI was separately registered with the Service Tax Department and admittedly paid Service Tax on various services including renting of immovable property, bandwidth services, co-location services and project consultancy. The controversy was confined to charges connected with activities under the STP Scheme, particularly SOFTEX certification and issuance of NoCs. The appellan
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad has held that charges collected by the Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) for SOFTEX certification and issuance of No Objection Certificates (NoCs) are taxable as “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994. In practical terms, the tribunal treated these services as taxable support services rather than as non-taxable or merely regulatory/administrative charges, meaning the amounts recovered by STPI for these certifications can fall within the service tax net.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the ruling affects entities that pay for or provide such certification-related services in the STPI context, particularly where the charges are linked to business facilitation for software exporters or similar regulated activities. No specific effective date, rate, threshold, exemption, or procedural deadline is stated in the provided text, but the legal consequence is that these SOFTEX certification and NoC fees are characterized as taxable consideration for service tax purposes under the pre-GST regime. Companies dealing with STPI certifications should therefore review whether historical service tax was charged, paid, or accounted for correctly on such fees and assess any exposure for past periods, credits, or disclosures.

rows.title: Income Tax | Madras HC Upholds Deletion of Penny Stock Gains Addition under Section 68
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12592 Case Name CIT Vs Sohanraj Uttamchand (Madras High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Madras High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); CIT Vs Sohanraj Uttamchand (Madras High Court) Summary: The Madras High Court dismissed the Revenue’s appeals in T.C.A.Nos.714 and 721 of 2018 and upheld the Tribunal’s deletion of additions of Rs.32.90 crore and Rs.38.05 crore made under Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in respect of gains claimed as exempt Long Term Capital Gains under Section 10(38). The Court held that although the Revenue’s investigation could give rise to strong suspicion regarding manipulation in the prices of PFL Infotech Limited and Risa International Limited shares, suspicion, however grave, could not substitute proof. The Court noted that the shares had been purchased and sold through recognised stock exchanges, Securities Transaction Tax had been paid, sale consideration had been received through banking channels, and there was no positive material establishing that either assessee had paid unaccounted cash to an operator or participated in an arrangement to manipulate share prices. The Court further held that the Tribunal’s findings of fact could not be interfered with under Section 260A in the absence of perversity. The Supreme Court decisions in CIT v. Durga Prasad More and Sumati Dayal v. CIT, dealing with the test of human probabilities, were distinguished on facts. The Court emphasised that the test of human probabilities does not dispense with the requirement of positive material connecting the assessee with an alleged tax-evasion design. Relying also on the principles stated in Dhakeswari Cotton Mills Ltd. v. CIT, Omar Salay Mohamed Sait v. CIT and Umacharan Shaw and Brothers v. CIT, the Cour
rows.summary:
The document reports a Madras High Court decision affirming the deletion of an income-tax addition made under Section 68 in relation to alleged “penny stock” gains. The court held that the tax authority cannot sustain an addition merely on suspicion or on the general view that the scrip was associated with price manipulation; there must be concrete evidence connecting the specific assessee to the alleged manipulation or to an unexplained credit scheme. In other words, the fact that a stock is low-priced or suspected of being a penny stock is not enough by itself to tax the gains as unexplained income.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is evidentiary: if an assessee has reported gains from share transactions, the Revenue must establish a direct link between that taxpayer and the fraud/manipulation before invoking Section 68. The decision reinforces that documentation of genuine transactions—such as purchase/sale records, contract notes, demat entries, payment trails, and other corroborating records—remains critical in defending against penny-stock related additions. The document does not announce a new statutory amendment, rate change, threshold, filing deadline, or procedural rule; it describes a judicial ruling that narrows the practical basis on which Section 68 additions can be made in penny-stock cases.

Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Dhukha Ram Vs ACIT (ITAT Jodhpur) Summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Jodhpur Bench, allowed the assessee’s appeal concerning the application of the special tax rate under section 115BBE to ₹6,25,000 surrendered during a survey. The appeal arose from the order dated 22.10.2025 passed by the Ld. Addl./JCIT(A)-5, Kolkata, in relation to the assessment framed under section 143(3) for Assessment Year 2016-17. The assessee was an individual engaged in retail trading of medicines and also derived income from operation of a sonography machine. A survey under section 133A was conducted at the business premises on 20.09.2016, during which ₹6,25,000 was surrendered. The assessee subsequently filed a return declaring total income of ₹14,81,960, including the surrendered amount, and paid tax at the normal applicable rate. During assessment, the Assessing Officer issued a show-cause notice proposing application of section 115BBE. The assessee contended that section 115BBE could apply only where the income fell within sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C or 69D, and that none of those deeming provisions applied to the surrendered business income. The AO rejected the explanation and taxed ₹6,25,000 at 30% under section 115BBE. Significantly, the AO did not invoke any particular provision from sections 68 to 69D or record a finding that the statutory requirements of any such provision were satisfied. The CIT(A) upheld the AO’s action, reasoning that the assessee had not explained the exact source of the surrendered income and that the deeming provisions would consequently apply. According to
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur held that income surrendered during a survey cannot automatically be taxed at the punitive rate under Section 115BBE unless the Revenue first brings that income within one of the deeming provisions in Sections 68 to 69D. In other words, a mere voluntary surrender in a survey does not, by itself, make the amount “deemed income” of the kind that triggers Section 115BBE’s higher tax treatment. The practical compliance point is that taxpayers who disclose income during a survey should not be assumed to face 115BBE taxation unless the tax authority can specifically classify the surrendered amount under the statutory deeming rules for unexplained cash credits, investments, money, bullion, expenditures, etc.

For affected entities, this ruling is relevant to businesses and individuals subject to tax surveys under the Income-tax Act, especially where income is offered to settle survey findings. It signals that the department must establish the legal basis for applying Section 115BBE rather than relying solely on the fact of surrender. There is no new statutory deadline or procedural filing requirement announced here; the key change is interpretive, limiting when the higher 115BBE rate can be imposed on survey-related surrendered income. Compliance teams should still document the source and nature of any surrendered amounts carefully, because if the income does fall within Sections 68 to 69D, Section 115BBE can still apply.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Co-operative Bank Conversion Mid-Recovery: Forum, Composite Notice & Cost of Delay
rows.desc: When a Co-operative Bank Changes Its Registration Midway Through Recovery – The forum, the composite notice and the cost of delay Summary: A State co-operative bank’s conversion into a multi-State co-operative bank during recovery can materially affect the forum, limitation and enforceability of proceedings against borrowers and guarantors. The article examines whether pre-conversion members automatically become members under the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002; whether claims against sureties fall within Section 84; and how the six-year limitation under Section 85 interacts with acknowledgments made only by the principal borrower. It also analyses whether a composite SARFAESI demand notice adequately identifies borrower-wise liabilities and secured assets, and whether prolonged delay after possession can reduce a guarantor’s liability under Sections 139 and 141 of the Contract Act where security loses value. Parallel SARFAESI and arbitration proceedings may be permissible, but multiple references arising from one composite secured transaction require transparent appropriation and consolidated accounts to prevent duplication. Conditional attachment before award must satisfy the statutory requirement of intent to defeat or delay execution, while indiscriminate freezes involving non-parties may exceed arbitral authority. The article further highlights objections concerning the Central Registrar’s appointment power, delegation, tribunal constitution and the distinction between the place and seat of arbitration. It concludes with a practical defence sequence: challenge constitution and membership promptly, raise limitation early, contest attachment within the appeal deadline, demand complete account and valuation records, and obtain independent evidence of security value and sale consideration. Table of Contents▸ Brief Introduction The law as it stands The present position Conversion does not carry the members across Is a claim against a surety arbitrable u
rows.summary:
The document addresses legal and recovery-process implications when a co-operative bank converts during an ongoing enforcement/recovery matter, with a focus on what happens to the proper forum, limitation, guarantor liability, SARFAESI notices, delayed asset sales, and attachment actions after conversion. The core compliance issue is that a bank’s conversion mid-recovery can change the legal characterization of the institution and may affect which authority or court has jurisdiction over the dispute or enforcement action, so recovery teams must confirm the correct forum before proceeding further. It also emphasizes the need to review whether previously issued notices remain valid after conversion, especially composite notices under recovery law and SARFAESI-based demand or enforcement notices, because a procedural defect in notice/service can later be used to challenge the recovery steps.

The document also highlights that guarantor liability remains a material issue in mid-recovery conversion cases, meaning compliance teams should not assume that a change in the bank’s structure automatically extinguishes or weakens enforcement rights against guarantors. Delays in asset sale or attachment are treated as legally significant, and the document suggests that postponement can create additional risk, including arguments about delay, prejudice, or invalidity of the enforcement timeline. In practical terms, the bank or recovery team should document the conversion date, map it against each recovery step already taken, verify whether any fresh or amended notices are needed, and reassess the legal basis for continued SARFAESI action, sale of secured assets, and attachment proceedings after the conversion event.

rows.summary:
The document reports a Chennai Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) ruling in **Sri Balaji Shopping World** in which the Tribunal **deleted an addition of ₹48.09 lakh** made by the tax authorities. The disputed amount related to **receipts from BSNL**, which the Assessing Officer had treated as **commission income** largely because the **gross receipts appeared in Form 26AS**; the ITAT held that **Form 26AS alone is not determinative of the true nature of income**.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Tribunal recognized the taxpayer’s position that the BSNL amounts were in the nature of a **trade discount** rather than commission, and it rejected the revenue’s attempt to recharacterize the receipts solely on the basis of tax-reporting data. The ruling reinforces that **third-party reporting in Form 26AS does not by itself establish the legal character of a payment or receipt**; the substance of the underlying arrangement and supporting evidence matter. rows.summary:
The document reports a Gujarat High Court decision involving AY 2013-14 in which the Revenue’s appeal was admitted on six tax issues, but the Court rejected the Revenue’s challenge to the taxpayer’s claim of a deduction under Section 35(2AB) of the Income-tax Act. rows.summary:
The document is a short tax-law update reporting that the ITAT Delhi granted relief to C L Educate Ltd across several income-tax disputes, specifically on share premium, bad debts, Section 14A disallowance, liabilities written back, and loan processing charges. The key point for compliance purposes is the ruling on shares issued as business acquisition consideration: the tribunal held that where shares are issued in connection with acquiring a business, the issue is treated as consideration for the acquisition and falls outside the scope of Section 56(2)(viib), which is the anti–share premium provision often used to tax excessive premium received by closely held companies.
