The update does not describe any new statutory amendment, rate change, filing deadline, or numeric threshold; instead, it summarizes a judicial interpretation that may be relied on in similar fact patterns. Compliance teams should therefore focus on whether share issuances in acquisition transactions are properly documented as acquisition consideration, with board approvals, acquisition agreements, valuation support, and transaction records showing commercial substance. The same article also notes the tribunal’s favorable outcome for the taxpayer on the other contested items, but it does not provide the detailed reasoning or operative compliance standards for those issues.

rows.summary:
The ITAT Chennai held that a mere delay in filing an amended trust deed or modifying objects, by itself, cannot be treated as a valid ground to reject applications for registration under Section 12AB or approval under Section 80G. In this matter, the tribunal restored the assessee’s applications and found that the authorities were not justified in denying registration/approval solely because the object modification was filed late, without first examining the merits of the trust’s objects and eligibility under the law.

The key compliance implication is that entities should still keep object clauses, trust deeds, and related amendments properly documented and aligned with their actual activities, but a late amendment, without more, should not by itself defeat a Section 12AB or 80G application.

rows.summary:
The document reports a CESTAT Hyderabad decision holding that once a taxpayer has received a valid discharge certificate under the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme (SVLDRS), the Revenue cannot continue or revive an appeal on the same settled dispute. In this case, the Tribunal dismissed the Department’s appeal because the underlying tax dispute had already been resolved through SVLDRS, and the discharge certificate operated as final settlement for that matter. For compliance teams, the key point is that an SVLDRS discharge certificate has binding finality with respect to the covered issue, so any later departmental challenge on the same demand should be barred.

The decision also addresses limitation in a fifth show-cause notice (SCN): the Tribunal rejected the Revenue’s attempt to invoke the extended period of limitation for that notice. This means the Department could not justify the additional time window for raising the demand, which is important where allegations depend on suppression, wilful misstatement, or similar grounds typically needed to extend the normal limitation period. Although the summary provided does not include the underlying tax amount, dates, or the exact factual basis for the fifth SCN, the ruling is significant for entities that have concluded disputes under SVLDRS or are facing late-issued service tax notices, because it reinforces both the finality of the SVLDRS settlement and the need for the Department to meet strict legal standards before relying on extended limitation.

The dispute concerned the computation of the permissible assessment block under Section 153C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in the case of a person other than the person searched. Relying principally on CIT v. Jasjit Singh and PCIT v. Ojjus Medicare (P.) Ltd., the Tribunal held that AYs 2010-11 and 2011-12 were outside the scope
rows.summary:
This document reports an ITAT Delhi ruling on **Section 153C of the Income-tax Act** concerning the **time limit for completing assessments** in cases involving seized material belonging to “the other person” (i.e., a person other than the one searched). The key holding is that the **limitation period for Section 153C proceedings starts from the date the Assessing Officer (AO) of the other person receives the seized material**, not from the date of the original search or seizure. Based on that rule, the Tribunal held that the assessments for **Assessment Years (AYs) 2010-11 and 2011-12** were **outside the permissible Section 153C limitation period** and therefore could not be sustained.

For compliance purposes, the practical significance is that when a company or related entity becomes subject to Section 153C proceedings because materials were found in someone else’s search, the department must be able to show **when the receiving AO actually got the seized material**, since that date governs the statutory block-period timeline. If the notice or assessment is issued beyond the limitation calculated from that receipt date, the assessment may be vulnerable to challenge as time-barred. The decision underscores the need to preserve records of the **date of transfer/receipt of seized documents between AOs**, because that date can determine whether the income-tax department’s action is valid.

rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court held that a GST adjudication order and the related appellate order could not stand where the department uploaded the show cause notice (SCN) only under the “Additional Notices” tab on the GST portal and did not separately intimate the taxpayer. The court found this mode of service violated natural justice because the taxpayer was deprived of a proper and effective opportunity to see and respond to the notice before adverse orders were passed. As a result, the HC quashed both the adjudication order and the appellate order.

For compliance purposes, the key point is procedural: GST authorities cannot rely on a buried portal upload alone if it does not reasonably alert the registered person to the SCN. Taxpayers should therefore monitor the GST portal carefully, including the “Additional Notices” section, and maintain internal controls to detect portal communications promptly. At the same time, if an SCN or order was issued without separate intimation and the taxpayer can show it was not effectively brought to its attention, this decision supports a challenge on natural justice grounds. The Court found that the show-cause notice, reminder and adjudication order bore neither digital nor physical signatures. Examining Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules, 2017, the Court held that electronic issuance and authentication are distinct and cumulative requirements and that mere generation of a document on the GST portal or allotment of a reference number cannot substitute authentication by signature. A signature authenticates the document, fixes accountability on the issuing officer and safeguards against arbitrariness by evidencing application of mind. Consequently, an unsigned show-cause notice or order is no notice or order in the eyes of law, and the defect is not a curable irregularity but goes to the root of the authority to proceed. The Court further noted that the documents had been uploaded only under “Additional Notices and Orders”, the petitioner learnt about the demand only upon bank recovery proceedings, and no effective personal hearing had been afforded contrary to Section 75(4). rows.summary: The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST show cause notice and the resulting order were invalid because they were unsigned, emphasizing that either digital authentication or physical signature is mandatory under Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules. In practical terms, the court found that GST notices/orders issued without proper authentication do not satisfy the legal requirement for validity, so taxpayers can challenge such documents on the ground that they were not duly signed. This ruling directly affects GST-registered entities that receive departmental notices or adjudication orders, because they should verify that any SCN, demand notice, or order is properly authenticated before treating it as enforceable. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is to check every GST communication for valid signature or digital authentication and to preserve a copy of any unsigned document as a potential ground for objection or appeal.

rows.summary:
This document reports an ITAT Delhi decision holding that a reassessment under the Income-tax Act cannot be sustained where it is based on stale investigation material that was already available to the tax department in earlier proceedings. In the case described, the tribunal found that the reassessment was improperly initiated because the “reasons to believe” did not rest on fresh, live information or a valid new basis; instead, the department attempted to reopen an assessment using the same information it had previously possessed and could have acted on earlier.

A key compliance takeaway is that the tribunal also held the approval under Section 151 to be mechanical, meaning the sanctioning authority had not applied independent, meaningful scrutiny before approving the reopening. That matters because reassessments require proper statutory approval, and the decision reinforces that such approval cannot be a rubber-stamp exercise; it must reflect real consideration of the facts and legal basis for reopening.

For companies and tax teams, the practical implication is that if the department issues a reassessment notice relying on old investigation material or information already on record, the notice may be challengeable as invalid, especially if the approval process appears perfunctory. This is not a substantive change in tax rates or filing deadlines, but a procedural ruling affecting the validity of reassessment actions under the Income-tax Act and the standards for Section 151 approval.

(Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by M/s. Saudi Arabian Airlines and set aside the penalty imposed for delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT), holding that delayed payment of FTT cannot be equated with failure or non-payment of tax for the purposes of Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979. The Court held that while Section 38(3) deals with non-payment of FTT, delayed deposit falls within Section 38(4) read with the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979. It further held that imposition of penalty under Section 38 is not automatic merely because a statutory timeline has been breached. The dispute arose from six instances of delayed deposit of FTT collected by the appellant airline. In five instances, the delay ranged from one day to eleven days, though the demand drafts had been purchased before the respective due dates. The appellant explained that the drafts could not be deposited because of security restrictions. In the sixth instance, involving December 1995, there was a delay of 63 days, which was attributed to the concerned employee being on emergency leave. The initial adjudication order had imposed a penalty of Rs.12,000 for the six cases of late payment, but after remand the penalty was enhanced drastically to Rs.71,29,140. Examining Section 38(3), the Supreme Court emphasised the expressions “fails to pay the foreign travel tax” and “the amount of the tax not so paid”. The Court held that “failure to pay” means non-payment and cannot be equated with delay in making payment.
rows.summary:
The document reports a Supreme Court holding that a **delay in paying Foreign Travel Tax (FTT) does not amount to “non-payment” under Section 38(3)** of the relevant law, and therefore **penalty cannot be imposed automatically solely because the tax was paid late**. In other words, the Court distinguished between **late payment** and **failure to pay**, limiting the automatic use of penalty provisions where the tax was eventually paid rather than wholly omitted.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that entities responsible for collecting/remitting Foreign Travel Tax should still **pay on time to avoid disputes**, but a delayed remittance by itself is **not treated as an outright default equivalent to non-payment** under Section 38(3). Any penalty action must be assessed in light of this ruling rather than assumed to follow mechanically from lateness. The document does not specify any new filing deadline, rate change, or revised procedure; it is primarily a **judicial clarification restricting automatic penalty imposition** for delayed FTT payment.

The document reports a Madras High Court ruling on reassessment procedure under the Income-tax Act: where the Income Tax Department had issued a Section 148 reassessment notice in the name of a deceased assessee, the court directed that a fresh notice must be issued to the deceased person’s legal representatives instead. rows.summary:

The practical effect is that taxpayers who have incurred PMS charges in relation to managing investments and then realized capital gains may be able to claim those charges as a deduction from capital gains, reducing taxable gains, subject to the facts of their case and the applicable judicial view.

As a result, the related penalties were also struck down as unsustainable.

The petitioner purchased the vehicle for USD 54,000, filed Bill of Entry No.7472252 dated 26.12.2024 and paid customs duty of Rs.99,78,795. Out-of-charge was granted on 02.01.2025. On 07.02.2025, however, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the petitioner’s residence, prepared a Panchnama and directed him not to deal with or part with the vehicle. No contemporaneous seizure order under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 was passed. During pendency of the writ petition, the DRI ultimately issued a seizure memo only on 17.04.2026, more than one year after the original detention, followed by a show-cause notice dated 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4). The Department also passed a provisional release order on 18.05.2026 requiring a bond for Rs.85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs.1.20 crore by relying upon paragraph 2 of Circular No.35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017. The High Court noted that the relied-upon part of the Circular had already been struck down by the Delhi High Court in Shanus Impex Vs Union of India & Ors. to the extent it curtailed the adjudicating authority’s discretion. The Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated the Department’s continued reliance upon that paragraph. The Court rejected the Department’s attempt to attribute the delay in initiating Section 110 proceedings
rows.summary:
The document reports a Gujarat High Court ruling that Customs authorities cannot avoid the statutory seizure framework under Section 110 of the Customs Act by simply keeping imported goods under prolonged detention without issuing a proper seizure order. The specific case involved an imported Land Cruiser that had been held by Customs, and the court directed its release, indicating that indefinite retention of imported goods is not permissible when Customs has not lawfully completed the seizure process.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that once Customs takes possession or control of imported goods, it must act within the legal limits and cannot continue detaining the property indefinitely as a substitute for seizure. The ruling reinforces that Customs enforcement actions must follow the prescribed statutory procedure, including timely issuance of a seizure order where required, rather than relying on open-ended detention. No specific monetary thresholds, deadlines, or rate changes are mentioned in the provided text, but the decision is significant for importers, customs brokers, and compliance teams handling detained shipments because it strengthens the ability to challenge prolonged detention that is not backed by formal seizure action.

The appellant had availed credit on the basis of three invoices, two issued in 2011 and one dated 22.01.2014. The Department sought reversal on the ground that the appellant had purchased the goods through M/s Ashis Enterprise, which did not possess dealer registration. The appellant contended that the invoices issued by M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal specifically showed Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. as the consignee, while Ashis Enterprise was shown as the buyer. The goods were directly dispatched to the appellant and were duly accounted for in RG 23A Part I. Ashis Enterprise separately issued a commercial invoice to facilitate payment, which could be correlated with the invoice issued by Roshanlal Bhagirathmal. On examining the invoices, the Tribunal found that the appellant was expressly shown as the consignee and that all particulars required for an invoice under Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 were fulfilled. The Tribunal further noted that there was no allegation that the goods had not actually been received by the appellant. The goods had also been accounted for in RG 23A Part I after receipt at the appellant’s factory. In these circumstances, the Tribunal held that the Revenue had failed to establish any contravention of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The demand was accordingly set as
rows.summary:
The document reports a CESTAT Kolkata ruling on excise/CENVAT credit, holding that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely because the manufacturer’s invoice named the assessee as the **consignee**, so long as the goods were actually received by the assessee and properly entered in its records/accounts. In other words, the tribunal recognized that the invoice description and consignee designation were sufficient to support credit when the underlying transaction was genuine and the receipt of goods was evidenced.  

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that credit eligibility should be evaluated based on **substance and documentation of receipt/use**, not only on rigid invoice-form terminology, where the assessee is clearly identified as the consignee and the goods are traced into inventory or accounting records. The ruling does not announce a new rate, threshold, or filing deadline; it is a judicial interpretation affecting how manufacturers and recipients defend CENVAT credit claims in excise audits or disputes. Firms should still retain invoices, goods receipt evidence, stock/accounting entries, and any supporting transport or inward records to substantiate that the goods were received and accounted for, because those facts were central to the credit being allowed.

rows.summary: The document reports a CESTAT Hyderabad ruling that upheld dismissal of a service tax appeal because the appellant did not comply with a pre-deposit direction. The tribunal had ordered a deposit of 50% of the disputed amount under the **unamended Section 35F**, and the appeal was dismissed when that condition was not satisfied. For compliance purposes, the key point is that, at least for appeals governed by the pre-amendment regime, failure to make the required pre-deposit can be a complete bar to appellate relief and can result in dismissal of the case without a merits hearing. The respondents relied on departmental practice and the Standard Operating Pr
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court has directed the income tax department to refund **Rs. 53.09 crore of TDS, together with applicable interest**, and held that the department could not insist on **Form 26B** or rely on **Rule 31A** in this situation. The key point is that, **after a Section 201 assessment has already been completed**, the court treated the request as one that did not require the payer to go through the usual Form 26B process for correction or refund processing.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that this ruling limits the tax department’s ability to reject or delay a TDS refund merely because **Form 26B was not filed**, where the liability issue has already been determined under **Section 201**. The decision appears to affect **deductors/payers seeking TDS refund after an adverse or completed Section 201 proceeding**, and it reinforces that procedural requirements under **Rule 31A** should not be applied mechanically to defeat a refund once the substantive assessment has been concluded.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has approved Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) to acquire an “aggregate holding” of up to 9.99% of the paid-up share capital or voting rights in ICICI Bank. The approval was communicated in an RBI letter dated September 4, 2026, and ICICI Bank said it received the letter at 9:09 p.m. on September 4, 2026. rows.summary:
The CBI has registered a criminal case against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra and three others—Pankaj Suroliya, Amish Pandya, and Rajeev Dholakia—based on a complaint from LIC Housing Finance Ltd. (LICHFL) alleging cheating, criminal breach of trust, and conspiracy in relation to housing finance exposures exceeding Rs 1,322 crore. According to LICHFL, the alleged fraud centered on financial disclosures used to obtain credit facilities: Chandra reportedly submitted a net worth certificate in 2018 stating his net worth was Rs 59,113 crore, and LICHFL says that certificate was used to secure loans for M/s Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt. Ltd. and other companies linked to him. The complaint says LICHFL relied on that certificate and subsequently extended credit to three companies associated with Chandra; LICHFL also disputes later statements made by Chandra during insolvency proceedings, particularly his denial that he had ever had a net worth of Rs 50,000 crore as reflected in the certificates submitted to the lender.

A specific transaction cited in the complaint is a Rs 500 crore loan facility to Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt. Ltd. and Pan India Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (as co-borrower), described as a Home Entity Loan (Takeover & Top-up for Business Expansion) under Loan Account No. 610700003341, secured by a Letter of Continuing Guarantee dated 28 March 2018 executed by Subhash Chandra. For compliance purposes, the key issue is that the allegations concern the accuracy and reliability of borrower/promoter net-worth declarations, the basis on which lender credit decisions were made, and whether guarantees and related-party/company linkages were properly documented and verified. No regulatory deadline or new general rule is announced in the article; rather, it reports an enforcement action and the lender’s allegations about prior conduct and loan origination documentation.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) withdrew more than ₹6 trillion of surplus liquidity from the banking system on Monday, responding to a record spike in cash parked by banks. The piece says the RBI received offers worth ₹3.53 trillion in an overnight liquidity operation, and this came immediately after banks placed ₹2.59 trillion into a separate 30-day auction, taking total absorption to over ₹6 trillion. The trigger for the intervention was that India’s banking-system liquidity surplus had reached ₹11.6 trillion on September 6, which the article says was nearly 4% of total banking-system deposits.

For compliance purposes, the document does not announce a new rule, filing requirement, or regulatory deadline for banks or corporates; it is a market/liquidity update describing RBI’s liquidity management actions. The main operational significance is that the RBI is actively draining excess system liquidity after an exceptional build-up, which may affect short-term funding conditions, money-market rates, and treasury positioning for banks and other market participants. The article is dated/reported as last updated on September 7, 2026 at 1:24 PM IST.

The company, which is set to become the first standalone asset reconstruction company to list in India, is also open to acquisitions of smaller ARCs. rows.summary:
The document is an interview-style market update, not a rulemaking notice, but it contains several material business and portfolio facts that compliance teams should track because they indicate ARCIL’s current risk mix, strategic direction, and planned corporate actions. ARCIL says the fastest growth in its portfolio is coming from retail assets originated by NBFCs, while bank-originated, corporate, and other retail portfolios continue to grow as well; management expects retail and SME assets to take a larger share over time because they are growing faster than corporate assets. As of FY26, retail and SME assets together made up a little over 31% of ARCIL’s portfolio, with corporate assets around 69%, and the retail/SME book has grown at a CAGR of nearly 56% over the last couple of years.

Operationally, ARCIL reports it currently handles about 32 lakh NPA accounts on the retail side and operates across roughly 24 states, which is relevant for scale, recovery operations, and state-by-state execution risk. The company says it resolves close to 25% of its opening AUM each year, supported by low leverage and cash flows from resolutions, indicating an active recovery and monetization cadence rather than a passive hold strategy. ARCIL also says around Rs 5.5 lakh crore of corporate assets written off by banks and NBFCs are now returning to the resolution ecosystem, which signals a potentially expanding pipeline of stressed assets.

Strategically, ARCIL says it is set to become the first standalone asset reconstruction company to list in India, which is a significant corporate event from a governance, disclosure, and public-market compliance perspective. The company is also open to acquiring smaller ARCs, but only where there is a willing seller, appropriate valuation, and strategic fit. ARCIL positions NARCL as both a competitor and a complement, with NARCL focused mainly on very large stressed assets; this matters for competitive and market-segmentation assessment, though the article does not describe any regulatory requirement, deadline, or filing obligation arising from that point.

rows.summary:
The document reports that the one-year median marginal cost of funds-based lending rate (MCLR) for scheduled commercial banks in India increased to 8.70% in August from 8.60% in July, and for the first time in 14 months it was also above the year-ago level of 8.60%. This is notable because the repo rate stayed unchanged at 5.25%, so the rise suggests continued funding-cost pressure even though overall banking system liquidity improved sharply.

The increase was not broad-based: it was driven entirely by foreign banks, whose one-year median MCLR rose to 7.33% in August from 7.20% in July. In contrast, the one-year median MCLR for public sector banks remained unchanged at 8.80%, and for private sector banks it remained unchanged at 9.35%. For compliance purposes, this is primarily a market-rate update rather than a new regulatory obligation, but it is relevant to any lending, pricing, or treasury decisions tied to MCLR benchmarks.

The article also notes that surplus liquidity in the banking system rose to around Rs 6.7 lakh crore by August 31, up from Rs 2.5 lakh crore at the end of July and Rs 1.4 lakh crore at the end of June. This improvement was largely attributed to the conversion of Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits into rupees, which eased near-term funding pressures for banks. The report further says that banks’ fresh spreads recovered in July, with the spread for scheduled commercial banks widening by 8 basis points, indicating some normalization in pricing dynamics despite the higher MCLR.

rows.summary:
The document says India’s 2026 FCNR(B) mobilisation under the FCNR(B) scheme raised **$127.2 billion**, making it far larger than prior diaspora-focused foreign-currency deposit programmes. For compliance purposes, the key point is that the scheme’s scale was exceptional: it equaled **3.1% of GDP**, compared with **1.4% of GDP** for the **2013 FCNR(B) scheme**, and it represented **76.8% of outstanding NRI deposits**, versus **38.3% in 2013**. The article characterizes this as evidence that the Reserve Bank of India’s **decision to close the scheme early** was justified because demand was overwhelming.  

It also places the 2026 result in historical context against earlier foreign-currency mobilisation drives: the **India Development Bond (1991)** raised **$3.3 billion**, the **Resurgent India Bonds (1998)** raised **$4.7 billion**, and the **India Millennium Deposit scheme (2000)** raised **$5.5 billion**—all far below the 2026 amount. The 2013 FCNR(B) mobilisation itself is cited as **$26 billion**, equal to **40% of annual private remittances**, while the 2026 scheme equaled **75.6% of annual private remittances**.  

No new compliance procedure, filing obligation, rate change, or deadline is described in the text beyond the fact that the **2026 FCNR(B) scheme was closed early** by the RBI. The document is therefore mainly informational: it reports the magnitude of the mobilisation and the comparative metrics, but it does not announce any fresh operational requirements for banks, deposit-taking entities, or NRI customers in the excerpt provided.

However, rising incomes, greater awareness and promotional campaigns by banks are supporting increased adoption.The integration with UPI could widen the range of transactions where credit cards can be used by enabling payments through UPI QR codes, including at merchants that do not accept cards through tradit
rows.summary:
The document is a market report, not a new regulation or rule change, but it does describe a significant payments development that compliance teams in banks, card issuers, fintechs, and merchant acquirers should monitor: credit cards are expected to see wider use in India as they become integrated with the Unified Payments Interface (UPI). Under this model, consumers will be able to pay with credit cards through widely accepted UPI QR codes, including at merchants that do not have traditional point-of-sale card infrastructure, which broadens the practical acceptance of credit cards beyond conventional card terminals. The report says this is likely to increase credit card utilization, especially for ecommerce and higher-value purchases, while UPI-powered digital wallets are expected to remain the main instrument for day-to-day spending.

The piece cites Reserve Bank of India data showing 122.9 million outstanding credit cards in India as of July, versus 1.03 billion debit cards, underscoring that debit cards still dominate in volume. It also notes that credit and charge card adoption remains relatively low because many consumers, especially in rural areas, lack formal credit histories and remain wary of interest costs and debt. In contrast, adoption is being supported by rising incomes, greater awareness, bank promotional campaigns, and the consumer value proposition of rewards, discounts, and installment payment options.

For compliance purposes, the key implication is operational rather than prescriptive: institutions involved in issuing, acquiring, or enabling UPI-linked credit card payments should expect broader transaction channels and potentially higher usage volumes as card payments migrate into QR-based acceptance. There are no explicit deadlines, mandatory thresholds, or new filing obligations stated in the document, but teams should treat this as a signal to review product, merchant acceptance, customer-disclosure, fraud-monitoring, and transaction-classification controls for UPI-enabled credit card payments, particularly where cards are used at merchants that do not accept traditional card swipes or chip-and-PIN infrastructure.

rows.summary:
The document is not a regulatory notice or financial rulemaking, but a news analysis of India’s latest national accounts data and the methodology behind reported GDP growth. It reports that India’s real GDP grew 7.8% year-on-year in Q1 FY27 (April–June), compared with 6.9% in the same quarter a year earlier; nominal GDP grew 10.3%, and real GVA grew 8.2%. This was stronger than the Reserve Bank of India’s 7.0% forecast and market expectations of about 7.1%, which is why the figures sparked scrutiny.

The controversy centers on whether the new GDP series—based on a new 2022-23 base year—plus changes in price measurement and revisions to prior estimates may be making real growth appear higher than it otherwise would be. Critics are questioning whether the updated methodology has produced an unusually high real GDP number, while the government says the higher growth reflects improved data sources and methodological changes consistent with national accounting practices, not an attempt to inflate growth.

The article specifically highlights the GDP deflator as the key mechanism affecting the real growth calculation. It describes the deflator as the implicit price index derived by comparing GDP at current prices with GDP at constant prices, meaning it captures price changes across the economy and is used to strip inflation out of nominal GDP to arrive at real GDP. The piece indicates that concern is focused on how this price measure, together with the rebasing and revisions, could materially affect the reported real growth rate.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that this is a methodology/reliability issue in official macroeconomic reporting, not a direct compliance obligation imposed on companies. However, it may matter for internal forecasting, covenant analysis, budgeting, and any disclosures or models that rely on India GDP growth assumptions, since the article suggests the headline growth figure could be sensitive to the underlying deflator and base-year changes.

In the March quarter, the players received 97.8% of funding and had a 94.1% AUM share. Advt The skewness towards large NBFC-MFIs is a reflection of banks and other financiers playing safer, lending largely to well-capitalised institutions during uncertain economic cycles. While the broader economy is facing US-Iran war-related anxiety, the microfinance sector itself is trying to come out of the woods after a couple of years of intense asset quality stress.“Funding is likely to remain the key differentiator. While larger NBFC-MFIs have better access to funding, smaller institutions continue to face tighter liquidity, higher borrowing costs and cautious lender appetite,” CareEdge Ratings said in a note last m
rows.summary:
The document reports a continuing funding concentration in India’s microfinance sector rather than announcing a new rule or formal regulatory requirement. In the first quarter of the current fiscal year, large microfinance companies received 98.1% of all funds extended to NBFC-microfinance institutions (NBFC-MFIs), even though they accounted for 93.8% of the sector’s assets under management; six months earlier the figure was 97.5% against 93.7% AUM, and in the March quarter it was 97.8% funding against 94.1% AUM. The article says this widening skew reflects banks and other financiers preferring to lend to better-capitalized, larger institutions in an uncertain economic environment, while smaller MFIs continue to face tighter liquidity, higher borrowing costs, and more cautious lender appetite.

The funding data cited for the quarter shows Rs 21,407 crore of debt funding to the sector, with banks contributing 80.4% of that amount. The article also notes that NBFC-MFIs remain the largest micro-credit providers, holding a 44.3% market share. From a compliance/risk perspective, the practical implication is that smaller NBFC-MFIs may face ongoing refinancing and liquidity pressure, which can affect their recovery pace and funding access, while larger players are likely to continue receiving a disproportionate share of lender support. There are no explicit deadlines, operational mandates, or regulatory filing instructions in the piece; it is a market update that should be used to assess counterparty funding concentration, liquidity risk, and lending exposure in the microfinance sector.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) took action on **September 7, 2026** to **absorb more than 6 trillion rupees of surplus banking liquidity** after system liquidity surged to a record level the previous day. Specifically, the RBI received **3.53 trillion rupees** of bids in an **overnight auction** and had already taken **2.59 trillion rupees** through a **30-day auction**, bringing the day’s total withdrawal to over **6 trillion rupees**; the RBI had originally sought to withdraw **7 trillion rupees** via the 30-day operation.

For compliance and treasury teams, the key point is that this is a **liquidity management move affecting banks participating in RBI operations**, not a new rule change, but it signals a materially tighter liquidity stance. Market participants reported **weak participation** in the 30-day auction and some traders cited **technical glitches**, though a person familiar with the matter said there were **no glitches** and that all bids were processed through the RBI’s **e-Kuber system**; the RBI did not publicly comment. The article indicates the RBI may conduct **another long-duration reverse repo later in the week**, so banks should expect continued liquidity-absorption operations.

The broader context is that India’s banking system liquidity surplus reached **11.6 trillion rupees on September 6**, equal to **nearly 4% of banking system deposits**. The article attributes part of the liquidity spike to India receiving a steeper-than-expected **$136 billion** under special one-off schemes intended to strengthen external balances. It also notes that the RBI’s **total liquidity withdrawals have exceeded 8.5 trillion rupees**, and that sustained large surpluses could raise **inflation** and boost **financial assets**, which is relevant because the RBI had recently signaled that **rate hikes could be ahead** as inflation and growth firm up.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) responded to a technical problem in its liquidity operations by announcing an additional overnight variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) on Monday, Sept. 7, 2026. The new operation is for **₹5 trillion** (about **$52.96 billion**), and it follows a prior **30-day auction** in which the RBI received bids/offers totaling only **₹2.59 trillion**; that longer-term auction had included an **early redemption option for banks**. According to market participants cited in the report, the bidding venue for the VRRR was moved away from the RBI’s normal **E-Kuber** platform because E-Kuber had “technical issues,” and as a result some banks were reportedly unable to participate because they were not aware of the platform change.  

For compliance and treasury teams, the key point is that this is an RBI liquidity-management action, not a broad rule change, but it may affect banks and other eligible counterparties that participate in RBI reverse repo operations, particularly those relying on E-Kuber access and auction notifications. Institutions should confirm their operational readiness for RBI auction participation, including contingency procedures for platform disruptions, alternate bidding channels, and internal communication controls so they do not miss same-day overnight liquidity operations or longer-term VRRR/redemption events. The article does not state any new permanent regulatory requirement or policy deadline beyond the **Sept. 7, 2026** operation itself.

rows.title: Smallcap mutual funds outperform with 21% return in 6 months. Should investors chase the rally or wait for correction?
rows.desc: Smallcap mutual funds outperform with 21% return in 6 months. Should investors chase the rally or wait for correction? India’s foreign-exchange reserves reached a record **$740.80 billion** in the week ended **August 28, 2026**, after rising **$11.475 billion** in that single week from **$729.328 billion** on **August 21**. This was the **ninth consecutive weekly increase**, with reserves up by nearly **$75 billion** over that nine-week span, and it surpassed the prior high of about **$728.5 billion** set at the end of **February 2026**.  

The article does **not describe a new rule, mandate, or filing requirement**, but it explains a material macro-financial development relevant to compliance and treasury planning: India’s reserve buildup is being driven in significant part by **foreign-currency deposits and borrowings mobilized with RBI support**, rather than only by export earnings or FDI. That means the external buffer has strengthened, but it also creates **future dollar repayment obligations** and **rupee-liquidity management challenges** for the RBI and, by extension, for institutions with exposure to RBI liquidity operations, foreign-currency funding, or cross-border balance-sheet management.  

For compliance teams, the key operational takeaway is that the environment is one of **heightened external volatility**: the article notes that wars are making capital more cautious, keeping **oil prices elevated**, pressuring currencies, and **constraining FDI**. Entities with India exposure should therefore monitor their **FX, funding, and liquidity risk positions** closely, especially where they rely on foreign-currency liabilities or are sensitive to RBI liquidity actions. The article’s substantive point is that India’s reserve “shield” is now stronger than ever, but the policy and liquidity costs of building it have increased as well.

rows.summary:
The document says the Reserve Bank of India is facing a major liquidity-management challenge because FCNR(B) scheme inflows have created an estimated ₹10.5 lakh crore of liquidity, far above earlier expectations. The immediate policy test is a 30-day variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auction to absorb ₹7 lakh crore, and the level of participation in that auction is described as a key indicator of whether the RBI can keep liquidity neutral without further intervention. If the auction does not sufficiently sterilize the inflow, the RBI may need to use additional tools, specifically sell-buy dollar swaps and bond sales through open market operations (OMOs), as well as more VRRRs, to drain excess rupees from the banking system.

The article also notes that the RBI could let all $36 billion of forward dollar positions mature over the next year, which would also help absorb rupee liquidity generated by the FCNR inflows. In addition, extinguishing those positions using current dollar inflows is presented as another liquidity-draining option. The underlying issue is that the total inflows from the special schemes are now said to be about $136 billion, versus an initial expectation of $80-90 billion, implying roughly an extra $50 billion, or about ₹5 lakh crore, of unanticipated inflows that the RBI must manage.

For a compliance team, the main takeaway is that this is a central-bank liquidity operation rather than a direct new regulatory rule, but it may affect market conditions, funding, and treasury positioning for banks and market participants. The key date mentioned is Monday, when the 30-day VRRR auction is scheduled, and the outcome may signal the RBI’s next steps on sterilization through reverse repos, dollar swaps, and OMOs.

rows.summary:
India launched a special June deposit window for its diaspora under the FCNR(B) program to attract foreign-currency deposits and help defend the rupee after it fell to record lows. Under this arrangement, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) agreed to protect participating banks from losses if the rupee weakens by offering a favorable currency-swap facility, which economists estimate costs roughly 3%–3.5% per year.  

The program drew far more money than anticipated, and the article says inflows are expected to rise further once overseas foreign-currency debt and external commercial borrowings are added. Because banks will convert the dollars raised into rupees, the RBI must also absorb excess liquidity injected into the banking system, creating an additional balance-sheet burden.  

Economists quoted in the piece estimate the combined cost to the RBI could reach about Rs. 1.2 lakh crore, or roughly $10.6 billion, with some commentary suggesting the burden could be even higher. The article also notes that the RBI may need to use foreign investments to offset these expenses, and that market attention has shifted to how these inflows will affect the RBI’s liquidity stance and operations.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that this is not a new ongoing reporting rule or filing requirement; rather, it is a description of a central bank fundraising/support program that created contingent costs and liquidity management obligations for the RBI and participating banks under the FCNR(B) special deposit window.

The document is a market analysis, not a new rule or regulatory notice, and it says India’s gold lending industry is expected to grow at roughly 28% CAGR over FY26–FY28E, driven by broader formalization of credit and the still-low level of monetization of household gold holdings. It states that gold lending has already overtaken personal loans to become the second-largest consumer lending category for banks and NBFCs, behind home loans. The report estimates Indian households hold about 28,000 tonnes of gold worth approximately Rs 380 trillion to Rs 390 trillion, but only a small share of that asset base is currently reaching the formal lending system.

For compliance and risk teams at banks and NBFCs, the key operational implication is that gold loans are becoming a much larger and more strategically important retail asset class, with the report saying they account for 15.7% of consumption loans across banks and NBFCs. By FY26, the outstanding gold loan portfolio is put at Rs 18.6 billion, ahead of personal loans at Rs 16.5 billion and auto loans at Rs 9.3 billion, though still behind home loans at Rs 44.4 billion. The report also says retail gold loans within the banking system grew at a 78% CAGR over the past three years, far faster than housing loans (18%), vehicle loans (13%), other personal loans (13%), and credit cards (10%).

A major point in the report is that only around 8% of India’s household gold stock has been monetized through the organized gold loan market, based on an assumed average industry loan-to-value ratio of about 60%. This is presented as evidence of a large untapped market and a structural shift away from informal moneylender-based lending toward organized institutions. The organized sector’s share of the total gold loan market rose from 26% in FY14 to 37% in FY24, and the report expects further gains as regulatory harmonization, digital KYC, and branch expansion by banks and NBFCs accelerate formalization.

There are no direct compliance deadlines, enforcement actions, or prescriptive regulatory requirements in the article itself. However, for a compliance officer, the document signals that institutions active in gold lending should expect continued portfolio growth, increased competitive pressure, and greater importance of maintaining robust KYC, valuation, LTV, collateral custody, and operational controls as the market expands.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has proposed draft restrictions that would ban or sharply limit revolving credit facilities offered by non-bank lenders (NBFCs), but the latest industry consultation suggests the final rule may be narrower than the original draft. RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu has already met with NBFCs and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) to hear concerns, and the RBI has reportedly received about 350 responses directly, while around 30–40 lenders have submitted feedback through FIDC; the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) is expected to forward the suggestions discussed to the RBI as well.  

The key compliance issue is that the RBI originally appeared to believe the impact would be limited to only three or four NBFCs, but industry feedback indicates the definition could affect a much broader segment of the NBFC sector, including products and lending structures that are not intended to function as perpetual rollovers. Because of that, the RBI is now considering a partial restriction rather than an outright blanket ban, and the final contours have not yet been finalized. Industry participants said the draft is particularly concerning because some products involve limited redraw or replenishment within an existing sanctioned facility, which NBFCs argue should not automatically be treated as prohibited revolving credit.  

The RBI’s policy objective, as described in the article, is to curb evergreening and strengthen borrower credibility and repayment discipline by preventing credit lines from remaining continuously available on a revolving basis. NBFCs are warning that if the definition is written too broadly, it could sweep in working-capital products and other lending structures that are operationally similar to revolving credit but are not intended to be captured by the regulation. rows.summary:
Ujjivan Small Finance Bank’s key leadership change is the early retirement of Managing Director and CEO Sanjeev Nautiyal on health grounds, effective September 1, 2026, after which he ceased to serve as MD & CEO and as a key managerial personnel; he will remain on leave during his three-month notice period ending November 30, 2026. The Reserve Bank of India has approved the appointment of Executive Director Carol Furtado as interim MD & CEO for three months, and the bank is expected to accelerate its succession process and submit shortlisted permanent candidates to the RBI within the next three to four months, with both internal and external candidates under consideration.

From a compliance and governance perspective, the bank states that Nautiyal’s departure is unrelated to strategy, governance, or operations, and that its near-term FY27 guidance and strategic priorities remain unchanged. Management says MSME growth remains in line with guidance and asset quality is broadly in line with Q1 performance, with no material deviations currently visible, so there is no indicated need for a near-term reset of disclosed operating targets.

The longer-term roadmap still being executed is substantial and remains the key continuity issue for oversight: Ujjivan is targeting a gross loan book of Rs 1 lakh crore by FY30, along with a secured-loan mix of 65–70% by FY30, up from about 50% in June 2026 and about 31% in June 2024. The bank’s FY30 plan also includes CASA of 35%, deposits at three times the Q1FY26 level, a branch network of 1,150 branches, a cost-to-income ratio of 55%, and a credit-to-assets ratio below 5%; the strategy centers on strengthening the liability franchise, expanding digital and physical distribution, and continuing the shift toward secured lending.

The article also notes an additional management change: Vikas Agarwal has been appointed head of the MSME business to strengthen leadership bandwidth, and he brings more than 25 years of experience across MSME, business banking, retail banking, credit, product, and distribution. Ujjivan remains non-committal on when it will reapply for a universal banking licence, so compliance and governance focus should remain on execution of the current business plan, succession continuity, deposit-franchise strengthening, and MSME expansion under the interim leadership until the RBI-cleared permanent CEO is chosen.

rows.title: Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules Non-banking finance companies have sought clarity from the Reserve Bank of India on whether recovery calls fall under the service-call category permitted through the 1600 numbering series, amid concerns that customers increasingly block calls originating from the series, sources part of the discussion told ETBFSI. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Updated On Sep 4, 2026 at 11:31 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133737944; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The issue was raised by NBFC CEOs and industry representatives during a meeting with RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu on Thursday, where the industry flagged concerns around the implementation of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s (TRAI) mandatory 1600-series framework for regulated financial entities.“Sales calls should be outside the 1600 series. We fully agree with that. But whether recovery calls fall under service calls is still a question. That needs to be clarified,” a source told ETBFSI.The 1600 series was allocated by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) for service and transactional voice calls by Government and BFSI entities. TRAI, in November 2025, subsequently mandated a phase-wise migration of RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities to the series, with the objective of allowing consumers to distinguish legitimate calls from regulated financial institutions from spam, promotional and potentially fraudulent calls. Advt For RBI-regulated entities, commercial banks were required to adopt the 1600 series by January 1, 2026, while large NBFCs with asset size above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks and small finance banks were given a February 1, 2026 deadline. Remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks and other entities were required to migrate by March 1, 2026.
rows.summary:
The article reports that NBFCs have asked the Reserve Bank of India to clarify whether loan recovery calls can be made through the TRAI-mandated 1600-numbering series, since the framework clearly allows “service calls” but the industry is uncertain whether collections/recovery calls qualify as service calls. Industry representatives raised this issue directly with RBI Deputy Governor S.C. Murmu, saying that while they agree sales calls should not use the 1600 series, recovery calls remain ambiguous and need explicit regulatory guidance.

The underlying rule is TRAI’s November 2025 mandate requiring a phased migration of RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities to the 1600 series, which was allocated by the Department of Telecommunications for service and transactional voice calls by Government and BFSI entities. The stated purpose of the framework is to help consumers distinguish legitimate calls from regulated financial institutions from spam, promotional, and potentially fraudulent calls. Under the rollout schedule for RBI-regulated entities, commercial banks had to adopt the 1600 series by January 1, 2026; large NBFCs with asset size above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks, and small finance banks had to comply by February 1, 2026; and remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks, and other entities had to migrate by March 1, 2026.

For compliance purposes, the key open point is not the existence of the mandate, but whether debt recovery/collections communications are permitted as “service calls” under the 1600 series or must be handled outside it. The article does not report any change to the deadline structure or any exemption being granted; instead, it shows that regulated entities are already expected to follow the migration timetable and are seeking clarification only on the scope of call types allowed within the series, particularly for recovery activity.

A compliance team should nonetheless note the key impact: shorter listing timelines will require tighter coordination of filing, approvals, exchange/listing submissions, and any settlement or post-issue documentation workflows to avoid non-compliance once the T+3 regime applies.

rows.summary:
SEBI’s informal guidance responds to Share India Securities Limited’s question about whether securities bought under a Discretionary Portfolio Management Service (D-PMS) can be pledged by the client. The company explained that under its D-PMS structure, clients open demat accounts with the approved custodian, trades are executed through empaneled brokers, and securities purchased remain in the client’s beneficial ownership and are held in the client’s name in the demat account. It asked whether a portfolio manager may allow a client to pledge those securities either directly or through instructions routed via the portfolio manager to the custodian, on the basis that the securities are still the client’s property.

The response is an informal guidance letter issued under SEBI’s Informal Guidance Scheme, 2025, dated August 17, 2026, and addressed to Share India Securities Limited, Unit No. 615 and 616, 6th Floor, X-Change Plaza, Dandi Street Commercial Co-operative Society Limited, Road 5E, Block 53, Zone 5, GIFT City, Gandhinagar, Gujarat 382050, attention Bhavya Vora, Principal Officer. The document is not a rule amendment or enforcement action; it is an interpretive response to the specific facts presented, and the key compliance issue is whether pledging would be permissible within the Portfolio Managers Regulations, 2020 for D-PMS-held securities.

Because the excerpt cuts off before the actual conclusion, the provided text does not include the final SEBI position, any conditions, or any express approval/rejection. For compliance purposes, the material takeaway from the visible portion is that SEBI was asked to clarify the legality and regulatory implications of client pledging of securities purchased through D-PMS, where the securities remain in the client’s demat account with the custodian and are beneficially owned by the client, and that the query specifically contemplates both direct client instruction and routing the pledge instruction through the portfolio manager to the custodian.

rows.summary:
SEBI issued an informal guidance letter in response to Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited’s request regarding whether the portfolio manager rules on “client level segregation of funds and securities” under Regulation 24(3A) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020, as reflected in paragraph 3.4 of the Master Circular for Portfolio Managers dated July 16, 2025, would require a specific operational change. The key issue was whether a portfolio manager may maintain the cash and securities belonging to different clients in one common bank account and one common demat account, provided that the portfolio manager’s internal books and records clearly allocate the assets to each client and the clients’ portfolios are separately identifiable.

SEBI’s response, on the facts presented, is that it would not object to this arrangement if the assets remain fully segregated in the portfolio manager’s internal records and systems at the client level, and the portfolio manager is able to demonstrate separate identification of each client’s holdings despite the pooled bank/demat structure. In other words, the guidance indicates that the segregation requirement is focused on accurate client-wise recordkeeping and traceability, rather than mandating physically separate bank and demat accounts for each client in every case.

The document is dated July 16, 2026, and references an applicant letter dated May 18, 2026. It should be treated as informal guidance tied to the specific facts described by Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited; it is not a formal amendment to the regulation itself, but it is relevant compliance clarification for portfolio managers subject to Regulation 24(3A) and paragraph 3.4 of the Master Circular. Compliance teams should therefore ensure that any pooled account structure still preserves strict client-level segregation in books, records, and reporting, because SEBI’s comfort is conditioned on that operational separability being demonstrable.

rows.summary:
SEBI issued an interpretive/informal guidance letter on the InvIT Regulations in response to a request from Sustainable Energy Infra Investment Managers Private Limited, under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003. The material issue addressed is whether a nominee director appointed by a foreign investor can be treated as an “independent director” of an infrastructure investment trust (InvIT) manager, and SEBI’s guidance is that such a person would **not** qualify as independent if they are a representative or nominee of a shareholder/investor with a right to appoint them, because that relationship undermines the independence standard under the InvIT Regulations.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that when determining board composition and independent-director eligibility for an InvIT manager, the company must look beyond the label of “independent” and assess whether the individual is in fact connected to a shareholder or investor through nomination/appointment rights. If a foreign investor (or any shareholder/investor) has the power to nominate a director, that director should not be counted as independent for regulatory compliance, board constitution, or any filings or disclosures that depend on the number of independent directors.

The document is an interpretive clarification rather than a new rule change, so it does not prescribe a new effective date, numerical threshold, or implementation deadline. However, it is still operationally important because it confirms the compliance position the applicant should follow immediately in structuring the board and in maintaining ongoing conformity with the InvIT Regulations’ independence requirements.

SEBI issued an informal guidance letter dated **March 20, 2026** in response to **FRR Shares and Securities Limited’s** request under the **SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2025**. FRR is a SEBI-registered intermediary, operating as a **trading member of NSE and BSE (SEBI Reg. No. INZ000279232)** and a **CDSL depository participant (IND 12068100)**. The company asked whether **client trade instructions sent via WhatsApp chat from a client’s registered mobile number** could count as evidence of client order placement under SEBI’s requirements for preventing unauthorized trading.

SEBI stated that the older circular on unauthorized trading, **CIR/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD2/CIR/P/2017/108 dated September 26, 2017**, has been **superseded** by the **SEBI Master Circular for Stock Brokers, SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/90 dated July 17, 2025**. Under **paragraph 35.2** of that Master Circular, a stock broker must retain **evidence of pre-trade confirmation from the client**, and that evidence may include **email, logs for internet transactions, SMS messages, or any other legally verifiable record**. SEBI’s interpretive position is that a **WhatsApp instruction from the client’s registered mobile number may qualify as a legally verifiable record**, but only if the broker’s logs/records are **retrievable and legally verifiable for investigation or legal proceedings**.

SEBI also made clear that, if there is a dispute, the broker must be able to **prove the legal verifiability of the WhatsApp communication under the applicable law governing electronic evidence** and must comply with **all other applicable requirements of the SB Master Circular**. This guidance is **fact-specific** and based only on FRR’s representation; SEBI expressly said different facts or conditions could lead to a different result, and the letter reflects the department’s **enforcement position only**, not a binding Board decision. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that merchant bankers should not assume an automatic insider-trading restriction on post-employment sale of ESOP shares solely because the individual was previously employed by the merchant banker; instead, they should assess whether the person was in possession of UPSI, remains subject to any continuing confidentiality or trading restrictions, and whether the proposed transaction is otherwise permissible under applicable internal and regulatory controls. The letter is informal guidance rather than a binding adjudication, so it should be used as interpretive support and not as a substitute for obtaining transaction-specific legal advice or clearing the trade under the firm’s insider-trading policy and ESOP documentation.

rows.summary:
SEBI responded to Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited’s informal guidance request regarding how a **close-ended Alternative Investment Fund (AIF)** may operate during an **extended tenure** under the **SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012**. The applicant, a SEBI-registered portfolio manager and investment manager for a **Category III AIF** (registration no. **IN/AIF3/16-17/0291**) and a **Category II AIF** (registration no. **IN/AIF2/17-18/0340**), asked whether, once the fund’s tenure is extended, the AIF may only **liquidate existing portfolio investments** or may also **make new investments in portfolio companies**.

SEBI’s view is grounded in **Regulation 13(5)** of the AIF Regulations, which permits extension of the tenure of a close-ended AIF by **up to two years**, but only with the approval of **two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment** in the AIF. SEBI also cites **Regulation 13(6)**, which requires close-ended AIFs to **cease from making fresh investments after the expiry of the tenure or extended tenure**, except in **special situations permitted under the regulations**. On that basis, SEBI’s position is that during the extended period, the AIF is **not permitted to make fresh investments in portfolio companies** and is limited to winding down / liquidating its existing portfolio, unless a specific regulatory exception applies.

For compliance purposes, this means managers of close-ended AIFs should treat any tenure extension as a **run-off period**, not as an additional investment period. The practical requirement is to ensure that, once the original term ends and an extension is approved by the required unit-holder majority, the fund’s activities are restricted to **exiting existing positions and managing liquidation**, and not deploying capital into new investments. This interpretation applies directly to **close-ended AIFs** under the AIF Regulations, and should be reflected in fund governance, investor approvals, and investment operations during the extended tenure.

rows.title: Consultation Paper on Review of Voluntary Delisting norms under SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021  Addendum- Executive Summary
rows.desc: Page 1 of 2 Addendum to Consultation Paper on Review of Voluntary Delisting Norms under SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021 The following is the executive summary of consultation paper on Review of Voluntary Delisting placed on the website of SEBI on August 14, 2023 for seeking public comments. 1. Review of the Counter-Offer Mechanism  As per the Delisting Regulations, an acquirer can make a counter-offer only after the cumulative shareholding of the shares held by acquirer and shares tendered by public shareholders in Reverse Book Building (“RBB”) mechanism reaches at least 90% of the paid-up capital of the company.  In order to facilitate cases where cumulative shareholding of the shares held by acquirer and shares tendered by public shareholders does not reach 90%, it is proposed to reduce the threshold for counter-offer to below 90% but equal to or more than 75% (75%-90%) of the paid-up capital of the company.  The floor price of such counter-offer shall be the Volume Weighted Average Price of the shares tendered by the willing shareholders in the delisting offer wherein the acquirer failed to reach 90%. 2. Review of “Floor Price” under the Delisting Regulations-  In addition to the current parameters for computing floor price, it is suggested to introduce an additional parameter i.e. Adjusted Book Value which will be applicable for delisting of frequently traded and infrequently traded shares. 3. Alternatives to the Reverse Book Building Process  Presently, exit price is determined by way of RBB mechanism only.  It is proposed to introduce delisting at fixed price as an alternative to RBB for companies whose shares are frequently traded. 4. Review of the Reference Date for Determination of the Floor Price-  Presently, the reference date for computing the floor price is the date of approval of the board meeting.  It has been proposed in the consultation paper to change the reference date to the date of the initial public announcement.  F
rows.summary:

The document is a SEBI “Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)” listings page, not a single substantive rule text, and it functions as a regulatory docket of AIF-related papers, circulars, master circulars, and guidance items over time. For compliance purposes, the most material items visible in the excerpt are current and recent regulatory actions affecting AIF managers, trustees, and related market participants: SEBI issued a **Master Circular for AIFs on 3 June 2026**; a **circular on regulatory reporting by AIFs on 4 March 2026**; and a **GARUDA “Green-Channel” mechanism on 30 July 2026** for processing AIF placement memoranda filed with SEBI upon document acknowledgement, indicating a new/streamlined filing workflow for placement memorandum processing. The page also shows that on **9 September 2025** SEBI issued a circular establishing a **framework for AIFs to make co-investment within the AIF structure**, which is relevant to how co-investment opportunities are structured and offered through the fund vehicle itself rather than outside it.

The listing also reflects several consultation papers that signal likely or proposed rule changes affecting compliance obligations, even though the page itself does not state the final rule text. This listing shows recent SEBI commodity derivatives regulatory materials and indicates that firms active in the commodity derivatives market need to monitor multiple updates across trading, clearing, settlement, and risk management obligations. The document itself is a search/listing page rather than a full circular, so it does not provide the detailed text of each rule change; however, it identifies the most material current items and their publication dates.

The newest items are a **12 Aug 2026 circular** on the **review of inclusion of historical scenarios in stress testing for the commodity derivatives segment**, and **11 Aug 2026 consultation papers** on both **expanding the scope of the SEBI (Vault Managers) Regulations, 2021** and **FPI participation in exchange traded commodity derivatives (ETCDs)**. These are currently consultation-stage items, meaning they are not yet operative rules, but they are important because they may affect how risk is modeled, how warehoused commodities are handled, and whether foreign portfolio investors can participate in commodity derivative products under revised conditions.

On **19 Jun 2026**, SEBI issued a circular on **clarification regarding the applicability of the benefit of early pay-in in the commodity derivatives segment**. Any exchange member, clearing member, or participant relying on early pay-in treatment should review this because it clarifies when the benefit applies and therefore affects margin, settlement, and operational processing.

On **16 Mar 2026**, SEBI issued a circular on the **coverage of the Settlement Guarantee Fund (SGF) for the commodity derivatives segment**, and on **5 Feb 2026** it released a related **consultation paper on draft circulars covering both historical scenario inclusion in stress testing and SGF coverage**. Together, these items indicate a broader review of default-risk backstops and stress-testing methodology for clearing corporations and commodity derivatives market infrastructure. Compliance teams at clearing corporations and exchanges should treat these as likely to affect risk parameter calibration, default fund coverage, and the documentation used for internal and regulatory risk controls.

The 2024 items are operationally significant and directly relevant to market infrastructure and members. On **30 May 2024**, SEBI issued a circular on **comprehensive guidelines for the Investor Protection Fund (IPF) and Investor Services Fund (ISF) for stock exchanges having a commodity derivatives segment**, and another circular on **revision of eligibility criteria for launching commodity futures contracts**. These affect exchanges that list commodity derivatives and may change the conditions that must be satisfied before a new commodity futures contract can be introduced, as well as the contribution/use framework for investor protection and services funds. On the same date, SEBI also modified the **requirement for inspection of accredited warehouses by clearing corporations**, which affects warehouse accreditation and ongoing supervision over deliverable inventory used in physical settlement.

Also on **27 May 2024**, SEBI issued a **standard operating procedure for handling stock exchange outages and extending trading hours in the commodity derivatives segment**, and a circular setting **eligibility criteria for launching options on commodity futures as underlying** for stock exchanges with commodity derivative segments. These require exchanges and members to have explicit outage-response procedures and could impose conditions on listing new options products, including product-launch controls, risk checks, and operational readiness. On **24 May 2024**, SEBI modified the **staggered delivery period in commodity futures contracts**, which is directly relevant to delivery-cycle planning, warehouse coordination, and member/client settlement processes.

Finally, the listing includes earlier 2024 and 2023 framework items such as **cross-margin benefits for offsetting positions with different expiry dates** (23 Apr 2024), a **notification of goods under the SCRA, 1956** (5 Mar 2024), a **Master Circular for the Commodity Derivatives Segment** (4 Aug 2023), a **revision in computation of the Core Settlement Guarantee Fund** (23 May 2023), and **direct market access (DMA) to SEBI-registered…** (10 May 2023, truncated in the listing). For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that commodity derivatives participants should check whether they are an exchange, clearing corporation, broker, FPI, warehouse/vault operator, or other market intermediary because different updates affect different parts of the market stack, and several of the newest items may still be under consultation rather than final implementation.

rows.summary:
This document sets out the contractual rights and obligations between a Beneficial Owner and a Depository Participant (DP) under the Depositories Act, 1996, SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 1996, and all related SEBI circulars, depositary bye-laws/business rules, and applicable government notifications as amended from time to time. A DP may open or activate a demat account only after receiving a complete account-opening form, KYC documents, and other supporting documents required by SEBI from time to time; in other words, account activation is contingent on full documentary compliance, not partial submission. The DP must keep all beneficial owner details, account-opening information, supporting documents, and any other related information confidential and may disclose them only when required by a statutory, legal, or regulatory authority.  

The Beneficial Owner has an ongoing duty to promptly notify the DP in writing of any change in the details provided in the account-opening form or later furnished to the DP. On fees, charges, and tariffs, the Beneficial Owner must pay the DP’s agreed charges for holding and transferring securities in dematerialized form and for depository services, as set out in the DP’s tariff sheet; the document specifically notes that no charges are payable for opening a demat account. It also states that for Basic Services Demat Accounts (BSDA), the DP must follow the charge structure prescribed under the applicable SEBI framework, meaning BSDA pricing is not left to free negotiation.  

For a compliance team, the key operational requirements are that account onboarding cannot proceed until the prescribed KYC/identity-supporting documentation is complete, confidentiality obligations apply to all BO data held by the DP, and any changes in BO particulars must be captured through written intimation and updated records. The fee disclosures must clearly reflect the tariff sheet and the rule that account opening itself is free, while BSDA accounts must be charged strictly in accordance with the applicable prescribed charge limits. The excerpt provided ends mid-sentence on the BSDA charge structure reference, so if this is part of a larger form, additional specific charge caps or conditions may appear in the omitted portion and should be checked separately.

rows.summary:
The document appears to summarize SEBI’s responses to comments on proposed changes for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs), with a focus on validation of SWAGAT-FI status, re-KYC timing, and fee-block duration. On SWAGAT-FI identification/validation for existing FPIs, commenters objected that requiring FPIs to prove diversification, independence of fund managers, regulator confirmation, blind-pool status, and absence of segregated portfolios would create unnecessary paperwork and operational burden; SEBI disagreed, but clarified that the verification requirements will be aligned with the existing exemption criteria under the Additional Disclosure Framework, which the industry has already implemented, rather than creating a separate burdensome documentation process.  

On re-KYC, commenters wanted the current periodicity to be retained and asked that the process not be expanded for FPIs, while also expressing concern about material changes such as UBO changes being caught through re-KYC. SEBI disagreed with removing re-KYC and stated that material-change reporting requirements will continue, because re-KYC remains necessary for FPIs in the same way as for other investors and helps identify unreported changes such as UBO updates. The document also addresses annual fees: commenters argued the current payment frequency should stay in place and that moving to a longer payment cycle would reduce SEBI’s flexibility to adjust fees. SEBI responded that there is no annual fee requirement in the current setup; instead, the fee “block period” is being extended from 3 years to 10 years, and this 10-year period is intended to coincide with the re-KYC cycle.  

The excerpt ends mid-comment at item 6, indicating there are additional proposals and responses not fully shown, but from the visible content the key compliance impact is that existing FPI validation and ongoing due diligence expectations are being formalized in line with existing disclosure/exemption criteria, re-KYC obligations are retained, material changes must still be reported, and the fee cycle/block period is moving from 3 years to 10 years.

This calculator would guide the User to arrive at the indicative settlement amount which is normally arrived at by inputting values to various factors identified under Regulation 10 and Schedule II of the Settlement Regulations, 2018. Such indicative settlement amount is subject to modifications as deemed fit by the Internal Committee, High Powered Advisory Committee and the Panel of Whole Time Members. In appropriate cases there may also be levy of non-monetary settlement terms in accordance with Regulation 9 of the Settlement Regulations, 2018. How to use the Settlement Calculator Guidelines for arriving at Settlement Terms (As per Schedule II of the Settlement Regulations, 2018) The settlement amount (SA) shall comprise of the Indicative Amount (IA) arrived at in terms of these guidelines and the factors provided in regulation 10 of the Settlement Regulations, wherever applicable. The IA shall not be less than Rupees 3 lakh for first time applicants or Rupees 7 lakh for others, as the case may be Explanation.-A ‘first time applicant’ is a person against whom no order has been passed by the adjudicating officer or by the Board or who has never obtained a settlement order from the Board as on the date of the present application. Based on the stage at which the proceeding(s), for which the application is made, is/are pending, the proceeding conversion factor (PCF) shall be applied when calculating the IA.
