rows.title: Deposits and Accounts – Accounts of Non-resident banks
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/251 A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 20 September 02, 2026 To All Authorised Dealer Category-I banks Madam / Sir Deposits and Accounts – Accounts of Non-resident banks Please refer to Para B.2(ii) and B.8(i) of Part B of the A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No.92, dated April 4, 2003, in terms of which AD banks were required to: a. Furnish an up-to-date list of all its offices/branches maintaining Rupee accounts of non-resident banks, as at the end of December each year before 15th January of the following year to the Central Office of Reserve Bank, and b. Report temporary overdrawals by overseas branches/ correspondents over permissible limit, if not adjusted within five days, to the Central Office of Reserve Bank. 2. On a review, it has been decided to dispense with the above reporting requirements with immediate effect. 3. The directions contained in this circular have been issued under sections 10(4) and 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (42 of 1999) and are without prejudice to permissions/approvals, if any, required under any other law. Yours faithfully (N. Senthil Kumar) Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has removed two reporting obligations that previously applied to Authorised Dealer Category-I (AD Cat-I) banks under Para B.2(ii) and B.8(i) of A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 92 dated April 4, 2003. Effective immediately as of September 2, 2026, AD banks no longer need to submit the annual list of all offices/branches maintaining rupee accounts of non-resident banks as at each December-end by January 15 of the following year to the RBI Central Office. They also no longer need to report temporary overdrawals by overseas branches/correspondents that exceed the permissible limit if those overdrawals are not adjusted within five days.

For compliance teams at AD Cat-I banks, the practical impact is that these two RBI-specific reporting workflows may be discontinued from the circular’s effective date, but the underlying permissions/approvals under other applicable laws remain unchanged. The circular states it is issued under sections 10(4) and 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, and expressly notes it does not affect any approvals that may still be required under other laws.

rows.title: Relief Measures in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities - Reporting through Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) Portal - Introduction of Half-Yearly Return
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/250 CO.FIDD.FSD.No.S544/05-10-001/2026-27 September 02, 2026 The Chief Executive Officer / Managing Director All Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks) All Local Area Banks/ Urban Cooperative Banks/ Rural Cooperative Banks/ Non- Banking Financial Companies / AIFIs Madam / Dear Sir, Relief Measures in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities - Reporting through Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) Portal - Introduction of Half- Yearly Return The regulatory framework governing the relief measures to be extended by the Regulated Entities (REs) in areas affected by natural calamities has been revised vide the amendment directions on Resolution of Stressed Assets dated April 29, 2026 (list enclosed), which came into effect from July 1, 2026. 2. These directions require REs to submit data relating to relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities through the CIMS portal on a half-yearly basis. Accordingly, in order to align the existing reporting mechanism with the revised regulatory framework, REs shall furnish the required information in the revised reporting format through the CIMS portal. 3. The return shall be submitted within 30 days from the end of each half-year, i.e., by October 30 for the half-year ending September 30, and by April 30 for the half-year ending March 31. 4. REs shall ensure that the information submitted through the CIMS portal is accurate, complete, and duly validated. Appropriate internal systems and processes may be 2 established to facilitate timely collection, verification, consolidation, and submission of the required information. 5. Further, the existing monthly return which was applicable to all Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Small Finance Banks and excluding Regional Rural Banks) on relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities stands discontinued with effect from July 1, 2026. Yours sincerely, (R Giridharan) Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The RBI’s September 2, 2026 circular requires regulated entities to report relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities through the CIMS portal using a revised reporting format, replacing the earlier mechanism to align with the amended “Resolution of Stressed Assets” directions issued on April 29, 2026, which took effect on July 1, 2026. The new requirement is a **half-yearly return** covering data on relief measures in calamity-affected areas, and it applies broadly to **all regulated entities addressed in the circular**: Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks), Local Area Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, Rural Cooperative Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, and AIFIs.

The return must be filed **within 30 days after the end of each half-year**, specifically **by October 30 for the half-year ending September 30** and **by April 30 for the half-year ending March 31**. RBI expects the data submitted through CIMS to be **accurate, complete, and duly validated**, and it directs entities to put in place internal systems and procedures for timely **collection, verification, consolidation, and submission** of the information. Compliance teams should note that the **existing monthly return** previously applicable to **all Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Small Finance Banks, but excluding Regional Rural Banks)** on these calamity-related relief measures is **discontinued effective July 1, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Second Amendment Directions, 2026
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/249 DOR.MRG.REC.No.217/00-00-011/2026-27 September 2, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 Please refer to Chapter VIII of Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025, on Investment in non-SLR securities. In view of the establishment of Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC) as the nation's central digital payment fraud intelligence platform and to enable UCBs to acquire its membership, there is a need to amend the extant instructions. 2. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (hereinafter called the Act), read with Section 56 thereof, and all other laws enabling the Reserve Bank in this regard, the Reserve Bank, being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in the public interest so to do, hereby, issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. (i) These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Second Amendment Directions, 2026. (ii) These Amendment Directions shall come into effect from the date of issue. 4. The Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025, are amended as provided below. (i) Paragraph 101.(5) shall be substituted by the following, namely:- “101.(5) Equity shares of Umbrella Organization (UO) of UCB sector and Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC) for acquiring membership;”. (ii) Paragraph 107.(1) shall be substituted by the following, namely:- “107.(1) Equity shares of Market Infrastructure Companies (MICs), Umbrella Organization (UO) of UCB Sector, IDPIC, and CCBs / StCBs, if it becomes necessary to do so for
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Second Amendment Directions, 2026 update the 2025 Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) investment rules specifically to permit UCBs to invest in the equity shares of the Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC), which has been established as the national central digital payment fraud intelligence platform, so that UCBs can become members of IDPIC. The amendment is issued under Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and takes effect immediately from the date of issue, September 2, 2026.  

Substantively, the amendment changes paragraph 101(5) of the 2025 Directions so that it now expressly allows investment in equity shares of the UCB sector’s Umbrella Organization (UO) and in IDPIC “for acquiring membership.” It also substitutes paragraph 107(1) to expand the set of equity-share holdings that may be relevant in the investment framework to include Market Infrastructure Companies (MICs), the UO of the UCB sector, IDPIC, and CCBs/StCBs where necessary, replacing the prior narrower language.  

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that UCBs now have explicit regulatory permission to acquire IDPIC equity shares for membership purposes, and the investment portfolio classification/valuation framework should be applied accordingly under the amended 2025 Directions. There are no numeric limits, thresholds, or filing deadlines stated in the amendment itself; the main requirement is to update internal investment policy, approval, and classification processes to reflect IDPIC as a permitted equity investment/membership-related holding effective immediately.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Second Amendment Directions, 2026
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/248 DOR.SOG(SPE).REC.214/13.03.00/2026-27 August 25, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 Please refer to the Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (hereinafter referred to as ‘Directions’), dated November 28, 2025 (Updated as on June 17, 2026), wherein temporary withdrawal of the interest rate ceiling on fresh FCNR(B) deposits of 3-5 year tenors and restriction on interest rates on NRE deposits of 3 year and above tenors, including the deposits that are renewed upon maturity, have been provided with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until September 30, 2026. On a review, it has been decided to amend the date ‘September 30, 2026’ to the date ‘August 31, 2026’ for the aforementioned temporary relaxation. 2. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act,1949 and all other laws enabling the Reserve Bank India (RBI) in this regard, the RBI, being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in public interest so to do, hereby, issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. These Amendment Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co- operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Second Amendment Directions, 2026. 4. These Amendment Directions shall come into force with immediate effect. 5. These Amendment Directions shall modify the Directions, as under: i. In paragraph 24(4) subscript ( 1 ), the phrase “with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until September 30, 2026” shall be substituted with “with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until August 31, 2026”. ii. In paragraph 29(7) subscript ( 2 ), the phrase “with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until September 30, 2026” shall be substituted with “with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until August 31, 2026”. (Dr. Sudarsana Sahoo) Chief Gene
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Second Amendment Directions, 2026** for **Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits** shorten the end date of a previously granted temporary relaxation on deposit pricing. Under the underlying 2025 Directions (updated June 17, 2026), rural co-operative banks were allowed, **from June 17, 2026**, a temporary withdrawal of the interest rate ceiling on **fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3-5 year tenors** and a relaxation of interest rate restrictions on **NRE deposits of 3 years and above**, including **renewals on maturity**; that relaxation had originally been set to run until **September 30, 2026**. This amendment changes that end date to **August 31, 2026** instead, meaning the temporary relief now applies only through **August 31, 2026**.

The RBI issues the amendment under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and states it is doing so in public interest. Under the amended rule, the exemption from **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** and **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** maintenance for **fresh FCNR(B) deposits** with a **minimum tenor of 3 years and maximum tenor of 5 years**, and for **fresh NRE term deposits** with a **tenor of 3 years or more** (including renewals on maturity), now applies only to deposits mobilized **between June 8, 2026 and August 31, 2026** instead of through **September 30, 2026**.

For compliance purposes, the key change is a **shortening of the eligibility window by one month** for both categories of deposits covered by the exemption. The amendment specifically modifies **paragraph 20(6)** and **paragraph 20(7)** of the underlying **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025** by substituting the relevant end date from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**. The directions were issued on **August 25, 2026** and **came into force immediately** upon issuance.

The legal basis cited is **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, read with **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. In practical terms, small finance banks must ensure that only deposits meeting the original tenor criteria and **mobilized on or before August 31, 2026** continue to receive the CRR/SLR exemption; deposits mobilized after that date will not qualify under this temporary relief.

rows.summary: The Reserve Bank of India’s Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026, issued on August 25, 2026, shorten the temporary CRR and SLR exemption window previously granted to commercial banks for certain fresh long-term NRI deposits. Under the underlying 2025 Directions, fresh FCNR(B) deposits with a minimum tenor of three years and a maximum tenor of five years were exempt from cash reserve ratio and statutory liquidity ratio maintenance if mobilized by banks between June 8, 2026 and September 30, 2026, and fresh NRE term deposits with a tenor of three years or more were similarly exempt if mobilized (including renewals upon maturity) between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026. This amendment changes both end dates from September 30, 2026 to August 31, 2026, so only deposits falling within those revised date windows remain eligible for the exemptions. The change is made under the RBI’s powers under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, read with Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934 and Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, and it applies specifically to commercial banks subject to the CRR and SLR Directions, 2025. The amendment takes effect immediately upon issuance, so banks must apply the revised cutoff date at once when determining whether qualifying FCNR(B) and NRE deposits may be excluded from CRR and SLR maintenance.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/237 DOR.CRE.REC.210/07-03-008/2026-27 August 25, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026 The Reserve Bank has issued the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 (hereinafter referred to as ‘Directions’ ). On a review, it has been decided to revise the large exposure framework for Infrastructure Debt Fund-Non-Banking Financial Company (IDF-NBFC) in the Upper Layer. 2. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred by Chapter III B of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and all other provisions / laws enabling the Reserve Bank of India (‘RBI’) in this regard, RBI being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in the public interest so to do, hereby, issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. These Amendment Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Non- Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026. 4. These Amendment Directions shall come into force with immediate effect. 5. These Amendment Directions shall modify the Directions as under: (1) After paragraph 39 in ‘Chapter IV - Guidelines Applicable to NBFC – Upper Layer’, a new paragraph 39A shall be inserted as under: 39A. The large exposure limits applicable to NBFC-IFC shall also be applicable to IDF-NBFC that are subject to Upper Layer regulations in terms of paragraph 60A of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 read together with 2 paragraph 18 (4) (i) of the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025. (Dr. Sudarsana Sahoo) Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** on **August 25, 2026**, and they take **immediate effect**. The amendment was made under the RBI’s statutory powers and specifically revises the **large exposure framework** for **Infrastructure Debt Fund–Non-Banking Financial Companies (IDF-NBFCs)** that fall within the **Upper Layer** regulatory category.  

The sole substantive change is the insertion of a new **paragraph 39A** after paragraph 39 in Chapter IV of the existing **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025**. This new paragraph states that the **large exposure limits applicable to NBFC-IFCs** will also apply to **IDF-NBFCs subject to Upper Layer regulation**, as determined under **paragraph 60A of the RBI (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025**, read with **paragraph 18(4)(i) of the RBI (Commercial Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025**.  

For compliance purposes, this means affected IDF-NBFCs in the Upper Layer must now monitor and comply with the same concentration-risk / large-exposure caps and related controls that already apply to NBFC-IFCs, effective immediately, with no transition period stated in the amendment. The document does not introduce new numeric thresholds in the text itself; instead, it imports the existing NBFC-IFC large exposure limits by reference into the IDF-NBFC Upper Layer framework.

rows.title: Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1267/ 1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List: Amendment of 21 Entries
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/236 DOR.AML.REC.204/14.06.001/2026-27 August 19, 2026 The Chairpersons/ CEOs of the Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Local Area Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, All India Financial Institutions Madam/Dear Sir, Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1267/ 1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List: Amendment of 21 Entries Please refer to Chapter IX on “Requirements/obligations under International Agreements - Communications from International Agencies” of the Reserve Bank of India - Know Your Customer, Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 (amended as on December 29, 2025) (“Directions”), as applicable, as per which, regulated entity shall ensure that in terms of section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) (UAPA) Act, 1967 and amendments thereto, it does not have any account in the name of individuals / entities appearing in the lists of individuals and entities, suspected of having terrorist links, which are approved by and periodically circulated by the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). 2. In this connection, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Government of India has informed about the UNSC press release SC/16435, dated August 18, 2026 wherein the Security Council pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da’esh), Al‑Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities enacted the amendments specified with strikethrough and underline in the entries mentioned in Annexure 1 on its ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List of individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2734 (2024), and adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations. 2 3. Press release dated August 18, 2026 regarding the above can be found at https://pres
rows.summary:
This RBI circular instructs all regulated entities covered by the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 — including commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, urban and rural co-operative banks, regional rural banks, local area banks, NBFCs, asset reconstruction companies, and all India financial institutions — to continue enforcing the section 51A UAPA, 1967 obligations that prohibit maintaining accounts in the names of persons or entities appearing on the UNSC-approved terrorist sanctions lists. The specific update being communicated is the UN Security Council press release SC/16435 dated August 18, 2026, which amended 21 entries on the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al‑Qaida Sanctions List under UNSC resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015), with those individuals/entities subject to asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo measures under resolution 2734 (2024).

Compliance teams are directed to act immediately in accordance with Chapter IX of the RBI KYC Directions, 2025, and to strictly follow the UAPA Order dated February 2, 2021 as amended on April 22, 2024. Practically, this means institutions must screen against the updated UNSC lists, ensure no accounts are held in the names of listed persons/entities, and take appropriate sanctions-response action whenever a match or new listing is identified. RBI also points institutions to the UNSC narrative summaries and sanctions detail pages for identifying information and the scope of the measures/exemptions.

On de-listing, the circular reflects MHA guidance that any delisting request received by a bank must be forwarded electronically to the Joint Secretary (CTCR), Ministry of Home Affairs for consideration. It also notes that listed persons or entities may submit delisting requests to the UN Secretary-General’s independent Ombudsperson. No separate RBI deadline is given for filing actions in this circular, but the operative expectation is immediate and ongoing compliance with the updated UNSC designations and the prescribed UAPA/RBI procedures.

The RBI is reminding regulated entities that, under Chapter IX of the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 (as amended on December 29, 2025), they must continue to ensure compliance with Section 51A of the UAPA, 1967 by not maintaining accounts in the name of any individual or entity appearing on the UNSC-approved sanctions lists circulated under that law. This circular, dated August 18, 2026 (RBI/2026-27/235), specifically conveys a Ministry of External Affairs communication about UNSC press release SC/16433 dated August 14, 2026, which updated the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida sanctions list under resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015), and the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo regime under UNSC resolution 2734 (2024).

The material change is that four list entries have been amended, so compliance teams must ensure their screening systems reflect the updated particulars immediately and that any existing or prospective relationships are re-screened against the revised data. The first amended entry is QDi.002, Amin Muhammad Ul Haq Saam Khan (also known as Amin Al-Haq / Muhammad Amin / Dr. Amin / Dr. Amin Ul-Haq), an Afghan national born on either 30 April 1963 or in 1960, associated with Kabul, Afghanistan as of June 2026; the entry notes his role as security coordinator for Usama bin Laden, that he was repatriated to Afghanistan in February 2006, was in Afghanistan as of August 2021, was arrested in Pakistan in 2024 and deported to Afghanistan in 2025, and that photo and fingerprints are available via the INTERPOL-UN Security Council Special Notice. The second amended entry is QDi.436, Abubakar Swalleh (also listed as Abubaker Swaleh / Tom Kiyurige; low-quality alias Isaac Mupeta), a Ugandan national born on 13 January 1992 or 16 March 1993, with Uganda passport number A00195974 expiring 16 December 2029, national ID CM920231090NZA, and an address at Luzira Prison, Kampala, Uganda; the entry states he provides financial, material, technological, and logistical support to ISIL (listed as Al-Qaida in Iraq/QDe.115), has acted since 2018 as an ISIL facilitator for East and Southern Africa, and includes a phone number (+963936016952) plus an INTERPOL notice reference. The third amended entry is QDi.439, Hamida Nabaggala (name in original script provided; also listed under low-quality aliases Nabaggala / Nabaggaka / Hamida / Hamidah), a Ugandan national born 23 February 1989, with Uganda ID CF89095102DDAE expiring 27 March 2025 and an address in the Democratic Republic of the Congo; the update says she works as a mediator in financing channels for ISIL in Central Africa, has been charged with financing a 2021 bombing in Kampala, and attempted to coerce her three children in Uganda to send them to ISIL camps in the DRC, with photo availability via the INTERPOL-UN Special Notice.

The Reserve Bank of India has issued a directive dated **August 10, 2026** assigning **Lead Bank responsibility** for **five newly created districts in the Union Territory of Ladakh**, following the UT Administration’s **Gazette Notification SG-LD-E-27042026-1712 dated April 27, 2026**. rows.summary: This RBI amendment directs banks to exclude certain lending linked to recently mobilized foreign currency and NRE deposit inflows from the calculation of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) for priority sector lending purposes. Specifically, advances made in India against fresh FCNR(B) deposits with a tenor of at least 3 years and up to 5 years, mobilized or renewed during the window from June 08, 2026 through September 30, 2026, must not be counted in ANBC; the same exclusion applies to advances against NRE term deposits of 3 years or more mobilized or renewed during the window from June 19, 2026 through September 30, 2026. The document ties this to the RBI’s earlier June 2026 measures that introduced a USD/INR swap facility for fresh FCNR(B) dollar funds of 3–5 year tenor and provided CRR/SLR exemptions for the same categories of deposits, indicating that the priority sector denominator treatment is being aligned with those deposit incentives. The compliance impact is on banks calculating PSL targets/classification: they must identify and carve out qualifying advances against these specified deposit types when computing ANBC for regulatory reporting and target compliance. The excerpt ends mid-sentence after “between June…”, so the full scope may include additional implementation details or operational instructions in the remainder of the direction, but the material rule clearly stated is the ANBC exclusion for these two deposit-backed advance categories within the specified mobilization periods and tenors.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) Third Amendment Directions, 2026** replace the existing recovery-agent guidance in Chapter X of the **Reserve Bank of India (Housing Finance Companies) Directions, 2025**. Specifically, the former **sub-section A.15 “Guidelines for engaging Recovery Agents”** and its **paragraph 170** are being **deleted and substituted** with a new provision titled **“A.15A Conduct of HFCs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agents”**. Under the new paragraph **170A**, an HFC must comply with the provisions of **paragraphs 100A.2 to 100AB under Chapter III of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025**, which means the HFC-specific recovery-agent rules are now aligned to the broader RBI conduct framework applicable to NBFCs.

These amendment directions are issued under **Section 30A of the National Housing Bank Act, 1987** and are stated to be necessary in the public interest. They are titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Housing Finance Companies) Third Amendment Directions, 2026** and **take effect on January 1, 2027**. The document also notes that RBI has separately reviewed the prior instructions on recovery agents and decided to issue **comprehensive conduct-related instructions for recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies** for most NBFCs under the Responsible Business Conduct framework.

For a compliance team, the key operational point is that HFCs should treat this as a **mandatory transition from the old HFC-specific recovery-agent paragraph to the new cross-referenced conduct regime** effective **1 January 2027**. The text indicates the new HFC obligation is not a standalone set of rules in the amendment itself, but a requirement to follow the referenced RBI conduct provisions in the NBFC Responsible Business Conduct Directions. Since the amendment expressly replaces the existing paragraph, HFCs should update internal recovery policies, agent engagement standards, staff and vendor training, complaint/escalation procedures, and any customer-contact scripts or oversight controls to ensure they are aligned with the incorporated Chapter III requirements by the effective date.

(2) These Directions shall come into effect from January 1, 2027. 4. These Amendment Directions shall modify the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 as under: (1) In paragraph 6, the following definitions shall be inserted after sub-paragraph 6( 11), namely: “6(11A) Recovery agency means an entity or individual (other than NBFC’s own employees) who has been engaged by an NBFC, irrespective of the contractual designation / nomenclature used for such engagement, under an outsourcing 2 arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a borrower in d
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Responsible Business Conduct) Third Amendment Directions, 2026** are issued under the RBI Act, 1934 and are designed to replace and expand earlier recovery-agent instructions with a more comprehensive framework governing **recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies**. The amendment applies to **all NBFCs** except **Mortgage Guarantee Companies, Core Investment Companies, NBFC-Account Aggregators, Standalone Primary Dealers, Non-Operating Financial Holding Companies, and NBFCs that do not have any customer interface**. It becomes effective **January 1, 2027**.

A key change is the insertion of a new definition of **“recovery agency”**: it means any **entity or individual other than the NBFC’s own employees** that is engaged by an NBFC, regardless of the contractual label used, under an **outsourcing arrangement** to assist in recovering loan dues from a borrower. This wording is important because it captures arrangements based on substance rather than the form or title of the contract, so firms cannot avoid the rules by using different nomenclature. Compliance teams should treat any third party or individual used for collections/recovery support as a recovery agency if they are not direct employees.

The document states that RBI reviewed the prior instructions and decided to issue **comprehensive instructions on conduct-related matters in recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies**, indicating a broader regulatory focus on borrower treatment, recovery conduct, and outsourcing controls. Although the excerpt provided only shows the start of the amendment text, the practical implication is that NBFCs in scope should prepare for updated requirements governing how recoveries are conducted and how recovery agents/agencies are selected, supervised, and controlled. Compliance officers should ensure internal policies, outsourcing agreements, and collection practices are aligned in advance of the **1 January 2027** effective date.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions (AIFI) – Responsible Business Conduct Third Amendment Directions, 2026** expand and formalize the rules governing **loan recovery conduct and outsourcing to recovery agencies** for all AIFIs. The RBI states that the earlier instructions on AIFI responsibilities when using recovery agents have been reviewed, and it is now issuing **comprehensive instructions on conduct-related matters in recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies** applicable to all AIFIs (whether referred to collectively as “AIFIs” or individually as an “AIFI”) under the 2025 Responsible Business Conduct Directions.

The amendment is issued under **Section 45L of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934** and is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions - Responsible Business Conduct) Third Amendment Directions, 2026**. The new directions **take effect on January 1, 2027**. They amend the 2025 Directions by inserting new definitions in paragraph **3A** after sub-paragraph **3A(6)**.

Two key definitions are added. **“Recovery agency”** is defined broadly as any **entity or individual other than the AIFI’s own employees** that is engaged by an AIFI under an **outsourcing arrangement** to assist in recovery of loan dues from a borrower in default, **including taking possession of a security**, regardless of the contractual label or nomenclature used. **“Recovery agent”** is defined as a **representative of a recovery agency** who is involved in recovery-related activities. For compliance purposes, this means institutions must look to the **substance of the arrangement and function performed**, not just the contract title, when determining whether the new recovery-related requirements apply.

The document as provided stops partway through the inserted definition of recovery agent, so no additional operational rules, timelines, reporting steps, or thresholds are visible in the excerpt. Based on the text shown, the immediate compliance impact is that AIFIs should prepare for **expanded conduct and outsourcing controls over external recovery providers** beginning **January 1, 2027**, with particular attention to how recovery agencies and their personnel are identified and governed under existing RBI responsible business conduct obligations.

The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) – Responsible Business Conduct Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** revise the 2025 Responsible Business Conduct framework to introduce **new, comprehensive conduct rules for loan recovery and for the engagement of recovery agencies**. The RBI states that the earlier recovery-agent instructions have been reviewed and replaced with broader requirements covering **all RCBs**, with the amendments issued under **Sections 21, 35A, and 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

These Directions are titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** and **take effect from January 1, 2027**. From that date, they modify the 2025 Directions by inserting a new definition of **“recovery agency”** in paragraph 4(23A). The definition is broad: it covers **any entity or individual other than the RCB’s own employees** that an RCB engages, regardless of the contract label used, **under an outsourcing arrangement** to help recover loan dues from a defaulting borrower, including **taking possession of security**.

Compliance teams should therefore review all third-party and BC recovery arrangements, because the RBI is signaling that the substance of the activity—not the name of the contract—determines whether the arrangement falls under the recovery-agency rules.

The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Responsible Business Conduct) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** (RBI/2026-27/227, dated **August 6, 2026**), which **take effect on January 1, 2027**. These amendments are made under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and are intended to replace the existing, narrower instructions on engagement of recovery agents by UCBs with **comprehensive conduct-related rules governing recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies** for all UCBs.

The key substantive change is the insertion of a formal definition of **“recovery agency”** into paragraph 4 of the 2025 Directions. A recovery agency is now defined broadly as **any entity or individual other than the UCB’s own employees** that is engaged under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a defaulting borrower, **regardless of the title or contractual label used**. The definition expressly includes situations where the agency helps in recovery actions such as **taking possession of security**.

The RBI also gives an explicit illustration to prevent circumvention through alternative labeling: a **Business Correspondent (BC)** that is involved in recovery-related activities on behalf of a UCB will be treated as a **recovery agency**. Compliance teams should therefore assume that any outsourced person or firm doing recovery work, even if not described as a “recovery agent,” will fall within the new regime and must be managed as such under the Responsible Business Conduct framework once the amendment is in force.

Because the document states that the extant recovery-agent instructions have been reviewed and replaced with comprehensive instructions, UCBs should review their current outsourcing arrangements, recovery practices, and borrower-contact procedures before the **January 1, 2027** effective date to ensure that all recovery-related vendors, BCs, and other third parties are brought within the compliance controls applicable to recovery agencies under the amended Directions.

The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Regional Rural Banks (Responsible Business Conduct) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** on **August 6, 2026**, and they **take effect on January 1, 2027**. The amendment is made under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and is directed at **all Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**. Its purpose is to replace the prior, narrower instructions on recovery agents with **comprehensive rules governing conduct in recovery of loan dues and the use of recovery agencies**.

A key substantive change is the insertion of a new definition of **“recovery agency”** in the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025. A recovery agency now means **any entity or individual other than the RRB’s own employees** that is engaged by an RRB, regardless of the contractual label used, under an outsourcing arrangement to help recover loan dues from a borrower in default, **including taking possession of security**. The RBI expressly clarifies by illustration that a **Business Correspondent (BC)** performing recovery-related activities on behalf of an RRB is to be treated as a recovery agency for these purposes. This means RRBs cannot avoid the recovery-agency rules simply by using a different contract description or outsourcing structure.

For compliance purposes, RRBs should treat the amendment as requiring their recovery-outsourcing arrangements, including BC-linked recovery activity, to be reviewed against the RBI’s forthcoming/updated conduct standards applicable from **1 January 2027**. The document itself does not list the full operational conduct requirements in the excerpt provided, but it makes clear that the new framework is intended to govern **how recovery of loan dues is conducted** and **how recovery agencies are engaged**, with the expanded definition capturing a broad range of third-party recovery participants.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026 revise the RBI’s Local Area Banks (LABs) responsible business conduct framework to replace the earlier, narrower recovery-related instructions with a comprehensive set of rules governing recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies. The amendment is issued under Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and it takes effect on **January 1, 2027**. It applies to **all Local Area Banks** and covers recovery from borrowers in default, including **taking possession of security**; where expressly stated, some provisions also apply “mutatis mutandis” to collection from borrowers who are **not** in default in the normal course.

A key definitional change is the insertion of two new terms in the RBI’s 2025 Directions. A **“recovery agency”** is now defined as any entity or individual other than the LAB’s own employees that the LAB engages under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues, including possession of security, regardless of the contractual label used; the RBI specifically states that a **Business Correspondent (BC)** involved in recovery activities on behalf of an LAB will be treated as a recovery agency. A **“recovery agent”** is defined as the representative of such a recovery agency who actually interacts with the customer on recovery-related activities. The amendment also clarifies that if an individual is directly engaged by the LAB under an outsourcing arrangement for recovery or possession-related activities, the rules for both recovery agencies and recovery agents apply to that individual.

The amendment deletes paragraphs **227 to 235** of Chapter VIII (“Responsible Lending Conduct”) and replaces them with a new section titled **“Conduct of LABs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agencies.”** Under the new framework, LABs must adopt a formal **policy on collection/recovery of loan dues and taking possession of security** by either their own employees or recovery agents. This policy must cover, at a minimum, the triggers for starting recovery, a **graded escalation matrix**, code of conduct standards for both employees and recovery agents, recovery handling when a borrower has died, and a structured process for financially distressed borrowers that includes **documented pre-escalation engagement** and guidance on available resolution options.

For recovery agency governance, the policy must also set out **eligibility and due diligence criteria**, performance evaluation standards, inspection/audit requirements, control mechanisms to ensure compliance with statutory and regulatory obligations, and procedures and/or **penal actions** for non-compliant recovery agencies and their agents. The policy must further include rules on **compensation to borrowers and guarantors** for losses arising from recovery actions that are not consistent with these Directions. In addition, LABs using a **technology-based mechanism** for recovery must follow whatever additional instructions are specified later in paragraph **235S** (the excerpt indicates this is contemplated, though the actual text of 235S is not included in the provided content). The new section also states that these rules do not override any **statutory rights or obligations** relating to security enforcement under other laws, nor any separate RBI directions on specific recovery actions such as **one-time settlement**.

rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** will take effect on **1 January 2027** and materially overhaul the rules governing **loan recovery, collection practices, and the engagement of recovery agents/agencies by Small Finance Banks (SFBs)**. The RBI says the earlier instructions on recovery agents have been reviewed and replaced with **comprehensive conduct requirements** for both recovery of loan dues and the use of recovery agencies. The amendment is issued under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and modifies the existing **SFB Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025**.

A major change is the addition of new definitions. A **“recovery agency”** is now defined broadly to mean any entity or individual, other than the SFB’s own employees, engaged by an SFB under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a defaulting borrower, **including taking possession of security**, regardless of the contractual label used. The RBI explicitly states that a **Business Correspondent (BC)** involved in recovery-related activities on behalf of an SFB will be treated as a recovery agency for these purposes. A **“recovery agent”** is defined as the representative of a recovery agency who actually interacts with the customer at the point of interface; if an individual is directly hired by the SFB under outsourcing for recovery or possession work, the rules for both recovery agencies and recovery agents apply to that person.

The amendment **deletes paragraphs 408 to 416 and 442 to 454** in Chapter VIII on Responsible Lending Conduct and replaces them with a new section, **“L. Conduct of SFBs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agencies.”** This new section applies to **recovery of loan dues from defaulting borrowers, including taking possession of security**, and it can also apply, where specifically stated, to normal-course collection from borrowers who are not in default. The RBI also clarifies that these provisions do **not** override any statutory enforcement rights or obligations a bank may have under other laws, and they do not displace other RBI directions covering specific recovery actions such as **one-time settlement**.

Under the new framework, each SFB must adopt a **formal policy** on collection and recovery of loan dues, including possession of security, whether recovery is conducted by the bank’s own employees or by recovery agents. That policy must cover, at a minimum: the **triggers for starting recovery**, a **graded escalation matrix**, a **code of conduct** for employees and agents, procedures for recovery in the event of the **borrower’s death**, and a **structured process for handling financially distressed borrowers**, including **documented pre-escalation engagement** and guidance on available resolution options. Where recovery agencies are used, the policy must also set out **eligibility and due diligence criteria**, **performance evaluation standards**, **inspection/audit mechanisms**, compliance controls to ensure adherence to statutory and regulatory requirements, and the **procedures and penalties** for dealing with non-compliant agencies or agents. The policy must further include rules on **compensation to borrowers or guarantors** for losses caused by recovery actions that are not consistent with the Directions.

The amendment also makes clear that the new section applies to SFB employees involved in recovery and possession work, by defining **“SFB employees”** for this purpose to include employees deployed for those activities. Although the excerpt provided ends partway through paragraph 454G, the document signals that SFBs using a **technology-based mechanism for recovery** under the forthcoming paragraph 454S will need to build that mechanism into their policy as well. For compliance teams, the key implementation task is to ensure that, by **1 January 2027**, all recovery arrangements, BC-related recovery activity, outsourcing contracts, conduct standards, escalation procedures, grievance/compensation processes, and oversight controls are aligned with the new RBI framework.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** applies to **all Commercial Banks except Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Regional Rural Banks, and Local Area Banks**. It **comes into effect on January 1, 2027** and replaces the earlier piecemeal instructions on recovery agents with a more comprehensive framework governing **recovery of loan dues, possession of security, and engagement of recovery agencies**. The RBI has issued these changes under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

The amendment first introduces two key defined terms into the Directions. A **“recovery agency”** is any entity or individual, other than the bank’s own employees, engaged by a bank under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovering loan dues from a borrower in default, including taking possession of security; the definition explicitly says that a **Business Correspondent (BC)** involved in recovery-related work for a bank is treated as a recovery agency for these purposes. A **“recovery agent”** is the representative of such a recovery agency who interacts directly with customers at the point of customer interface. If an individual is directly engaged by the bank under an outsourcing arrangement for recovery or possession-related work, that person is subject to the requirements applicable to both recovery agencies and recovery agents.

The amendment then **deletes paragraphs 408 to 416 and 442 to 454** of Chapter VIII on Responsible Lending Conduct and inserts a new section titled **“Conduct of Banks in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agencies.”** This new section applies to **recovery of loan dues from borrowers in default, including taking possession of security**, and, where expressly stated, also applies **mutatis mutandis to dues collection from borrowers who are not in default**. It also makes clear that these provisions are **without prejudice to any statutory enforcement rights or obligations under other laws** and do not override other Directions dealing with specific recovery actions such as **one-time settlement**.

Under the new section, a bank must have a formal **policy on collection/recovery of loan dues and possession of security** by both its own employees and recovery agents. That policy must specify, at minimum, the **trigger points for starting recovery**, a **graded escalation matrix** for recovery actions, a **code of conduct** for employees and recovery agents, procedures for cases involving the **death of a borrower**, and a **structured framework for dealing with financial distress**, including documented pre-escalation engagement and guidance on available resolution options. The policy must also cover the **eligibility and due diligence standards** for appointing recovery agencies, their **performance evaluation criteria**, **inspection/audit/control mechanisms** to ensure compliance with legal and regulatory requirements, and the **procedures and penalties** for dealing with non-compliant recovery agencies or their agents.

The amendment further requires the policy to include provisions for **compensating borrowers or guarantors for losses arising from recovery-related actions** of the bank or its recovery agencies that are not in compliance with applicable requirements, and it is clear from the structure of the inserted section that the RBI expects banks to tighten governance over outsourcing, borrower treatment, escalation discipline, and remedy mechanisms. Although the excerpt cuts off before the remainder of paragraph 454F and any additional paragraphs, the material change is already clear: banks will need to review and likely revise their recovery and outsourcing policies, staff and agent conduct rules, due diligence and monitoring processes, and borrower-redress/compensation arrangements so they are compliant by **1 January 2027**.

rows.summary:
This Master Direction consolidates all operative RBI instructions on Relief/Savings Bonds as updated through **June 30, 2018**, and states that the direction set is maintained on the RBI website and will be revised whenever rules, regulations, or policy change. It is addressed to the **State Bank of India, all nationalized banks (except Punjab and Sind Bank and Andhra Bank), Axis Bank Ltd., ICICI Bank Ltd., HDFC Bank Ltd., and Stock Holding Corporation of India Ltd. (SHCIL)**, indicating these entities are within the distribution/receiving-office framework for these bonds.

On **broker enrollment/registration**, Receiving Offices are permitted to use a **simple registration procedure**: a broker must apply on its **business letterhead** and include **business data**; the Receiving Office must then assign a **code number** to that broker, and that code must be quoted on all applications submitted to claim brokerage. Because the text provided does not include the substantive paragraphs of those sections, no new rate, threshold, or date beyond the **June 30, 2018** cut-off can be confirmed from the excerpt, but compliance teams should treat the document as the governing compilation for operational handling, broker onboarding, brokerage claims, and nominee-related processing for these bond products.

rows.summary:
The Master Direction on Operational Guidelines for Primary Dealers, updated as of November 22, 2018, reiterates and governs several ongoing compliance obligations for Primary Dealers (PDs) in the Government securities market. For primary auctions, PDs must continue to comply with RBI/2008-09/479 dated May 22, 2009, as amended, on submission of non-competitive bids in G-Sec auctions. If a PD sells securities allotted in a primary issue on the same day, it must follow the RBI circulars dated October 6, 2000, May 11, 2005, and July 16, 2012 that prescribe how such same-day sales are to be undertaken; the direction expressly permits PDs to use brokers to execute those sale contracts.

A key operational requirement is the settlement of primary auctions: primary auction settlement is separate from secondary market settlement and must therefore be funded separately. Successful PDs must ensure sufficient funds are available in their current account with the RBI by 3:00 p.m. on the auction settlement day to cover their primary-auction obligations; any shortfall is treated as an instance of “SGL bouncing” and attracts the applicable penal provisions.

In the secondary market, PDs are required to act as market makers in Government securities by providing two-way prices through NDS-OM, the OTC market, and recognized stock exchanges in India, and by taking principal positions in the secondary market for G-Secs. They must also meet annual turnover benchmarks: a minimum turnover ratio of 5 times for Government dated securities and 10 times for Treasury Bills/Cash Management Bills, calculated against average month-end stocks. For outright transactions specifically, the minimum turnover ratio is lower but still mandatory—at least 3 times for Government dated securities and 6 times for T-Bills/CMBs—using the same turnover concept of total annual purchases and sales in the secondary market divided by average month-end stocks.

The excerpt also begins to address secondary market short-selling by PDs, stating that they must follow RBI-issued guidelines, but the text provided cuts off before the detailed short-selling requirements are set out.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2026 Directions on “Conduct of Government Business by Agency Banks (ABs) – Payment of Agency Commission and Oversight of ABs” govern how banks appointed as agency banks may conduct Central and State Government business and how they are paid for that work. The Directions are issued on April 30, 2026 and set the framework for appointment of agency banks, eligible and ineligible government transactions for commission, reporting requirements to the RBI, the rate and method of agency commission claims, treatment of challans, documentation standards, and oversight expectations for banks handling government receipts and payments. They apply to agency banks conducting government business on behalf of Governments and are therefore relevant to any bank that is appointed—or seeking appointment—as an AB.

A central focus of the document is payment of agency commission for government business. It specifies which government transactions qualify for commission and which do not, including distinct treatment for transactions under various government schemes. It also requires ABs to report relevant transaction data to the RBI in the prescribed manner, and it lays out the applicable commission rates, the rule that a single challan is to be treated as a single transaction for commission purposes, and the process for submitting commission claims. ABs must also provide the supporting documents required by the RBI when claiming commission, follow the clarifications in the Directions when determining whether a claim is valid, and account for penal interest where commission is claimed incorrectly or in excess. Chapter IV, titled “Oversight of Government Business in ABs,” indicates that RBI will actively supervise how agency banks carry out this work, so compliance teams should expect ongoing monitoring, reporting, and procedural adherence obligations in addition to the payment rules.

Because the table of contents specifically identifies separate sections for appointment of ABs, eligible and ineligible transactions, scheme-related transactions, reporting to RBI, agency commission rates, claims procedure, documentation, clarifications, and penal interest, the document is not merely informational—it creates an operational compliance framework for agency banking. Any bank engaged in government business should review the final text to confirm the precise categories of transactions that generate commission, the exact claim timelines and documentary requirements, and any scheme-specific exceptions or thresholds that affect whether payment is allowable.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India [Disbursement of Government Pension by Agency Banks (ABs)] Directions, 2026 (Updated as on June 24, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Disbursement of Government Pension by Agency Banks (ABs) Directions, 2026”** sets out the operating rules that agency banks must follow when paying government pensions and related pension benefits, with the version provided being **updated as of June 24, 2026** and issued under reference **DGBA/2026-27/399 CO.DGBA.GBD.No.S43/31.02.007/2026-27 dated April 30, 2026**. It applies to **agency banks that disburse government pension**, and its stated structure covers commencement, applicability, definitions, implementation of government orders, recovery/refund of excess payments, withdrawal by old/sick/disabled/incapacitated pensioners, reimbursement of pension payments, and life-certificate related requirements. For compliance teams, the key point is that these directions are the operative framework governing how ABs must process pension payments, respond to government instructions, and handle exceptions and corrections.

A central requirement is that **government orders on Dearness Relief (DR) and related pension changes must be implemented promptly by agency banks**, meaning banks cannot delay updating pension payments once the government issues the relevant order. The directions also require ABs to follow the **timing rules for pension disbursement** prescribed in the document so that pensions are credited/disbursed on schedule. In practice, this means the bank must maintain a process to track and apply government pension notifications quickly, accurately, and without unnecessary internal delay, with the bank’s pension operations aligned to the government’s effective dates for DR or similar revisions.

The directions also address **recovery and refund of excess pension payments**, distinguishing between errors caused by the **agency bank** and those caused by the **government**. Where the excess payment arises from a bank-attributed error, the bank must take the prescribed steps to recover or regularize the excess; where the excess results from a government-attributed error, the handling differs and is governed by the relevant recovery/refund framework in the directions. This is a material compliance point because it means banks must be able to identify the source of an overpayment, document it, and apply the correct recovery or refund pathway rather than using a one-size-fits-all adjustment approach.

For **old, sick, disabled, or incapacitated pensioners**, the directions require banks to provide specific assistance and permit withdrawal of pension in a manner designed to accommodate their condition. The document also requires **display of these instructions in bank branches**, which means branches handling pensioners must visibly communicate the available withdrawal support and procedural guidance. Compliance teams should ensure branch staff are trained to apply these accommodations consistently and that branch notices are kept current and accessible.

The directions further cover **reimbursement of pension payments** and **life certificate** requirements, which are critical for ongoing pension continuity. Although the excerpt does not include the detailed mechanics, the inclusion of these chapters indicates that agency banks must follow RBI-prescribed procedures for claiming reimbursement from the government and for verifying pensioner eligibility through life certificates. Operationally, this means the bank needs controls for submission, recordkeeping, and certification management so that pension payments are not interrupted and reimbursement claims remain valid under the RBI framework.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026** under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** to strengthen banks’ internal grievance redress framework and ensure customer complaints are reviewed at an apex level before rejection. These Directions apply to **commercial banks with 10 or more banking outlets in India as of March 31, 2025**, whether incorporated in India or outside India; “commercial banks” for this purpose means **banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks**, as well as **corresponding new banks** and the **State Bank of India** as defined under the Banking Regulation Act.

The Directions take **immediate effect** on issuance, but three specific provisions—**clause 7(2), 14(2), and 14(4)**—must be complied with **no later than June 30, 2026**. The RBI also reserves the power to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, either generally or for a particular regulated entity, and may **extend any suspension period** by further order. This means affected banks must review their internal complaint handling and escalation structures immediately, while also tracking the June 30, 2026 deadline for the specified clauses.

Substantively, the Directions require banks within scope to operate an **Internal Ombudsman mechanism** as a final internal review layer before complaint rejection, so that unresolved or proposed-to-be-rejected customer complaints are considered by a senior, independent apex authority within the bank. For compliance purposes, the key operational implication is that eligible banks must ensure their grievance redress process is designed so that complaint rejections are not finalized without the mandated internal ombudsman review, and they must confirm their policies, procedures, staffing, escalation criteria, and implementation timelines align with the new RBI framework.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued new **Directions on capital charge for credit risk under the Standardised Approach for commercial banks**, dated **April 27, 2026**, with **effect from April 1, 2027**. The directions set out the RBI’s revised framework for how commercial banks must calculate regulatory capital against credit risk exposures, and they apply broadly across the entire credit-risk book, including sovereign, bank, corporate, retail, MSME, real estate, non-performing asset, off-balance-sheet, securitisation, and various other asset classes.

A major part of the document is the detailed classification of exposures and the **risk-weight framework** that banks must apply to each class. It specifies separate treatment for **domestic sovereigns, foreign sovereigns and foreign central banks, public sector entities, multilateral development banks/BIS/IMF, banks, corporates, subordinated debt/equity/other capital instruments, retail exposures, MSME exposures, real estate exposures, NPAs, fund investments, specified categories, unhedged foreign currency exposure, other assets, and off-balance-sheet items**. The directions also include a distinct chapter on **capital adequacy for securitisation exposures**, meaning banks must follow prescribed capital treatment for securitised positions rather than treating them like ordinary credit exposures.

The directions tighten and formalize **due diligence requirements** for banks before relying on regulatory risk weights or external ratings. They also create a full framework for **external credit assessments**, including which credit rating agencies are eligible, how ratings may be mapped and used, how **long-term and short-term ratings** are to be applied, how to treat **unsolicited ratings**, how to handle **multiple ratings**, and how to deal with **issuer-not-cooperating (INC)** situations. The document further states when an **issue rating** can be extended to the issuer or other claims, which is important for banks’ capital calculations and rating reliance procedures.

The final major section covers **credit risk mitigation (CRM)**, setting the conditions under which banks may recognize **collateral, netting, guarantees, and other mitigation techniques** for capital purposes. It addresses the general principles, **legal certainty** requirements, **maturity mismatch** treatment, **currency mismatch** treatment, collateralized transactions, **on-balance-sheet netting**, and guarantees, so banks will need legally enforceable documentation and internal processes aligned to these rules before taking capital benefit. The document also includes a **repeal chapter**, indicating that prior conflicting directions are being superseded from the effective date, so compliance teams should review existing RBI capital/risk-weight policies and transition them to the new framework before **April 1, 2027**.

The directions explicitly cover the **methodological framework for calculating ECL**, how to handle **fair valuation on transition**, **initial recognition and subsequent measurement**, how to determine **SICR**, how to measure ECL for different instrument types, how to decide the **period over which lifetime ECL is measured**, and the use of **probability-weighted outcomes**. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025” are comprehensive KYC/AML requirements for commercial banks, issued under RBI powers and updated as of December 29, 2025. The directions apply to commercial banks and govern customer identification, customer due diligence, beneficial ownership identification, ongoing monitoring, and related board-approved policy and risk-management controls. The document replaces or consolidates prior KYC expectations into a structured set of obligations that banks must implement through formal policies, internal controls, and documented procedures.

A core requirement is that each bank’s board of directors must approve and oversee a KYC/AML framework, including risk-based customer acceptance policies, account-opening controls, CDD standards, recordkeeping, monitoring, and staff accountability. Banks must maintain a customer identification procedure before establishing a relationship or carrying out relevant transactions, and must apply due diligence commensurate with the customer’s risk profile rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach. The directions also require banks to identify and verify beneficial owners for legal persons and arrangements, and to perform ongoing due diligence throughout the relationship, not only at onboarding.

The document distinguishes between CDD requirements for individuals, sole proprietorships, and legal entities, indicating that the documentation and verification burden varies by customer type but remains mandatory in all cases. For individuals, banks must verify identity using approved official documents and supporting information; for sole proprietors and legal entities, banks must establish the existence of the business and the authority/identity of the persons acting for it. The beneficial ownership chapter is especially important for compliance teams because it requires banks to look through ownership and control structures to determine the natural persons ultimately owning or controlling the customer, with enhanced scrutiny where ownership is layered or opaque.

The directions also provide for enhanced due diligence and simplified due diligence, meaning banks may apply lighter procedures only where the risk profile justifies it and heavier procedures where risk is higher, such as for politically exposed persons, unusual transactions, or customers from higher-risk geographies or business sectors. Banks must maintain ongoing monitoring of account activity to ensure transactions are consistent with the customer’s profile and source of funds, and must escalate discrepancies, unusual behavior, or incomplete information through internal review and decision-making. The document’s structure indicates that it also includes detailed provisions on risk management and customer acceptance controls, so a compliance team should expect specific operational rules for periodic review, escalation, and documentation rather than merely principles.

Because the content provided is only the table of contents and title page, the exact substantive thresholds, documentary lists, time periods, and any special exemptions are not visible here. However, based on the title and chapter structure, the material compliance takeaway is that commercial banks in India are required to run a formal, risk-based KYC program covering onboarding, identification, beneficial ownership, and ongoing monitoring under RBI supervision, with implementation anchored in board-approved policies and documented procedures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets” Directions, 2025 (updated through July 1, 2026) set out a comprehensive framework for how commercial banks must identify, report, resolve, disclose, and provision for stressed loan exposures. The directions apply to commercial banks and govern the bank’s internal policies, borrower monitoring, inter-lender coordination, and supervisory reporting around stressed assets; the document is structured around mandatory board-approved policies, early warning and reporting requirements, a formal resolution process, and additional provisioning consequences if resolution is delayed. Since this is a prudential supervisory framework, compliance teams should treat it as an end-to-end operational requirement, not merely a credit policy update.

At the governance level, banks must have board-approved policies for dealing with stressed assets, and those policies must cover early identification of stress, escalation, monitoring, and resolution decision-making. The directions require banks to identify stress early and report it through prescribed internal and supervisory channels, rather than waiting until accounts become severely delinquent or non-performing. The document also requires disclosures, so banks must maintain reporting discipline and ensure that stressed exposures are reflected accurately in any mandated financial or regulatory disclosures. Supervisory review provisions indicate that the RBI will expect demonstrable adherence to the framework and will assess the bank’s handling of stressed accounts as part of its oversight.

The resolution process is built around a defined “review period,” during which lenders must assess the borrower’s stress and work toward an agreed resolution plan. Where multiple lenders are involved, an inter-creditor agreement is required so that creditors coordinate on the terms and timing of resolution rather than acting in a fragmented manner. The resolution plan itself must be prepared and implemented within the framework and timelines set by the directions, and failure to implement within the required time triggers additional regulatory consequences. In particular, the document includes a chapter on “Delayed Implementation of Resolution Plan – Additional Specific Provisioning,” meaning banks face extra provisioning burdens if they do not execute the agreed resolution plan on time.

For compliance purposes, the key operational obligation is to ensure that stressed exposures are identified early, documented, escalated to the right decision-makers, and managed under board-approved procedures with proper lender coordination. Banks should confirm that their internal policies align with the RBI’s framework, that reporting and disclosure processes capture all covered stressed assets, and that any multi-lender cases use enforceable inter-creditor arrangements. The document’s effective date is November 28, 2025, with the version provided updated as of July 1, 2026, so institutions should verify they are using the latest updated text and associated implementation guidance when testing compliance controls.

It applies to **commercial banks** and covers the full lifecycle of loan and credit exposure monitoring, including board oversight, lending prudence, disclosures, automation of IRAC processes, NPA identification, and provisioning treatment. From a compliance perspective, the document is not merely definitional: it imposes ongoing governance, system, and reporting obligations on banks to ensure income is not recognized on impaired assets, exposures are classified correctly and promptly, and provisioning is made in line with RBI-prescribed rules.

A key compliance theme is **board responsibility and internal control**: the board is expected to set the tone for prudent lending, approve policies, and ensure that the bank’s systems and staff are aligned with income-recognition and asset-classification requirements. The directions also require **consumer education and disclosure discipline**, meaning banks must ensure borrowers and other stakeholders are not misled about the nature of asset classification, repayment status, or the consequences of delinquency. The disclosure requirements in Chapter II indicate that the bank’s public and regulatory disclosures must be consistent with the IRAC treatment applied in the books.

The document places special emphasis on **automation of income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning processes**. Banks are required to implement automated or system-driven processes so that asset classification and related provisioning are triggered accurately and on time, reducing manual discretion and the risk of delayed recognition of stress. For compliance teams, this means the bank must ensure its core banking and risk systems can identify delinquency, move accounts into the appropriate classification buckets, and stop accrual of income where required under RBI rules, with audit trails and controls sufficient to demonstrate compliance.

On **asset classification**, the directions prescribe the general rules for moving accounts into non-performing status, handling regularisation near the balance-sheet date, and dealing with special situations and specific categories of NPAs. The document includes separate treatment for “specific cases of asset classification” and for the “categories of non-performing assets,” which implies compliance must monitor not only standard overdue accounts but also special exposures that may require different classification judgments. This is especially important around the **balance-sheet date**, where regularisation of an account shortly before reporting may still be subject to RBI scrutiny and may not automatically permit a return to standard status if the underlying default behavior indicates otherwise.

The directions also include **upgradation rules** for NPAs, meaning once an account improves, it can only be moved back to a performing category when the RBI’s conditions are satisfied; compliance should assume that mere payment after default may not be enough unless the governing criteria are met. Overall, the document requires banks to maintain strong governance over lending, account monitoring, classification triggers, and provisioning calculations, with the updated 2026 version serving as the operative reference for RBI compliance as of that date.
