rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Setting Up of Wholly Owned Subsidiaries by Foreign Banks) Guidelines, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.desc: DOR/2025-26/144 November 28, 2025 Reserve Bank of India (Setting Up of Wholly Owned Subsidiaries by Foreign Banks) Guidelines, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026) A. Background The global financial crisis of 2008 demonstrated that the growing complexity and interconnectedness of financial institutions, coupled with the lack of effective cross- border resolution regimes, severely constrained the ability of home and host authorities to cope with the failure of too big to fail (TBTF) and too connected to fail (TCTF) institutions. Globally, several policy options have been proposed to address these challenges, including measures to contain the negative externalities arising out of size and interconnectedness, strengthening the capital and liquidity buffers, and enhancing the resolvability of such institutions. The lessons from the global financial crisis support the case for domestic incorporation of foreign banks. The main advantages of local incorporation include: (1) Creation of separate legal entities with their own capital base and local board of directors; (2) Clear delineation between the assets and liabilities of the domestic bank and those of its foreign parent, with ring fenced capital and assets within the host country; (3) Clarity and certainty regarding the applicability of the laws of country of incorporation on the locally incorporated subsidiary; (4) A locally incorporated bank has its own board of directors which are required to act in the best interests of the bank and safeguard the interests of depositors and creditors; (5) Local incorporation provides effective control to the local regulators. Accordingly, several jurisdictions require foreign banks to adopt local incorporation mainly for (i) protecting local retail depositors, (ii) easing the resolution process, and (iii) affording greater regulatory comfort. In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) allowed foreign banks, if eligible, to establish presence through a single mode i.e. either the branc
rows.summary:
The RBI’s 2025 Guidelines on Setting Up of Wholly Owned Subsidiaries by Foreign Banks, updated as of April 1, 2026, explain the policy basis for requiring or permitting foreign banks to operate in India through locally incorporated entities rather than branches. The document ties this framework to post-2008 financial stability concerns—especially “too big to fail” and “too connected to fail” risks—and says local incorporation is intended to create a separate legal entity with its own capital base and board, ring-fence Indian assets and liabilities from the foreign parent, clarify that Indian law applies to the local subsidiary, and give Indian regulators more direct supervisory and resolution control. It also states that India had already allowed eligible foreign banks to enter through a single mode of presence, and these guidelines are issued in that context.

For compliance purposes, the key substantive point is that the RBI is advancing a regulatory preference for foreign banks to use a wholly owned subsidiary (WOS) structure in India because it better protects local retail depositors, simplifies resolution, and provides greater regulatory comfort. A WOS must operate as a separate Indian-incorporated bank, with its own capital and local governance, and its board is expected to act in the interests of the bank and its depositors and creditors rather than the foreign parent. This means compliance teams at foreign banks considering India operations should assess whether their proposed structure, governance, capital, and resolution planning align with the local-incorporation model described in the guidelines.

The document is primarily background and policy framing in the excerpt provided; it does not yet set out specific numerical capital thresholds, filing deadlines, approval timelines, or procedural forms in the text shown. For compliance purposes, the key substance is that **the board of each small finance bank must take direct responsibility for ALM/liquidity risk governance**. The board is required to approve the bank’s liquidity risk management policy, define and periodically review limits and tolerances, and ensure management has appropriate systems, processes, and reporting for identifying, measuring, monitoring, and controlling liquidity risk. The document indicates that the framework covers both **strategy and governance**, meaning compliance is not limited to a single liquidity ratio or report: banks must maintain a structured policy, clear accountability, and ongoing review mechanisms.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Small Finance Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio” Directions, 2025 (DOR/2025-26/193, dated November 28, 2025 and updated through May 18, 2026) set the prudential and accounting rules Small Finance Banks must follow for their investment portfolios. The document applies to small finance banks and governs how they classify, value, and operate investments, with the board required to approve and oversee an investment policy framework. The directions are structured to cover general governance, classification of investments, valuation treatment, and specific rules for investments in associates and joint ventures, so compliance teams should expect both policy-level obligations and transaction-level accounting controls.

A key feature is the formal classification of investments into held to maturity (HTM), available for sale (AFS), and fair value through profit and loss (FVTPL), with a subcategory of held for trading (HFT) under FVTPL. This means the bank must determine, at initial recognition and thereafter, which bucket each instrument belongs in because that classification drives valuation, income recognition, and likely reclassification constraints. The directions also address initial recognition and subsequent valuation, so compliance and finance functions need controls to ensure instruments are booked correctly from inception and not moved or remeasured inconsistently with the RBI’s prescribed treatment.

Because the table of contents shows a dedicated chapter on the role of the board, the directions are not just accounting rules but governance requirements: the board must set the investment policy framework and ensure it is implemented. The policy framework is the bank’s core internal compliance document for investment activities, and it should be aligned with the RBI’s classification and valuation requirements. The document also includes rules for investments in associates and joint ventures, indicating that equity-method or similar special-purpose holdings are treated separately from routine debt and marketable securities and must be monitored as a distinct compliance category.

The extract provided does not include the detailed thresholds, percentages, valuation haircuts, or specific time-bound deadlines beyond the document’s issuance date and the fact that it is updated as of May 18, 2026. From the content shown, the compliance obligation is to implement the RBI’s framework for investment portfolio governance, classification, valuation, and operation across all relevant small finance bank investment holdings, with special attention to the board-approved policy, correct bucket allocation (HTM/AFS/FVTPL/HFT), and the separate treatment of associate/joint venture investments.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Credit Risk Management Directions, 2025** (updated **July 1, 2026**) consolidate and replace the RBI’s credit-risk related rules for **small finance banks (SFBs)** and set out the minimum governance, lending, monitoring, and reporting framework they must follow. The document requires SFBs to maintain **board-approved credit risk policies**, with clear internal systems for credit appraisal, sanction, monitoring, recovery, and exposure management, and it makes these requirements binding across a range of credit activities including retail, MSME, and other borrower segments. It also formalizes a number of specific regulatory controls on lending exposures, documentation, and collateral/asset registration, with some provisions updated to reflect later RBI amendments through July 1, 2026.

A major focus of the directions is **credit risk evaluation and lending discipline**: banks must assess borrower repayment capacity, use robust underwriting standards, and ensure that credit decisions are based on documented risk analysis rather than relationship-based lending. The directions also impose **statutory and regulatory restrictions** on certain forms of exposure and require compliance with RBI-prescribed concentration limits and prudential norms, so SFBs need to verify that no prohibited or excess exposure is booked and that exceptions are not processed outside the permitted framework. Where the bank extends credit to borrowers with foreign currency exposure, it must also comply with the **country risk management** requirements and the separate rules on **unhedged foreign currency exposure (UFCE)**, meaning the bank must identify, measure, and price that risk and ensure appropriate capital/risk treatment.

The directions add or restate borrower-level compliance requirements around **Legal Entity Identifier (LEI)** and collateral documentation. Where applicable, borrowers must obtain and maintain an LEI, and the bank must not proceed with covered transactions unless the LEI requirement is satisfied; this is intended to improve borrower identification and systemic transparency. In addition, SFBs must ensure proper **valuation of properties** through empanelled valuers meeting RBI’s standards, and they must file security interests for **immovable property (other than equitable mortgage), movable assets, and intangible assets** with **CERSAI**, so the bank must build controls to ensure these filings occur within the required timelines and are not omitted before/after disbursement as applicable.

The document also addresses **current account, cash credit, and overdraft account maintenance**, including restrictions on how banks may open and operate such accounts when borrowing arrangements exist with other lenders, and it continues the RBI framework for the **loan system for delivery of bank credit**, which generally requires closer discipline in working capital lending and related account conduct. Finally, the directions include **repeal and savings provisions**, meaning older instructions on the same subjects are superseded to the extent covered here, and banks should treat this as the operative RBI framework as of the updated date. For compliance purposes, the key action is to map all lending, collateral, account-opening, and borrower-onboarding processes to this consolidated direction set and confirm that policies, forms, due diligence checklists, and monitoring systems are aligned to the updated 2026 version.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025** set out a mandatory framework for how **small finance banks (SFBs)** must participate in and report to **credit information companies (CICs)**. The directions apply to **all small finance banks** and require them to maintain CIC membership, report credit data in the prescribed formats, and follow RBI’s reporting, correction, and dissemination rules. The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and is shown as **updated as on July 01, 2026**, so compliance teams should treat the text as including whatever amendments or refinements were in force by that date.

A key requirement is that SFBs must be **members of CICs** and must provide credit information in the formats and timelines specified by RBI. The directions require banks to report both **positive and negative credit information** accurately and on time, and to keep their data current through periodic updates rather than treating reporting as a one-time activity. The document also includes specific procedural requirements for **reporting timelines and updation**, meaning banks need operational processes that ensure loan and customer account changes are captured promptly and transmitted to CICs in the required format.

The directions also address **data quality and rejected-data handling**. Where submitted information is rejected, the bank must **rectify and resubmit** the data in accordance with RBI’s instructions, and it must also review its **Data Quality Index (DQI)**, which is explicitly referenced as part of the compliance framework. This means compliance is not limited to sending data, but also requires active monitoring of rejection reasons, internal remediation, and ongoing quality improvement so that reporting remains acceptable to CICs and to RBI’s standards.

The document further requires banks to have procedures for **correction of Credit Information Reports (CIRs)** when customers dispute or identify inaccuracies. It also requires SFBs to use credit information reports in **credit appraisal**, indicating that CIC data must be incorporated into lending decisions rather than treated as optional reference material. In addition, there are rules on the **display of information**, which means certain credit-related information must be shown or made available in the manner RBI prescribes, likely affecting customer-facing disclosures and internal access controls.

Finally, the directions clarify the **applicability of other Department of Regulation instructions**, so SFBs cannot treat these rules in isolation; they must also comply with any related RBI instructions that continue to apply. The chapter structure also indicates the existence of a **Technical Working Group** and **customer-related provisions**, suggesting the framework includes governance/support mechanisms and customer complaint or correction processes. From a compliance perspective, the document requires a fully documented reporting control environment covering membership, reporting accuracy, periodic updates, rejection remediation, DQI monitoring, correction handling, and integration of credit bureau information into lending and disclosure processes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** (as updated **July 15, 2026**) sets out the binding prudential, conduct, technology, and product-specific rules that apply to **small finance banks (SFBs)** when extending credit. It consolidates requirements across traditional lending, credit linked to specific payment instruments, and digital lending, and it also includes special rules for **lending against gold and silver collateral**. For compliance teams, the key point is that this is not just a high-level policy statement: it is a detailed operating framework that affects lending governance, board oversight, customer disclosures, partner management, data handling, reporting, and collateral-based lending controls.

At the governance level, the directions assign an explicit role to the **Board** of the SFB, meaning lending policies and controls must be board-approved and supervised at the highest level rather than left only to management discretion. The document also creates a separate chapter for **credit facilities linked to specific payment instruments**, indicating that if an SFB offers products tied to designated payment rails or instruments, those products are regulated under additional provisions beyond ordinary loan origination. Compliance teams should treat this as requiring product-by-product review to confirm whether any facility falls into these specially governed categories.

A major operational component is the **digital lending** framework, which governs **bank–LSP arrangements** (where the bank uses a lending service provider) and the related conduct, technology, and reporting obligations. The directions require SFBs to implement customer-protection controls in digital lending, maintain appropriate technology and data safeguards, and ensure that credit information and digital lending applications are properly reported through the required channels. The document also addresses **loss-sharing arrangements in the event of default**, meaning any contractual allocation of credit loss between the bank and an outsourcing/LSP counterparty must comply with the specified rules rather than being structured freely by the parties.

The directions further impose dedicated requirements for **lending against gold and silver collateral**, including general conditions and specific **restrictions and ceilings**. That means SFBs offering secured loans against these metals must check both the permissibility of the facility and the applicable caps/limitations before sanctioning, renewing, or rolling over such exposures. Because the document explicitly separates “general provisions” from “restrictions and ceilings,” compliance staff should expect product-level controls, collateral valuation standards, monitoring of exposure limits, and checks on whether the borrower/loan structure fits within the permitted framework.

The document is dated **November 28, 2025**, with an update as of **July 15, 2026**; the table of contents confirms the principal operative areas but does not itself show the substantive numeric thresholds or all procedural details. For implementation purposes, an SFB should assume the directions are intended to be fully operational policy requirements and should map existing lending products, third-party arrangements, digital lending workflows, data/reporting processes, and gold/silver-backed loan programs against the final text of the directions to identify any gaps, required policy revisions, and staff training needs.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025** set out the interest-rate framework that all **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** must follow for **domestic rupee deposit accounts**, with the stated update reflecting the text as of **August 25, 2026**. The directions establish the rules for **current accounts, savings deposits, term deposits, additional interest, overdue deposits, floating-rate term deposits, interest payment frequency, and interest payable after a depositor’s death**, so compliance teams should treat this as the governing deposit-pricing and interest-crediting framework for SFBs unless a specific carve-out applies.

At a high level, the document requires SFBs to use a **board-approved interest rate framework** and to ensure deposit interest is determined transparently and consistently within RBI-prescribed constraints. The directions apply to **domestic rupee deposits** maintained by SFBs and are intended to regulate how interest is offered, calculated, disclosed, and paid across deposit products, including any special treatment for categories such as **senior citizens**, **employees**, and certain **deceased depositor** scenarios where extra interest or continued interest may be permitted under the RBI rules.

For compliance purposes, the key operational obligation is that SFBs must align product terms and system processing to the RBI rules for: **no interest or restricted interest on current accounts**, the **minimum interest floor/structure for savings deposits**, the manner of setting and changing **term-deposit rates**, and the conditions under which **additional interest** may be paid above the advertised rate. The directions also address what happens when a deposit becomes **overdue** and whether/when it may continue to earn interest, as well as how **floating-rate term deposits** must be benchmarked and repriced.

The document further specifies how interest must be credited on savings deposits, including the **periodicity of interest payment**, and contains rules for the **interest payable on the domestic deposit account of a deceased depositor**, which is a common audit and customer-treatment risk area. It also preserves limited discretion for banks to pay interest on the **minimum credit balance in a farmer’s composite cash credit account**, but only within the regulatory framework stated in the directions.

Because this is a prudential conduct document rather than a one-time filing requirement, the most important compliance takeaway is ongoing: SFBs should ensure their deposit product terms, rate sheets, customer disclosures, core banking system logic, and exception-handling procedures are all consistent with these directions and any RBI updates through **August 25, 2026**. rows.desc: DOR/2025-26/257 DOR.CRE.REC.176/07-03-004/2025-26 November 28, 2025 Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks - Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025 Table of Contents Chapter I - Preliminary ................................................................................................................... 2 Chapter II - Exposure Norms ........................................................................................................ 5 Chapter III - Repeal and other provisions .................................................................................... 7 Annex - I .......................................................................................................................................... 8 2 Introduction The concentration of a bank’s exposures to a single borrower or a group borrower poses significant risks. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), recognizing the imperative of robust risk management, therefore introduced prudential exposure limits for Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) in October 1995. These limits restricted banks’ exposures to individual borrower and group borrowers to a certain percentage of capital funds, laying the foundation for mitigating concentration risk on assets side of their balance sheets. These prudential norms were further revised in March 2000 and June 2001 and the reference parameter was changed to owned funds. In addition, banks were advised in October 1999 to implement the recommendations of High-Level Committee on Credit SSI, which required, inter alia, banks to have their own sectoral exposure limits. These limits restrict banks’ exposures to individual borrower and group of interconnected borrowers, laying the foundation for mitigating concentration risk on assets side of their balance sheets. Categorization of UCBs for Regulatory Purposes 2. Given the heterogeneity in the urban cooperative sector, a four-tiered regulatory framework has been adopted to balance the spirit of mutuality and cooperation more prevalent in banks of smaller sizes and those with limited area of operation vis-à-vis the growth ambitions of the large-sized UCBs to spread their area of operation and undertake more complex business activities. Accordingly, the UCBs are categorized into the following four tiers for regulatory purposes: (1) Tier 1 - All unit UCBs and salary earners' UCBs (irrespective of deposit size), and all other UCBs having deposits up to ₹100 crore; (2) Tier 2 - UCBs with deposits of more than ₹100 crore and up to ₹1000 crore; (3) Tier 3 - UCBs with deposits of more than ₹1000 crore and up to ₹10,000 crore; (4) Tier 4 - UCBs with deposits of more than ₹10,000 crore. 3. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This 2026 RBI Supervisory Directions consolidate and restate the Reserve Bank of India’s expectations for commercial banks on a wide set of operational, conduct, governance, and control matters. They are issued by the Department of Supervision on 31 July 2026 under RBI/DoS/2026-27/416 and apply to commercial banks as covered by the document’s applicability section. The directions span IT system access, monitoring of end-use of funds, Prompt Corrective Action (PCA), interest-charging practices, inoperative and unclaimed accounts, nomination, fraud prevention, protected disclosures, and vigilance governance.

A major theme is tighter control over access, accountability, and monitoring. Banks must ensure controlled access to IT systems and maintain procedures that support traceability and supervision of user activities. They also must implement monitoring of end use of funds, which means they are expected to track whether borrowed or sanctioned funds are actually used for the stated purpose, with heightened controls where misuse risk is present. The PCA chapter establishes RBI’s framework for supervisory escalation when banks’ financial condition deteriorates; affected banks may be placed under corrective actions once specified trigger points are breached, and they must then comply with the RBI-directed restrictions and remediation steps that accompany the framework.

The directions also reinforce customer-protection requirements. Banks must follow the Fair Practices Code on charging of interest, meaning interest must be levied in a transparent, non-exploitative manner and in line with RBI’s fair-lending expectations. For inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits, banks are required to maintain systems and procedures to identify dormant accounts, handle unclaimed balances appropriately, and support claim resolution. The nomination chapter requires banks to provide and administer nomination facilities so depositors and other eligible customers can designate nominees for account balances and related claims.

Fraud prevention is a substantial component of the document and covers multiple scenarios that compliance teams should treat as control requirements. The directions address frauds involving collusion by bank officials, large-value frauds, bulk retail-loan sanctions, frauds using fake title deeds of property, frauds in non-resident accounts, and safekeeping of critical documents. Banks must also manage accounts opened by employees with enhanced scrutiny, maintain a legal compliance certificate and a legal compliance audit process, and carry out forensic scrutiny where needed. The document further addresses the exercise of discretionary powers and sets out a “best practices” code for banks, indicating that internal decision-making authority must be documented, disciplined, and subject to control review rather than left to informal discretion.

The Protected Disclosure Scheme chapter requires banks to provide a protected complaint mechanism for reporting wrongdoing. It covers the scheme’s scope, the procedure for lodging complaints, and the protected disclosure policy, meaning banks must be able to receive complaints confidentially and protect whistleblowers from retaliation while ensuring appropriate inquiry and handling. The vigilance chapter then adds governance expectations for anti-corruption and integrity controls: it introduces vigilance-angle assessment, the role and appointment of a Chief of Internal Vigilance, tenure expectations, restrictions on association with sensitive matters, and reporting/return submission and review requirements. It also requires preventive vigilance measures, staff rotation, and mandatory leave in sensitive roles, plus established complaint-handling and investigation arrangements, including the use of investigation agencies and review of cases entrusted to them.

The document also places responsibility on banks to maintain a **robust data architecture and IT infrastructure** that supports accurate, complete, and timely supervisory reporting, which means banks need systems capable of producing regulatory data reliably and in a controlled manner.

The directions further require banks to ensure the **accuracy and integrity of reporting**, including processes to verify returns before submission and to correct errors when identified. In practice, this means banks must have procedures for **validation, reconciliation, review, and authorization** of supervisory data, with clear internal controls to prevent misreporting. The document also contemplates **operational guidelines, a list of applicable returns, timelines, exceptions, penalties, and other instructions** in Chapter III, indicating that banks will need to monitor the specific return-wise filing calendar and comply with any format- or event-driven reporting obligations prescribed by RBI from time to time.

Finally, the directions include standard legal provisions on **repeal and saving**, application of other laws not barred, and interpretation, meaning these directions sit alongside other applicable statutory and regulatory requirements rather than replacing them wholesale. Based on the text provided, **no specific numeric filing deadlines, thresholds, or penalty amounts are stated in the excerpt**, so a compliance team should review the full Chapter III tables and instructions for the exact return list, due dates, exception handling, and any consequences for late or inaccurate submissions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Commercial Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026” take effect immediately on issuance and apply to commercial banks in relation to the appointment and reappointment of their Statutory Central Auditors (SCAs) and Statutory Auditors (SAs). The directions are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, and the State Bank of India Act, and they supersede the prior RBI framework for statutory audit of commercial banks. The document is directed at banking companies, except where the text later distinguishes specific bank categories or overseas branches for special treatment.

For compliance purposes, the core change is that the RBI is formalizing detailed governance, eligibility, tenure, appointment, and reporting requirements for bank statutory auditors, with explicit board and senior management responsibility for the process. The board must ensure a robust auditor selection process, monitor auditor independence and performance, and make sure audit-related governance is documented and escalated appropriately. The directions also require banks to follow prescribed procedures for appointment/reappointment, including any limits on the number of auditors, branch coverage rules, and coordination for overseas branches where applicable.

The directions set out detailed eligibility and independence criteria for SCAs/SAs, including professional standards, fit-and-proper expectations, and restrictions intended to avoid conflicts of interest. They also establish tenure and rotation requirements so that auditors cannot remain indefinitely, and they prescribe how audit fees and expenses are to be determined and handled. In addition, there are specific procedural requirements for appointing auditors, including the submission and approval steps banks must follow and the special process for appointing auditors for overseas branch(es).

A major operational requirement is the Long Form Audit Report (LFAR), for which the directions establish both procedure and timelines and separately address the reports prepared by SCAs and by branch auditors. The LFAR framework includes defined objectives, strategy, scope, and coverage expectations, along with indicative coverage areas that auditors must examine. Banks must ensure that the required LFAR information is gathered, reviewed, and submitted within the stipulated deadlines, and that any findings are integrated into governance and remediation processes.

Finally, the directions include repeal-and-saving provisions and clarify that they do not bar the application of other laws. The document also contains annexes that appear to provide the operational detail, forms, and implementation guidance needed to execute the audit framework. For a compliance team, the key action is to review whether current auditor appointment practices, audit committee/board oversight, independence checks, rotation tracking, and LFAR workflows align with the new RBI requirements as of the issuance date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Internal Audit Function Directions, 2026** require all **commercial banks**—defined to include **banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Local Area Banks, corresponding new banks, and the State Bank of India**—to operate under a **Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA)** framework rather than a purely transaction-centric audit model. The directions are issued under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **take effect immediately upon issuance**; the document is dated **July 31, 2026**. The RBI states that the purpose is to strengthen banks’ internal control and risk management systems by aligning internal audit with current governance standards and international best practices.

At the governance level, the **Board of the bank** (or the **Local Advisory Board** in the case of a foreign bank) must approve a **formal RBIA policy** and the **risk assessment methodology** used by the Internal Audit Department. The directions make clear that internal audit is expected to evaluate not just transactions but also the **adequacy of risk management systems and internal controls**, so the board’s oversight must extend to how audit coverage is planned and prioritized based on risk. Senior management is expected to support implementation of the RBIA framework and ensure the audit function has the information, access, and organizational support needed to operate independently and effectively.

The directions also require each bank to put in place an **internal audit policy and framework** that is **risk-based, documented, and periodically reviewed**, with the scope of audit determined through a structured risk assessment. The Internal Audit Department must use a methodology that identifies, measures, and ranks risks across the bank’s activities, so that audit frequency, depth, and coverage reflect risk significance rather than simply transaction volume. The framework must include procedures for **functional independence**, so internal audit is not placed in a position where its judgment is compromised by the business lines it reviews.

The document further addresses **scope, communication, performance evaluation, and outsourcing** of internal audit, indicating that banks must define what activities and functions are covered by RBIA, how audit findings are escalated and reported, how the effectiveness of internal audit is assessed, and under what conditions audit work may be outsourced. It also creates specific requirements for the **Head of Internal Audit**, including provisions on **authority, stature, independence, tenure, and reporting line**, to ensure the function has sufficient standing and direct access to appropriate senior governance bodies. Finally, the directions include **repeal and saving provisions**, preserve application of other laws where not inconsistent, and provide interpretive guidance for implementation.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026** establish a mandatory framework for commercial banks to **prevent fraud, detect it early, escalate red flags, and report incidents promptly to law enforcement and the RBI**. The directions are issued under **Sections 21 and 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and apply to the entities covered under the document’s applicability provisions (commercial banks). They are intended not just to govern reporting after a fraud is found, but also to require governance, internal controls, early warning systems, staff accountability, and procedures for cases under resolution or involving third parties.

A major requirement is that banks must maintain a **fraud risk management governance structure** with clear oversight responsibilities, and must implement an **Early Warning Signal (EWS) / Red-Flagged Account (RFA) framework** for both **credit facilities/loan accounts** and **other banking or non-credit transactions**. This means banks are expected to identify suspicious indicators early, classify affected loan accounts appropriately as red-flagged, and follow specified internal escalation and reporting processes before losses deepen. The document also requires banks to obtain **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, where relevant, so reliance on outsourced or external inputs does not weaken fraud controls.

The directions impose explicit obligations on **reporting frauds to LEAs and to RBI**, including reporting incidents of fraud, using the **Central Fraud Registry**, following RBI’s specified reporting modalities, and completing closure reporting for fraud cases once resolved/closed. In addition, there is a separate reporting obligation for **cheque-related frauds**, which must be reported both to law enforcement and RBI under the dedicated chapter. The framework further addresses the treatment of accounts classified as fraudulent and then **sold to other lenders or asset reconstruction companies**, indicating that fraud classification and related consequences do not simply disappear on transfer.

The document also covers **staff accountability and penal measures**, meaning banks must investigate internal responsibility and apply consequences where employee conduct, negligence, or collusion is implicated. For larger exposures, banks must conduct a **legal audit of title documents for large value loan accounts**, and the directions state that auditors have a role in the fraud risk environment as well. Finally, the directions include a separate reporting requirement for **cases of theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery**, and a repeal/saving section clarifying how these directions interact with earlier RBI instructions and other laws. The title indicates a 2026 instrument, and the document itself is dated **July 31, 2026** (RBI reference **RBI/DoS/2026-27/412** and **DoS.CO.FMG.6/23.04.001/2026-27**).

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on 31 July 2026 and effective immediately upon issuance, applies to **commercial banks** only—specifically banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Local Area Banks, as well as corresponding new banks and the State Bank of India. It requires those banks to implement RBI-prescribed digital payment security controls for **digital payment products and services** used for both financial and non-financial functions, including balance enquiry, PIN set/change, mobile banking registration, OTP generation, mini-statements, transaction status checks, and customer dispute/grievance raising; the scope also explicitly extends to related IT assets such as applications, systems, and infrastructure, whether the service is provided directly by the bank or through an RBI-operated system or an RBI-authorised Payment System Operator (PSO).

The document is structured as a comprehensive security-control framework covering board oversight, general controls, internet banking, mobile payment applications, and card payment security. It states that the bank’s **Board must approve policies** governing these security controls, so compliance is not just an IT obligation but a governance requirement at board level. The controls are intended to address governance and management of security risks, generic security controls, application security lifecycle requirements, authentication framework requirements, fraud risk management, reconciliation, and customer protection/awareness/grievance redressal obligations.

Although the excerpt provided does not yet include the detailed control clauses, the introductory material makes clear that the directions are binding regulatory requirements issued under the RBI’s powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **Chapter IV of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**. The document also indicates that its definitions are drawn from the **FSB Cyber Lexicon**, unless otherwise specified, which signals that terms such as cyber risk, assets, and controls are likely to be interpreted in a standardized, regulatory manner. The directions include later chapters on **internet banking security controls, mobile payment application security controls, and card payment security controls**, so compliance teams should expect specific operational, technical, and customer-protection obligations across all major digital payment channels.

The final chapter references **repeal and saving**, application of other laws not being barred, and interpretation provisions, which means these directions likely supersede or replace prior RBI instructions on the same subject while preserving certain actions already taken and leaving other legal/regulatory obligations intact. For compliance purposes, the key immediate takeaway is that commercial banks must confirm their digital payment products, associated IT infrastructure, and outsourced/RBI-platform-based channels fall within scope and must operate under board-approved security policies aligned to this new RBI framework from the date of issuance.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026”** is a comprehensive supervisory directive issued on **July 31, 2026** by RBI’s Department of Supervision. It replaces or updates the RBI’s baseline expectations for **commercial banks** on IT governance, cybersecurity, resilience, outsourcing/third-party controls, and assurance, and it is structured as a binding directions framework with requirements flowing from the board level down to operational teams. The document is aimed at ensuring that banks maintain a formal governance structure, document and periodically review IT/cyber risks, and implement minimum technical and procedural safeguards across their technology environment.

At the governance level, the directions require the **board of directors** to approve and oversee key policies, including an **information security policy** and **cybersecurity policy**, and to establish or use designated board-level committees for oversight of IT risk and technology strategy. The framework assigns explicit responsibilities to **senior management**, the **IT Steering Committee**, the **Information Security Committee**, the **Head of IT**, and the **Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)**, indicating that IT and cyber risk management must be embedded in operating governance rather than treated as an isolated control function. Banks must maintain an IT governance framework that covers project management, architecture, service management, and risk ownership, with regular review of IT-related risks and documented risk identification and assessment processes.

A substantial portion of the directions sets **baseline cybersecurity and resilience requirements** for day-to-day controls. Banks are required to maintain an inventory of information assets, implement a **data leak prevention strategy**, control **data migration**, prevent execution of **unauthorised software**, and maintain physical/environmental protections for systems. The framework also requires controls for **capacity management**, **secure configuration**, **network management and security**, **application security throughout the software development life cycle**, and ongoing maintenance/monitoring/analysis of **audit logs**. Banks must also have structured **patch, vulnerability, and change management**, strict **user access control/management**, controls for **teleworking**, and a formal **authentication framework for customers**; the document additionally covers secure mail/messaging, removable media, cryptographic controls, and **straight-through processing** requirements.

The directions also impose obligations around **third-party arrangements**, meaning banks must manage cybersecurity and technology risks arising from vendors, service providers, and other external dependencies. This includes oversight of outsourced technology services and controls to ensure external relationships do not weaken confidentiality, integrity, availability, or operational resilience. The framework further introduces a requirement for **continuous surveillance** of the technology environment, indicating that banks are expected to monitor for anomalies, threats, and control failures on an ongoing basis rather than relying only on periodic reviews.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that the document requires a bank-wide, board-backed control framework with documented roles, periodic risk review, and a detailed operational cybersecurity program covering assets, access, systems hardening, monitoring, patching, authentication, telework, third parties, and secure communications. The document title and table of contents indicate this is a **directional framework** rather than a voluntary guidance note, so affected commercial banks should treat it as a mandatory supervisory standard and ensure internal policies, committee charters, technical controls, and vendor oversight processes are aligned to the RBI’s expectations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Concurrent Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Concurrent Audit Directions, 2026** apply to **commercial banks** only—specifically **banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Local Area Banks**, as well as **corresponding new banks and the State Bank of India**. The directions are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, are **effective immediately upon issuance**, and are intended to strengthen internal controls by ensuring a short interval between a transaction and its independent review, with a particular focus on detecting errors, irregularities, fraudulent transactions, and supporting preventive vigilance.

On governance, the **Audit Committee of the Board (ACB)**, or **Local Management (LM) in the case of foreign banks**, must approve the **detailed scope** of the concurrent audit. The same ACB/LM must also determine the **maximum tenure of external concurrent auditors** and the **remuneration** payable to them, so these are no longer left to operational discretion alone. The document defines an **“audit firm”** broadly to include a **proprietorship firm, partnership firm, or LLP**, and otherwise relies on the meanings already assigned in the RBI Act, the Banking Regulation Act, the Companies Act, or other RBI regulations and common commercial usage.

Although the excerpt provided stops before the full operational requirements, the stated structure makes clear that the directions will also cover: **which activities must be included in concurrent audit coverage, how auditors are appointed, their accountability, tenure, remuneration, reporting, and repeal/saving provisions**. For compliance purposes, the immediate practical action is to confirm that the bank’s concurrent audit framework, audit-firm appointment process, audit scope approval, auditor tenure limits, and remuneration approvals are aligned to the ACB/LM’s formal oversight role and to the new RBI directions as of the issuance date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Compliance Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Compliance Function Directions, 2026** are effective **immediately upon issuance on July 31, 2026**, and apply to **all commercial banks**. The Directions establish minimum standards for how a bank must organize and run its compliance function, while allowing each bank to structure the function in a way that is commensurate with its **size, complexity, risk profile, and organizational structure**. RBI also states that the principles are aligned with the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision** framework and are intended to extend to **bank-led financial conglomerates** for group-wide compliance risk management.

At a governance level, the **board of directors** is responsible for approving and overseeing the bank’s compliance framework, while **senior management** must implement it and ensure compliance is embedded in operations. The bank must maintain a formal **compliance policy**, and the compliance function must cover the relevant regulatory obligations of the bank and, where applicable, the group. The Directions emphasize that compliance is not optional or purely advisory: it is treated as a core part of corporate governance and an assurance function alongside internal audit and risk management.

The document requires banks to define the **scope, structure, staffing, roles, and responsibilities** of the compliance function, including a group-wide approach where relevant. It also requires banks to cultivate a **compliance culture** and to put in place **quality assurance and internal audit** mechanisms to assess the effectiveness of the compliance function. A key structural requirement is the appointment of a **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)**, with specified expectations around the CCO’s **authority, stature, independence, reporting lines, and responsibilities**. The CCO must have sufficient standing within the organization and must report on compliance matters in a way that supports independent oversight.

The Directions also introduce requirements on the **use of technology for monitoring**, indicating that banks should leverage technology to support compliance oversight and monitoring of regulatory obligations. Finally, the document includes **repeal and saving provisions**, states that other laws are **not barred** by these Directions, and provides for **interpretation** provisions. For compliance teams, the practical effect is that the bank must review its governance documents, compliance policy, reporting lines, staffing, and monitoring tools to confirm they meet the RBI’s minimum standards from the moment the Directions take effect.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Miscellaneous Supervisory Directions, 2026** consolidates and updates a broad set of supervisory, governance, consumer-protection, anti-fraud, vigilance, and disclosure requirements applicable to **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)**. It is issued by RBI’s Department of Supervision under **RBI/DoS/2026-27/425** and is dated **July 31, 2026**; the document is organized into multiple chapters covering access to IT systems, monitoring end-use of funds, fair-practice rules on charging interest, treatment of inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits, nomination facilities, fraud prevention, protected disclosures, and vigilance processes. For a compliance team, the key point is that these are not merely advisory expectations: they impose operational controls, governance responsibilities, review/audit obligations, and complaint-handling procedures that SFBs must embed in policy and practice.

A major compliance theme is **fraud prevention and internal control**. The directions address frauds arising from **collusion of bank officials**, **large-value frauds**, **bulk sanctioning of retail loan proposals**, **fake title deeds used as property security**, and **frauds in non-resident accounts**, and they also require safeguards around **safe custody of critical documents** and **accounts opened by employees**. The document contemplates formal **legal compliance certificates**, **legal compliance audits**, **forensic scrutiny**, and clear standards for the **exercise of discretionary power**, along with a “best practices” framework for banks and other related instructions. Compliance officers should treat these as requiring documented controls, escalation and review protocols, and evidence that management decisions, especially in high-risk or large-value cases, are subject to independent checks.

The directions also place emphasis on **protected disclosures and whistleblowing**. They set out a **Protected Disclosure Scheme**, including the **scope and coverage**, the **procedure for lodging complaints**, and the required **protected disclosure policy**. This means SFBs need a channel for reporting misconduct that preserves confidentiality and protects complainants under the scheme, with internal processes capable of receiving, recording, and handling allegations without compromising the identity of the whistleblower. The structure indicates that the bank must have an implemented policy rather than simply an informal reporting route.

Another substantial area is **vigilance governance**. The document provides a full vigilance framework, including a definition of the **“vigilance angle,”** the role of the **Chief of Internal Vigilance**, requirements for that officer’s **appointment**, **tenure**, and restrictions on association with **sensitive matters**, as well as requirements for submission of **reports and returns** and periodic review. It also mandates **preventive vigilance**, **staff rotation**, and **mandatory leave** in appropriate cases, and it sets procedures for handling **complaints**, selecting the **investigation agency** for inquiries, and reviewing cases entrusted to external or internal investigating agencies. The vigilance chapter also addresses **action against persons making false complaints**, so the bank must distinguish bona fide disclosures from malicious allegations while preserving due process.

Finally, the table of contents shows that the directions cover core operational compliance issues that are likely to require policy updates and customer-facing process changes, including **access to IT systems**, **monitoring the end use of funds**, **interest-charging fairness practices**, **inoperative accounts/unclaimed deposits**, and **nomination facilities**. Although the excerpt does not reproduce each chapter’s operative text, the structure makes clear that SFBs must review their systems, product terms, account-management workflows, and customer communication to ensure alignment with the revised supervisory expectations. A compliance team should treat the directions as a comprehensive SFB governance and control manual and confirm, chapter by chapter, that existing policies, controls, audit trails, and escalation mechanisms are updated to match RBI’s requirements effective from the **31 July 2026** issuance date, or any specific implementation date stated in the full text of each chapter.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks (Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026** apply **immediately upon issuance** and are mandatory for **all Small Finance Banks**. The Directions are issued under the RBI’s statutory powers and set the framework for how these banks must manage, validate, and submit supervisory information to the RBI, including all periodic and ad hoc data submitted in prescribed formats, regardless of the technology platform or submission method. The document defines **“CIMS”** as the RBI’s online platform for return submission and data dissemination, and treats **“supervisory returns”** broadly to include all such reports.

From a governance perspective, the **Board and Senior Management** are required to explicitly include **data quality risk identification, assessment, and management** within the bank’s overall risk management framework. That framework must cover both **in-house and outsourced** data-related risks and must include policies addressing **data confidentiality, integrity, availability, and risk management**. The bank must ensure its **risk data aggregation capabilities and risk reporting practices** are fully documented and subject to high validation standards; the text indicates these standards must be aligned with the RBI’s expectations, meaning compliance teams should expect a formalized control environment around supervisory reporting data and not just operational submission processes.

The Directions also create a compliance obligation around the **accuracy and integrity of reporting**, meaning banks are expected to maintain strong documentation, validation, and governance controls over the data used in supervisory submissions. The document establishes that it governs the **filing of supervisory returns**, including operational guidelines, applicable return lists, timelines, exceptions, penalties, and other instructions, which means the compliance team must review the specific return schedule and submission deadlines contained later in the Directions and ensure internal processes are built to meet them. The excerpt provided does not include the detailed return-by-return deadlines, threshold values, or penalty amounts, but it clearly signals that failure to meet the supervisory return requirements may trigger **penalties** and that the RBI expects a structured, validated reporting process under board oversight.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Statutory Audit Directions, 2026** were issued under **Section 30(1A) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling powers, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance** on **31 July 2026**. They apply to **all Small Finance Banks** and govern the **appointment and reappointment** of their statutory auditors: the document uses the term **Statutory Central Auditors (SCAs)** for banks that also appoint separate **Statutory Branch Auditors (SBAs)**, and **Statutory Auditors (SAs)** for banks that do not use a branch-auditor model.  

For compliance purposes, the Directions reorganize and replace the RBI’s statutory-audit framework for SFBs, beginning with governance requirements for the **Board and senior management**, followed by detailed rules on **how many auditors may be appointed, branch coverage, auditor eligibility, independence, professional standards, tenure/rotation, audit fees and expenses, and appointment procedure**. The structure of the document also shows that RBI expects banks to maintain formal oversight over the audit process and to follow the specified appointment and reappointment rules rather than treating auditor selection as a purely internal matter.  

A major portion of the Directions addresses **Long Form Audit Reports (LFARs)** and the **timelines and procedures** for their submission. The document distinguishes between LFAR obligations for **SCAs** and for **SBAs**, and it sets out the **objectives, audit strategy, scope, and indicative coverage** that auditors must follow, indicating that compliance teams should ensure audit planning, field coverage, and report production are aligned to RBI’s prescribed framework rather than standard external-audit practice alone.  

The Directions also include a final chapter on **repeal, saving, and interpretation**, meaning the RBI has formally consolidated the statutory-audit regime for SFBs into this 2026 instrument and preserved or clarified the effect of prior actions where applicable. For a compliance officer, the immediate action point is that any **current or upcoming SCA/SA appointment or reappointment process** for a Small Finance Bank must be checked against these Directions as of **31 July 2026**, including the specific eligibility, independence, tenure, fee, branch-coverage, and reporting requirements contained in the later chapters and annexes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026** on **July 31, 2026**, and they take effect **immediately upon issuance**. These Directions apply to **all Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** and require them to move away from a mainly transaction-checking audit approach to a **Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA)** model, with internal audit focused on evaluating the bank’s **risk management systems and internal controls**, while still performing selective transaction testing. The RBI states that this is being issued under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and related enabling powers.

For compliance purposes, the key change is that each SFB must have an internal audit framework that is **risk-based, governance-driven, and aligned with evolving standards and international best practices**. The directions cover governance and oversight by the board and senior management, the internal audit policy, functional independence, risk assessment, audit scope, audit communication, performance evaluation, outsourcing, and the role of the Head of Internal Audit. The document also includes a chapter on repeal and saving, application of other laws, and interpretation, indicating that these directions are intended to sit within the broader RBI/regulatory framework rather than replace all other applicable legal obligations.

Although the excerpt provided does not show the detailed chapter provisions, the structure makes clear that SFBs will need to ensure the board and senior management formally oversee the internal audit function, that internal audit has sufficient independence, and that audit coverage is determined by risk rather than only by transaction volume or periodic checklists. Compliance teams should expect mandatory internal policies and procedures governing how internal audit is planned, executed, reported, evaluated, and, where applicable, outsourced, as well as specific expectations on the stature, authority, independence, tenure, and reporting line of the **Head of Internal Audit**.
