DAY-NRLM adopts a demand driven
rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular dated **April 1, 2025** consolidates and updates all prior instructions on **Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)** and **replaces the earlier Master Circular dated April 16, 2024**. It is addressed to **Public Sector Banks and Private Sector Banks, including Small Finance Banks**, and it restates the framework for bank participation in the Government of India’s flagship rural poverty-reduction program, which was originally launched as NRLM on **April 1, 2013** and renamed **DAY-NRLM on March 29, 2016**. The scheme is designed to build strong institutions of the poor, especially women, and help them access financial services and livelihoods through a demand-driven, state-specific approach.

The circular confirms that DAY-NRLM primarily promotes **affinity-based women Self Help Groups (SHGs)**, with an exception allowing **men and women together only for SHGs formed for persons with disabilities and other special categories such as elders and transgenders**. Standard women SHGs must have **10 to 20 members**; however, in difficult areas, groups with disabled persons, and remote tribal areas, the minimum may be **5 members**. Federations of SHGs formed at village, gram panchayat, cluster, or higher levels may be **registered under the relevant state law**. For financial support, the Ministry of Rural Development will provide a **Revolving Fund (RF) of ₹20,000 to ₹30,000 per SHG** to strengthen institutional and financial management capacity and help build internal credit history, but only SHGs that have existed for at least **3/6 months**, follow the “**Panchasutras**” (regular meetings, regular savings, regular internal lending, regular recoveries, and proper books of account), and have **not previously received RF** are eligible. The circular expressly states that **no capital subsidy** will be sanctioned to any SHG under DAY-NRLM. It also notes that **Community Investment Support Fund (CIF)** will be provided to SHGs in all blocks, routed through village- or cluster-level federations and **kept in perpetuity** by those federations; CIF may be used by the federations to make loans to SHGs and/or finance common collective socio-economic activities. In addition, the scheme includes **interest subvention for women SHGs**, with the detailed features set out in **Annex II**.

For banks, the circular makes clear that their role begins with **opening savings/current accounts for all SHGs and SHG federations**, including groups with members who have disabilities. SHGs are eligible to open savings accounts when they are engaged in promoting savings among members. For **KYC of SHG members**, banks must follow the **Master Direction on KYC dated February 25, 2016, as updated from time to time**; for **PAN/Form 60**, banks must follow **Section 33A(b) of the Master Direction on KYC**. The circular also permits **Business Correspondents (BCs)** to open SHG savings accounts, but only if this is done in accordance with existing BC guidelines and the bank’s **Board-approved BC policy**. The excerpt provided ends mid-sentence after beginning a further instruction on opening savings accounts for all members, so any additional account-opening requirement appears to continue beyond the visible text and should be checked in the full circular and annexes before implementation.

rows.title: Master Circular on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme
rows.desc: RBI/2025-26/01 FIDD.CO.FID.BC.No.4/12.01.033/2025-26 April 01, 2025 The Chairman/ Managing Director/ Chief Executive Officer All Scheduled Commercial Banks Madam/ Dear Sir Master Circular on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme The Reserve Bank of India has, from time to time, issued a number of guidelines/instructions to banks on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme. The enclosed Master Circular c onsolidates the circulars issued by Reserve Bank on the subject up to March 31, 2025, as indicated in the Appendix. Yours faithfully (Nisha Nambiar) Chief General Manager-in-Charge Encl: As above 2 Master Circular on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme Self Help Groups (SHGs) have the potential to bring together the formal banking structure and the rural poor for mutual benefit. Studies conducted by NABARD in a few states to assess the impact of the linkage project have brought out encouraging and positive features like increase in loan volume of the SHGs, definite shift in the loaning pattern of the members from non-income generating activities to production activities, nearly 100 per cent recovery performance, significant reduction in the transaction costs for both the banks and the borrowers etc., besides leading to a gradual increase in the income level of the SHG members. Another significant feature observed in the linkage project is that about 85 per cent of the groups linked with banks were formed exclusively by women. 2. Recognizing the importance of SHG Bank linkage, banks have been advised to meet the entire credit requirements of SHG members, as envisaged in Paragraph 93 of the Union Budget announcement for the year 2008-09, made by the Honorable Finance Minister, wherein it was stated as under: "Banks will be encouraged to embrace the concept of Total Financial Inclusion. Government will request all scheduled commercial banks to follow the example set by some public sector banks and meet the entire credit requirements of SHG members, namely, (a) income generation activities, (b) social ne
rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, dated April 1, 2025, consolidates all prior RBI instructions on the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme up to March 31, 2025 and is addressed to all Scheduled Commercial Banks. It does not announce a wholly new regime, but it restates and consolidates the compliance expectations that banks must follow when opening accounts for, and lending to, Self Help Groups (SHGs), with the goal of supporting “total financial inclusion” and ensuring banks meet the full credit needs of SHG members, including income-generating activity, social needs such as housing/education/marriage, and debt swapping.

Banks must allow both registered and unregistered SHGs that promote savings among members to open savings bank accounts, even if the group has not previously borrowed from a bank. While doing so, banks must apply the simplified customer due diligence (CDD) requirements applicable to SHGs under Chapter VI of the Master Direction on KYC (2016, as updated). The circular also emphasizes that banks should not impose rigid formal structures on SHGs and should keep the process hassle-free, including permitting consumption expenditure as part of the financing approach.

For lending, SHG credit must be built into the bank’s branch, block, district, state, and corporate credit plans, with “utmost priority” in those plans. NABARD operational guidance permits SHG loans generally within a savings-to-loan ratio of 1:1 to 1:4; however, for mature SHGs, banks may lend beyond four times the savings at their discretion. Banks are required to simplify loan applications, procedures, and documentation, eliminate operational bottlenecks, and delegate sufficient sanctioning authority to branch managers so that credit can be sanctioned and disbursed quickly.

On pricing and charges, banks may decide the interest rate on SHG and SHG member loans, but only within the limits of the RBI’s Master Direction on Interest Rate on Advances (March 3, 2016, as updated). The circular also points to the separate RBI priority sector lending instructions for service/processing charges on SHG loans, meaning any applicable charge waivers or restrictions must be followed under those directions. The document’s stated “effective” status is as a consolidation of the extant instructions as of March 31, 2025, so compliance teams should treat it as the current master reference for SHG-bank linkage requirements unless and until superseded.

rows.title: RBI invites comments on the Draft “Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026”
rows.desc: August 12, 2026 RBI invites comments on the Draft “Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026” In pursuance of the announcement made in the Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies dated August 05, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India has today issued the Draft Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026 for public comments. 2. The Reserve Bank has issued various instructions from time to time on interest rates on loans and advances for regulated entities (REs), with the objectives of ensuring effective monetary policy transmission, appropriate pricing of credit risk, and fair and non-discriminatory treatment of borrowers. At present, regulatory framework on interest rate on advances are applicable for Commercial Banks (including Small Finance Banks and Local Area Banks), covering, inter alia, instructions on internal and external benchmark-based lending frameworks for floating rate loans and determination of spreads over such benchmarks. Regulatory instructions on interest rates on loans and advances extended by other REs (i.e., Non-Banking Financial Companies, All India Financial Institutions, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, and Rural Cooperative Banks) are largely with regard to conduct related aspects. Further, with respect to Commercial Banks, divergent practices have been observed in certain aspects, including determination of MCLR (internal benchmark) and its components. In addition, the extant guidelines contain very limited regulatory instructions regarding fixed rate loans. Accordingly, it is proposed to issue harmonised Directions for all REs, prescribing a broad, principles-based framework for the determination of interest rates on both fixed rate and floating rate loans, commensurate with the nature, complexity, and scale of the operations of the REs. 3. For the purpose of public consultation / feedback, a draft Direction applicable to all REs is being issued. Upon
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued, on August 12, 2026, draft “Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026” for public comment, in line with the RBI’s August 05, 2026 Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies. The draft is intended to replace the current patchwork of instructions and create a harmonized, principles-based framework for how all regulated entities determine interest rates on both fixed-rate and floating-rate loans and advances, with the stated policy goals of improving monetary policy transmission, ensuring credit is priced for risk, and promoting fair, non-discriminatory treatment of borrowers.

At present, the RBI’s more detailed interest-rate rules mainly apply to commercial banks, including Small Finance Banks and Local Area Banks, particularly for internal and external benchmark-based floating-rate lending and spread-setting, while other regulated entities—Non-Banking Financial Companies, All India Financial Institutions, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, and Rural Cooperative Banks—are subject mostly to conduct-related requirements. The RBI says it has observed divergent practices among commercial banks, especially in how MCLR (the internal benchmark) and its components are determined, and that existing rules on fixed-rate loans are very limited; the new draft is meant to standardize these areas across all regulated entities, with requirements calibrated to the nature, complexity, and scale of each institution.

For compliance teams, the key point is that the draft is not limited to banks: it is proposed to apply to all regulated entities covered by RBI supervision, and it will likely impose broader governance and pricing expectations for loan and advance interest-rate setting than the current framework. The notice itself does not provide the final operative rules, implementation date, or comment deadline in the excerpt shown, but it makes clear that this is a consultation draft and that the final directions, once issued, are expected to govern both fixed and floating rate lending practices across the sector.

rows.desc: August 7, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’ Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) reflects the adjustment to the default risk-free prices of derivatives to account for potential counterparty default. CVA risk refers to losses resulting from changes in CVA values, driven by shifts in counterparty credit spreads and market risk factors. The CVA capital charge ensures banks hold sufficient capital to cover these risks. 2. The extant CVA framework was issued by the Reserve Bank in 2011, which was based on the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) standards issued in 2010. The BCBS has, since, issued revised CVA guidelines under the final Basel III framework. Accordingly, it has been decided to issue revised instructions on CVA framework permitting banks in India to adopt the basic approach (BA-CVA). Banks may choose to implement either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. Alternatively, in line with BCBS guidelines, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may calculate their CVA capital charge as 100 per cent of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge. 3. The revised instructions: (a) allow eligible banks to choose a simpler approach; (b) clarify the eligibility and recognition of CVA hedges; (c) increase the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties by sector and credit quality; and (d) separate systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation, addressing imperfect alignment of indirect CVA hedges. These revisions enhance risk sensitivity and improve consistency in the CVA framework. 4. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank has released today the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026. 5. rows.summary:
On August 7, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released draft **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026** and invited public comments on them through **August 28, 2026**. The draft updates India’s CVA capital framework, replacing the earlier RBI framework from **2011** that had been based on **2010 BCBS standards**, because the Basel Committee has since issued revised CVA rules under the final Basel III framework.

The key substantive change is that **banks in India may now adopt the BCBS basic approach (BA-CVA)** for CVA capital calculation, rather than only the prior framework. Under the draft, eligible banks can choose either the **full BA-CVA** or a **reduced BA-CVA** version; alternatively, banks with an **insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives** may calculate the CVA capital charge as **100% of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge**. This is a significant compliance choice because it changes how banks measure and hold capital against derivative counterparty-default-related losses.

The revised instructions also make several technical but important regulatory clarifications: they define more clearly **which CVA hedges are eligible and recognized**, increase the **sensitivity of supervisory risk weights** by **counterparty sector and credit quality**, and, in the full BA-CVA calculation, separate **systematic** and **idiosyncratic** CVA risk components to address imperfect alignment of **indirect CVA hedges**. RBI states that these changes are intended to improve risk sensitivity and consistency in the CVA framework.

For compliance teams at regulated banks, the practical implication is that institutions should assess whether they qualify for the simpler approaches, whether their derivative portfolios are sufficiently small in non-centrally cleared contracts to use the **100% of CCR** method, and whether existing hedge documentation and capital models will need revision to match the new eligibility and recognition rules. RBI is seeking comments not only from **Regulated Entities** but also from **market participants and other interested parties** by the **August 28, 2026** deadline.

rows.summary:
On August 6, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India issued draft directions for public comment in connection with the August 5, 2026 Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies. The package has two parts: a new draft **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) – Directions, 2026** that would replace the existing 2025 concentration-risk directions for rural co-operative banks, and a draft **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) – Amendment Directions, 2026** that would amend selected provisions of the 2025 credit facilities directions.

Substantively, the draft framework is intended to set **prudential exposure limits for single and group counterparties**, impose **enhanced housing loan limits**, and establish **prudential limits on unsecured advances** for rural co-operative banks (RCBs). It also proposes a differentiated treatment for housing loans: **larger RCBs with deposits above ₹1,000 crore** would be given flexibility to decide the **tenor and moratorium** for housing loans, while the **caps for tenor and moratorium would be increased for other RCBs**. In addition, the RBI proposes to **withdraw the prescribed prudential sectoral exposure limits for all sectors except real estate**, meaning the sectoral concentration constraints would be relaxed generally but **retained for real estate exposure**.

The draft directions are not yet final; they have been released for comment. **Regulated entities and other stakeholders / members of the public must submit feedback on or before August 28, 2026**, either through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website using the hyperlink provided for each document, or by **email** with the subject line **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Directions)”**. Compliance teams at RCBs should assess whether they are affected by the proposed exposure-limit changes, housing-loan flexibility, and unsecured-advance framework, and should consider submitting comments before the deadline if the draft requirements would materially affect operations or risk appetite.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued draft rules, dated July 21, 2026, to rationalize the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, following the Union Budget 2026–27 announcement of a comprehensive review of the foreign investment framework. The draft is the product of a Central Government committee review and stakeholder consultation, and it is intended to create a more contemporary, user-friendly regime for foreign investment into India. It does not itself set out new numerical thresholds, ownership caps, approval requirements, or sector-specific limits in the text provided; instead, it describes the policy direction of the rewrite.

For compliance purposes, the most material change is structural: the proposed rules aim to simplify and rationalize the existing framework, harmonize definitions, and make the regulatory architecture more principle-based. The draft also says it will more clearly separate FEMA procedural requirements from FDI policy and sector-specific conditions, which should reduce confusion about what is governed by RBI/FEMA rules versus what is imposed by policy or sectoral regulators. This is meant to improve clarity, reduce compliance complexity, and allow policy updates to be made more quickly when needed.

The draft further signals a move toward “investee-neutral and investor-neutral” provisions, indicating that the new framework is intended to be more flexible across different types of foreign investors and Indian investee entities while still preserving regulatory safeguards. The stated objective is to streamline procedures, reduce compliance burden, and improve operational flexibility for foreign investment transactions. From a compliance standpoint, organizations should expect changes to rule drafting, definitions, and procedural mechanics rather than a simple amendment to isolated provisions.

No effective date or transition deadline is provided in the text. The document explicitly says the rules will be finalized only after wider public consultations, so the current draft is not yet operative. Compliance teams should treat this as an early-stage consultation document and monitor the final issuance for any concrete changes to reporting, approvals, pricing, sectoral compliance, or transaction conditions once the rulemaking is completed.

rows.summary:
On July 15, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance”** for public comment. The draft is **not yet final**, but it signals the RBI’s expected supervisory direction on how regulated entities should govern data in light of increasing digitization and technology-led business models. Comments are due **by August 17, 2026**, and may be submitted through RBI’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** portal or sent by email/post to the Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, RBI, Mumbai, with the specified subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance.”**

The draft guidance applies broadly to a wide set of RBI-regulated entities: **commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), asset reconstruction companies, and credit information companies**. Compliance teams at any of these entities should assume the draft is intended to set expectations for enterprise-wide data governance, not just IT or information security functions, because the RBI explicitly links weak data governance to **financial, operational, compliance, and reputational risk**.

The document states the objective is to ensure data remains **accurate, consistent, secure, and fit for purpose across functions and systems**. While the excerpt provided does not include specific operative standards, thresholds, or technical mandates, the compliance relevance is that the RBI is formalizing supervisory expectations around how regulated entities manage data as a critical business asset, likely across collection, storage, quality, access, use, and oversight. Entities in scope should review their current data governance framework, ownership model, controls, and monitoring arrangements against this stated objective and prepare to respond to the consultation before the **August 17, 2026** deadline.

That means firms active in call, notice, and term money markets—especially **banks, standalone primary dealers, and other market participants that may seek to borrow or lend in these markets**—should review whether the draft would change their trading, funding, counterparty-access, or internal limit frameworks.

On June 24, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management”** for public comment. The draft is intended to apply broadly across RBI-regulated entities, specifically: **commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), asset reconstruction companies, and credit information companies**.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’
rows.desc: June 10, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’ The extant guidelines require the use of the Current Exposure Method (CEM) for the computation of Counterparty Credit Risk (CCR) exposure. In 2016, RBI issued final ‘Guidelines for Computing Exposure for Counterparty Credit Risk arising from Derivative Transactions’ and ‘Guidelines on Capital Requirements for Bank Exposures to Central Counterparties’, both based on the Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR), with an intended implementation date of April 1, 2018. However, the implementation of these guidelines was subsequently deferred. 2. Since then, the Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020, has been enacted, while the margining framework has been implemented under the Reserve Bank of India (Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives) Directions, 2024. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) has also, over time, issued various FAQs providing further clarity on the SA-CCR guidelines. 3. Considering the time elapsed and the recent legal and regulatory developments, the guidelines have been comprehensively reviewed. The key changes between the 2016 guidelines (currently part of the Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions, Directions, 2025) and the proposed draft Directions include, inter alia, (i) clarification on the scope of CCR across both banking and trading book exposures, (ii) treatment of multiple margin agreements and multiple netting sets elaborated in view of the legal / regulatory developments in netting and margining guidelines, (iii) guidance on the treatment of transactions where a bank acts as a clearing member of SEBI- recognised stock exchanges in the equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments, (iv) treatment for deferment of option premium, (v) guidance on computation of effective notional for options, and (vi) inclusion of disclosure
rows.summary:
On June 10, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft Amendment Directions on the **Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)** and invited public comments. The draft reflects a comprehensive review of the earlier 2016 SA-CCR-based guidelines, which had originally been intended to take effect on **April 1, 2018** but were later deferred; under the extant framework, banks still compute counterparty credit risk exposure using the **Current Exposure Method (CEM)**. The review was prompted by subsequent legal and regulatory changes, including the enactment of the **Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020**, the implementation of the margining framework under the **Reserve Bank of India (Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives) Directions, 2024**, and additional clarification issued by the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)** through FAQs.

The draft directions make several substantive changes relevant to compliance and risk systems: they clarify the scope of counterparty credit risk across **both banking book and trading book exposures**; expand guidance on **multiple margin agreements** and **multiple netting sets** in light of the new netting and margining regime; address transactions where a bank acts as a **clearing member of SEBI-recognised stock exchanges** in the **equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments**; provide treatment for **deferment of option premium**; explain how to compute the **effective notional for options**; and add **disclosure templates** for SA-CCR. RBI states that it has now issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Amendment Directions, 2026**, which implies affected institutions should review whether their CCR calculation methodologies, margin/netting documentation handling, and disclosure processes need to be updated once these amendments are implemented.

Comments on the draft are due by **July 1, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Market Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Mumbai 400 001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’”**. The consultation is open to **regulated entities, market participants, and other interested parties**.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued **revised draft Amendment Directions** on **“Conduct of Regulated Entities in Recovery of Loans and Engagement of Recovery Agents”** after receiving substantial stakeholder feedback on the version released for public comment on **February 12, 2026**. The RBI says the earlier draft has been **materially revised** in several key areas based on that feedback, including changes to provisions related to lenders’ proposed use of **technology-based mechanisms to restrict or disable certain functions of financed mobile devices** (such as **mobile phones and tablets**) in order to recover dues from borrowers in default.  

The revised draft is now being issued for **another round of public consultation** and applies across a broad set of RBI-regulated institutions through entity-specific amendment directions, namely: **commercial banks, small finance banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies, and housing finance companies**. The press release does not set out the substantive final rules yet; rather, it announces that these revised drafts have been published and remain open for comment.  

**Comments/feedback must be submitted on or before May 31, 2026.** Regulated entities and other stakeholders may file comments either through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website using the hyperlink for each document, or by **email** with the subject line formatted as **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions (including the type of Regulated Entity))”**.  

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that RBI is signaling a potential change in how recovery practices and recovery-agent engagement will be regulated, and that the revised drafts may affect debt-recovery procedures, borrower-device restrictions, and related conduct controls once finalized. Organizations in any of the covered entity categories should review the revised drafts promptly and determine whether their current loan-recovery, collections, outsourcing, and technology-enabled recovery practices would need policy, process, legal, customer-notice, or governance updates.

rows.summary:
The RBI has issued draft amendment directions and is seeking public comments on proposed changes to the framework used to identify NBFCs in the Upper Layer (NBFC-UL), as well as on the treatment of Government-owned NBFCs. The two draft instruments are the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Second Amendment Directions, 2026** and the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Concentration Risk Management) Third Amendment Directions, 2026**. Comments from NBFCs, members of the public, and other stakeholders are invited **until May 04, 2026** and may be submitted through RBI’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** portal or emailed/mailed to the Department of Regulation (SIG-NBFCs), with the specified subject line referencing the draft amendment directions.

Substantively, the RBI says the current Scale Based Regulatory framework identifies NBFC-UL using a **two-pronged methodology**: the **top ten eligible NBFCs by asset size** and a **parametric scoring methodology**. The draft proposal would replace that approach with a more transparent, simple, and absolute **asset-size criterion** for identification of NBFC-UL. The press release states that this new threshold is **currently proposed at ₹1,00,000** (the text is truncated, but this clearly refers to an asset-size threshold; compliance teams should review the full draft for the exact unit and final wording). No.: NSE/CML/2026/19 Date: August 07, 2026 To, All Listed Entities Subject: Adherence to Compliance Requirements for Handling Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 Suggested Best Practices SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 “(PIT Regulations)”, as amended from time to time, and the relevant circulars issued by SEBI and the Stock Exchanges detail, inter-alia, the manner in which the listed companies are required to deal with Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI). The provisions of the PIT Regulations are further supplemented and clarified through the Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) issued by SEBI. In light of the observations made in certain cases, it is considered imperative that listed companies diligently adhere to best practices to ensure full compliance with the PIT Regulations as amended from time to time including the following: 1. Listed companies shall maintain a structured digital database containing the nature of UPSI, the names and PANs (or any other identifier authorized by law) of persons who have shared the information, and the names and PANs of persons with whom such information has been shared. In case where UPSI is shared with a listed company, intermediaries, or fiduciaries, the names and identifier of the individuals handling such information shall be recorded. 2. Listed companies shall diligently implement and periodically review internal policies designed to prevent the leakage of UPSI. Such measures must be in alignment with the statutory and regulatory provisions prescribed under the PIT Regulations. 3. To ensure a culture of compliance, companies shall conduct periodic training and awareness programs for all employees and fiduciaries regarding the prescribed manner of handling UPSI. 4. Listed companies shall ensure compliance with the Code of Conduct formulated by the company wi
rows.summary:
This NSE circular, dated **August 7, 2026** and addressed to **all listed entities**, reiterates and reinforces compliance expectations for handling **Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)** under the **SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (PIT Regulations)**, as amended, along with SEBI/stock exchange circulars and SEBI FAQs. It does **not introduce a new rule change or numerical threshold**, but it emphasizes that listed companies must strictly follow the existing PIT framework and the “best practices” described in the circular because of compliance concerns observed in certain cases.

The key operational requirement is that listed companies must maintain a **structured digital database** recording the **nature of the UPSI**, the **names and PANs (or other legally authorized identifiers)** of the persons who shared the information, and the **names and PANs/identifiers of the persons with whom it was shared**. Where UPSI is shared with a **listed company, intermediary, or fiduciary**, the company must also record the **names and identifiers of the individuals actually handling the information**. The circular also requires companies to **diligently implement and periodically review internal policies** intended to prevent UPSI leakage, ensuring those policies align with the PIT Regulations and related requirements.

In addition, listed companies are expected to run **periodic training and awareness programs** for **all employees and fiduciaries** on the proper handling of UPSI, so that compliance is embedded as a routine practice rather than handled ad hoc. The circular further states that companies must ensure compliance with the **company’s Code of Conduct** formulated under the PIT regime; although the final sentence in the provided text is truncated, the substance clearly signals ongoing responsibility to align internal conduct rules with the insider trading framework. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that documentation, access tracking, policy review, and staff training around UPSI should be treated as active, auditable controls under the listed entity’s insider trading compliance program.

rows.summary:
This FAQ explains the NSE process context for corporate action record dates under SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, and confirms that **all listed entities** may fix a **record date** for a corporate action under **Regulation 42**. For **InvITs and REITs**, the document states that the record date must be disclosed under the applicable SEBI regulations **at least two working days prior to the record date**. The FAQ is presented as a general guidance note only, and it expressly says that if there is any conflict between this FAQ and the underlying NSE circulars, **the circulars control and are final and binding**.

The document also makes clear that the guidance is not a standalone rulebook and should not be relied on without checking the governing circulars and regulations. It advises readers to do their own diligence because NSE disclaims liability for errors, omissions, or any losses from reliance on the FAQ. A corporate compliance team should therefore treat this as a summary aid, not as the operative legal requirement, and should verify the exact filing/disclosure steps and timing against the relevant NSE circulars and SEBI provisions before taking action.

rows.title: Norms for Base Price, Price Bands, Call Auction in pre-open session and Close-out procedure for Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs)
rows.desc: Circular Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2026/18 Date: July 03, 2026 Department: LISTING To, All Listed Entities Subject: Norms for Base Price, Price Bands, Call Auction in pre-open session and Close-out procedure for Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) Dear Sir/Ma’am, This is with reference to the SEBI Circular No. HO/47/11/11(1)2026-MRD-POD3/I/13804/2026 dated June 15, 2026, issued by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) titled “Norms for Base Price, Price Bands, Call Auction in pre-open session and Close-out procedure for Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs)”. A copy of SEBI Circular dated June 15, 2026, is enclosed for your reference and for necessary action at your end. The copy of the circular is also available on the NSE website (www.nseindia.com). This is for your information please. For and on behalf of National Stock Exchange of India Limited Snehal Mariappa Manager Encl: SEBI Circular
rows.summary:
The document is an NSE circular dated July 3, 2026, addressed to all listed entities, forwarding SEBI Circular No. HO/47/11/11(1)2026-MRD-POD3/I/13804/2026 dated June 15, 2026, on “Norms for Base Price, Price Bands, Call Auction in pre-open session and Close-out procedure for Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs).” As written, the NSE letter itself does not set out the substantive ETF trading rules; it simply notifies listed entities that SEBI has issued the circular, encloses a copy for reference, and states that the circular is available on the NSE website for necessary action. The only compliance implication stated in this document is that affected parties should review the enclosed SEBI circular and take any action required under that SEBI framework.

From a compliance perspective, this means the operative requirements, including any changes to ETF base price determination, price band application, pre-open call auction mechanics, or close-out procedures, are contained in the referenced SEBI circular rather than in this NSE cover note. No implementation date, deadline, numerical threshold, or specific procedure is provided in the text of the NSE letter itself. If your organization issues, lists, trades, or supports ETFs, the practical next step is to read the attached SEBI circular and assess any rule changes applicable to your trading, listing, surveillance, or risk/compliance controls.

rows.title: Update of single filing system through API-based integration between Stock Exchanges
rows.desc: National Stock Exchange of India CONFIDENTIAL CIRCULAR Department: Listing Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2026/17 Date: June 19, 2026 To, The Compliance Officer, All Listed Entities Subject: Update of single filing system through API-based integration between Stock Exchanges This has reference to Exchange Circular No. NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024, with respect to single filing system through API-based integration between Stock Exchanges. In this connection, we are pleased to inform you that the single filing system has been extended for the XBRL filing pertaining to the below mentioned event with effect from June 20, 2026, along with the release of the few new XBRL utilities as mentioned in the below table. At the initial stage, the PDF filings will be considered by the Exchange as compliance under Regulation 30 of the SEBI LODR Regulations 2015. Further, all listed entities would be required to submit the filings in XBRL mode within 24 hours of submission of the said PDF filing. The XBRL utility for the new events mentioned in the table below will be made available at the path COMPLIANCE >> Common XBRL Upload>> Equity Announcement- XBRL. Further, it may be noted that the said XBRL filing, will also be made available in iXBRL format (readable format) to the listed entities/stakeholders on the website of the Exchange at path https://www.nseindia.com/companies-listing/corporate-filings-announcements-xbrl (selection of announcement type) Further, please note that the XBRL utility and filing of single event of Para B of Part A of Schedule III of SEBI LODR 2015 i.e. Awarding, bagging/ receiving, amendment or termination of awarded/bagged orders/contracts not in the normal course of business, will be discontinued effective June 20, 2026 and will be merged with the single utility of Para B events. With this, the Single filing system through API-based integration shall now be available for below mentioned disclosures: - National Stock Exchange of India CONFIDENTIAL
rows.summary:
This circular updates the NSE’s single filing system under the API-based integration between stock exchanges, building on Circular No. NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024. Effective **June 20, 2026**, the single filing system is being **extended to XBRL filing** for the newly specified event categories, and the Exchange is also releasing new XBRL utilities for those events. For the initial transition period, **PDF filings will be treated by the Exchange as compliance under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**, but listed entities must then **file the corresponding XBRL version within 24 hours of submitting the PDF**. The new XBRL utility will be available in the path **COMPLIANCE >> Common XBRL Upload >> Equity Announcement- XBRL**, and the same XBRL filing will also be made available to stakeholders in **iXBRL (readable) format** on NSE’s website at the specified corporate filings/announcements XBRL page.

The circular also states that the **existing XBRL utility and separate filing workflow for the Para B of Part A of Schedule III event** relating to **“Awarding, bagging/receiving, amendment or termination of awarded/bagged orders/contracts not in the normal course of business”** will be **discontinued effective June 20, 2026** and **merged into the single utility for Para B events**. In practical terms, compliance teams of all listed entities should be prepared to use the updated single filing/API-based process for the newly covered disclosures, ensure the PDF-to-XBRL conversion and submission happens within the 24-hour deadline, and note that the previously separate utility for the specified contract/order event will no longer be used after the effective date.

rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India Limited issued Circular NSE/CML/2026/16 dated June 12, 2026, addressed to all listed entities, attaching FAQs for the submission of the quarterly “Integrated Filing – Governance” report (formerly the Corporate Governance Report). The circular asks listed entities to take note of the FAQs and comply accordingly, and it states that the FAQ document is guidance only for filing the quarterly Integrated Filing – Governance through the XBRL utility; it does not override or replace any applicable law, SEBI regulation, or exchange circular.

The key filing deadline confirmed in the FAQs is that the Integrated Filing – Governance Report must be submitted within 30 days from the end of each quarter, in line with Regulation 27(2) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations. A newly listed entity must begin filing from the quarter ending immediately after the date of listing, so the obligation starts with the first full quarter after listing rather than the listing date itself.

The FAQs also clarify that the filing is for listed entities and is meant to be done in the quarterly governance format through XBRL. Beyond the deadline and start date, the document is primarily a reference guide for the reporting process and points users to different sections covering board composition, committee composition, board meetings, committee meetings, “others,” and quarterly disclosures under Schedule III of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015.

From a compliance perspective, the important operational point is that this circular does not introduce a new substantive governance rule; it reinforces the existing quarterly reporting obligation and directs listed entities to follow the detailed FAQ guidance for accurate submission. Compliance teams should ensure the report is filed every quarter within the 30-day window, that newly listed entities begin with the correct quarter, and that the filing is made in the prescribed XBRL format in accordance with the governing SEBI/Exchange requirements.

rows.title:
Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 54L of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy 
Code, 2016.
rows.desc: National Stock Exchange of India Circular Department: Listing Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2026/15 Date: June 01, 2026 To All Listed Companies, Sub: Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 54L of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. Attention is invited to the provisions relating to Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (“PPIRP”) under Chapter III-A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (“IBC”). In this regard, as advised by SEBI, it is clarified that, the exemptions available under various SEBI Regulations in respect of a Resolution Plan approved under Section 31 of the IBC are not available in case of a Resolution Plan approved under Section 54L of the IBC under the PPIRP framework. Accordingly, listed entities undergoing PPIRP shall be required to comply with all applicable procedural and regulatory requirements prescribed under the relevant SEBI Regulations. The listed companies are advised to take note of the above and ensure compliance of the same. For and on behalf of National Stock Exchange of India Limited Yukti Sharma Head - Listing
rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India, by Listing Circular No. NSE/CML/2026/15 dated June 1, 2026, has clarified how listed companies must treat a **Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP)** under **Section 54L of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC)**. The key change is that the **SEBI regulatory exemptions that are available when a resolution plan is approved under Section 31 of the IBC do not apply** when a resolution plan is approved under **Section 54L** in the PPIRP framework.

For compliance purposes, this means that **listed entities undergoing PPIRP must continue to comply with all applicable procedural and regulatory requirements under the relevant SEBI Regulations**, rather than assuming any relaxed treatment based on the insolvency resolution process. The circular does not create a new filing form or numerical threshold, but it imposes an important compliance obligation: companies in PPIRP must review the applicable SEBI regime and ensure that all normal obligations remain met where required. The circular expressly directs all listed companies to take note and ensure compliance.

rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) has updated its single filing system through API-based integration between stock exchanges, extending the XBRL-based single filing facility to additional disclosure events under the listed-company disclosure framework. This update is issued under Circular No. NSE/CML/2026/14 dated May 29, 2026, and it expressly references the earlier circular NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024, which introduced the single filing system. The new extension applies to XBRL filings for the listed events identified in the circular and becomes effective on the dates specified for each event, meaning companies must use the single-filing/API route for those disclosures from those dates onward where applicable.

For disclosures relating to the **schedule of analysts’ or institutional investors’ meetings, investor presentations, transcripts, and audio/video recordings**, the requirement under **Regulation 30 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**, read with **sub-para 15 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**, is available through the single filing system from **May 29, 2026**. The same effective date, **May 29, 2026**, also applies to disclosures concerning **actions initiated or orders passed by any regulatory, statutory, enforcement authority or judicial body** under **Regulation 30 read with sub-para 19 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**, and **actions taken or orders passed by any regulatory, statutory, enforcement authority or judicial body** under **Regulation 30 read with sub-para 20 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**. These filings are marked in the circular as enabled for **equity** and **equity + debt** listed companies, but not for **exclusively debt** listed companies or **REITs/INVITs** for those items.

The circular also brings **initiation of forensic audit** filings under the single-filing system, effective **May 05, 2026**, pursuant to **Regulation 30 read with sub-para 17 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**. In addition, disclosures under the **SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015**, specifically **Regulation 7(2) and 7(3)**, are included in the single filing system from **May 05, 2026**, and the applicability matrix in the circular indicates this item is available for **equity**, **equity + debt**, and **REITs/INVITs**, but not for **exclusively debt** listed companies. The circular’s table is structured by listed-company type, so compliance teams should confirm whether their entity falls into the categories covered for each disclosure event before relying on the API-based single filing route.

The document is fundamentally a process/update notice rather than a substantive change to the underlying disclosure obligations: it does **not** create new reporting triggers, but it changes the **filing mechanism** by expanding which XBRL disclosures can be submitted through the stock exchange single-filing/API integration. Compliance officers should ensure internal disclosure workflows, XBRL preparation, and exchange filing procedures are updated so that the above events are filed through the integrated system from the stated effective dates, and that the entity-specific applicability shown in the circular is followed to avoid misfiling or filing through the wrong channel.

rows.title: Filing of disclosures in XBRL format under Regulation 7(2) and Regulation 7(3) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
rows.desc: National Stock Exchange of India Circular Department: Listing Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2026/12 Date: May 04, 2026 To, The Company Secretary, All Listed Entities Subject: Filing of disclosures in XBRL format under Regulation 7(2) and Regulation 7(3) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 Dear Sir/Madam, This is to inform you that disclosures under Regulation 7(2) and Regulation 7(3) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 were previously being filed through the following path: NEAPS  Compliance  Disclosures  Insider Trading The above-mentioned filing path has now been discontinued, and a new XBRL based utility has been introduced for submission of such disclosures. Accordingly, all listed companies, REITs and InvITs are required to submit the aforesaid disclosure only in XBRL format through the revised process as detailed below: To download XBRL utility: NEAPS  Compliance  Download XBRL Utilities For Submission of disclosures: NEAPS  Compliance  Common XBRL Upload  Prohibition of Insider Trading Please note that previously filed disclosures shall continue to be available at the following link: https://www.nseindia.com/companies-listing/corporate-filings-insider-trading-archive-data Further, with reference to Exchange Circular No. NSE/CML/2026/11 dated May 04, 2026, the said utility will also be available for Single Filing system through API-based integration. You are requested to take note of the above and ensure compliance. Yours faithfully, For National Stock Exchange of India Limited Harshad Dharod Chief Manager-Listing Compliance
rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India has changed the filing mechanism for disclosures required under Regulation 7(2) and Regulation 7(3) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. The earlier NEAPS path — **Compliance → Disclosures → Insider Trading** — has been **discontinued**, and these disclosures must now be submitted **only in XBRL format** using the new utility.

This requirement applies to **all listed companies, REITs, and InvITs**. The new process is: download the utility from **NEAPS → Compliance → Download XBRL Utilities**, then upload disclosures through **NEAPS → Compliance → Common XBRL Upload → Prohibition of Insider Trading**. The circular does not specify a separate grace period or filing deadline, so the operational change should be treated as **effective immediately from the circular date, May 04, 2026**.

The Exchange also states that **previously filed disclosures will remain available** at the NSE archive link provided in the circular, so historical filings are still accessible for reference. In addition, the same XBRL utility will be available for **Single Filing system through API-based integration** pursuant to Exchange Circular **NSE/CML/2026/11 dated May 04, 2026**.

For compliance teams, the key action is to ensure internal filing workflows are updated so that insider-trading disclosures under Regulations 7(2) and 7(3) are no longer routed through the old NEAPS disclosure path and are instead filed through the new XBRL upload process, with any automated/API-based filing arrangements aligned to the new utility.

rows.summary:
This circular updates the “single filing system” established under Exchange Circular NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024, by extending the API-based integration between stock exchanges to additional XBRL disclosures. The extension is already effective for the first added item as of **April 25, 2026**, and other listed items become available from **May 5, 2026**. The practical effect is that filings made to one exchange for the covered disclosures can be transmitted through the API-based single filing mechanism rather than requiring separate manual filings to each exchange, but only for the event types and issuer categories specifically listed in the circular.

The circular states that, with effect from **April 25, 2026**, the single filing system covers XBRL filing for the **“Outcome of Board Meeting for Dividend, Buyback, Bonus and Voluntary Delisting events”** under **Regulation 30 of SEBI (LODR) read with sub-para 4 of Para A Part A of Schedule III**. From **May 5, 2026**, it also covers **“Initiation of Forensic audit”** under **Regulation 30 of SEBI (LODR) read with sub-para 17 of Para A Part A of Schedule III**, and **“Prohibition of Insider Trading”** disclosures under **Regulation 7(2) and 7(3) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015**. For the insider trading item, the matrix indicates applicability to **equity**, **equity + debt**, and **REITs/InvITs**, whereas the forensic audit and board-meeting outcome items are marked for **equity** and **equity + debt** listed companies only.

The circular also indicates that the single filing system remains applicable for several other Regulation 30 disclosures already covered under the API integration framework, including **Agreements/Contracts/Arrangements/MOU under Para A** (**sub-para 5 and 5A**), **Notice of Shareholders’ Meeting** (**sub-para 12**), **Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process events** (**sub-para 16**), and **Issuance/Allotment/Alteration/Restriction on transferability of securities under Para A** (**sub-para 2**, though the text provided is truncated after this item). The issuer-category matrix shown in the circular uses checkmarks to indicate where the single filing mechanism applies, with the main coverage shown for **equity** and **equity + debt** listed entities, and in some cases also **REITs and InvITs**. Compliance teams should treat the listed effective dates as the point from which these disclosures must be routed through the updated API-based single filing process for the covered entities, and verify internal filing workflows are aligned to the applicable event type and issuer category.

rows.title: XBRL based filing for Violations related to Code of Conduct (CoC) under SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
rows.desc: National Stock Exchange of India Circular Department: Listing Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2026/13 Date: May 04, 2026 To, The Company Secretary, All Listed Entities/Intermediaries/Fiduciaries Subject: XBRL based filing for Violations related to Code of Conduct (CoC) under SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 SEBI vide Circular No. SEBI/HO/ISD/ISD/CIR/P/2020/135 dated July 23, 2020, prescribed the format for reporting violations of the Code of Conduct under SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. To enhance accuracy and efficiency in disclosures, the Exchange has introduced an XBRL utility for reporting such violations through NEAPS with effect from May 05, 2026. rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India has introduced an XBRL-based filing process for reporting violations of the Code of Conduct under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. This change is stated to improve accuracy and efficiency in disclosures, and it becomes effective on **May 05, 2026**. It applies to **all listed companies**, as well as **intermediaries and fiduciaries** that are required to report Code of Conduct violations under the SEBI PIT framework.

For **listed entities**, the reporting must now be filed **only through NEAPS in XBRL mode**, and the Exchange explicitly states that **no PDF submission is permitted** for these filings. The NEAPS workflow is: **Compliance → Download XBRL Utilities** to obtain the utility, and **Compliance → Common XBRL Upload → Violation of Code of Conduct under SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015** for submission. Any filing by a listed entity made through another mode will **not be taken on record and will be treated as invalid**.

For **unlisted entities acting as intermediaries or fiduciaries**, the existing process remains unchanged: they must continue to submit disclosures by **email to pit_coc@nse.co.in**, in line with Exchange Circular **NSE/CML/2020/44 dated August 26, 2020**. The circular also clarifies that disclosures relating to Code of Conduct violations **will not be disseminated on the Exchange website**. Compliance teams should ensure the new NEAPS XBRL-only requirement is implemented immediately for listed entities, with internal controls updated so that no PDF or alternate-mode submission is used after the effective date.

rows.summary:
NSE has updated its “single filing system” through API-based integration between stock exchanges, originally introduced under Circular NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024. Effective March 07, 2026, the single-filing mechanism is expanded to cover additional XBRL filings for specified disclosures, but only to the extent expressly listed in the circular and only for the listed entity categories shown in the table.

For **equity-listed entities** and **equity + debt listed entities**, the new single-filing coverage now includes XBRL submissions for: prior intimation of board meeting under Regulation 29 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015; closure of trading window under the SEBI PIT Regulations; fraud/default/arrest disclosures under Regulation 30 of SEBI LODR and sub-para 6 of Part A of Schedule III; corporate debt restructuring disclosures under Regulation 30 and sub-para 9 and 10 of Part A of Schedule III; resolution plans/restructuring related to bank/financial institution borrowings, inter-creditors agreements, and one-time settlement (OTS); issue summary document (ISD) for buyback via open and tender route; integrated filing–financials under Regulations 23(9), 30 read with Section V-B of the Master Circular, and Regulations 32(1) and 33(3) (effective January 03, 2026); annual secretarial compliance report under Regulation 24A(2) (effective September 15, 2025); integrated filing–governance under Regulations 13(3), 27(2), and 30 (effective March 01, 2025); meetings of shareholders and voting results under Regulation 44(3) (effective December 28, 2024); reconciliation of share capital audit report under Regulation 76 (effective November 15, 2024); corporate governance report under Regulation 27(2) (effective October 26, 2024), which has been merged into Integrated Filing–Governance pursuant to the SEBI circular dated December 31, 2024; and investor grievance report under Regulation 13(3) (effective October 01, 2024).  

The circular makes an important limitation clear: **for Regulation 29, Regulation 30 of SEBI LODR, and trading window disclosures, listed entities must continue filing PDF submissions at both exchanges and these are not yet covered by single filing except for the XBRL events specifically listed in the table**. Likewise, for all other Regulation 29 and Regulation 30 events not included in the table, entities must continue to make submissions separately on all exchanges, in PDF and XBRL where applicable. NSE also instructs listed entities to avoid duplicate filings of the same disclosure on both exchanges, because the objective is to move toward a true single-filing process. If an exchange later asks for clarification after submission, the listed entity must respond only to the exchange that requested it.  

In practical compliance terms, affected listed entities should update their disclosure workflows from March 07, 2026 to route the newly covered XBRL filings through the single-filing/API process for the exact events identified above, while continuing legacy dual filing where the circular expressly says single filing does not yet apply. Questions are to be directed through NEAPS at **NEAPS > Help > Contact Us > Listing Compliance** or by email to **takeover@nse.co.in**.

The key change is that, **effective February 21, 2026**, the single-filing/API route will now be available for the specified Regulation 30 events listed in the circular.

rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India is seeking comments and feedback on a proposed move from the current application-based, manual QIP filing process to an XBRL-based filing framework for Qualified Institutional Placement applications. Today, listed entities seeking QIP approval must submit applications to the Exchange for in-principle approval, post-allotment approval, and trading approval, with companies manually entering data and uploading supporting documents in PDF form; the proposed change would replace that document-based process with standardized XBRL submissions.

The proposal specifically targets QIP-related filings for “In-Principle approval” and “Post-Allotment Listing Approval,” and states that these filings would need to be submitted in XBRL exclusively rather than through the existing application system. The Exchange says the purpose is to standardize securities-market data, improve regulatory efficiency, and make the filing process easier for listed entities while also improving data analysis and monitoring by the Exchange.

The circular ties the proposal to existing legal requirements under the SEBI LODR Regulations, 2015 and the SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018, along with other applicable provisions, circulars, and guidance notes as amended from time to time. The document does not set an implementation date, transition deadline, or compliance deadline in the excerpt provided; it is only a consultation document requesting comments/feedback on the planned XBRL framework and noting that the XBRL formats are being made available. Compliance teams should therefore treat this as an advance notice of a likely mandatory filing-format change for listed entities undertaking QIPs, with the key operational shift being exclusive XBRL submission for the specified approval stages.

rows.summary:
This circular updates the National Stock Exchange’s single filing system through API-based integration between stock exchanges and extends that system to **Integrated Filing (Financials)** under **Regulation 33 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**, effective **January 3, 2026**. For compliance teams, the practical change is that the single filing/API-based transmission will now cover financial disclosure filings for applicable listed entities, instead of requiring separate exchange submissions in the traditional manner.

The circular specifies that the API-based single filing facility is available for the following categories of disclosures and dates: **Integrated Filing (Financials)** under **Reg. 23(9), Reg. 30 read with Section V-B of the SEBI Master Circular, Reg. 32(1), and Reg. 33(3)** from **January 3, 2026**; **Annual Secretarial Compliance Report** under **Reg. 24A(2)** from **September 15, 2025**; **Integrated Filing (Governance)** under **Regs. 13(3), 27(2), and 30** from **March 1, 2025**; **Meetings of shareholders and voting results** under **Reg. 44(3)** from **December 28, 2024**; and **Reconciliation of Share Capital Audit Report** under **Reg. 76** from **November 15, 2024**. The circular also notes that **Corporate Governance Report** filings under **Reg. 27(2)** were **merged into Integrated Filing (Governance)** pursuant to the **SEBI circular dated December 31, 2024**, meaning that separate corporate governance report filing is no longer the operative standalone treatment under this system.

The applicability matrix shows that these API-based single filing provisions apply to **equity-listed companies** and **equity + debt listed companies** where marked with a check, while for **exclusively debt-listed entities** and **REITs/InvITs**, the circular states **“shall be communicated later”** for several items, indicating those categories are not yet brought into the single filing framework for those disclosures. The document therefore does not impose a new filing obligation on those excluded categories yet, but it does confirm that listed entities in the equity and equity+debt buckets should use the integrated API-based route for the covered disclosures as of the respective effective dates above.

The circular is a follow-up to **NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024**, so compliance teams should treat it as an implementation update rather than a new substantive disclosure law. The key compliance action is to align internal reporting calendars, approval workflows, and data preparation processes so that the relevant filings are ready for submission through the integrated single-filing/API mechanism on the applicable dates, particularly the new **financials integration starting January 3, 2026**.

This SEBI circular dated October 13, 2025 (circulated by NSE on October 14, 2025) informs all listed entities that the earlier SEBI Master Circular dated November 11, 2024 and SEBI Circular dated June 26, 2025 already required companies to follow the Industry Standards Forum’s “Minimum information to be provided to the Audit Committee and Shareholders for approval of Related Party Transactions” when seeking approvals for related party transactions. The new circular updates those standards through a revised set of minimum information requirements that listed entities must now use for Audit Committee and shareholder approval processes; it is intended to standardize the disclosures that must be placed before these approving bodies for RPTs.

For compliance purposes, the key obligation is not a new approval threshold or monetary limit, but a mandatory disclosure-format requirement: listed entities must ensure that the minimum information prescribed by the ISF standards is furnished in RPT approval papers submitted to the Audit Committee and, where required, to shareholders. The circular is addressed to all listed entities and all recognized stock exchanges, and was also issued to ASSOCHAM, FICCI, and CII, indicating it is a market-wide governance requirement rather than an issuer-specific exemption or industry carve-out. The document also indicates that SEBI’s updated circular ref. no. SEBI/HO/CFD/CFD-PoD-2/P/CIR/2025/135 is the operative reference to consult for the exact revised disclosure contents.

rows.title: Filing of Financial Results by REITs & InvITs in XBRL Mode
rows.desc: National Stock Exchange of India Circular Department: Listing Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2025/38 Date: October 09, 2025 To, All Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) All Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) Subject: Filing of Financial Results by REITs & InvITs in XBRL Mode This is in reference to the SEBI Master circular SEBI/HO/DDHS-PoD-2/P/CIR/2025/99 dated July 11, 2025, for REITs & SEBI Master circular SEBI/HO/DDHS-PoD-2/P/CIR/2025/102 dated July 11, 2025, for InvITs, regarding Chapter 4 - Continuous Disclosures and Compliances by REITs & InvITs wherein the format for submission of financial results by REITs & InvITs has been revised as per the aforesaid Master circulars. In this regard, we wish to inform you that the excel utility for submission of Financial Results-REITs & InvITs as per the revised format has been made available on NEAPS portal on the below path: Compliance > Common XBRL Upload > Invit/Reit- Financial Results The REITs & InvITs are required to submit the financial results in XBRL mode within 24 hours of submission of the financial results in PDF mode using the excel utility “Financial Results_Invits_Reits” In case of any queries concerning the captioned subject, you may contact the respective team members on the contact details available in the NEAPS platform at path NEAPS > Help > Contact Us > Listing Compliance or send an email to listingfr@nse.co.in Yours faithfully, For National Stock Exchange of India Limited Mandar Walavalkar Vice President-Listing
rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India has issued a circular to all listed REITs and InvITs requiring them to file financial results in XBRL mode using the revised format prescribed under SEBI’s updated master circulars for REITs and InvITs (SEBI/HO/DDHS-PoD-2/P/CIR/2025/99 and /102, both dated July 11, 2025). The circular states that the format for submission of financial results has been revised under Chapter 4 on continuous disclosures and compliances, and that the corresponding Excel utility is now available on the NEAPS portal at Compliance > Common XBRL Upload > Invit/Reit- Financial Results.

For compliance purposes, the key obligation is procedural and time-bound: REITs and InvITs must submit their financial results in PDF mode first, and then file the same financial results in XBRL mode within 24 hours of the PDF submission. The prescribed utility for the filing is the Excel file named “Financial Results_Invits_Reits,” which must be used for the XBRL upload. The circular does not introduce a new quantitative financial threshold or rate, but it does impose a specific filing workflow and a strict 24-hour deadline tied to the PDF submission date/time.

If there are filing questions, the circular directs users to the contact details available in NEAPS under Help > Contact Us > Listing Compliance, or to email listingfr@nse.co.in. The circular is dated October 09, 2025 and is addressed specifically to all REITs and all InvITs listed or filing through NSE.

rows.summary:
The NSE has updated its single filing system through API-based integration between stock exchanges and extended it to cover the **Annual Secretarial Compliance Report required under Regulation 24A(2) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**, with **effect from September 15, 2025**. This means listed entities that fall within the applicable categories can now submit this report through the single-filing/API mechanism rather than separately filing it across exchanges, subject to the rollout status noted by NSE for certain other security types. The circular is addressed to **all listed entities** and is an update to the earlier NSE circular **NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024**.

The circular also restates the broader list of disclosures already brought into the single-filing system and their rollout dates: **Investor Grievance Report under Regulation 13(3)** effective **October 1, 2024** (later **merged with Integrated Filing (Governance)** pursuant to the SEBI circular dated **December 31, 2024**); **Corporate Governance Report under Regulation 27(2)** effective **October 26, 2024**; **Reconciliation of Share Capital Audit Report under Regulation 76** effective **November 15, 2024**; **Meetings of shareholders and Voting Results under Regulation 44(3)** effective **December 28, 2024**; and **Integrated Filing (Governance) under Regulations 13(3), 27(2) and 30** effective **March 1, 2025**. For these disclosures, the circular indicates the system is already available for **equity-only listed companies** and **equity + debt listed companies** where marked with a check, while availability for **exclusively debt listed entities** and for **REITs/InvITs** is in some cases still noted as **“shall be communicated later.”**

For the newly added **Annual Secretarial Compliance Report**, the applicability is shown as available for **equity-only** and **equity + debt** listed companies from **September 15, 2025**, while availability for **exclusively debt** entities and **REITs/InvITs** is again marked as **to be communicated later**. The document is essentially a procedural compliance update: it does not change the underlying reporting obligation itself, but it changes the **filing method/timing framework** by extending the API-based single-filing integration to another mandatory disclosure. Compliance teams should therefore ensure that, from the effective date, their filing workflows are aligned to the single-filing system for the Annual Secretarial Compliance Report and monitor NSE communications for any later rollouts affecting debt-listed entities, REITs, and InvITs.

rows.summary:
This NSE circular dated September 4, 2025 forwards FAQs on the SEBI-mandated Industry Standards for the minimum information to be placed before the Audit Committee and shareholders for approval of related party transactions (“RPTs”). The circular makes clear that these Industry Standards **replace** the earlier RPT disclosure formats in **Section III-B of the NSE Master Circular dated November 11, 2024**, from the **specified effective date**, but if any part of the Industry Standards conflicts with later amendments to the LODR Regulations or subsequent SEBI circulars, the **LODR Regulations/SEBI circulars prevail**.

For compliance purposes, the Industry Standards are described as setting only the **minimum** information to be disclosed; listed entities may provide **additional information** to the Audit Committee and/or shareholders if management believes it is in the interest of public shareholders, and the Audit Committee may itself seek further information where it considers that necessary and reasonable to assess the proposed RPT. The FAQs confirm the **effective date is 1 September 2025** under SEBI Circular No. **SEBI/HO/CFD/CFD-PoD-2/P/CIR/2025/93 dated June 26, 2025**.

The applicability is broad: the Standards apply not only to direct RPTs of the listed entity, but also to RPTs involving **foreign subsidiaries of Indian listed companies** and to transactions undertaken by **subsidiaries where the listed entity itself is not a party**, so long as those transactions require Audit Committee and/or shareholder approval of the listed holding company under the LODR Regulations. The FAQs also state that where the listed entity has RPTs with **fellow subsidiaries**, the holding company may provide a **duly certified summary of financial information** for the relevant subsidiaries to support Audit Committee/shareholder review, but this is subject to a caveat that the information is based on data collected for preparation of the listed entity’s **consolidated financial statements**.

The FAQs further clarify that the Standards are not limited to the specific transaction types covered in Part B and Part C; **Part A of Para 4 applies to all related party transactions unless exempt under Para 1(3)**. The document begins to address a threshold aggregation example involving three RPTs of **₹30 lakh each** and a fourth proposed transaction of **₹11 lakh**, indicating that numerical aggregation/threshold treatment is a compliance issue under the Standards, but the provided text cuts off before the answer is completed.
