rows.summary:
The IRDAI (Indian Insurance Companies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021 were issued by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India on 7 July 2021 and took effect immediately on publication in the Official Gazette. Their stated purpose is to harmonize IRDAI insurance-company regulations with the Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2021 and the Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2015, by amending several existing regulations that apply to Indian insurance companies.

The most significant change is the insertion of a new regulation 5A in the Registration of Indian Insurance Companies Regulations, 2000 for Indian insurance companies with foreign investment. It requires that a majority of the board directors be Resident Indian Citizens, a majority of Key Management Persons also be Resident Indian Citizens, and at least one of the chairperson, managing director, or chief executive officer must be a Resident Indian Citizen. “Resident Indian Citizen” is defined by reference to rule 2(1)(o) of the Foreign Investment Rules, 2015.

A new regulation 5B is also inserted for Indian insurance companies with foreign investment exceeding 49%. If such a company pays dividend on equity shares in a financial year and, at any time in that year, its solvency margin is below 1.2 times the control level of solvency, then at least 50% of that year’s net profit must be retained in general reserve. In addition, unless the chairperson of the board is an independent director, at least 50% of the directors must be independent directors; if the chairperson is independent, then at least one-third of the board must be independent directors.

The amendment also changes the application/registration filing requirements in regulation 10. The foreign investment threshold in regulation 10(2)(e) is increased from 49% to 74%, clauses (f) and (g) of regulation 10(2) are omitted, and new affidavit requirements are introduced: where the applicant has foreign investment, the managing director, chief executive officer, or whole-time director together with the promoters must file an affidavit certifying compliance with regulation 5A; where the applicant has foreign investment exceeding 49%, a separate affidavit is required confirming compliance with the more stringent requirements applicable to that level of foreign ownership. The document also makes corresponding textual amendments to Regulations 29, 30, and 31, and to other linked provisions, to align those regulations with the new foreign-investment framework and Resident Indian Citizen requirements.

rows.summary:
The Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Amendment Rules, 2021, issued by the Ministry of Finance on 19 May 2021, take effect immediately on publication in the Official Gazette. They amend the Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2015 and were made under section 114(2)(aaa) of the Insurance Act, 1938, read with section 2(7A)(b); the government had earlier published draft rules on 15 April 2021 and considered public comments before finalizing them.

The most significant change is that the foreign investment ceiling in an Indian insurance company is raised from 49% to 74%. The definition provisions are also revised: several definitions in rule 2 are deleted, the definition of “Resident Indian Citizen” is replaced so that it now means what is provided in the Central Government’s current FDI policy, and “Total Foreign Investment” is redefined to mean the sum of direct and indirect foreign investment by foreign investors, calculated in the manner specified by the Authority’s registration regulations. A new interpretive clause is added so that undefined terms take their meanings from the Insurance Act or rules/regulations made under it.

Governance requirements are tightened for insurers with foreign investment. In any Indian insurance company with foreign investment, a majority of directors must be Resident Indian Citizens, a majority of Key Management Persons must be Resident Indian Citizens, and at least one of the chairperson of the board, the managing director, or the chief executive officer must be a Resident Indian Citizen. The rule expressly applies the existing corporate-governance meaning of “Key Management Person.” Companies that already had foreign investment on or before the commencement date must comply with these governance requirements within one year of commencement.

The amendment also adds a new dividend restriction for companies with foreign investment exceeding 49%. For any financial year in which equity-share dividends are paid and at any time during that year the solvency margin is below 1.2 times the control level of solvency, at least 50% of net profit for that financial year must be retained; the text provided cuts off after “not less than fifty per cent. of the net profit for the finan…,” so any remaining sub-clauses are not visible in the excerpt. Compliance teams should therefore treat the visible portion as clearly imposing a profit-retention condition tied to dividend distribution and solvency status, effective from the amendment’s commencement date.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI notification, titled **“Obligatory Cession for the financial year 2021–22,”** was issued on **28 December 2020** under **Section 101A(2) and (4) of the Insurance Act, 1938**, with prior Central Government approval and consultation with the Advisory Committee. It applies to **Indian reinsurers and other insurers to whom Section 101A applies**. For all **general insurance policies attaching during 1 April 2021 through 31 March 2022**, insurers must cede **5% of the sum insured** to the Indian reinsurer(s), but **the cession is NIL for terrorism premium and for premium ceded to the Nuclear Pool**. The notification also specifies that **the entire obligatory cession must be placed only with General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re)**, not with any other reinsurer.

The document then sets out operational conditions for the cession. It states that there is **no sum-insured cap** for cessions made during the financial year, and it prescribes a **three-tier distribution of the obligatory cession between different classes of general insurance business**: the effective cession percentages differ by business segment, with some categories subject to **5%, 10%, 7.5%, 15%**, and in one case **50%**, and a corresponding allocation split of **50:50** in one instance and **78% / 14%** in another, indicating that the cession is not uniform across all general insurance lines. Compliance teams should treat this as a mandatory placement requirement for the relevant financial year, requiring insurers to route the stated obligatory cession amounts to GIC Re and to exclude terrorism and nuclear-pool-related premium from the ceded amount. The notification is effective for **business attaching in FY 2021–22**, and the required treatment must be applied from the start of that financial year onward.

IRDAI has upgraded its Business Analytics Platform (BAP) and moved several reinsurance-related regulatory filings and approvals into the new integrated portal. The migration covers Reinsurance Regulatory Returns, Reinsurance Summary Formats (Advance and Final), applications for File Reference Numbers (FRNs) for Cross Border Reinsurers (CBRs), and applications for appointment and remuneration of the Chairperson/CEO of reinsurers and foreign reinsurer branches (FRBs). The circular applies to all insurers, reinsurers, foreign reinsurer branches (FRBs), and, where relevant, Lloyd’s India and its constituents. The submission timelines are specified by filing type: Reinsurance Regulatory Returns must be filed on the integrated BAP portal starting from FY 2024–25; Corporate Governance Returns from FY 2025–26; Pool Administrator Returns from FY 2024–25; and Reinsurance Programme Summary Returns (Advance and Final) from FY 2024–25. The document also indicates that the FRN application process for CBRs is now part of BAP, so any CBR seeking an FRN must use the updated platform process.

The circular is dated 28 August 2026 and is issued by IRDAI under reference number IRDAI/REINS/CIR/MISC/114/08/2026. Compliance teams should ensure that internal filing procedures, responsible users, and approval workflows are updated immediately to route the affected reinsurance submissions and related applications through BAP, and that filings for the specified financial years are prepared in the new system format and submitted theregoing forward.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular dated **27 August 2026** to **all insurers** permitting investment in **“Onshore Rupee Bonds” / Maharajah INR Bonds** to be issued by the **New Development Bank (NDB)**, and to treat those bonds as **“approved investments”** for insurers, subject to specific conditions. NDB has represented that it intends to raise **INR 25,000 crores over five years**, and the bond proceeds are intended for **general corporate purposes** tied to **financing/onward lending for sustainable development, sustainable infrastructure, and green/social projects in India**.

The circular states that these onshore rupee bond issuances are **“securities” under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956**. IRDAI’s permission is not blanket approval; insurers may invest only if the bonds comply with applicable **Government of India norms**, the **public issue is approved by SEBI**, and the insurer complies with **Section 27E of the Insurance Act, 1938** when making the investment. In addition, the bonds must satisfy the **rating criteria for “Approved Investments” under Schedule III of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment functions of insurers) Regulations, 2024, as amended from time to time**.

The circular also contemplates a situation where **SEBI exempts the rating requirement** because the bond has already obtained a rating from an **international rating agency**; in that case, insurers can rely on that SEBI exemption framework, but they still remain subject to the other statutory and regulatory conditions in the circular. The practical compliance action for insurers is to confirm, before investing, that each NDB Maharajah INR Bond issuance is **properly approved, qualifies as an approved investment, and meets the required legal/rating conditions** under the applicable IRDAI, SEBI, and insurance law framework.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI circular, dated **31 July 2026** and addressed to **all CEOs/CMDs of all insurance companies, including life insurers and stand-alone health insurers**, responds to the **natural disaster/floods that began on 19 July 2026** in Assam and affected the districts of **Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, and Golaghat**. It instructs insurers to take immediate action to reduce hardship for insured persons and to **speed up claim registration and settlement** in the affected areas.

The circular requires insurers to **mobilize all available resources**, including **surveyors and investigators**, and to **appoint senior Nodal Officers** to supervise claims operations in the affected districts. The appointment of the Nodal Officer must be **communicated immediately to the Chief Secretary**, and insurers may also designate a **District Claims Service Head** for each district to oversee local claims handling.

Insurers must also activate and publicize **24x7 customer support helplines** to assist claimants and launch an **extensive awareness campaign** explaining the measures taken. The **contact details of the district heads** must be published on the insurer’s **website**, and the same information may also be given publicity through the **press and digital media**.

For claims processing, insurers are directed to use **special, empowered district desks** to ensure **prompt survey, claim registration, and settlement**. The document’s substance is operational rather than punitive: it does not create a monetary penalty or specific filing deadline, but it does impose an immediate service-response obligation on all affected insurers to ensure faster claims support in the four named districts following the flood disaster.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI has issued a circular dated **July 23, 2026** addressed to **all insurers except reinsurers** requiring them to improve the timeliness and completeness of submissions made to the **Office of the Insurance Ombudsmen (IOs)**. The trigger for the circular is a reported pattern, discussed with IOs during a recent orientation programme, of **inordinate delays** by insurers in submitting **Self-Contained Notes (SCNs)**, supporting documents, and later requests for additional information/documents, often in **piecemeal form**. IRDAI says these delays are causing avoidable delays in the disposal of complaints filed by policyholders/beneficiaries.

The circular emphasizes that when IOs seek documents or information under **Rule 15(2) of the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017**, insurers must provide them **promptly** so the IO can examine the complaint and decide the matter. IRDAI links this to **Rule 17(4)**, which requires that a complaint be decided **within 90 days of receipt of all requirements from the complainant**; delayed or fragmented insurer submissions interfere with that timeline and the spirit of the rule. The practical compliance expectation is therefore not just to respond, but to provide the complete set of required materials without unnecessary delay.

Although the extracted text is truncated before the full list of instructions, the circular clearly begins directing insurers to **submit the required SCNs duly supported by relevant documents**, indicating that the compliance burden includes preparing a complete, properly documented SCN package and responding fully to any further IO requests. Based on the text shown, there are no monetary thresholds, rates, or penalties stated in the excerpt, but the affected entities are all insurers other than reinsurers, and the compliance risk is operational/regulatory: failures may contribute to delayed complaint resolution and could draw regulatory concern regarding adherence to the Ombudsman process.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI has issued a further circular on 14 July 2026, referenced as **IRDAI/IFRS/CIR/MISC/94/7/2026**, addressed to **all insurers**, providing **additional clarifications on implementation of Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)**. This circular follows IRDAI Circular No. **IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/45/4/2026 dated 1 April 2026** and is intended to ensure consistent application of the regulatory framework based on insurer representations.

A key clarification concerns the **role of the Appointed Actuary** in preparing financial statements under Ind AS. Under **Clauses 6 and 7 of Part II of Schedule I of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, the Appointed Actuary must provide actuarial expertise and support for Ind AS financial statement preparation, but the circular makes clear that the **responsibility for the financial statements remains with the insurer’s Board/management**, not the Appointed Actuary. The Appointed Actuary’s role is therefore advisory/technical in nature, focused on actuarial inputs needed for Ind AS compliance rather than ownership of the statements themselves.

The circular also addresses **Independent Validation** for Ind AS-compliant financial statements used for consolidation. For the **financial year 2026–27 and onwards**, insurers are required to have the relevant Ind AS financial statements independently validated by an appropriate professional, and the circular states that this validation process must be in place **from 1 April 2026 onward** for the specified statements used in consolidation. The circular clarifies the scope of the statements subject to this validation requirement, indicating that where an insurer’s Ind AS-compliant numbers feed into a group/consolidated reporting process, those numbers must be subject to this independent review.

Another important clarification concerns the **preparation and use of Ind AS-compliant financial statements for consolidation purposes**. Insurers must ensure that the statements used in consolidation are prepared in a manner consistent with Ind AS and with the insurer’s regulatory reporting obligations. The circular identifies the statements/inputs to which this applies and clarifies that the insurer must maintain controls and procedures so that the data used for consolidation is reliable, properly reviewed, and aligned with the applicable accounting and actuarial requirements.

The circular also refers to the interaction with the **IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, including provisions under **Clause 5 / Clause 6 / Clause 7** and related schedules, and explains how those provisions should be applied when insurers are transitioning to or operating under Ind AS. It reiterates that insurers must maintain the required actuarial and financial governance processes, including documented roles, review mechanisms, and internal accountability, so that Ind AS reporting is prepared in a controlled and compliant manner.

Finally, the circular indicates an implementation timeline under which insurers must align their processes for the relevant financial-year reporting cycles, with the new clarifications operative for **FY 2026–27 onward** and the relevant independent validation requirement tied to **1 April 2026**. Compliance teams should therefore ensure that: the Appointed Actuary’s role is limited to providing actuarial expertise; management retains responsibility for the final financial statements; independent validation arrangements are in place for consolidation-related Ind AS statements; and the insurer’s internal controls, approvals, and reporting workflows are updated to reflect these clarifications.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular dated **8 July 2026** to **all insurers and reinsurers** updating the **formats for publishing financial results under the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**. The change is driven by the **adoption of Ind AS by insurers** and replaces the existing stock-exchange reporting formats for insurers that now prepare financial statements under Ind AS; the updated formats apply to **listed Life Insurers, General Insurers, Health Insurers, and Reinsurers**.

The circular states that the earlier SEBI master circular on financial-results formats, issued on **11 July 2023** and updated on **30 January 2026**, required listed insurers to use IRDAI-prescribed formats. Because Ind AS implementation changes the underlying presentation, IRDAI has now updated the formats for **unaudited/audited quarterly financial results** to be filed with stock exchanges. The new reporting format for **quarterly financial results** is prescribed in **Annexure I**.

In addition to the main quarterly results format, insurers must also provide **segment-wise Revenue, Results, and Capital Employed** with the quarterly results, in the format prescribed in **Annexure II**. The circular also notes that the applicable reporting format for **financial year 2026-27** includes additional structure in **Annexure IV** for disclosures required under **Regulation 47(1)(b) of the LODR Regulations, 2015**. For balance-sheet/related disclosures under the 2026-27 reporting cycle, the circular references updated formats in **Annexure III** as well.

An important carve-out is that insurers who have been **granted forbearance for financial year 2026-27 for Ind AS implementation** are excepted from the revised Ind AS-based format changes; the updated formats apply to the remaining listed insurers/reinsurers required to report under Ind AS. The circular also references earlier IRDAI communications from **25 August 2016** and **30 January 2017**, indicating that these earlier directions are being superseded or supplemented by the new formats.

The practical compliance obligation is that affected listed insurers and reinsurers must now align their **stock-exchange financial results filings** to the updated IRDAI annexures, rather than continuing with the prior submission templates, for the relevant reporting periods beginning with the applicable **2026-27** cycle.

Those circulars were issued because the amended regulations under the Insurance Act, 1938, as amended by the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025, had not yet been notified; the earlier transitional period had been set to run only until 30 June 2026.

IRDAI now states that these transitional arrangements will continue beyond 30 June 2026 until the relevant amended regulations governing annual fee payment and related matters are formally notified. Specifically, paragraph 4.3 of the 16 March 2026 circular is extended from 30 June 2026 to 31 August 2026, or to the date of notification of the amended regulations, whichever is earlier. The same extension applies to paragraph 4.1 of the 7 April 2026 circular. In practical terms, intermediaries and, where applicable, surveyors and loss assessors remain covered by the temporary fee-payment and certificate-issuance process during this extended period, and compliance teams should continue following the transitional procedure until the new regulations are notified or the new end date arrives.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated **25.05.2026** and referenced **IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/72/5/2026**, updates how insurers may determine and pay **remuneration to Key Management Persons (KMPs)** under the **IRDAI (Corporate Governance for Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, which were issued on **21.03.2024** and later amended on **22.05.2024**. The circular specifically revises the wording of **Regulation 8.3** and related definitions in **Regulation 9.2** so that KMP remuneration can be computed and governed on the basis of the policyholder premium measure used in the regulation, and it introduces more explicit treatment for commission-linked or sales-linked compensation components, including the requirement that certain calculations be made with reference to prescribed premium figures and the defined salary/remuneration components in the CG regulations.

A key practical change is that, for **FY 2026-27**, the circular prescribes the way the remuneration benchmark under **Regulation 8.3** is to be read and applied. The document lays out a graduated framework tied to premium slabs and references percentages such as **90%**, **15%**, **30%**, **60%**, **7%**, and **50%**, indicating that KMP remuneration limits and/or benchmarking are now to be applied using these specific slab-based mechanics rather than a single flat approach. The circular also makes clear that certain remuneration components are to be measured only on the basis of the defined remuneration items under the CG Regulations and excludes or separately treats specified forms of incentive/variable compensation where the circular and amended regulation distinguish between fixed and variable pay.

The document further introduces a compliance formula and reporting structure for insurers to calculate the relevant remuneration amounts using a specified ratio-based approach, and it embeds the need to use the regulatory premium base and the defined premium categories when determining whether compensation falls within the allowed limits. It also references **thresholds of 15, 30, and 60** in the context of the remuneration computation and indicates that insurers must align internal compensation structures for KMPs with the revised rules before paying or approving such remuneration. Where a KMP’s pay includes components linked to performance, the circular appears to require those components to be tested against the revised ceilings/benchmarks and to be supported by the insurer’s documented calculation.

From a compliance perspective, the circular affects **all insurers regulated by IRDAI** that pay remuneration to KMPs, particularly where compensation is structured as fixed pay, variable pay, or performance-linked incentives. Insurers should review board-approved compensation policies, KMP appointment terms, and payroll practices to ensure the remuneration basis now matches the amended **Regulation 8.3** and the updated definitions in **Regulation 9.2**. The effective operational period highlighted by the circular is **FY 2026-27**, so firms should treat the new calculation method and associated remuneration limits as mandatory for that financial year and ensure the revised approach is implemented before compensation decisions for that period are finalized.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular dated 7 April 2026 clarifies how the transitional arrangements for annual-fee payment and issuance of the Certificate of Registration under the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025 apply specifically to **Surveyors and Loss Assessors (SLAs)**. It applies to **all insurance surveyors and loss assessors** and is issued as a continuation of IRDAI Circular Ref. **IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/41/3/2026 dated 16 March 2026** on transitional arrangements for intermediaries.

The core substantive change is that, after the SBSR Act amended **Section 42D of the Insurance Act, 1938**, an intermediary’s registration remains in force only subject to payment of the annual fee prescribed by regulations, unless the registration is suspended or cancelled by IRDAI. For SLAs, IRDAI is providing a special transition because they have a distinct operational and fee framework, and the circular is meant to ensure a smooth move to the revised registration/fee regime.

The circular states that where an SLA’s registration falls due for renewal between **5 April 2026 and 30 June 2026**, the SLA must pay the applicable annual fee for the **remaining period of the certificate**, and the fee is expressly stated as **exclusive of 18% GST**. The document provides example amounts showing the net fee, GST, and total payable: a fee of **₹400 + ₹72 GST = ₹472** and a fee of **₹2,000 + ₹360 GST = ₹2,360**. It also clarifies that if an SLA has already paid the annual fee on or after **4 April 2026** under the previous framework, the payment will be treated in accordance with the transitional arrangements under the **Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors (Payment of Annual Fee) Regulations, 2015**.

A final implementation date is given: the clarifications are stated to **come into effect on 5 April 2026**. Compliance teams overseeing SLA registrations should therefore verify renewal dates in the 5 April–30 June 2026 window, confirm whether annual fee payments have been made under the prior framework since 4 April 2026, and ensure GST is applied correctly at 18% when calculating the amount due for the remaining term of the registration.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular dated **1 April 2026** titled **“Clarifications on implementation of Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)”** to **all insurers**. The circular is issued under **Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938**, **Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999**, and **Regulations 7 and 8 of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**. It follows recent amendments to those 2024 regulations and is intended to clarify how insurers should implement Ind AS in light of the amended framework.

The document’s key substantive point is that insurers must apply the clarified Ind AS implementation approach beginning **1 April 2026** (the circular refers to the amended regulations and related implementation provisions effective from that date). The circular indicates that implementation issues are being addressed through specific clarifications connected to the amended 2024 regulations and related schedules/annexures, which appear to affect insurers’ **financial reporting, actuarial, finance, and investment functions**. In particular, it references provisions tied to the **Insurance Act, 1938** and the **Companies Act, 2013**, showing that the clarifications are meant to align insurance-sector accounting treatment with both the sectoral regulatory regime and the applicable accounting standard requirements.

A notable compliance deadline in the circular is **30 April 2026**, which is specifically mentioned in connection with the transition/implementation process. The document also references the **financial year 2026–27** as the period from which the clarified arrangements are to operate for insurers covered by the circular. Compliance teams should therefore treat this as a near-term reporting and implementation change requiring readiness before the new financial year begins.

The circular also points to specific regulatory provisions being impacted or interpreted, including **Section 11 of the Insurance Act, 1938**, **Section 13 of the Insurance Act, 1938**, **Section 49 of the Insurance Act, 1938**, and **Section 64 / 64VB**-related references, along with the amended regulations and associated annexures. While the excerpted content does not reproduce all the detailed prescriptions, it makes clear that insurers will need to revise internal accounting/financial-reporting processes to comply with IRDAI’s clarified Ind AS implementation instructions and any linked filing, valuation, or reporting treatment under the applicable insurance-law provisions.

Finally, the circular directs insurers to seek any further clarification by email at **indas-team@irdai.gov.in**. For a compliance officer, the practical takeaway is that this is a mandatory sector-specific accounting implementation circular affecting all insurers, with immediate preparation needed for the **30 April 2026** deadline and full operational compliance from **FY 2026–27** onward.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a transitional circular for insurance intermediaries under the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025 (“SBSR Act”), which took effect on 5 February 2026. The circular applies to all categories of registered insurance intermediaries, including insurance brokers, corporate agents, insurance marketing firms, web aggregators, common service centres, insurance surveyors and loss assessors, insurance repositories, third party administrators, and any other entity registered as an insurance intermediary under applicable regulations.

The key change is that, because Section 42D of the Insurance Act, 1938 has been amended by the SBSR Act and new sub-section 42D(4A) now governs the payment of annual fee, IRDAI has prescribed a temporary framework for how annual fee and registration certificate issuance will operate during the transition. For the period from 5 February 2026 through 30 June 2026, intermediaries must follow the transitional arrangements set out in the circular for payment of annual fee and issuance of the Certificate of Registration; the circular indicates that these provisions are meant to bridge the period immediately after the amendment came into force. The document also states that any fee or registration-related requirement should be understood in the context of the amended Section 42D framework, rather than the pre-amendment regime.

For compliance purposes, the important operational point is that the transition window is fixed and short: the circular is expressly effective from 5 February 2026, with the transitional arrangements applicable up to 30 June 2026. Intermediaries should therefore review whether any annual fee payments, certificate renewals, or registration issuance steps fall within that period and ensure they are handled under the new transitional process. The circular is aimed at all affected intermediaries, so firms should treat this as a broad compliance update rather than an entity-specific exemption, and align internal procedures, renewals, and payment workflows accordingly.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued Circular No. IRDAI/PP&GR/CIR/MISC/02/01/2026 dated 6 January 2026 to all insurers and insurance intermediaries, directing immediate preparation for compliance with TRAI’s mandatory 1600-series adoption requirement for customer-facing voice communications. The circular explains that TRAI’s Direction dated 16 December 2025, issued under section 13 read with section 11(1)(b)(i) and (v) of the TRAI Act, 1997, requires all IRDAI-regulated entities to use the 1600-series for all service and transactional voice calls made to consumers, with the stated objectives of reducing unsolicited commercial communication (UCC), preventing impersonation-based fraud, and improving consumer trust.

The key compliance deadline is 15 February 2026, by which insurers and insurance intermediaries must complete adoption of the 1600-series for all service and transactional voice calls. After that date, no service or transactional voice calls may be initiated from any number other than numbers allocated under the 1600-series, even where the customer has given explicit or implied consent. This means consent does not provide an exception to the numbering requirement once the deadline passes.

The circular also warns that any UCC complaint against an entity that does not comply may trigger action under the TRAI regulatory framework applicable to unregistered telemarketers, in addition to whatever further action the Authority may deem appropriate. In other words, non-compliance may create both TRAI-related exposure and separate supervisory consequences from IRDAI.

Operationally, insurers and intermediaries are instructed to coordinate with their Telecom Service Providers for timely allocation, activation, and operationalization of 1600-series numbers. They must also submit the status reports required by TRAI on a timely basis and send a copy of those reports to IRDAI. The circular references an Annexure containing contact details of the nodal officers of the access providers to support implementation, and the overall instruction is to ensure strict compliance.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated **19 December 2025** and addressed to **all insurers and reinsurers**, expands the set of permissible fixed-income investments for insurers by allowing investment in securities issued by **RBI-regulated All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**. Specifically, insurers are now permitted to invest in **(i) AT1 bonds** and **(ii) debt capital instruments and preference share capital instruments forming Tier 2 capital**, with the explicit exception of **Perpetual Cumulative Preference Shares**. The circular states that this change is intended to broaden insurers’ investment options and support portfolio diversification.

The permission applies to instruments issued by AIFIs that are regulated by the RBI, which began issuing **Additional Tier 1 Bonds and Tier 2 capital instruments from 1 April 2024** under the Basel III prudential framework. IRDAI is not creating a new investment regime from scratch; instead, it requires insurers to follow the **same investment provisions that already apply to insurer investments in banks**, specifically the rules in **paragraphs 1.6(b) and 1.6(d) of Chapter 3 of the Master Circular on Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers dated 17 May 2024**. In other words, the existing bank-investment compliance framework is to be used as the operational benchmark for these AIFI investments.

For compliance and reporting purposes, insurers must also use the **existing category codes used for investments in the corresponding instruments of PSU banks** when booking these AIFI holdings. The circular is issued under **clause 12(6) of Schedule III of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, so compliance teams should treat it as a formal regulatory instruction rather than guidance. No separate implementation deadline is specified beyond the circular date, so the effective position is that insurers may apply this permission immediately, subject to the existing bank-investment limits and requirements referenced above.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has announced that it is ending the long-standing practice of permitting an individual Surveyor/Loss Assessor (SLA) to add an additional line of business (LOB) to a surveyor licence merely on the basis of the categorization letter issued in 2001–02. The circular explains that, under the earlier categorization exercise, individual SLAs who held valid licences before the 2000 Licensing/Professional Requirements/Code of Conduct Regulations were categorized across multiple departments/LOBs, and they were originally allowed only 3 LOBs on their licence from that categorized list. Then, by Circular Ref. IRDA/SUR/CIR/MISC/042/02/2020 dated 4 February 2020, IRDAI had allowed additions to an individual SLA’s licence based on that old categorization letter if the person had the relevant educational qualification and had continuously renewed the licence without break, and it also removed the earlier cap on the number of LOBs.

IRDAI says it is now receiving modification applications from SLAs seeking to add LOBs even though they have not done any survey work in that LOB since 2002, and it considers pre-2001/02 experience and knowledge in those areas to be obsolete because of technological change over the last 23 years. To ensure fair assessment of insured losses, IRDAI has decided to stop this practice entirely. As a result, Circular Ref. IRDA/SUR/CIR/MISC/042/02/2020 dated 4 February 2020 is repealed with immediate effect, meaning applications relying on the 2001–02 categorization letter as the basis for adding LOBs should no longer be entertained under that route.

Going forward, an individual surveyor may still be eligible for any LOB on the surveyor licence, but only if the person meets the eligibility criteria under Regulation 3 of the IRDAI (Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors) Regulations, 2015, as amended. In addition, to add an LOB, the individual SLA must now comply with the Proviso under Regulation 27 of the same 2015 Regulations, as amended from time to time. The notice is effective immediately and was issued with the approval of the Competent Authority.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular (No. **IRDAI/RBC/CIR/MISC/94/8/2025**, dated **14 August 2025**) requires insurers to participate in **Quantitative Impact Study-2 (QIS 2)** as part of the development of India’s **Risk Based Capital (RBC)** framework. The circular explains that IRDAI had already conducted **QIS 1 in 2023** to assess the initial impact of the RBC framework, and that feedback from insurers and the first study led IRDAI to determine that a second study was necessary to further refine the framework.

The requirement applies broadly to **all Life Insurers, General Insurers, Standalone Health Insurers, Reinsurers, Branches of Foreign Reinsurers, and Lloyd’s India**. For QIS 2, insurers must carry out the exercise **using the data used for actuarial valuation as at 31 March 2025**. IRDAI states that the **Technical Guidance document**, the **data submission template**, the **requirements for the associated results template**, the **mode of submission**, and **supplementary information** will be communicated separately, so compliance teams should expect additional operational instructions beyond this circular.

The circular also specifies the timing: the **QIS 2 exercise is to be carried out by 15 September 2025**. In substance, this means affected entities must prepare the required actuarial-valuation-based data set for the 31 March 2025 valuation date, complete the QIS 2 calculations and submissions in the format later prescribed by IRDAI, and ensure they are ready to meet the separate submission requirements once those are issued. The document positions QIS 2 as a **key/pivotal step** toward implementation of the RBC framework, so it is not optional or exploratory for the covered entities.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI Master Circular, issued on 25 July 2025 as Ref. IRDAI/NL/CIR/RSS/85/07/2025, consolidates and updates the compliance framework for insurers’ rural sector, social sector, and motor third-party obligations under the Insurance Act, 1938, the IRDAI Act, 1999, and the relevant 2024 regulations. It supersedes earlier circulars and implements the applicable 2024 regulatory requirements for FY 2024-25, while also setting out the obligations to be followed for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27. The circular is organized around new consolidated definitions and reporting structures for “rural sector,” “social sector,” and motor third-party compliance, with separate annexures/forms (Annexure 1 and Annexure 2) referenced for reporting and operational details.

For rural and social sector obligations, the circular restates the method for calculating compliance and specifies the minimum business/coverage requirements that insurers must meet over the coming years. For the rural sector, insurers must track compliance against the prescribed benchmarks for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 using the regulatory percentages and numerical thresholds stated in the circular, including the figures of 25,000 and 50,000 as the relevant volume thresholds and the required proportionate compliance levels of 15%, 25%, and 10% for the specified categories in those years. For the social sector, the circular likewise preserves the statutory reporting structure and sets out the applicable yearly targets, again with the 25,000/50,000 thresholds and the compliance percentages that apply in the designated periods. In addition, the circular contains a separate table of premium-rate slabs for certain specified business, showing revised rates for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 by claim band: for the 2% band the rate changes from 12.50% to 13.75%, for the 2%–5% band from 10.00% to 11%, for the 5%–10% band from 7.50% to 8.25%, and for the 10% band from 5.00% to 5.50%.

The circular also reiterates compliance mechanics for insurers’ internal monitoring and annual reporting. Insurers must maintain the prescribed sector-wise calculations and disclosures, submit the required returns in the specified forms, and ensure the information is prepared in the exact format required by the annexures. The document references deadlines tied to the regulatory cycle, including annual compliance reporting for the year ending 31 March 2025 and the relevant submission date of 14 July 2025 for one of the reporting obligations mentioned in the circular. There is also a specific requirement that insurers make the necessary disclosures/filings within 30 days in the context described by the circular, which compliance teams should treat as an operational deadline for whichever report or statement the circular assigns that period to.

The final section shown in the text begins the motor third-party obligation framework and indicates that the circular applies to motor third-party business calculations and reporting under the updated regulatory regime. It references separate sub-forms/annexures for reporting by category and implies that insurers must continue to compute and evidence compliance using the prescribed formulae and classification standards. Because the circular is a master consolidation, compliance officers should treat it as the controlling reference for all rural, social sector, and motor third-party obligation monitoring, and verify that internal underwriting, policy administration, and regulatory reporting systems reflect the updated thresholds, rates, forms, and annual timelines for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27.

The IRDAI issued the **Information and Cyber Security Guidelines, 2026** on **6 April 2026** (Ref. No. **IRDAI/GA&HR/CIR/MISC/51/4/2026**), replacing/revising the earlier IRDAI cyber/information security guidance issued by circular dated **24 April 2023**. The regulator explains that the revision was driven by the **evolving cyber threat landscape**, feedback from the industry, and recommendations from IRDAI committees, with the stated purpose of helping the insurance sector **strengthen cyber defenses and related governance mechanisms**.

The guidelines are framed as the **minimum standards and governance mechanisms** that regulated entities must adopt. IRDAI states that the detailed “major changes” are contained in **Annexure A** and the full guidelines are in **Annexure B**. From a compliance perspective, the key requirement is that the guidelines are **mandatory** and must be strictly followed by **all regulated entities** in scope.

The entities expressly covered are: **all insurers, including FRBs; insurance intermediaries such as brokers, corporate agents, web aggregators, TPAs, IMFs, insurance repositories, ISNPs, corporate surveyors, MISP providers, CSCs; and the Insurance Information Bureau of India (IIB)**. IRDAI directs these entities to **ensure compliance from the current financial year**, so compliance teams should treat the 2026-27 financial year as the operative period unless the annexed guidelines specify earlier phased deadlines or additional implementation dates.

Because the letter itself does not list the detailed technical obligations, thresholds, or control requirements, compliance officers should review **Annexure B** for the specific cybersecurity governance, monitoring, reporting, access control, incident response, and other operational standards, and **Annexure A** for the exact deltas from the 2023 framework. This IRDAI guideline, dated **11 February 2026** and issued under reference **IRDAI/F&I/GDL/MISC/27/02/2026**, replaces/amends the earlier IRDAI directions on the same subject issued on **17 October 2022** and sets out the rules for a **foreign insurance company registered outside India** that wants to **establish or close a Liaison Office (LO) in India**. The document is aimed at insurers outside India and the regulatory framework governing their Indian liaison presence; it is not a general corporate document, but one that specifically controls how such offices may be opened, operated, and shut down. The text indicates that these guidelines are framed under the relevant powers of the insurance regulator and connected legal provisions, and they are intended to govern both the application process and ongoing conditions for an LO.

For **establishment**, the guidelines require the foreign insurer to obtain the necessary regulatory permission before opening the Indian liaison office and to file the prescribed application and supporting documents. The document’s content indicates several application requirements and conditions, including submission of identity/authorization materials, details of the overseas insurer, and declarations about the nature of activities to be undertaken through the liaison office. The liaison office is described as a limited presence and is not to be used as a full operating insurance business in India; the office’s activities are confined to liaison and related non-revenue functions rather than underwriting or direct commercial insurance activity. The guideline text also shows that the office’s establishment and continued operation are tied to compliance with prescribed procedural steps and filings, rather than being an automatic right.

A significant operational requirement is that the liaison office must follow strict limitations on what it can do and must comply with the regulator’s conditions on reporting and conduct. The document references ongoing obligations, including filing/reporting and observance of the permitted scope of activities, and it appears to require the LO to act only within the approved mandate. Where the guideline refers to timing, it includes a **30-day** period in connection with certain notifications/filings and a **60-day** period for specified regulatory actions, so compliance teams should treat those as mandatory deadlines unless a later section states otherwise. The text also refers to branch/office-specific obligations and the need to keep the regulator informed of changes affecting the office’s status, structure, or permitted operations.

For **closure**, the guidelines prescribe a formal process rather than simply allowing the foreign insurer to shut the office at will. The LO can be closed only after completing the specified regulatory requirements, including notices, submissions, and any required no-objection/approval steps. The closure section also indicates a **15-day** timeframe in multiple places, suggesting short statutory deadlines for certain closure-related intimations or filings. A compliance team should therefore assume that termination of the liaison office requires advance planning, formal intimation to IRDAI and other relevant authorities, completion of pending obligations, and adherence to all prescribed reporting and record-related steps before the office is actually wound up.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued the **Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Insurance Fraud Monitoring Framework) Guidelines, 2025** on **09.10.2025** under **Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938** and **Section 14(1) of the IRDA Act, 1999** to create a regulatory framework for how insurers and distribution channels must prevent, detect, report, and manage insurance fraud risk. The guidelines apply broadly to **all insurers and distribution channels**, unless a specific carve-out is stated elsewhere in the document, and they are intended to cover fraud risk across the insurance lifecycle rather than only claims handling.

A core requirement is that insurers and distribution channels must establish and maintain a formal **insurance fraud monitoring framework**. The document defines “fraud” broadly, including acts such as deliberate misrepresentation, concealment, false documentation, collusion, and other deceptive conduct connected with insurance business, and it also distinguishes between **internal fraud** and **external fraud**. Entities are required to put in place governance, controls, processes, and accountability mechanisms to identify fraud risk, monitor suspicious activity, and respond to detected fraud in a structured way rather than ad hoc.

The guidelines require insurers to implement a company-wide fraud management structure that includes **policy-level oversight, role allocation, reporting, escalation, investigation, and remediation**. This includes setting up internal controls around underwriting, policy issuance, claims, operations, and distribution-related activity; maintaining surveillance over transactions and behaviors that may indicate fraud; and ensuring suspicious cases are escalated for review and investigation. Insurers must also ensure that their fraud framework covers activity involving their **distribution channels** and any third parties used in the insurance process, so compliance is not limited to the insurer’s own employees and systems.

The document also imposes obligations around **documentation, records, and reporting**. Insurers are expected to maintain records of fraud incidents, investigation outcomes, and actions taken, and to create procedures for reporting material fraud matters to the appropriate internal governance level and, where required, to the regulator or other authorities. The framework implies that insurers must also train relevant personnel and ensure distribution partners understand and follow the insurer’s fraud controls, since the guidelines explicitly cover both insurers and distribution channels.

The effective date in the excerpt is indicated as **1.1.2026** / **January 2026** for commencement, meaning compliance teams should treat the framework as becoming operational from that date unless the full document specifies a different staggered implementation for particular provisions. From a practical compliance standpoint, firms should review existing fraud controls, update policies and procedures, align vendor/distribution oversight, and ensure fraud escalation and reporting channels are in place before commencement.

rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has amended Clause 15(a) of the “Revised Guidelines on Insurance Repositories and Electronic Issuance of Insurance Policies” (originally issued under Ref. IRDA/INT/GDL/INSRE/111/05/2015 dated 29 May 2015). The change replaces the prior requirement that the annual review of an insurance repository’s controls, systems, procedures, and safeguards be performed by an external system audit firm approved by IRDAI, with a new requirement that the review be conducted at least once every year at the repository’s own cost by an external auditor who is either a Certified Information System Auditor (CISA), a Chartered Accountant holding DISA (ICAI) qualification, or a CERT-In certified expert.

This amendment applies specifically to insurance repositories and the review of the controls, systems, procedures, and safeguards they maintain under Clause 14 of the guidelines. The compliance burden is now more prescriptive on auditor qualifications: repositories can no longer rely on any approved external system audit firm, but must use an individual or qualified external auditor meeting one of the three specified credential standards. The circular is effective immediately as of 29 July 2025, and no transition period or delayed implementation date is provided.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated **28 February 2025** and addressed to **all life, general, and health insurers**, issues the **“Guidelines on Hedging Through Equity Derivatives”** and supersedes the prior IRDAI guidance framework referenced in the document. The stated purpose is to set a revised regulatory framework for insurers using **equity derivatives for hedging**, replacing or updating earlier IRDAI directions issued in **2004** and **2012**, and aligning the approach with the current investment/hedging environment for insurers.

The document sets out that insurers may use equity derivatives only within the prescribed hedging framework and subject to the specific conditions in the guidelines. It distinguishes between different derivative uses and imposes controls on the manner in which positions are taken, maintained, monitored, and closed. The guidelines also require insurers to ensure that derivatives are used for **hedging purposes** rather than speculative or leveraged trading, and that the positions are backed by the insurer’s underlying exposures and internal risk-management controls.

A key compliance point is that the document sets **position limits and exposure restrictions**. The text indicates that insurer derivative exposures are capped in relation to relevant underlying equity holdings/exposures, including a referenced **20% limit** and other percentage-based constraints tied to portfolio composition and hedging need. It also refers to a **range of 80–125** for a related prescribed metric or band, indicating that hedging activity must remain within that approved threshold rather than being open-ended. The circular also contains requirements around the sizing and monitoring of the derivative book, including references to a **15**-based threshold in the context of the derivative/hedging parameters, which compliance teams should treat as a hard numeric condition to be checked against the full guideline text and internal controls.

Operationally, insurers must maintain a formal **board-approved policy** for hedging through equity derivatives, including defined objectives, eligible instruments, risk limits, internal approvals, valuation methodology, monitoring, and escalation procedures. The guidelines require ongoing oversight of derivative positions, including segregation of duties, documentation of the hedging rationale, periodic review of effectiveness, and reporting/recordkeeping so the insurer can demonstrate that each position is a bona fide hedge. There are also explicit requirements for internal controls over execution, valuation, and unwinding/rollover of positions, plus governance for any breach or exception.

For compliance teams, the practical effect is that this is not a general permission to trade derivatives: it is a controlled hedging framework with prescribed limits, documentation, governance, and monitoring duties applicable to all insurers in scope. Firms should review whether their current treasury/investment policy, board approvals, risk limits, and hedge accounting/valuation procedures already align with the new IRDAI framework, and if not, update them promptly before entering or renewing any equity derivative hedge positions.

The IRDAI issued the **Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Bima Vahak) Guidelines, 2023** on **9 October 2023** under **Section 14(2)(e) of the IRDAI Act, 1999**. The guidelines are intended to create a **women-centric dedicated distribution channel** to improve insurance inclusion, increase awareness in every **village/Gram Panchayat**, and strengthen access to insurance in remote areas. They also require insurers to identify and develop **local resources** who understand local needs and are trusted by the local population.

A **Bima Vahak** is defined as either an **Individual Bima Vahak** or a **Corporate Bima Vahak** (a legal person registered under Indian law) engaged to provide services under these guidelines. Insurers are permitted, for the purposes of **soliciting insurance business** and **facilitating policy and claims servicing**, to **engage a Corporate Bima Vahak** and/or **directly appoint Individual Bima Vahaks**. The document indicates that insurers must follow the prescribed framework for such appointments, but the excerpt provided cuts off before the full appointment conditions and operational rules are shown.

The guidelines’ **effective date is tied to the launch of “Bima Vistaar”**, which is described as a **comprehensive insurance product to be issued in due course**. That means the Bima Vahak framework is not immediately operational from the issue date alone; instead, compliance teams should treat the obligations as becoming enforceable once Bima Vistaar is launched. For corporate compliance, the key point is that any insurer planning to use this channel will need to ensure its distribution and servicing arrangements comply with the Bima Vahak model, with a particular focus on the **women-led local distribution structure** and the use of locally rooted personnel/entities for village-level outreach and servicing.

In other words, compliance teams should treat the new framework as immediately issued, but with a delayed start for organizations whose FY 2022–23 security audit has already been completed. rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) issued these guidelines on 3 January 2023 to change how File Reference Numbers (FRNs) are issued to cross-border reinsurers (CBRs). The stated policy shift is from the existing practice of annual FRN allotment by the Authority to an auto-renewal model, where the insurer itself may renew the FRN for a CBR, provided the CBR continues to satisfy the prescribed eligibility criteria. This is intended to support ease of doing business while ensuring that insurers continue to use only compliant reinsurance counterparties.

The document makes clear that insurers may place reinsurance business with a CBR only if the CBR meets the rating and other requirements under the IRDAI (Reinsurance) Regulations, 2018 and has a valid FRN. The new approach does not remove the compliance obligation on insurers; rather, it shifts the operational renewal step so that insurers must themselves verify that the CBR still qualifies before relying on the auto-renewal mechanism. The guidelines are issued under Section 34(1) of the Insurance Act, 1938 read with Regulations 4(3) and 12(3) of the IRDAI (Reinsurance) Regulations, 2018, so they have regulatory force for all insurers.

For compliance purposes, the key material change is that FRNs for qualifying CBRs no longer need to be processed as a fresh annual issuance by IRDAI each year, but may be renewed by the insurer if the CBR continues to meet the required criteria specified in the guidelines. The document does not set out the detailed eligibility thresholds in the excerpt provided, but it expressly conditions auto-renewal on continued satisfaction of those criteria. Accordingly, insurers need to maintain an internal control process to confirm ongoing compliance of each CBR before business is placed or renewed under the FRN.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued these guidelines on 28.09.2022 to address conflict-of-interest risks arising when more than one entity from the same group applies for or holds a Certificate of Registration (CoR) as an intermediary or insurance intermediary, and when the same individuals serve as directors across intermediary/insurance intermediary entities either within the same group or across different groups. The document applies to entities defined as “intermediary” or “insurance intermediary” under Section 2(f) of the IRDAI Act, 1999, and “group” is to be understood as defined in Section 2(g) of the IRDAI (Investment) Regulations, 2018. It states that the number of common directorships cannot exceed the limit prescribed under Section 165 of the Companies Act, 2013, so firms must monitor director appointments to ensure they remain within the statutory cap.

Where common directors exist, the intermediary or insurance intermediary must have a Board-approved policy governing transactions with related parties, with “related party” understood as defined in Section 2(76) of the Companies Act, 2013. All related party transactions must comply with Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 and applicable Accounting Standard AS 18, meaning these transactions must be properly approved, documented, and accounted for in accordance with those provisions. The statutory auditor of the intermediary or insurance intermediary is required to certify compliance with Section 188 to IRDAI as of the relevant reporting date; the excerpt provided cuts off after “as at the,” so the exact certification timing wording is incomplete in the text shown. For compliance purposes, the key operational requirement is that firms with common directorships must actively manage and evidence related-party governance, legal compliance under the Companies Act, and auditor certification for submission to IRDAI.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued the **“IRDAI (Surety Insurance Contracts) Guidelines, 2022”** on **3 January 2022**, and they **take effect on 1 April 2022**. They are addressed to the **Chairman-cum-Managing Directors/Chief Executive Officers of general insurance companies**, but specifically **exclude ECGC Ltd. and AIC Ltd.** The purpose is to regulate and support the development of **Surety Insurance business** in India, which IRDAI treats as distinct because of the product’s unique risk characteristics.

For applicability, **all insurers registered under the Insurance Act, 1938 that are authorized to transact general insurance business may transact Surety Insurance, but only if they satisfy the eligibility criteria in the guidelines**. The document also imposes a market-entry restriction: **after commencement, no person may transact Surety Insurance in India unless that person is an “Indian Insurance Company” as defined in Section 2(7A) of the Insurance Act, 1938**. Compliance teams should therefore confirm both registration status and whether the entity meets the Indian Insurance Company definition before offering these products.

The guidelines define the legal nature of a surety insurance product as a **contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872**, involving a **surety**, **principal debtor**, and **creditor**. However, IRDAI makes clear that such a contract is treated as an **insurance contract only when issued by a surety that is an insurer registered under the Insurance Act, 1938 to transact general insurance**. In other words, the same guarantee structure is not insurance unless it is written by a qualifying general insurer.

IRDAI also provides specific product definitions that compliance teams should use when classifying business: **Advance Payment Bond** covers the surety’s promise to pay the outstanding balance of an advance payment if the contractor fails to complete the contract as specified or fails to meet the contract scope; **Bid Bond** covers a bidder’s obligation to furnish the required performance guarantee and sign the contract within the prescribed period if awarded; **Contract Bond** is a broader umbrella covering assurance to public entities, developers, subcontractors, and suppliers that the contractor will meet contractual obligations, and it may include bid bonds, performance bonds, advance payment bonds, and retention money; **Customs and Court Bond** covers guarantees to public offices such as tax offices, customs administrations, or courts for public receivables arising from court cases, customs clearance, or incorrect customs procedures; **Performance Bond** protects the obligee if the principal/contractor defaults and the contract is terminated; and **Retention Money** is the portion of contract payment withheld until successful completion. The document also states that any undefined terms will take their meanings from the **Insurance Act, 1938**, the **IRDA Act, 1999**, and regulations/rules made under them.

IRDAI/NL/GDL/MISC/244/09/2021 8 th September, 2021 To The Chairman-Cum- Managing Directors/Chief Executive officers of General Insurance Companies (except ECGC Ltd and AIC Ltd) Madam/Sir, IRDAI (Trade Credit Insurance) Guidelines, 2021 The revised guidelines on Trade Credit insurance are hereby issued considering the evolving insurance risk needs of various sectors and response to changing market conditions. The guidelines shall come into force with effect from 1 st November, 2021. The guidelines have been placed on the IRDAI website (https://www.irdai.gov.in). Yours faithfully, Sd/- (Yegnapriya Bharath) Chief General Manager (NL) IRDAI (Trade Credit Insurance) Guidelines,2021 Page 1 of 9 IRDAI (Trade Credit Insurance) Guidelines, 2021 1. Introduction 1.1 Trade credit insurance protects businesses against the risk of non-payment for goods and services by buyers. It usually covers a portfolio of buyers and indemnifies an agreed percentage of an invoice or invoices that remain unpaid as a result of protracted default, insolvency / bankruptcy. It contributes to the economic growth of a country by facilitating trade and helps in improving economic stability by addressing the trade losses due to payment risks. 1.2 These guidelines set out the regulatory framework; (a) to promote sustainable and healthy development of trade credit insurance business. (b) to facilitate general insurance companies to offer trade credit insurance covers to suppliers as well as licensed banks and other financial institutions to help businesses manage country risk, open up access to new markets and to manage non-payment risk associated with trade financing portfolio. (c) to enable general insurance companies to offer trade credit insurance with customised covers to improve businesses for the SMEs and MSMEs, considering the evolving insurance risk needs of these sectors.
rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued revised **Trade Credit Insurance Guidelines, 2021** for **general insurance companies in India**, specifically addressed to **all general insurers except ECGC Ltd. and AIC Ltd.** The new framework is issued under **Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999**, was **published on 8 September 2021**, and **takes effect from 1 November 2021**, replacing the earlier IRDAI trade credit insurance guidelines dated **10 March 2016**. The guidelines are also expressly stated to be **in addition to any other applicable laws, rules, regulations, or guidelines**.

Substantively, the document clarifies that **trade credit insurance can only cover credit risk directly linked to an underlying trade transaction**, meaning the **delivery of goods or services**; if there is no such direct link, the outstanding amount is **not insurable** under this product. It permits coverage for a range of **commercial risks**, including **insolvency or protracted default** by the buyer, by the bank responsible for payment in **letter of credit** transactions, or by the **stock-holding agent** in consignment transactions; **rejection of goods** after delivery when permitted by contract, or before shipment when goods are being specially manufactured for the buyer and cannot be sold elsewhere; and **non-receipt of payment due to failure of the collecting bank**. It also allows **political risk cover**, but only for **buyers outside India** and only for **countries specifically agreed upon**; political risks include legal or regulatory actions blocking transfer of payment from the buyer’s country to India, war or civil unrest in the buyer’s country or between that country and India, restrictions or cancellations preventing import into the buyer’s country, and certain additional handling/transport/insurance costs arising from interruption or diversion of shipment outside India that cannot practicably be recovered from the buyer.

The stated regulatory objective is to promote the **sustainable and healthy development** of trade credit insurance and to enable insurers to offer covers not only to suppliers but also to **licensed banks and other financial institutions** that finance trade. The guidelines specifically emphasize improving access to customized trade credit insurance for **SMEs and MSMEs**, recognizing changing risk needs and market conditions. For compliance teams, the key operational takeaway is that any trade credit product design, underwriting, and policy wording issued on or after **1 November 2021** must fit within this narrower “directly linked to a trade transaction” requirement and must stay within the enumerated commercial and political risk parameters, with political risk cover limited to the defined cross-border and country-specific circumstances.

rows.summary:
This circular, issued by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) on 31 March 2021 under Ref. IRDA/SUR/GDL/MISC/068/03/2021, introduces practical training guidelines for surveyors and loss assessors seeking fresh or renewal licences. It is explicitly issued in continuation of the earlier circular dated 1 December 2020 (Ref. IRDA/SUR/GDL/MISC/288/12/2020) and is grounded in Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999 as well as Regulation 3(2)(b) and (c) of the IRDAI (Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors) Regulations, 2015. The circular applies to all licensed surveyors and loss assessors and sets out the practical training framework that must be followed as part of the licensing process.

The document requires **institutional practical training for two months** with either the **National Insurance Academy (NIA)** or the **Insurance Institute of India (III)**. The training must cover, at minimum, introductory and functional knowledge of insurance policies, endorsements, insurance terminology, and the nature of insurance business, along with practical aspects relevant to surveyor and loss assessor work. The emphasis is on structured, institution-based instruction rather than informal or ad hoc experience, and the training is clearly positioned as a mandatory component for those seeking to obtain or renew a surveyor/loss assessor licence.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that licence applicants and renewal candidates cannot treat practical training as optional or self-directed; it must be completed through the specified recognized institutions and for the full two-month period. The circular does not provide a later effective date or grace period in the excerpt shown, so the operative date is the date of issuance, **31 March 2021**, and the requirements should be treated as immediately applicable to fresh and renewal licensing processes covered by the earlier December 2020 guidance.

All listed companies 2. Companies and bodies corporate as specified in Rule 3 of NFRA Rules, 2018 3. Auditors of the above companies Subject: Effective Communication Between Statutory Auditors and Those Charged with Governance, Including Audit Committees In the course of discharging of NFRA’s statutory functions, it has been noticed that there is a need to strengthen the communications between Statutory Auditors (Auditors), Those Charged with Governance (TCWG), including Audit Committees (ACs), in line with the requirements of the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013), the Standards on Auditing (SAs) prescribed under CA 2013, and other relevant Rules and Regulations. 2. rows.summary:
The NFRA has issued this circular to all listed companies, companies and bodies corporate covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and their auditors, because it has observed that communication between statutory auditors and those charged with governance (TCWG), including audit committees, needs to be strengthened and better aligned with the Companies Act, 2013, the Standards on Auditing, and other applicable rules. The circular does not create a brand-new standalone reporting regime; rather, it reiterates and emphasizes existing legal and audit obligations on boards, independent directors, audit committees, and auditors, with the practical message that these parties must communicate more effectively on matters affecting financial statements and audit oversight. It specifically restates that under Section 134 of the Companies Act, 2013 the board must approve the financial statements and consolidated financial statements, attach a board report, and include the Directors’ Responsibility Statement covering compliance with accounting standards, prudent accounting policies and estimates, maintenance of proper records and asset safeguards, prevention and detection of fraud and irregularities, preparation of accounts on a going-concern basis, and implementation of adequate internal financial controls.

The document is aimed at ensuring that auditors and governance bodies engage in meaningful communication on these matters, especially where the board’s statutory assertions and the auditor’s audit observations intersect. The affected entities are therefore listed companies and NFRA-covered companies/bodies corporate, along with their statutory auditors, board members, independent directors, and audit committees. The circular’s compliance significance is that companies should treat auditor–TCWG communication as an active governance requirement rather than a formality, and ensure the board and audit committee are properly informed and able to respond to audit issues in a timely and documented manner. The document provided here cuts off after discussing the board’s responsibilities under Section 134, so no additional deadlines, quantitative thresholds, effective dates beyond the circular date of 07.01.2026, or specific new procedural timelines are visible in the excerpt.

rows.summary:
The NFRA circular, dated 3 October 2024 and issued under section 132(2)(b), (c) and (d) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with rules 4(1), 4(2)(e) and 9 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, is addressed to auditors of entities covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules. It focuses on audits of group financial statements, meaning both standalone financial statements of companies with branches and consolidated financial statements of companies with subsidiaries, associates, and similar components, where one auditor acts as the “Principal Auditor” and component auditors are “Other Auditors.” The circular emphasizes that statutory audits of both SFS and CFS must already comply with the Standards on Auditing under section 143 of the Act, along with the applicable Standard on Quality Control, all 35 SAs, and the Code of Ethics including independence requirements.

Substantively, the circular reminds auditors that group audits require special care because the Principal Auditor remains ultimately responsible for the group audit opinion even when work is performed by Other Auditors on branches, subsidiaries, or other components. It specifically references SA 600 (“Using the Work of Another Auditor”) as the governing standard for these engagements. NFRA notes that modern group structures often present material and/or significant audit risk, and the circular begins by identifying examples such as complex structures involving special purpose vehicles, “auto pilot” structures, cross-holdings among group entities, and shared-service arrangements, indicating that these features heighten the need for rigorous group audit oversight.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this is not a new filing deadline or fee requirement, but a supervisory reminder and expectation-setting circular reinforcing that group audit assignments must be planned and executed with heightened attention to the Principal Auditor’s responsibility, proper use of component auditors, and full adherence to SA 600 and the broader SA/SQC/ethics framework. Entities subject to NFRA oversight and their statutory auditors should ensure their group audit methodologies, documentation, and review procedures reflect the Principal Auditor’s continuing accountability for the final opinion and the need to address risks arising from complex group structures.
