Auditors of the Entities Regulated by the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) Subject: Statutory Auditors’ Responsibilities in relation to Fraud in a Company In course of discharge of its statutory functions, NFRA has noticed that auditors are not fulfilling their statutory responsibilities relating to reporting of fraud as mandated under the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013) read with the relevant Rules and the applicable Standards on Auditing (SAs). 2 The CA 2013, the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order (CARO) and the Standards on Auditing (SAs) place mandatory reporting obligations on auditors to report fraud and/or suspected fraud to the Central Government and the Board/Audit Committee. 2.1 Section 143 (12) of CA 2013 and related Rules places certain reporting obligations on the auditor, in relation to frauds: “Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, if an auditor of a company in the course of the performance of his duties as auditor, has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving such amount or amounts as may be prescribed, is being or has been committed in the company by its officers or employees, the auditor shall report the matter to the Central Government within such time and in such manner as may be prescribed: ....” Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014, prescribes detailed steps that need to be followed by the auditor if he has reason to believe that an offence of fraud, which involves or is expected to involve individually an amount of rupees one crore or above, is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees. The auditor is required to report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee and to the Central Government in the form of a statement as specified in Form ADT-4. 2.2 Clause (xi) of Companies
rows.summary:
This NFRA circular dated **26 June 2023** reminds auditors of entities regulated by NFRA that they are **not meeting their statutory fraud-reporting obligations** under the **Companies Act, 2013**, the **Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order (CARO)**, and the **Standards on Auditing (SAs)**. NFRA states that auditors must report fraud and suspected fraud where required, and that these duties are mandatory rather than discretionary.

The circular specifically highlights **Section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013** and **Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014**. Under these provisions, if an auditor has reason to believe that an offence of fraud has been or is being committed in the company by its officers or employees, and the fraud **involves or is expected to involve an amount of ₹1 crore or more**, the auditor must follow the prescribed reporting process. That process includes reporting the matter to the **Board or Audit Committee** and also to the **Central Government**, using **Form ADT-4**. The circular also notes that the legal obligation applies when the auditor, in the course of performing audit duties, has reason to believe fraud has occurred or is occurring, so the trigger is not limited to proven fraud.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that NFRA is warning auditors of regulated entities that they must ensure their fraud-detection and reporting procedures are aligned with these statutory requirements, including the required reporting chain and form. The circular is aimed at **statutory auditors of NFRA-regulated entities**, and it reinforces that failures to report fraud in the manner and within the framework required by law are viewed as non-compliance with audit responsibilities.

All listed companies 2. Unlisted companies specified in Rule 3 of NFRA Rules, 2018 3. Auditors of the above companies Subject: Instances of non-compliance with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind ASs) on Accounting Policies for measurement of Revenue from Contracts with Customers and Trade Receivables As per sub-section 2(b) of section 132 of the Companies Act 2013 (the Act) read with rule 4(2)( c) of the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules 2018 (NFRA Rules 2018), the National Financial Reporting Authority is mandated to monitor and enforce compliance with accounting standards and auditing standards. Further, NFRA is required by sub-section 2( d) of section 132 of the Act read with rule 4(2) (g) of NFRA Rules, to perform such other functions and duties as may be necessary or incidental to the aforesaid functions and duties. 2. NFRA monitors compliance with accounting standards by Companies as part of its review of published financial statements of companies. During its recent review, instances of apparent non­ compliance with the prescriptions of the Ind ASs in the critical areas of Revenue Recognition and Measurement, and Initial Measurement of corresponding Trade Receivables have come to light. In order to ensure adherence to high-quality Ind AS Reporting Framework, which is substantially aligned with globally accepted IFRS Standards, the instances of non-compliance are highlighted below for the urgent attention of the Company Management/Audit Committees and the Statutory Auditors. Revenue from Contracts with Customers - Recognition and Measurement 3. Para 46 of Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, requires that the entity shall recognise as revenue the amount of the transaction price, excluding the estimates of variable conside
rows.summary:
The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) issued this circular on 29 March 2023 to all listed companies, all unlisted companies covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and the auditors of those companies. NFRA says that, in reviewing published financial statements, it found apparent non-compliance with Indian Accounting Standards in the key areas of revenue recognition/measurement and the initial measurement of related trade receivables, and it is flagging these issues for immediate attention of management, audit committees, and statutory auditors.

For revenue from contracts with customers, the circular points to Ind AS 115, paragraph 46, which requires revenue to be recognized at the transaction price excluding estimates of variable consideration to the extent those estimates are constrained under the standard. The concern is that companies may be recognizing revenue without correctly applying the Ind AS 115 rules on transaction price and variable consideration. The circular emphasizes that this affects both the reported revenue amount and the accounting policy disclosures and requires companies and auditors to ensure strict compliance with Ind AS 115 in reporting.

The circular also highlights the related issue of initial measurement of trade receivables arising from revenue contracts, indicating that the receivable should be recorded consistent with the revenue recognized under Ind AS 115 rather than using an amount that is not aligned with the standard’s measurement principles. NFRA’s message is that these are not merely presentation issues but potential accounting policy and measurement failures that could materially affect published financial statements. There are no new numerical thresholds, filing deadlines, or transition dates set out in this circular; instead, the immediate obligation is to review current accounting policies and financial statement practices, correct any departures from Ind AS requirements, and ensure auditors and audit committees challenge and remediate non-compliant revenue and receivables accounting.

rows.summary:
NFRA’s Order No. 24/2024, dated 21.10.2024, disposes of the show-cause notice dated 13.10.2023 issued to CA Chirag Doshi (ICAI Membership No. 119079), who was the Engagement Partner for the statutory audit of Ushdev International Limited (UIL), Mumbai, for FY 2017–18. The order is issued under Section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11(6) of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and concerns NFRA’s suo motu review of the auditor’s professional conduct in relation to UIL, a public interest entity.

The key finding is that, although the auditor ultimately issued a disclaimer of opinion on both the financial statements and the internal financial controls over financial reporting for FY 2017–18, NFRA concluded that he failed to exercise due diligence and acted with gross negligence, particularly in relation to the statutory duty to report fraud under Section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 and SA 240. NFRA says the audit file showed several indicators of fraud, yet the auditor did not respond appropriately. The order also concludes that the auditor failed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence in the course of the audit.

For a compliance team, the material point is that NFRA treated the audit failures as serious professional misconduct, not merely technical shortcomings: the deficiencies included failure to detect, evaluate, and report fraud indicators despite the presence of warning signs. The order is aimed at the individual engagement partner rather than the company itself, but it reinforces that statutory auditors of PIEs must meet the heightened standards imposed by the Companies Act and auditing standards, including active fraud vigilance and documentation sufficient to support any audit conclusion, even where the final outcome is a disclaimer of opinion.

rows.summary:

rows.summary:
The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) issued Order No. 020/2024 dated 19 August 2024 disposing of a show cause notice dated 17 January 2024 issued to M/s BSR & Associates LLP, CA Aravind Maiya (engagement partner), and CA Amit Somani (engagement quality control reviewer) in connection with the statutory audit of Coffee Day Enterprises Ltd. (CDEL) for FY 2018–19. NFRA conducted a suo motu review under section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, prompted by a SEBI investigation report alleging diversion of Rs. 3,535 crore from seven CDEL subsidiary companies, and examined the auditors’ conduct in relation to both the consolidated financial statements (CFS) and standalone financial statements (SFS). The order addresses major audit failures, lapses in audit documentation, and alleged violations of SQC 1 and SA 230, and it specifically evaluates the firm as well as the individual EP and EQCR as the principal auditors responsible for the audit.

From the material provided, the order is not merely a procedural disposition; it is a disciplinary action concerning whether the auditors failed in their professional duties in the audit of CDEL’s FY 2018–19 financial statements. NFRA’s review covered the consolidated and standalone reporting areas separately and also considered the auditors’ documentation practices, indicating that the regulator was assessing both substantive audit shortcomings and compliance with audit quality-control and recordkeeping standards. The order states that it includes findings on the articles of charge for professional misconduct and then moves to penalties and sanctions, so compliance teams should treat it as an enforcement order with potential reputational, regulatory, and professional-practice consequences for the audit firm and the named partners.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaways are that NFRA treated the case as a serious statutory-audit oversight matter involving a listed/regulated corporate group context and a large alleged fund diversion issue, and that the named auditors were scrutinized for their roles as EP and EQCR, not just as firm personnel. The order’s scope indicates that deficiencies in audit procedures, audit evidence, and documentation can independently trigger enforcement under the Companies Act framework and auditing standards, especially where there is a large-scale fraud/diversion allegation connected to the audited entity’s group structure. If your team uses external auditors, this order is a reminder that NFRA expects auditors to properly examine consolidation risks, subsidiary transactions, and governance red flags, and to maintain audit files that substantiate their judgments and conclusions.

rows.title: Request for public comments – Draft SA 600 (Revised)
rows.desc: SA 600 (REVISED) Request for Public Comments by 30.10.2024 (Refer accompanying note on NFRA website) SA 600 (Revised), SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS—AUDITS OF GROUP FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (INCLUDING THE WORK OF COMPONENT AUDITORS) (Applicable to PIEs under Rule 3 of NFRA Rules 2018 except PSUs, PSBs and PSIs and their branches) Introduction Scope of this SA 1. The Standards on Auditing (SAs) apply to an audit of group financial statements (a group audit). This SA deals with special considerations that apply to a group audit, including in those circumstances when component auditors are involved. rows.summary:
NFRA has issued **Draft SA 600 (Revised), “Special Considerations—Audits of Group Financial Statements (Including the Work of Component Auditors)”** for **public comments due by 30.10.2024**. The draft is intended to apply to **PIEs under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018**, **except PSUs, PSBs and PSIs and their branches**. It updates the audit standard governing **group audits**, including situations where **component auditors** are used, and it ties the requirements to related standards such as **SA 220 (Revised), SA 230, SA 300, SA 315 (Revised), and SA 330**.

Substantively, the draft clarifies that **group financial statements** are those that include the financial information of **more than one entity or business unit through a consolidation process**. The “consolidation process” is defined broadly to cover not only normal **consolidated financial statements** prepared under the applicable reporting framework, but also **combined financial statements** and the **aggregation of financial information** for entities or business units such as **branches or divisions**. It also notes that the standard may be useful, even outside a group audit, when the engagement team includes a person from another firm—such as for attending a physical inventory count, inspecting property, plant and equipment, or performing procedures at a remote shared service center.

The opening sections further explain that a group can be structured in different ways, including by **legal entities** or other organizational units, which means the standard is meant to be applied flexibly to the actual structure of the reporting group. For compliance purposes, the key action item is to review the draft standard and submit any comments by the stated deadline, and to assess whether the organization’s audits of group financial statements—or audits involving other-firm personnel at remote locations—would fall within the scope of the revised requirements once finalized.

rows.summary:
The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) issued this 16 January 2023 invitation for public comment to statutory auditors of NFRA-regulated Public Interest Entities (PIEs) on a proposal to require auditors/audit firms to publish Annual Transparency Reports (ATRs). The document does not itself impose a final rule yet; it explains the policy rationale and signals that NFRA is considering a disclosure obligation similar to requirements already used in some overseas jurisdictions, where audit firms that audit PIEs must prepare and publish annual transparency reports.

The stated purpose is to improve transparency around the audit profession’s capabilities and independence in auditing PIEs, given the increasing complexity of PIE financial reporting and the growing use of network firms, alliances, multidisciplinary teams, non-audit services, digital audit tools, and separate management/governance structures. NFRA notes that PIE audits are critical to the credibility and integrity of general purpose financial statements and that regulators are increasingly expecting high-quality information from both PIEs and their auditors.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the affected population is the statutory auditors and audit firms serving NFRA-regulated PIEs in India. If NFRA proceeds with the proposal, those firms would likely need to prepare and publicly release an ATR on an annual basis, meaning firms should anticipate new reporting, governance, and internal data-collection obligations covering both financial and non-financial aspects of their audit practice and quality capabilities. The document does not specify the ATR filing format, publication deadline, content template, or any monetary thresholds; it is an invitation for comments rather than an operative requirement.

rows.summary:
This document is a **Regulatory Impact Assessment by NFRA** responding to ICAI’s proposal to **revise the existing Accounting Standards (ASs)** under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013 for companies **not required to apply Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)**. The document explains that ICAI has submitted an **Approach Paper** and draft texts for **18 revised ASs out of an expected total of 32 revised standards**, as part of a broader project that began after Ind AS implementation for public interest entities; the revised ASs are intended to create a second set of standards for non-Ind AS companies. NFRA notes that these revised ASs would be **mandatory for all companies for which Ind AS is not mandatory**, which means the change would affect a **large number of Micro, Small and Medium-size Companies (MSMCs)** in addition to other non-Ind AS companies.

The material compliance point is that these revised standards would **replace the existing Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules**, so affected companies would need to transition from the current AS framework to the revised AS framework once prescribed. The document does **not** provide a final effective date, implementation deadline, or specific numerical accounting thresholds in the excerpt provided, but it makes clear that the revisions are being developed for compulsory application to the non-Ind AS population rather than as a voluntary option. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that companies outside the Ind AS regime should anticipate a **future mandatory accounting standards overhaul**, with potential impact especially on MSMCs, and should monitor NFRA/MCA action on the remaining standards and final notification of the revised AS package.

This consultation paper/report from India’s National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA), issued by its Technical Advisory Committee in March 2021 and circulated in June 2021, does not itself impose new binding legal requirements; rather, it sets out stakeholder feedback and recommendations for how NFRA should engage with the financial reporting ecosystem going forward. The report is focused on strengthening NFRA’s role in the accounting/auditing framework by improving consultation, transparency, guidance, enforcement processes, communication, and regulatory capacity. It describes the financial reporting “supply chain” and the perspectives of key groups affected by NFRA’s work: auditors, preparers of financial statements, users/investors, other regulators, academics, and other stakeholders.

A major theme is that NFRA should expand and systematize stakeholder engagement through more structured consultation before decisions are made, clearer communication of its positions and work programs, and stronger two-way interaction with the profession and other affected parties. The report also addresses NFRA’s inspection, investigation, and enforcement functions, recommending better processes for handling disciplinary matters, including settlement and remediation mechanisms rather than relying only on punitive action. It further recommends that NFRA provide timely guidance on accounting and auditing issues so that entities and practitioners know the regulator’s expectations before disputes arise, and that it improve dissemination of data and information to support market discipline and informed decision-making.

The document specifically highlights the need for a “road map” for NFRA’s future priorities, along with regulatory capacity building inside the authority so it can execute its expanded responsibilities effectively. Another emphasized area is audit quality oversight: the report discusses audit quality indicators and evaluation of audit firms as tools to assess performance and drive improvement in audit quality. It also considers independence, funding, and accountability as core governance issues that affect NFRA’s credibility and ability to operate.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that this paper signals a more active, data-driven, and transparent NFRA posture toward audit firms, preparers, and other regulated or affected parties, with greater expectation of engagement, timely response to guidance requests, and readiness for more robust inspection/enforcement and audit-quality evaluation processes. No numeric thresholds, rate changes, or specific effective dates for enforceable compliance obligations are set out in the material provided, and the text appears to be a policy/consultation report rather than an operative rule change.

rows.title: The PCAOB will hold an open meeting to consider adopting proposed amendments to QC 1000, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, and related proposed amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule, set to become effective on December 15, 2026.
rows.desc: At September 9 Open Meeting, PCAOB to Consider Adopting Amendments to Quality Control Standard WASHINGTON, Sep. 3, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) will hold an open meeting at 10:00 a.m. ET on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. At the meeting, the Board will consider adopting proposed amendments to QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, and related proposed amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule set to become effective on December 15, 2026. The meeting is open to the public and will take place in the PCAOB’s Multi-Purpose Room (301) at 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC. rows.title: The PCAOB announced the appointment of George Kostolampros as General Counsel.
rows.desc: George Kostolampros Named PCAOB General Counsel WASHINGTON, Jul. 1, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that George Kostolampros has been appointed the PCAOB’s General Counsel. As General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros will provide legal advice and counsel on all PCAOB operations and will manage the Office of the General Counsel (OGC). “OGC’s work underpins the PCAOB’s ability to execute its mission to protect investors,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We are grateful that George is joining us to fill this critical leadership role.” Mr. Kostolampros brings more than 25 years of experience advising organizations and senior leaders on complex legal, regulatory, governance, compliance, and risk-management matters. Prior to his appointment as General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros was a partner at Venable LLP, where he advised public companies, boards of directors, audit committees, financial institutions, and senior executives on compliance, governance, and regulatory matters, and represented clients in internal investigations, government enforcement matters, regulatory proceedings, and complex litigation. Before returning to private practice, he served as Senior Counsel in the Division of Enforcement at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Mr. Kostolampros received his J.D., magna cum laude, from Widener University School of Law and his B.A. from Syracuse University. “I am honored to join the PCAOB, and I look forward to working with the talented OGC staff to advance the PCAOB’s priorities and mission,” said Mr. Kostolampros. Matt Goldin, who was named Acting General Counsel in January 2026, will resume his role as Deputy General Counsel, advising the Board on PCAOB programs and operations and assisting with OGC’s management. “Matt is a valued member of the OGC team, and we thank him for his distinguished service as Acting General Counsel,” said Chairman Logothetis.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corp
rows.summary:
The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) announced on July 1, 2026, that George Kostolampros has been appointed General Counsel, making this a leadership change within the PCAOB rather than a rulemaking or enforcement action. In this role, Mr. Kostolampros will provide legal advice and counsel across all PCAOB operations and will manage the Office of the General Counsel (OGC), which the PCAOB says is central to its mission of protecting investors. The announcement does not impose any new compliance obligations, deadlines, filing requirements, or substantive standards on registrants, auditors, or other regulated entities.

The release notes Mr. Kostolampros brings more than 25 years of experience in legal, regulatory, governance, compliance, and risk-management matters. Before joining the PCAOB, he was a partner at Venable LLP, where he advised public companies, boards of directors, audit committees, financial institutions, and senior executives on compliance, governance, and regulatory issues, and represented clients in internal investigations, government enforcement matters, regulatory proceedings, and complex litigation. He also previously served as Senior Counsel in the SEC’s Division of Enforcement.

The PCAOB also stated that Matt Goldin, who had served as Acting General Counsel since January 2026, will return to his prior role as Deputy General Counsel. In that capacity, he will advise the Board on PCAOB programs and operations and assist in managing the OGC. The announcement includes biographical information and expressions of appreciation from PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis, but it does not describe any change in PCAOB policy, supervisory approach, or compliance timetable.

rows.title: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB after more than 17 years of service.
rows.desc: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich to Depart the PCAOB WASHINGTON, Jun. 26, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB on July 15, 2026, after more than 17 years of service. “I have greatly valued Barb’s expert advice – her accomplishments at the PCAOB have been extraordinary,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We thank her for her leadership and dedication, and we wish her well as she embarks on a new professional opportunity.” Ms. Vanich joined the PCAOB in February 2009. After serving in several roles at the PCAOB – including Associate Chief Auditor, Special Adviser to a Board Member, Deputy Chief Auditor, and Acting Chief Auditor – she was named Chief Auditor in October 2022. During her tenure as Chief Auditor, the PCAOB adopted several new standards that represented important milestones in the PCAOB’s work to improve audit quality and protect investors. Most notably, the PCAOB in May 2024 adopted QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control. The standard, which will become effective December 15, 2026, features a risk-based approach designed to drive continuous improvement in audit quality. Additionally, Ms. Vanich oversaw the development of other major standard-setting projects, the creation of resources to help audit firms with implementation of new standards, the launch of the PCAOB’s Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program, the PCAOB’s first-ever request for comment on potential future areas of focus for standard setting, and the creation of a Firm Consultation Process through which registered public accounting firms can submit standards-related questions directly to PCAOB staff and receive informal staff views. “It has been an honor to advance the PCAOB’s investor-protection mission, together with my talented colleagues in the Office of the Chief Auditor and so many others across the PCAOB,” said Ms. Vanich. The PCAOB is beginning a search to fill the Chief Auditor

rows.summary:
On June 25, 2026, the PCAOB announced a new **Firm Consultation Process** administered by the Office of the Chief Auditor (OCA) to give registered public accounting firms a more direct way to obtain **informal staff views** on how PCAOB requirements should be interpreted and applied. The process is intended to improve the **timeliness and consistency** of PCAOB guidance, particularly for questions involving the **implementation of new standards** and the **application of existing standards**.

The process is available to **registered public accounting firms** and covers questions about PCAOB **auditing, attestation, and quality control standards**, as well as related **rules and forms**, and PCAOB **ethics and independence** standards and rules. If a firm wants to use the process, it must submit a request by completing the **Consultation Intake Form**. The PCAOB stated that it does **not plan to make individual consultation requests public**, although it may later issue **public guidance** if it receives questions that are asked frequently or that would be broadly useful. There are no specific compliance deadlines, numerical thresholds, or effective-date phase-ins stated beyond the announcement date itself; the key operational change is the availability of this new consultation channel for firms seeking interpretive guidance.

rows.title: The PCAOB has launched an open comment period for stakeholders to provide input on its standard-setting and research agendas.
rows.summary:
The PCAOB is requesting public comment on three related items: updating its standard-setting and research agendas, potentially revisiting its overall approach to standard setting, and assessing the possible effect of the SEC’s recent proposal to permit optional semiannual reporting. The Board says the purpose of the request is to improve transparency and ensure its priorities reflect stakeholder views, and it is specifically asking commenters to address the need for, priority of, and possible scope of any reconsideration of its standard-setting approach.

This is not a rule change itself, but a consultation that may influence future PCAOB standards and research projects affecting audits of public companies and registered broker-dealers. The document states that the PCAOB uses this process to identify current and emerging audit issues and decide whether to undertake standard setting or research on standards-related topics, in support of its mission to protect investors and promote informative, accurate, independent audit reports. It also highlights two specific topic areas within its agenda-setting work: data and technology, including artificial intelligence and digital assets, indicating these are active focus areas for potential future standard-setting or research.

For compliance teams, the immediate obligation is to decide whether to submit comments and, if so, prepare them by the deadline. Comments must be submitted by August 7, 2026, and can be sent by email to comments@pcaobus.org, through the PCAOB website, or by postal mail to the Office of the Secretary, PCAOB, 1666 K Street, NW, Washington, DC 20006-2803. Submissions must reference “Request for Public Comment on PCAOB Standard Setting” in the subject or reference line, and all comments received will be publicly posted on the PCAOB website.

The release is dated June 23, 2026 (PCAOB Release No. 2026-005). The PCAOB invites all interested parties to comment, and any questions about the request may be directed to Barbara Vanich, Chief Auditor, at (202) 207-9363 or vanichb@pcaobus.org, or to Dima Andriyenko, Deputy Chief Auditor, at (202) 207-9130 or andriyenkod@pcaobus.org.

rows.summary: The PCAOB announced on June 15, 2026 that George G. Demos has been appointed Director of its Division of Enforcement and Investigations (DEI). In this role, he will lead the PCAOB’s investigations and enforcement actions involving violations of PCAOB rules, professional standards, and other applicable securities regulations, so the appointment signals continued and potentially intensified oversight of audit firms, public company audits, and other regulated PCAOB activity. His appointment does not itself create new compliance requirements or deadlines, but for firms subject to PCAOB oversight it underscores the need to maintain strong audit quality, documentation, and internal controls because the PCAOB has emphasized detection and deterrence of misconduct as central to its enforcement mission. rows.title: The PCAOB has published its annual report on broker-dealer audits.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s **Annual Report on the Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers** (PCAOB Release No. **2026-003**, dated **June 11, 2026**) summarizes the Board’s **2025 inspections approach** and **2025 inspection observations** for auditors of SEC-registered broker-dealers. The report is issued under **PCAOB Rule 4020T**, which governs the interim inspection program for broker-dealer audits and related reporting.

For compliance purposes, the document restates the core broker-dealer annual reporting framework under **Exchange Act Rule 17a-5**: broker-dealers registered with the SEC generally must file annually with the SEC a **financial report** (financial statements plus supporting schedules/supplemental information), either a **compliance report** or an **exemption report** depending on whether they claim an exemption from the **Customer Protection Rule (Exchange Act Rule 15c3-3)**, and the related **independent public accountant reports**. If the broker-dealer does **not** claim an exemption from the Customer Protection Rule, it must file a **compliance report** and its auditor must issue an **examination report** under **PCAOB Attestation Standard No. 1 (AT No. 1)**. If the broker-dealer **does** claim an exemption, or is otherwise eligible to do so under SEC rules, it must file an **exemption report** and the auditor must issue a **review report** under **PCAOB Attestation Standard No. 2 (AT No. 2)**. The report emphasizes that these AT No. 1 and AT No. 2 engagements are collectively referred to as **attestation engagements**.

The report also clarifies which broker-dealers are typically in each bucket. Broker-dealers that **carry customer accounts, maintain custody or control of customer cash or securities, or clear securities transactions for customers** generally **cannot** use the exemption and therefore must file **compliance reports**. By contrast, **most broker-dealers, including introducing broker-dealers**, file **exemption reports**. The document notes that broker-dealer audit attestation engagements are complex and involve professional judgment, and that any deficiency described in the annual report reflects information communicated to the PCAOB by the inspection team rather than a final Board determination that the firm committed sanctionable conduct.

From a compliance-team perspective, this document does **not** announce a new rule or deadline change; rather, it is an annual PCAOB inspection report that reinforces the existing filing and auditor-reporting structure and signals how the PCAOB is supervising broker-dealer audit work. The most important operational takeaway is that a broker-dealer must ensure it has correctly determined whether it is required to file a **compliance report** or an **exemption report**, because that decision drives the type of auditor engagement and the required PCAOB report under the relevant attestation standard.

rows.title: The PCAOB today issued for public comment a proposal regarding narrow, targeted amendments to QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control.
rows.desc: PCAOB Release No. 2026-002 June 9, 2026 PCAOB Rulemaking Docket Matter No. 057 Summary: The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (“PCAOB” or the “Board”) is issuing a supplemental request for comment on potential amendments to certain provisions of QC 1000 and related amendments to the QC reporting rule and PCAOB forms. This supplemental request for comment seeks commenters’ views on proposed amendments and other matters discussed in this release. Public Comment: Interested persons may submit written comments to the Board. Comments should be sent by e-mail to comments@pcaobus.org or through the Board’s website at pcaobus.org. Comments also may be sent to the Office of the Secretary, PCAOB, 1666 K Street, NW, Washington, DC 20006-2803. All comments should refer to PCAOB Rulemaking Docket Matter No. 057 in the subject or reference line and should be received by the Board no later than July 9, 2026. Board Contacts: Barbara Vanich, Chief Auditor, Office of the Chief Auditor (202/207-9363, vanichb@pcaobus.org); Jessica Watts, Senior Associate Chief Auditor, Office of the Chief Auditor (202/207-9376, wattsj@pcaobus.org); Karen Wiedemann, Senior Associate, Chief Counsel, Office of the Chief Auditor (202/591-4411, wiedemannk@pcaobus.org). SUPPLEMENTAL REQUEST FOR COMMENT: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO QC 1000, A FIRM’S SYSTEM OF QUALITY CONTROL, AND RELATED RULE AND FORMS PCAOB Release No. 2026-002 June 9, 2026 Page 2 Staff Contributors: Ekaterina Dizna, Associate Chief Auditor; Linnette Klinedinst, Assistant Chief Auditor; Schuyler Simms, Assistant Chief Auditor; David Ellam, Assistant Chief Auditor; Carla Del Monico, Assistant Chief Auditor; Kevin Lombardi, Associate Chief Counsel; Erik Durbin, Acting Director and Chief Economist, Office of Economic and Risk Analysis; Nick Galunic, Assistant Director, Economic Analysis; Zhoudan (Zoey) Xie, Financial Economist. PCAOB Release No. 2026-002 June 9, 2026 Page 3 TABLE OF CONTENTS I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY .............................
rows.summary:
The PCAOB issued this June 9, 2026 supplemental request for comment on targeted amendments to QC 1000, the standard governing a firm’s system of quality control, plus conforming changes to the QC reporting rule and PCAOB forms. This is not yet a final rule: it is a public-comment release seeking views on specific proposed revisions and related issues, with comments due by July 9, 2026 and submitted by email, web portal, or mail, referencing PCAOB Rulemaking Docket Matter No. 057. The release applies to PCAOB-registered firms and, where relevant, to the persons responsible for firm quality control governance, including firms that will need to design, implement, operate, evaluate, and document a QC system under QC 1000.

The supplemental request indicates the Board is considering amendments in several areas of QC 1000, including the requirement to design, implement, and operate the QC system, roles and responsibilities, the use of an external QC function, information and communication processes, monitoring and remediation, evaluation and reporting on the QC system, and documentation. It also proposes related changes to Rule 2203A and Form QC, as well as amendments to other PCAOB forms to align reporting and filing requirements with the revised QC framework. Because this is a proposal, no new compliance deadline is imposed yet beyond the comment deadline, but firms should review whether the proposed changes would require new governance, escalation, monitoring, and recordkeeping procedures if adopted.

The document’s operative compliance point at this stage is to identify whether a firm’s existing QC program would need redesign or enhancement under the proposed amendments, especially in the areas of accountability, use of outside QC resources, communications within the firm, remediation of QC deficiencies, and formal evaluation/reporting of QC effectiveness. The Board also flags “implementation support efforts” and “recent rulemaking history,” suggesting the proposal is part of a broader QC 1000 rollout and refinement process. For a compliance team, the immediate action item is to assess the proposal against current internal QC policies and, if desired, submit comments before July 9, 2026.

rows.title: The PCAOB will hold an open meeting to consider issuing proposed amendments related to QC 1000, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, for public comment.
rows.desc: At June 9 Open Meeting, PCAOB to Consider Issuing Proposed Quality Control Related Amendments for Public Comment WASHINGTON, Jun. 3, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) will hold an open meeting at 10:00 a.m. ET on Tuesday, June 9, 2026. At the meeting, the Board will consider issuing for public comment proposed amendments to QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control, the PCAOB’s quality control standard that is set to become effective on December 15, 2026, and related amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule. The meeting is open to the public and will take place in the PCAOB’s Multi-Purpose Room (301) at 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC. The public may also view the meeting via a livestream on the PCAOB’s event page, and a recording will be available after the meeting concludes. *****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws.
rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced that it will hold an open meeting on **June 9, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. ET** to consider whether to issue **proposed amendments to QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control**, for public comment. QC 1000 is the PCAOB’s quality control standard and is currently **scheduled to become effective on December 15, 2026**; the contemplated proposal would also include **related amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule**.  

For compliance purposes, the notice does **not itself impose new requirements yet**; it signals that the PCAOB is preparing a public-comment proposal that could change the final QC 1000 framework, associated form filings, and reporting obligations before the effective date. The meeting is **open to the public** and will be held in the PCAOB’s **Multi-Purpose Room (301), 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC**, with a **livestream available on the PCAOB event page** and a **recording posted after the meeting**.  

The underlying PCAOB standard matters to **PCAOB-registered audit firms** because QC 1000 governs a firm’s system of quality control, and any amendments could affect how firms design, document, implement, and report on their quality control systems before the standard takes effect. The PCAOB also reiterated its broader oversight role over audits of **public companies** and **SEC-registered brokers and dealers**, including compliance reports filed under federal securities laws, but the specific action described here is limited to the Board’s consideration of proposed QC 1000-related amendments.

rows.title: The PCAOB is seeking investors, audit committee members, auditors, financial executives, and other experts to serve on a new advisory body: the Inspections Modernization Council. Applications are due on June 15, 2026.
rows.desc: PCAOB Announces Inspections Modernization Council, Seeks Participation From Outside Experts Focused on modernizing PCAOB inspections, the new advisory body will leverage perspectives from a cross-section of capital markets experts; Deadline for applications is June 15, 2026 WASHINGTON, May 28, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) announced today that it is forming a new advisory body, the Inspections Modernization Council, and is seeking outside parties with a stake in the PCAOB’s inspection activities to participate in its work. Since its creation more than 20 years ago, the PCAOB inspection program has played a significant role in enhancing audit quality. Today, opportunities exist to modernize PCAOB inspections so they remain relevant and resilient. Consultation with outside experts can facilitate such modernization. For the Inspections Modernization Council, the Board seeks participants with capital markets expertise and knowledge of the PCAOB’s inspection program, including investors, audit committee members, financial executives at public companies, academics, technologists, other regulators, and practitioners from public accounting firms of varying sizes. Applicants should have a demonstrated commitment to the interests of investors and the public. “Modernization of PCAOB inspections has the potential to bring improved audit quality and other significant benefits to investors and other stakeholders,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “The Inspections Modernization Council will help us shape the future of PCAOB inspections, and we invite individuals of the highest integrity to join us in this effort.” Application and other information can be found on the Inspections Modernization Council page. The application period will close on June 15, 2026. *****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interes
rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced on May 28, 2026 that it is creating a new advisory body, the **Inspections Modernization Council**, to help modernize its audit inspection program so it remains relevant and resilient after more than 20 years of operation. The Council is intended to draw on outside expertise from people with a stake in PCAOB inspection activities and capital markets generally, and the PCAOB is specifically looking for **investors, audit committee members, financial executives at public companies, academics, technologists, other regulators, and practitioners from public accounting firms of varying sizes**. Applicants are expected to have **capital markets expertise, knowledge of the PCAOB inspection program, a demonstrated commitment to the interests of investors and the public, and high integrity**.

For compliance teams, the immediate action item is not a new inspection rule but a **call for participation**: organizations or individuals who fit the profile and want to contribute to PCAOB inspection modernization can apply for the Council. The PCAOB states that application materials and additional information are available on the Council’s web page, and the **application deadline is June 15, 2026**. No new substantive compliance obligations, thresholds, or reporting requirements are imposed by this announcement itself, but it signals that the PCAOB is actively seeking external input on future inspection modernization that could affect audit oversight practices going forward.

In that role, he will oversee and direct PCAOB investigations and enforcement actions involving violations of PCAOB rules, professional standards, and other applicable securities regulations. The PCAOB emphasized that detecting and deterring misconduct remains central to its mission of improving audit quality and protecting investors, and Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis specifically linked Demos’s enforcement background to advancing those goals. Demos joins from DLA Piper LLP, where he represented companies in federal and state investigations and performed internal corporate reviews. He previously served as Senior Counsel in the SEC Division of Enforcement, where he led investigations and prosecutions involving accounting fraud, insider trading, and market manipulation, and he has also taught at UC Davis School of Law.

The appointment also changes DEI leadership structure: William Ryan, who had served as Acting DEI Director since December 2025, will return to his prior role as DEI Chief Counsel, a position he has held since 2023. The document includes no new reporting obligations, filing dates, or numerical thresholds, but from a compliance perspective it indicates that PCAOB enforcement matters will now be led by a senior attorney with direct SEC enforcement experience, which may affect the tone, pace, and rigor of future investigations.

In its **December 4, 2025** Order (PCAOB Release No. **105-2025-037**), the Board **censured** TPS Thayer, imposed a **$100,000 civil money penalty**, and required the firm to complete **contingent remedial actions** described later in the Order. The PCAOB found that TPS Thayer **failed to appropriately plan** those five audits and **failed to reasonably supervise** the unregistered China-based firm’s work, which is significant because the Board is emphasizing auditor oversight and the use of non-registered firms in issuer audit engagements.

The Order also states that TPS Thayer **failed to properly disclose** the unregistered accounting firm’s participation both in its **Form AP filings** with the PCAOB and in **communications to the audit committees** of the affected issuers. The action was brought under **Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002** and **PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1) and (2)**, reflecting the Board’s view that the conduct implicated investor protection and the integrity of audit reporting. Compliance teams should note that the document is not just a financial penalty; it also signals a governance and disclosure failure in the firm’s audit supervision process, especially where outsourced audit work is performed by a non-registered foreign accounting firm.

The Order further notes that TPS Thayer had filed a **Form 1-WD on April 7, 2025** seeking to withdraw from PCAOB registration, and that request would be handled separately under **PCAOB Rule 2107**. For compliance purposes, the key takeaways are that firms using outside audit providers in issuer engagements must ensure the outside firm’s registration status is confirmed, that planning and supervision are robust enough to support reasonable oversight of substantial-role participants, and that **Form AP** and audit committee disclosures must accurately reflect any such participation.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered a settlement order on June 12, 2025 against Heaton & Company, PLLC (doing business as Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah) and its partner Kristofer Heaton, CPA, for audit documentation and quality-control failures tied to five issuer audits. The Board found that the firm did not timely assemble a complete and final set of audit documentation for retention on those five audits, and that Heaton did not adequately perform the required engagement quality reviews (“EQRs”) for those same five issuer audits; the Board also found that the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards and that Heaton directly and substantially contributed to those quality-control violations. The sanctions are severe: the firm is censured, its PCAOB registration is revoked, Heaton is barred from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, and both respondents must pay civil penalties—$35,000 for the firm and $25,000 for Heaton.

The order also imposes forward-looking compliance conditions. If the firm seeks to reapply for PCAOB registration in the future, it must first complete remedial measures required by the order before submitting any new application. Heaton must complete 40 hours of continuing professional education, in addition to any CPE required for his state or other professional licenses, before he may file any petition seeking PCAOB consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. The order states that both the firm and Heaton may reapply/petition only after two years from the date of the order, meaning no earlier than June 12, 2027.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that the PCAOB treated the failures as serious enough to warrant registration revocation and a bar, not merely a reprimand, because the conduct involved repeated audit-documentation breakdowns and deficient EQR performance across multiple issuer engagements. The order was entered pursuant to Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the respondents settled without admitting or denying the findings except as to PCAOB jurisdiction.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s April 22, 2025 Order (Release No. 105-2025-020) censures Adeptus Partners LLC, a registered public accounting firm, and Howard S. Krant, CPA, for audit-related failures tied to supervision, review, and quality control. Krant is suspended for one year from acting as an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and he must pay a $50,000 civil money penalty; Adeptus must pay a $75,000 civil money penalty. In addition, the firm is required to engage an independent consultant to review Adeptus’s system of quality control and make recommendations, with the consultant work to be performed under the conditions specified in Section IV of the Order.

The sanctions were imposed because the PCAOB found that Krant violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with the audits of two issuers—Blockchain of Things, Inc. and Applied UV, Inc.—and that Adeptus violated PCAOB rules and quality control standards. Krant was the engagement partner for both audits, so the misconduct directly implicates engagement-level supervision and review responsibilities. Adeptus is headquartered in New York, New York, and is registered with the PCAOB; it is also licensed in New Jersey and Maryland, which may matter for broader state practice oversight, though the PCAOB action itself is under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB rules.

The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the respondents resolved it through settlement offers under PCAOB Rule 5205 without admitting or denying the findings, except as to the PCAOB’s jurisdiction. The Board stated that the conduct met the statutory standard for sanctions because it involved intentional or knowing conduct, including reckless conduct, or repeated negligent conduct resulting in violations of applicable standards. The order is aimed at protecting investors and promoting informative, accurate, and independent audit reports, so the key compliance takeaway for audit firms is that deficient engagement supervision, review, and quality control can lead not only to firm censure and monetary penalties, but also to individual suspension and mandated third-party quality-control remediation.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s March 25, 2025 order against James Pai CPA PLLC and its sole partner, Yu-Ching James Pai, resolves disciplinary proceedings over audit failures in two issuer audits and imposes both firm-level and individual sanctions. The Board censured both respondents, revoked the firm’s PCAOB registration, barred Pai from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposed a $40,000 civil money penalty jointly and severally on the firm and Pai. The order states that the firm may reapply for PCAOB registration only after three years from the date of the order, and Pai may seek PCAOB consent to associate with a registered firm only after three years from the date of the order.

The sanctions are based on findings that the respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with two audits of one issuer client’s financial statements; that the firm failed to obtain the required engagement quality review (EQR) for those audits; that the firm filed inaccurate PCAOB Form APs in connection with one of the audits; and that the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards. The PCAOB also found that Pai directly and substantially contributed to the EQR, Form AP, and quality control violations, and that the conduct met the statutory standard for sanctions under Section 105(c)(5) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act because it involved intentional or knowing, reckless, or repeated negligent conduct. These findings were made pursuant to settlement offers, which the respondents submitted without admitting or denying the findings, except for the Board’s jurisdiction.

Beyond the monetary penalty and prohibitions, the order requires the firm to undertake specific remedial actions to its system of quality control before it can submit any future PCAOB registration application, and to provide evidence of those remedial measures with any future application. Pai is also required to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education, in addition to any CPE required for licensure, before filing any petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. For compliance teams, the key operational takeaway is that PCAOB registration status, public-company audit eligibility, and future association rights are restricted for at least three years, and any re-entry effort must be supported by documented quality-control remediation and Pai’s additional education completion.

The PCAOB’s March 11, 2025 order censures Jaslyn Sellers, CPA, bars her from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposes a $15,000 civil money penalty. The Board found that Sellers, acting as engagement partner on BF Borgers CPA PC’s audits of NetSol Technologies, Inc. (NTI) for fiscal years ended June 30, 2021 and June 30, 2022, repeatedly violated PCAOB rules and auditing standards by failing to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence in areas she had identified as significant risks, including revenue recognition and accounting estimates. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB treated these as serious, repeated audit-quality failures involving core audit areas and independence compliance. The matter involved an issuer audit, a registered public accounting firm, and an associated person under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), so firms should view this as a reminder that engagement partners must ensure adequate evidence for significant-risk areas and strict adherence to independence rules before audit reports are issued, including where critical audit matters are described in the report.

The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that in connection with the Firm’s administration of Personal Independence Compliance Testing (“PICT”), the Firm violated PCAOB rules and quality control standards over approximately two years. I. The Board deems it necessary and appropriate, for the protection of investors and to further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports, that disciplinary proceedings be, and hereby are, instituted pursuant to Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, as amended (“Act”), and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1) against Respondent. Order PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-018 March 11, 2025 2 denying the findings herein, except as to the Board’s jurisdiction over Respondent and the subject matter of these proceedings, which is admitted, Respondent consents to entry of this Order as set forth below. 1 III
rows.summary:
The PCAOB, in Release No. 105-2025-018 dated March 11, 2025, sanctioned PwC Singapore (PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, a PCAOB-registered public accounting firm in Singapore) for violations of PCAOB rules and quality control standards connected to the firm’s Personal Independence Compliance Testing (PICT) process. The Board found that, from 2022 through mid-2024, the firm failed to establish and implement adequate policies and procedures governing PICT and failed to foster an ethical culture within its Independence Office, which undermined the integrity of its quality control system. While those weaknesses existed, personnel in the Independence Office created and used methods to influence the PICT results reported to the PCAOB’s Division of Registration and Inspections and to understate the rate at which firm personnel failed to timely report financial interests and relationships.

As sanctions, the PCAOB censured PwC Singapore, imposed a civil money penalty of $1,500,000, and required the firm to undertake remedial actions described later in the Order. The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the Board accepted PwC Singapore’s settlement offer under Rule 5205; the firm did not admit the findings except for the PCAOB’s jurisdiction. The document makes clear that the Board viewed the conduct as intentional/knowing or at least reckless, or alternatively as repeated negligent conduct, meeting the statutory conditions for sanctions.

For compliance purposes, the key substantive requirement is that PCAOB-registered firms must maintain and properly operate a system of quality control with documented policies and procedures that provide reasonable assurance that personnel perform professional responsibilities with integrity, and that responsibility assignments and documentation are adequate to make the system effective. This order signals that misleading internal compliance-testing results, especially where they affect reported independence-deficiency rates, can itself be treated as a serious PCAOB violation even if the underlying issue is within an internal independence or quality-control function rather than an audit engagement. The remedial actions referenced in Section IV are part of the enforcement outcome and should be reviewed as compliance obligations imposed on the firm, though the excerpt provided does not specify those steps.

(KPMG Brazil), imposes a $700,000 civil money penalty, and requires remedial actions described in the order, based on conduct occurring between 2020 and 2023. The specific filing failures involved Form 2 omissions tied to six issuer audits and two inaccurate Form AP filings, underscoring the need for controls over regulatory reporting of audit reports/consents and audit participants. The order also states that the Board found KPMG Brazil violated PCAOB quality control standards, indicating deficiencies not just in isolated filings but in firmwide policies or monitoring processes. The proceedings were instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the firm entered the settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s February 25, 2025 Order sanctions Natalie Murphy, CPA, a former engagement partner at Heaton & Company, PLLC (doing business as Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah), for multiple violations tied to her audit work and her conduct during a PCAOB inspection. The Board censured her, barred her from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty, and required her to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education in addition to any CPE already required by any professional license she holds before she may seek Board consent to re-associate with a registered firm. Murphy may not petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm until five years from the date of the Order.

The findings underlying the sanctions are compliance-relevant because they identify three distinct failures in PCAOB-regulated audit work. First, Murphy failed to cooperate with the PCAOB’s 2022 inspection of Heaton & Co. by giving misleading information to inspectors in connection with two issuer audits. Second, she failed to adequately document work paper additions and modifications made after the documentation completion date for those same two issuer audits, meaning post-completion changes were not properly supported in the audit file. Third, she failed to timely assemble for retention a complete and final set of audit documentation in a total of five issuer audits, which indicates deficient audit-file completion and retention practices across multiple engagements.

For a corporate compliance team, the key operational takeaway is that the PCAOB treated both obstruction/misleading statements to inspectors and audit documentation failures as sanctionable misconduct, especially where issuer audits are involved. The order reinforces that registered firms and their personnel must cooperate fully and truthfully with PCAOB inspections, maintain clear documentation for any post-completion work-paper changes, and timely compile a complete final audit file for retention. The sanctions also show that such conduct can lead not only to individual discipline but to a multi-year bar from association with registered public accounting firms and a monetary penalty of $50,000.
